  keep-alives keeping it, and open as many as it liked. A machine now takes as many such
  connections at once as it holds open invitations, as each invitation enrolls one client,
  and none while it holds none: the rest are refused as their handshake ends. And it lets
  each go that has not joined within the idle bound, as long as a client waits for its
  daemon. Its client says such a refusal in the words its stream would have said (the
  join's refusal for a join, `this machine has not enrolled you` for a command), so that
  what a stranger learns is whether an invitation is free, nothing of which or whose.
  focal has no such peers: its invitations issue a credential its TLS checks (../focal
  docs/network-startup.md), where shards' prove their secret over the session, after its
  handshake.

And a client that sends a command no stdin sends its end at once, as a command that reads
it would otherwise wait for good. Tested in `tests/loopback.rs`, each test a daemon of its
own that stops when the test ends, so that a test that fails fails rather than waits: a
daemon that writes a command's every frame and its stream's end at once, 20 times; a client
that finishes its stream with the last of its stdin, the command reading it all and then its
end; 8 MiB of stdin through `cat`; a command given no stdin, and one that ends without
reading an endless stdin; a command that reads none of an endless stdin while another
client's command runs; a daemon that stops a client's stdin at once and answers 200 ms
later; a connection kept open over two commands, the first's stdin and state let go once
its exit is sent and its client asked to send no more; a client not enrolled refused by its
frame's header; a command whose client resets its stream, and one whose client stops
reading it, hung up and let go; a command whose client went writing on after the next
client connected, which hears none of it; a machine with one invitation taking one stranger
at a time, and with none, none, each refused as its handshake ends; a stranger let go at
the idle bound, and an enrolled client's command running past it; and
`only_a_clients_two_way_streams_open`. Each
fix was mutation-checked against its test: the end dropped from the last bytes; a read
after each frame; a finished stream, a stopped one and a reset one kept; stdin given by a
blocking send; no judging by the header; a connection's number given again; streams one
way, or a daemon's, allowed; a stopped stdin failing the command; no end for no stdin; no
STOP_SENDING at the last frame; the client's end ending no stdin; room again resuming no
stream; strangers taken past the invitations; no time to join, or one bounding enrolled
clients too; and a refusal at the handshake's end said in other words.

**A client's environment, and its owner's (part 1).** Docker's CLI takes a bare `-e NAME`
from its own environment (docker/cli opts/env.go, ValidateEnv), and its own credentials to
each registry a request reaches, which it sends with the request (cli/command/registry.go,
RetrieveAuthTokenFromImage); `docker --context NAME login` keeps a login with the CLI. A
command shards runs over a context is a CLI of that machine's, which the daemon gave its
whole environment: a client's `-e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` took the value the daemon's owner
had there, a client's pull went with the owner's logins, and `--context NAME login` wrote
the owner's store, their keychain among it. Now each side keeps its own:
- **A client's command has of the daemon's environment shards' settings of the machine
  alone** (`SHARDS_*`, but its tests' credentials and the client's own settings below), and
  where its programs, user and temporary files are, and its network's proxies
  (`shards_ipc::spawn_in`, which gives a child nothing else). None of `HOME`,
  `DOCKER_CONFIG`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or the auth variables, under which a registry's logins,
  a cloud's credentials and SSH keys are kept: with no config, a registry is asked with
  what the client sent alone, no credential helper asked (shards_registry::credentials,
  lookup). A build there will want the machine's cache, which macOS finds under `HOME`:
  part 3's.
- **What is the client's crosses from the client.** A bare `-e NAME` takes its value here,
  `--env-file` and `--label-file` cross as the `--env` and `--label` values their files here
  hold, ahead of the rest (the order a `docker` script's values take), by where shards' parser finds
  each flag's value (`flags::Parsed::positions`); the variables Docker's CLI reads for
  itself cross with the request (`frame::ENV`: how it prints, `SHARDS_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` and
  `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM`); and the client's credentials for the registry a pull, push,
  run, create or search reaches, found here as a pull here finds them, cross as
  `SHARDS_AUTH_CONFIG` for that registry alone, a token as `config.json` keeps one. A run
  or create with `--pull never` reaches no registry, so none are found for it: as docker/cli
  asks a credential helper only to pull (cli/command/container/create.go, `pullImage`), no
  helper is asked, and one that never answers holds up no such run (on 2026-10-17 this
  host's `docker-credential-desktop` answered no caller for over half an hour, and each
  such run over a context waited on it; `a_run_that_never_pulls_asks_no_credential_helper`).
  `login` and `logout` run here.
- `SHARDS_AUTH_CONFIG` itself reached no daemon until now: `REGISTRY_ENV`, what a client
  sends its daemon of the variables a pull reads, named `DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG` alone, though
  D157 put shards' own first. It now names both.

Tested in `tests/context.rs`: the owner's secret absent where `-e` named it and the client's
own variables and an env file's present
(`a_clients_command_has_the_clients_environment_not_the_owners`); and a registry that
wants a login, the owner logged in to it there (`a_clients_logins_are_its_own`): a client
logged in nowhere refused, a client's login and logout through the context kept here, the
owner's store unchanged, and the client's pull there taking its credentials. And
`a_clients_variables_and_files_are_its_own`, `a_flags_values_are_found_where_they_sit`,
`a_clients_command_takes_shards_settings_alone` and `a_clients_credentials_cross_as_they_were`.
Mutation-checked: the daemon's whole environment given, or its `DOCKER_CONFIG`; a bare `-e`
unresolved here; an env file read there; the client's credentials not sent; a login sent
there; `SHARDS_AUTH_CONFIG` not carried to the daemon.

**Part 2, built: the client's terminal, and its signals.** A context carries them as
`ssh -t` does (OpenSSH session.c, do_exec_pty; clientloop.c, enter_raw_mode):
- **The command's stdio is the client's.** The request says which of the client's stdin,
  stdout and stderr its terminal is, and its size; the daemon gives the command a
  pseudo-terminal of that size for those, and pipes for the rest, so that the command sees
  the stdio it would here and prints as it would: shards' own pages on a terminal, and in
  a pipe what a script written for `docker` reads, where part 1's commands saw pipes alone.
- **A terminal of its own, as a login's.** The command leads a session whose controlling
  terminal that is, which it takes itself first thing (`SHARDS_TAKE_TERMINAL`), as
  posix_spawn(3) has no action that makes one on macOS; so the terminal there does what a
  terminal does: echo, line editing, ^C as SIGINT, SIGWINCH on a resize. The client's
  terminal goes raw while the command reads it, and back as it was after.
- **What steers it crosses beside its data.** A resize, and each signal the client
  receives, cross on a control stream of the command's, a second QUIC stream, as SSH's
  window-change and signal requests cross beside a channel's data (RFC 4254 §6.7, §6.9): on
  the command's own stream they would wait behind stdin that a command does not read. A
  signal crosses by its Linux number, the guest's numbering, which the daemon's system
  numbers its own (SIGUSR1 is 30 on macOS, 10 on Linux); the command, a client of its
  daemon as any run's CLI is, does with it what it would here (`--sig-proxy`).
- So `run -it`, `exec -it` and `attach` need nothing of their own over a context, and `-it`
  with no terminal here is refused there, in a run's own words. Every
  command a client runs leads a session of its own, out of reach of the signals a terminal
  of the daemon's sends its group.

Tested in `tests/context.rs` on tests/tty.rs's terminal, a pty the test holds: the client's
terminal the command's own there, raw here while it runs, its size, what is typed echoed and
read, and given back as it was; a resize reaching the command; ^C interrupting it, and the
detach keys leaving it running on its machine; `exec -it` in a running microVM, and
`attach` to a command's terminal, through the context; and with no terminal, SIGINT and
SIGUSR1 to the client reaching the command as 2 and 10. In `tests/loopback.rs`: a resize and a signal
reaching a command whose stdin waits for room it does not get; a control stream naming no
command of its connection's refused, and a stranger's refused by its header. And
`a_signals_linux_number_names_it_on_every_system` (`shards_ipc`). Each mutation-checked:
the command given no terminal of its own, the terminal not taken as its controlling one,
the client not raw, signals steering nothing, SIGWINCH sent as a signal with no resize, and
a signal's Linux number taken for the daemon's system's.

**Part 2b, built: a Windows client's console.** Until D195 brought shards' daemon to
Windows, a context was how a Windows machine ran microVMs at all; its console is its
terminal as a Unix client's is:
- **Raw, so that keys reach the command there as a terminal's**: no echo, line editing or
  processed input, so ^C is a key the command's terminal there makes SIGINT of; no mouse
  events; insert and quick-edit mode, and keys as the escape sequences a terminal sends
  (ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT) where the console gives them (the modes moby/term v0.5.2
  sets, termios_windows.go, makeRaw, which the `docker` CLI's users' consoles are in). Its
  window events it keeps, which moby/term turns off. stdout takes escape sequences, which
  the command there writes, and both modes are given back after.
- **Its keys and its resizes read as the console's records** (ReadConsoleInputW,
  cli/terminal.rs `ConsoleInput`), where Rust's stdin reads its text: each key's text in
  UTF-8, a pair of surrogates whole, an Alt code's character; ^Z a key, which a read of
  text ending in it would have ended stdin with (std sys/stdio/windows.rs); and each
  record of the screen buffer's size (WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT) sizes the command's
  terminal as it comes. A console has no SIGWINCH, and docker/cli looks at its size every
  250 ms instead (MonitorTtySize, cli/command/container/tty.go). Where a resize leaves no
  record, a window showing part of its buffer (conhost's, with lines kept above it), or
  stdin not the console, its size is still looked at every 250 ms; a size changed before
  the command is there to take it is sent as it is. Held on a pseudo console of its test's
  own (`a_pseudo_consoles_keys_and_resizes_reach_the_command`, CI's Windows runner: keys,
  ^Z, ^C, an arrow, text past the BMP, and a resize, each reaching a child in it).
- **Its terminal's type**: a Windows console names none, and one taking escape sequences
  is xterm-256color to the command there, as Microsoft's own Linux is told its Windows
  console is (microsoft/WSL 4609b0c, src/windows/service/exe/DistributionRegistration.h,
  TERM's default), where the client's TERM says nothing (D16's choice then reads it).
- **Its events are signals as Go's runtime makes them** for a Windows process (go1.25.0
  runtime/os_windows.go, ctrlHandler), and so for docker/cli's signal proxy: ^C and ^Break,
  where the console's input is not raw, SIGINT; its closing, a logoff and a shutdown
  SIGTERM, whose handler waits, as Go's does, so that the command's end ends the client
  before Windows does.

Tested in `tests/context_client.rs`, the client against a daemon of the test's own, which
runs on every system: with no terminal, the client sends its command, its stdin and the
variables that shape what it prints, and exits as the command does with what it wrote (on
Unix also SIGUSR1, as 10); and on Windows, the client on a pseudoconsole the test holds
(ConPTY, made as Microsoft's "Creating a Pseudoconsole session" makes one): its terminal
the console's stdin, stdout and stderr at the console's size, keys reaching the command as
typed (`ab` and Enter as `ab\r`, ^C as byte 3), and a resize of the console sizing the
command's terminal. Unit tests hold raw mode's flags to moby/term's and the events' signals
to Go's. The Windows tests run on CI's Windows jobs; this host runs none.

**Part 3a, built: the archives a client writes and reads.** Images and a microVM's files
move between a laptop and the machine that runs its microVMs as archives: an image saved
here loads there (`shards save image app -o app.tar`, then `shards --context gpu load image
-i app.tar`), and what a job there wrote comes back (`shards --context gpu export vm job -o
job.tar`). Docker's CLI writes `save -o` and `export -o`, and reads `load -i` and
`import FILE`, itself (docker/cli v29.8.1 cli/command/image/save.go runSave, load.go
runLoad, import.go runImport, container/export.go runExport); a command shards runs over a
context is a CLI of the machine's, which would have written and read the machine's files,
so a context refused them. Now:
- **The file is the client's, the command there writes its stdout or reads its stdin.**
  The client reads the command line as shards' parser does, where each flag's value and
  each argument sits (`flags::Parsed::positions`, and `arg_words`, new), and takes the file
  out of it: `-o` and `-i` however they are given, the last one named, as pflag keeps it,
  and the flags a short one ran together with kept (`-qi FILE` is `-q`); `import`'s file
  sent as `-`, a URL still the machine's to fetch, as the CLI leaves one to its daemon; and
  `make agentfile -o`, shards' own. Neither is a terminal there, the client's though it be:
  a save refuses to write an archive to a terminal.
- **Whole or not at all.** docker/cli writes `-o` through moby/sys atomicwriter v0.1.0,
  whose Close renames its temporary file into place whenever no write to it failed
  (`writeErr == nil && written`), and runSave and runExport defer it and drop its error:
  an archive cut short by a lost connection, a daemon that fails part-way or a cancelled
  request is renamed into place under the name asked for, as a save here was measured to
  leave one (cli/save.rs: Docker 29.3.1, 60,300,800 bytes of an interrupted save), and a
  rename that fails goes unsaid, the save exiting 0. shards keeps the file once the
  command's exit says it is whole and every byte of it was written here: a command that
  fails, a signal that ends it, a lost connection, a write here that fails (said, exit 1),
  and a signal that ends the client before the command runs each leave the file as it was
  and nothing beside it, and a rename that fails is said. `make agentfile -o` writes so too,
  on one machine as over a context, where it wrote in place before.
- **A signal before the command is asked for ends the client.** The client gave what steers
  the command (resizes, signals) to its signal handling before it connected, so a signal
  then waited for a command that did not exist yet: ^C without a terminal, or SIGTERM,
  waited out the 10 s handshake of a machine that does not answer. What steers it now comes
  once the command is asked for (`client.rs`, `steering`), and a SIGINT or SIGTERM before
  then ends the client with status 128 and the signal's number, its file removed first, as
  docker/cli v29.8.1 ends on its first one (cmd/docker/docker.go, notifyContext and
  getExitCode); a resize meanwhile is sent once the command is asked for.
- **Shards' own artifacts are carried (part 3d, below)**: `build agent DIR` (and a
  harness's, an MCP server's) is the machine's build of its copy of the client's directory,
  and `sign agent` signs with the client's key or identity.

Tested in `tests/context.rs`, on a machine that runs microVMs: an image saved here from
there, removed there and loaded from here; a microVM's files exported here and imported
there; an image's Agentfile written here; nothing of them written where the command ran; a
failed save leaving nothing; and from a terminal, a save to a file and a load from one
(`a_clients_archives_are_its_own_files`). In `tests/context_client.rs`, against the test's
own daemon, on every system: a file kept whole, and kept as it was when the command fails,
a signal ends it or the connection is lost
(`a_file_the_command_writes_is_the_clients_whole_or_not_at_all`); a write that fails here,
under a 4-byte RLIMIT_FSIZE (`a_file_not_written_whole_here_is_kept_by_no_exit`); a client
signalled while its machine never answers (`a_client_ended_before_its_machine_answers_leaves_no_file`);
and `load -qi` and `import` sending their files (`a_file_the_command_reads_is_the_clients`).
Unit tests: every form of the rewrite, and what a context refuses. Mutation-checked: the
client's files not taken out, a file kept whatever the exit, a lost connection keeping
what it has, a failed write unrecorded, an ending signal leaving the file, controls given
before the command is asked for, the client's terminal left the command's stdout or stdin,
a short group keeping the flag's letter, an artifact's build carried.

**What else a command names of the client's (part 3a).**
- **A seccomp profile's file.** Docker's CLI reads `--security-opt seccomp=FILE` and sends
  the profile's JSON (docker/cli v29.8.1 cli/command/container/opts.go, parseSecurityOpts);
  a command over a context read the machine's file of that name, a profile not the
  client's, silently, where one was there. The client reads it, and sends
  `seccomp=JSON`, which the command there takes as the profile where no file is named so,
  as the Engine API takes one (cli/request.rs, `seccomp_profile`); a file not here is
  refused here, in the words and with the status the command would refuse it with (run's
  and create's `shards: …` and their help's line, 125; exec's plain, 1), as an
  `--env-file` not here is now too.
- **A pull's Agentfile** (D78): the pull there, then its Agentfile asked of the machine
  once it is through, written in the client's file whole.
- **The client's logins for shards' own commands**, as for Docker's (part 1): the image
  `make agentfile` names, which it pulls where it is not there, and the artifact an
  agent's, harness's or MCP server's push, pull or referrer's removal names.

Tested in `tests/context.rs`: a profile in the client's directory, which the command
there does not run in, refusing mkdir there, and one not here refused here
(`a_clients_command_has_the_clients_environment_not_the_owners`); a pull's Agentfile in a
directory here, as `make agentfile` writes it (`a_clients_archives_are_its_own_files`);
an agent pushed and an image's Agentfile made of a pull with the client's logins, refused
without (`a_clients_logins_are_its_own`). Unit tests: the rewrites, and what shards' own
commands name. Mutation-checked: the profile read there, its JSON not taken there, the
pull's Agentfile not asked for, shards' own commands' logins not sent, `make agentfile`'s
not sent.

**Part 3b, built: a copy is the client's.** `shards copy vm` (`cp`) moves files between a
microVM and the machine its client is on: a dataset into a job's microVM on the GPU
machine, its results back. Docker's CLI does its half of a copy itself (docker/cli v29.8.1
cli/command/container/cp.go: a path's stat, then an archive of it fetched, or one put into
it, laid out by go-archive's copy rules), and shards' CLI does too, against its daemon
(cli/cp.rs). Over a context the client drives the copy here, as its CLI drives one, and
each step is asked of the machine's daemon: the request names the step as the CLI asks it
(the copy step's IPC name, which no command line can carry), and the machine's daemon
takes it as its own CLI would, over its socket, the stream's pipes the step's descriptors
(remote.rs, `copy_step`: an archive's written into the stream, an extract's read from
it). So the paths here are the client's, relative ones from its own directory, the
archive passes through the stream once, staged nowhere, and what the copy says is what it
says here (its sizes, Docker's errors). What steers a command steers no step: a signal
ends the client, and a step there ends with its stream. A Windows client copies as the
Windows Docker CLI does (below).

Tested in `tests/context.rs` (`a_microvms_files_are_copied_to_and_from_the_client`): a
directory here into a running microVM there and back, as it was; a file into a directory
there said with its sizes; an archive to stdout; a file not there, said as a copy here
says it;
nothing written where the command runs. Mutation-checked: a step spawned as a command,
a copy sent whole, an archive's output not into its pipe, an extract's input not from
its pipe, an archive's pipe not given the daemon.

**Part 3c, built: a build of the client's context, kept in step on the machine.** A
laptop's source tree is built where the builder microVMs run: an x86_64 or a GPU machine.
buildx sends a context over its session, fsutil's walk of it, into the copy BuildKit kept
of the last transfer of the same directory, by its shared key (the source's name, hint and
session's key), the receiver asking for what changed alone (BuildKit v0.33.0, which buildx
v0.37.1 pins: source/local/source.go, `searchSharedKey` then `filesync.FSSync`); Docker's
classic builder sends the whole context, a tar in `POST /build`'s body, each build. A context refused builds: the command there
would have read the machine's directory. Now (crate::synced):
- **The machine keeps a copy of each context a client builds** (`synced/CLIENT/KEY`, KEY
  the context's path hashed, the client's name its directory, so a client reaches its own
  alone). The client walks its context as the build walks one (fsutil's walk,
  shards_build::context, with the excludes of the ignore file the build reads: beside the
  build file, else the context's, `.agentignore` before `.dockerignore`), asks the copy's
  manifest (its own walk of the copy), and sends what changed as a layer the copy is
  brought in step by: each entry new or changed whole, the directories each change is in
  again for their times, and a whiteout for the topmost of what went
  (shards_archive::pack_changes, go-archive's addTarFile with times to the nanosecond, which
  go-archive's headers drop and a copy compared by its times needs; `apply_layer`,
  confined to the copy by its root, as it confines an image's layer). An entry is changed
  where its mode, size, time or link is: a directory's size and a symlink's mode are its
  filesystem's, and are not compared.
- **The build file and the ignore file beside it go whole each time**, ahead of the
  layer, a few kilobytes, so a build file outside the context, or another one, costs no
  copy of its own; `-f -`'s, read from the client's stdin. The build runs there of the copy,
  under its lock, so two builds of one context take turns, as a client's command runs:
  its output and status the client's; its build file not there said in the build's own
  words, by its name.
- **What it names of the client's is the client's:** a build arg named alone takes the
  client's value, or none: the value where the build was asked for; and the logins of the
  registries the build's plan asks for, planned here with a resolver that answers every
  image empty (its bases and the images it copies from, by their names after its args),
  go with it, those alone.
- A client removed takes the copies of its contexts with it.

What a build names of the client's otherwise crosses too: its secrets (part 3e); its
outputs, `--iidfile` and `--metadata-file` (part 3f); its named contexts, local caches and
policies' files (part 3g); its SSH agents (part 3h); and on a terminal, the build is drawn
there as here (part 3i). Not yet: extended attributes (go-archive's archives carry
`security.capability` alone). A new name of a file the copy holds, unchanged,
goes as a link to the copy's file (part 3d's), no byte of it again, where it went as a file
of its own, and the copy's tree was not the client's.

Measured by the test, to the byte: the first build sends the context's files whole as the
ignore file leaves them; the next, nothing; one after two files changed, their bytes
alone; one after a file went, nothing, the file gone there. Tested in `tests/context.rs`
(`a_build_through_a_context_is_of_the_clients_context_kept_in_step`: also each image the
context as it was, an ignored file never sent, a changed directory's time the client's, a
build file outside the context sending no context bytes, a build arg named alone taking
the client's value, a client removed taking its copies; and in
`a_clients_logins_are_its_own`, a build of a base that wants a login, built with the
client's), `crates/archive/tests/changes.rs` (a copy brought in step: times to the
nanosecond, hard links, symlinks, a file's and a directory's removal, what did not change
untouched), and unit tests of the plan and of a copy's key. Mutation-checked: the layer not
applied, everything sent each time, the ignore file not applied here, what went not
removed, a change's directories not set again, the build file not the copy's, a base's
login not sent, a build arg named alone the machine's.

**Part 3j, built: a run's `--cidfile` through a context is the client's, and a context refuses
less.** A script on the laptop starts a job on the GPU machine and keeps its ID, to stop it
later: `shards --context gpu run vm -d --cidfile job.id IMAGE`, then `shards --context gpu
stop vm $(cat job.id)`. A `--cidfile` is a file of the client's, and a command over a
context runs as the machine's CLI, which would have made the machine's file instead, so a
context refused it.
- **Made here.** The client makes the file before the command is asked for, its path from
  the client's working directory as a run here makes it, in one step that fails where one
  is there (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL`), and refuses one that is there as a run or a create here
  refuses it, its status a `docker` script's, its words on a terminal shards' own. A platform that does not
  parse goes to the machine, which refuses it first, the order a `docker` script sees
  (docker/cli v29.8.1 create.go parses the platform before newCIDFile).
- **The ID told as it is made.** The client names its path in the command after a marker
  no command line can carry; the machine gives the command a pipe for it instead, told by a
  variable no client can send (`SHARDS_CIDFILE_FD`, taken and let go first thing, as a
  terminal is), so the command writes the ID there as the microVM is made and closes it; the
  machine sends it on as the stream's `Made` frame, the exit only after it; and the client
  writes its file, an attached run's while it runs. The run records the client's path,
  which `inspect` reports (HostConfig.ContainerIDFile). A run never made
  leaves no file, a file that cannot take the ID fails the command as here, and the
  command there is hung up.
- **What a context refuses, now only what needs this machine's files**: `buildx policy eval`
  and `test`, which read a policy of the client's in its own process, and `shards copy vm`
  from Windows. `buildx du` and `prune`, and `builder`'s, ask the machine's builder alone,
  and `compose`, no command of shards' (Compose reaches a context by its Engine socket,
  part 4), is the machine's to say so of, as this machine's would.

Tested in `tests/context.rs` (`a_cidfile_through_a_context_is_the_clients`: a relative
name made here, the ID the one `run -d` printed, the client's path recorded; one there
already refused with a run's words and status, left as it was; a create's; an attached
run's while it runs, kept once it ends; a run never made leaving none; and
`a_context_runs_commands_on_its_machine_whole`, `buildx policy eval` refused), and in
context.rs's unit tests (what a context refuses), and in `crates/remote`'s
(`what_a_command_made_comes_before_its_exit`: an ID told only once its command has exited,
the order a busy host may run them in, still reaches the client before the exit status).
Mutation-checked: the cidfile sent as it is, the ID not told (the command's own file), the
told descriptor ignored, the ID dropped by the client, the exit sent before the ID, the
told file held open as the run runs.

**Part 3i, built: a build through a context on a terminal is drawn as here, and a command's
terminal there ends whole.**
- **The build's display, shards' own.** Where the client's stderr is a terminal, the
  machine's build has a terminal of its own for its stderr, of the client's size and
  resized with it, as a command's is, its stdin and stdout the step's streams still; so it
  draws the display a build draws on one (build/live.rs), where it printed BuildKit's
  plain lines. Nothing the display draws names the copy: a step says a build file by its
  base name and a layout by its store's, and a build file the client could not read is
  not sent, the build naming it by its name; what the build prints after the display, which
  may name it, passes through what says the client's paths, as a plain build's does.
- **A command's terminal there ends whole.** At a terminal's last close XNU waits 60 ticks
  for what is unread to be read, then discards it, and the controller reads nothing of a
  replica no longer open (PM M246): a client reading slowly, its stream full as its command
  ended, lost the last of the command's output, up to the terminal's queue (59 of 60
  trials, a reader 600 ms late or more), and the command waited 0.6 s to end. Now the
  machine keeps a writer of each terminal of a client's command (a build's, `run -t`'s,
  `exec -t`'s) until the command has ended and nothing is unread (TIOCOUTQ): closed then by
  the command's waiter, or by the reader once it has read the rest. The command's close is
  never the last, and nothing waits on a timer: a build's close waits for nothing, and a
  command's exit, which drains its controlling terminal (kern_exit.c), for its client to
  read, as long as it reads. A client gone, its hang-up lets the writer go, its queue
  flushed first, so that no command's exit waits on a reader that will not come.
- **A tree's copy said as the client's.** The paths a client names for what its build
  prints now include each tree's (part 3g), by its key: an error naming a layout's
  directory names the client's, where it named the machine's copy of it.

Tested in `tests/context.rs` (`a_build_through_a_context_on_a_terminal_is_drawn_as_here`:
shards' display on the client's terminal, no plain lines; resized to 36 columns as its step
runs, the build's end laid out to them; and in
`what_a_build_names_of_the_clients_is_carried_through_a_context`, a directory that holds no
layout refused, named as the client names it), and in remote.rs's unit tests
(`what_a_command_writes_to_its_terminal_is_read_however_late`: a reader a second late reads
all, through what says the client's paths; a terminal written nothing more ends with its
command; one whose client is gone ends, what it held unread). The tests' guest gained
`sleep-for MS`, a step that lasts. Mutation-checked: a build asking for no terminal, given
none, its terminal never resized; the kept writer closed with output unread, never closed
by the reader, kept for a client gone; a tree's copy shown as it is, a tree's path not
said. A command's end not told its terminal survives on macOS, whose exit revokes the
command's controlling terminal and the kept writer with it (kern_exit.c, VNOP_REVOKE): it
is Linux's to catch, where the kept writer would hold the terminal open, in CI.

**Part 3h, built: a build's SSH agents through a context, the client's.** A step there that
clones a private repository over SSH (`RUN --mount=type=ssh`) signs with the laptop's keys,
which never leave it.
- **A descriptor there for each agent the build names, its connections relayed here.** The
  client resolves `--ssh` as a build here does (`buildflags::ssh_agents`: an agent's socket,
  `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`'s by default, or the keys of files, held in memory here). The machine
  gives the build one end of a socket pair for each id, told by a variable no client can
  send (`SHARDS_AGENT_FDS`, taken first thing, as `SHARDS_CIDFILE_FD` is); for each
  connection a step's builder makes, the build asks on it (`DIAL`), and is answered with
  one end of a pair made for that connection (`GRANTED`), which it says it has (`TAKEN`,
  so the machine lets its own end go and the step's close is the end the relay sees: M24).
  The other end is held, told to the client on the build's stdout with a token (the frame
  `AGENT`), and relayed once the client claims it by that token (the step `agent`), to the
  client's agent, or answered from its keys as the keyring answers. A connection no client
  claimed goes with the build.
- **No path to dial.** At first each agent was a socket file in the machine's home, which
  any process of the machine's user could connect to while the build ran, the client's
  agent answering it. A descriptor reaches the build alone, as a run's vsock ports became
  pairs; a descriptor the build was not told is asked nothing, so `--ssh default=/dev/fd/N`
  on a command line keeps its meaning (`build::ssh::take_agents`, `asked_of`).
- **Read-only, there and here.** The builder relays only what BuildKit's read-only agent
  answers (keys, signatures, unlocking; D51); the client refuses anything else itself,
  whatever a machine lets by, so that no machine, its builds' steps or itself, has the
  client's agent forget, add or lock a key. What it can ask is what agent forwarding asks:
  signatures, for as long as the build runs.
- A connection a relay each, its own QUIC connection, a handshake each: a step's agent
  connections are a few, where its signatures are what take the time.

Tested in `tests/context.rs` (`a_builds_ssh_agents_through_a_context_are_the_clients`,
against a real `ssh-agent` holding a key `ssh-keygen` made: the step there lists the key and
has it sign, and is refused its removal; the agent keeps its key; a key file answered here,
its comment dropped as x/crypto drops it; none of the client's paths in what the machine was
asked; no socket in the machine's home), and in context.rs's unit tests
(`a_relayed_agent_answers_only_what_a_read_only_agent_does`: a request to forget every key
refused here, never reaching an agent that would do it), remote.rs's
(`an_agent_connection_ends_with_its_step_once_the_build_has_it`) and build/ssh.rs's
(`a_build_asks_its_daemon_for_agent_connections_on_what_it_was_told`, a socket it was not
told asked nothing). Mutation-checked: the client's agent unfiltered, its own `--ssh` words
sent too, a step's agent connection not told, not relayed; the told descriptors not taken,
not told; a socket file in the machine's home; `TAKEN` letting nothing go, not said; a
socket not told asked.

**Part 3g, built: the rest of what a build names of the client's.** A build reads more of the
client's than its context: a named context's directory (`--build-context NAME=DIR`) or an
OCI layout's (`oci-layout://DIR`), a local cache to import (`--cache-from
type=local,src=DIR`) or export (`--cache-to type=local,dest=DIR`), a policy's file
(`--policy filename=FILE`).
- **Each tree a copy of its own, kept in step before the build.** A named context's or a
  layout's directory, or a cache to import, is a tree with a copy of its own there,
  apart from any other's of the same directory: before the build, the client asks what the
  copy holds and sends what changed alone (the `put` step, its own stream), as a build's
  context is sent; the build's words name the copy (`\0tree/KEY`). A named context's
  directory is walked with its own ignore file, as the build reads one. A cache to export
  comes back as an output does (part 3f).
- **A policy's file is found where the build finds it**: buildx reads it within the build's
  context (an `os.Root` of it), so a name inside the context is said as it is there,
  relative, of the copy, which holds it whatever the ignore file leaves out, as the build
  reads the directory itself; one outside the context goes as it was given, which the
  build refuses here as it does there. A word's placeholder is placed wherever it stands,
  a field of a CSV value as a flag's whole value is.
- **None of the client's paths cross.**

A layout made here by one build there (`-o type=oci,dest=DIR,tar=false`) is the base of the
next (`--build-context base=oci-layout://DIR`). Tested in `tests/context.rs`
(`what_a_build_names_of_the_clients_is_carried_through_a_context`: a named context's files
and not what its ignore file leaves out; a cache exported here and imported from here; a
layout made here and built on; a policy inside the context, left out by its ignore file,
named relative and absolute, refusing the build in its words; none of the client's paths
in what the machine was asked), and unit tests of the placeholders.
Mutation-checked: a named context's directory sent as its path, a tree not brought in step,
a tree's placeholder left as it is, a local cache's export sent as its path, a policy the
ignore file leaves out not kept, a policy's absolute name sent as it is.

**Part 3f, built: a build's outputs through a context, the client's own files.** What a build
on the GPU machine makes comes back to the laptop: its result as a directory (`-o
type=local,dest=DIR`, an OCI layout's with `tar=false`) or a tar (`-o type=tar,dest=FILE`,
`oci`'s, `docker`'s), its image's ID (`--iidfile`), its metadata (`--metadata-file`).
- **Written there to a directory of the build's own, sent back as it ends.** The client
  names each as a place of the machine's (`\0out/NAME`, the output's own fields kept, its
  `dest` the machine's); the machine's step writes them under its copy, frames its stdout
  (the stream's version 3): the build's own stdout as it comes, then, once the build is
  through, each output, its name, its bytes, a directory's as its archive, and its end
  (`synced::send_outputs`); and it removes them once sent, all under the copy's lock, so
  that no build's outputs outlive it there or meet another's. A step that sent them apart,
  after, would have left a client's outputs on the machine where the client ended between.
- **Kept here as a build here writes them, and better.** A directory's archive is unpacked
  into it as the local exporter writes one; a file is written beside its path and renamed
  to it at its end, its mode a new file's, so that a file is whole or not at all, where a
  build here writes its ID in place; one a signal ends goes. An output not kept fails the
  build, in the build's words. `-o -` is the build's stdout, as it was.
- **None of the client's paths cross**: where they would be read on the machine, each was
  the machine's own to misread.

Tested in `tests/context.rs` (`a_builds_outputs_through_a_context_are_the_clients_files`: a
directory's files, a tar's entries, an image's ID, its metadata, a tar on stdout, none of the
client's paths in what the machine was asked, and nothing left under its copies), and unit
tests of the framing (a step's frames, cut anywhere, coming apart as they were said) and the
placeholders.
Mutation-checked: the outputs not sent, the outputs kept there, an output's path sent as it
is, the step's stdout not taken apart.

**Part 3e, built: a build's secrets through a context, and its `RUN` steps.** A build on
the GPU machine reaches private packages as a build on the laptop does, its tokens the
laptop's:
- **Read here, held there in memory alone.** Each `--secret` is read by the client as a
  build here reads it (`buildflags::store`: its file, else its variable, else its id's,
  the last of an id counting, each within a step's frame), and crosses with the build's
  stream (`synced::send`, the format's version 2), the client's words of it (its file's
  path, its variable's name) left behind. The machine takes as many as the build's words
  name and no more, each into a buffer of its own length held as a secret
  (`SecretBytes`, overwritten when dropped), and gives the build each on a pipe of its
  own, which the build reads once as its file (`src=/dev/fd/N`): no file of the machine's
  ever holds one. Where a build here would read a file Docker's daemon is sent over its
  session, a context needs no SSH account to carry it.
- **`RUN` steps run there, which they did not.** A command a client runs is given none of
  the owner's variables, `HOME` among them, which keeps the owner's logins in reach of no
  client; but a `RUN` step's microVM needs the VM process shards writes out to its cache,
  which was found by `HOME` ("no cache directory: HOME is not set": part 3c's builds copied
  files alone). The cache is named outright now: `SHARDS_CACHE`, a user's to set too, and
  the daemon's for its clients' commands.

Tested in `tests/context.rs`
(`a_builds_secrets_through_a_context_are_the_clients_held_in_memory_alone`: a `RUN` step
there reading a secret file and a secret variable of the client's, saying only what each
hashes to (`testguest digest`); no file of the machine's home holding either; neither the
file's path nor the variable's name in what the machine was asked; and a secret not here
said in the build's words, `ERROR: failed to stat ...`), and unit tests of the stream (more
secrets than the build names refused), the placeholders and Go's CSV field.
Mutation-checked: the secrets not sent, no pipe given the build, a secret's placeholder left
as it is, no cache named, the client's own words of its secrets sent too, more secrets than
named taken.

**Part 3d, built: shards' own artifacts through a context.** An agent, a harness or an MCP
server is made where it is to run: on the GPU machine, of the agent's directory on the
laptop, its signature by the laptop's own key or identity.
- **Built there, of the machine's copy of the directory**, kept in step as a build's
  context is (part 3c): the first build sends its files' bytes, each once; each after,
  what changed alone. A copy of its own, apart from an image build's of the same
  directory, which holds what that build's ignore file leaves, where an artifact takes all
  its directory holds. Its words are the build's own (`agent.rs`, `build_args`, read here
  and there alike), the directory the copy's; `--platform` and `--sbom` run there, the
  SBOM's scanner pulled with the client's login for its registry, as a base is.
- **Byte for byte the artifact made here.** Its layer records each file's name, mode, time
  and hard links: the copy keeps the times to the nanosecond, the modes, and now the
  links, a new name of a file the copy holds going as a link to it
  (`shards_archive::pack_changes`, seeded with the copy's names `synced::plan` finds by
  their inodes), so that the copy's tree is the client's and its digest the one a build
  here makes.
- **What the build says names the client's paths.** A command of a copy prints the
  copy's path (`.../synced/CLIENT/KEY/context/agent.json`), a path on another machine; the
  machine's step says it as the client's own (`SHARDS_SYNCED_AS`, the only variable a
  client sends that no command is given), as it comes, holding back only a tail that may
  yet begin one: `ERROR: /Users/me/agent/agent.json: ...`. An image build's too.
- **Signed by the client, kept by the machine.** A signature is made where its signer
  is: the machine says what a signature of the name is of (its manifest, or its index,
  `sign_step subject`); the client signs that statement with its own cosign key and
  password, or keylessly with its own OIDC identity, neither of which crosses; and the
  machine keeps the bundle as the name's referrer (`sign_step keep`), only where the name
  resolves to what was signed still and the bundle's envelope holds that digest's
  statement: a bundle of anything else, or of what the name named before it moved, is
  refused. A push carries it with the artifact, as one made there.

Measured by the test, to the byte: the first build sends 65,590 bytes of files, its
config's 33, its script's 21 and its 64 KiB of data once, the data's second name a link; the
next, after the script was rewritten and the data given a third name, 28, the script's
alone. Tested in `tests/context.rs`
(`an_artifact_through_a_context_is_made_of_the_clients_files_and_signed_by_its_key`: the
digest there the digest here, twice; the bytes; a malformed config said at the client's
path, no copy's path said; signed by the client's key, pushed there to a registry, its
referrer's subject the agent and its envelope verified by the key's public half), the
archive's (`a_new_name_of_a_file_the_copy_holds_is_linked_to_it_there`), the plan's and the
shown paths' unit tests, and agent.rs's (`a_signature_is_kept_only_of_what_its_name_names`).
Mutation-checked: the copy's names not seeded, no partner named, the copy's paths shown as
they are, an artifact's build not of a copy, a signature not made here, a signature kept of
what its name named before, a bundle kept whatever it signs.

**Part 4, built: Docker's tools through a context.** What speaks Docker's API (its CLI,
Compose, the SDKs, Testcontainers) reaches the machine's microVMs:
- **An engine socket for each context, served with the daemon's own.** The client's daemon,
  while it runs, serves the engine of each context its home joined at a socket of its own
  (`e/KEY.sock` in the home, KEY the first six bytes of the name's SHA-256, so that the path
  fits a socket's address whatever the name: 71 bytes in a macOS home of a nine-letter user,
  of sun_path's 104). `shards inspect context NAME` names it (`Engine`), for `DOCKER_HOST`.
  Its listener is polled with the daemon's own sockets, not a thread of its own, so it
  lives and ends as they do:
  - the daemon watches the home's contexts (as it watches its images): a context joined
    while it runs is served as its record comes, one removed let go of as it goes;
  - a socket someone removed is bound again as the daemon next looks, as its own are, and
    so is one a context's removal took before the context was made again, which a socket
    kept by name alone would have left unserved;
  - as the daemon closes, the sockets go first and the clients that reached one by then are
    relayed, as those at its own sockets are served: no client is cut off as it exits;
  - a socket is bound beside its name and renamed to it once it listens, as `engine.sock`
    is now too: a client that found the name between bind(2) and listen(2) was refused,
    and Docker's clients do not ask again (the full suite found it, under load).
  A record is written whole under a name no record has and then linked to its own, so that
  a reader (this daemon, woken as the name comes, or `list contexts`) finds it whole or not
  at all: written in place, a record read as it was made failed the whole list.
- **A QUIC stream each connection.** Each connection there is relayed whole to the
  machine's Engine API (D170): its bytes as a command's stdin, the API's as its stdout, the
  end of each side's writing the other's end of reading, so that an attach's half-close
  (`docker run -i`'s end of stdin) reaches the command, and a hijacked stream's end reaches
  the client. The machine's daemon takes such a stream as a connection of its own user's to
  its own `engine.sock`; the client's daemon relays only its own user's connections, by
  their peer's credentials, as its own Engine API serves only them.
- **Ended at either end.** A client gone ends its stream there: its end of writing is the
  stream's end there, and a write that finds it gone hangs the stream up, where the relay
  would have read on and thrown away all a followed log or an attach said for as long as
  it ran. A daemon that stops hangs its relays up itself (`Controls::hang_up`, beside its
  API's connections, which it ends): ending its client's connection only half-closes the
  stream there, and an attach outlasts that, so the stop would have waited on the machine.
- **A machine that does not answer is said to be so.** Where the machine refuses the client,
  or cannot be reached, before any of its answer has come, the client's call is answered
  with why, as the API says an error (502, a gateway's): Docker's CLI prints `Error response
  from daemon: context gpu: this machine has not enrolled you: join it by an invitation
  first`, where a connection closed unanswered would have it print an EOF.
- **A context made again joins again.** A machine refused a join by a key it had enrolled,
  saying the invitation was not one it held, so a client that removed its context could not
  make it again, the record's address and key being the invitation's to give. A key
  enrolled already that brings a valid invitation now joins as it was enrolled, under the
  name it has; the invitation is redeemed, so that no other key takes it, and no second name
  is made.
- **What crosses of the client's is what Docker's CLI sends:** its own registry logins with
  each request (`X-Registry-Auth`), a build's context in its request's body; the paths a
  request names are the machine's.

The same end for shards' own commands through a context: a command whose output nobody
reads here any more (`shards --context gpu watch logs web | head -1`) is hung up there, and
the client ends with status 1, saying nothing, as such a command ends here; its client read
and threw away the rest for as long as the command ran, for ever for a followed log. A save
to a file whose write fails here ends the save there too, at once, said in the save's words,
where the machine sent the rest of the archive first.

Where Docker's `ssh://` context starts `docker system dial-stdio` through a shell account
for each connection, this needs neither; how they compare is part 5's to measure. Not yet:
each relayed connection opens a QUIC connection of its own, a handshake each, where one
connection kept for the context, a stream each, would not (part 5 measures both); a Windows
client, whose daemon serves no Engine API yet (D195; the parity plan's step 8), has no
engine socket (Docker's `npipe://`).
Tested in `tests/context.rs` (`a_contexts_engine_is_its_machines`): `_ping` through the
socket; a microVM made through the context, listed there and not by the client's own engine;
Docker's CLI where the host has one, its `ps`, a `run`, whose attach takes the connection
over, and a `run -i` of `cat`, its stdin to its end; a client that reads its answer to the
end; the context's removal taking its socket; the context made again while the daemon runs,
served with no other command, one client of its key, the invitation redeemed; a socket
removed served again; an attach through the socket ended as the daemon stops, in 5 ms, its
socket gone with it; served again by the next daemon; and a machine that refuses the client,
its words in the answer and in what the `docker` CLI says of it. In `tests/context_client.rs`
(`a_command_whose_output_nobody_reads_is_hung_up_there`), on every system: the command hung
up there once its reader here has gone, the client ending with status 1 and nothing said.
Mutation-checked: the engine's stream run as a command; either end's half-close not passed
on, the machine's or the client's; an enrolled key's join refused; the contexts unwatched; a
removed socket not bound again; the sockets kept as the daemon closes; the relays not hung
up as it stops; a machine's refusal unsaid; the client's writer failing and its command run
on; a reader gone said as an error.

### D181. `--use-api-socket`: a run's command reaches its own microVM's engine (slices 1 to 3 built)

The need: a CI job, a test suite with testcontainers, or an agent's tool runs `docker run`
from inside its workload, as on a host with Docker. The user's call (2026-10-16): what it
reaches is the microVM's own engine. Docker's flag (docker/cli v29.8.1
cli/command/container/create.go, marked experimental) does two things, both what shards
does not: it binds the host engine's own socket into the container, so the workload
controls the host's Docker, every container and image of it, as root does; and it writes
every registry credential the CLI holds into the container's files
(`/run/secrets/docker/config.json`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`), which its own comment says stay
there where the container is not removed.

- **What the command gets.** An Engine API endpoint of its own microVM's: a socket in its
  own files, `/run/shards/engine.sock`, and `DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/shards/engine.sock`
  where its run's options name none (over its image's own, which names an engine the
  flag replaces), so that the docker CLI, Docker's SDKs and testcontainers find it
  unchanged. No socket of the host's, and nothing at Docker's own path. The socket is the
  standby's to make, in the command's own view of its files, after the run's mounts (a
  tmpfs over `/run` holds it) and before its root is made read-only (`--read-only` keeps
  it), mode 0666: whoever the command runs as or becomes reaches it, and no process but
  the run's own sees the path.
- **On Windows**, where a VM's process gives its daemon no handle (D195: a child's end
  takes handles only from its spawner), the VM asks for each connection whose token
  holds (`ENGINE_CONN`, no handle), and the daemon makes a pair of pipes written in
  messages (`Stream::plain_pair`): it serves one end as the connection, scoped to the
  microVM as Unix's, and gives the VM the other, onto which the VM relays its guest's
  connection each way on a thread of its own (warm.rs `relay_engine`), each side's end of
  writes passed on: the pipe's message of no bytes one way, the socket's half-close the
  other. A run with no engine of its own is answered with no pipe, and its connection
  closed. Tested on jupiter: tests/engine.rs's own-engine tests and the docker CLI's
  `--use-api-socket`.
- **What it makes: joiners of its own microVM.** A container it creates there is a joiner
  of its microVM (D119): its own image, its own mount, PID, IPC and UTS namespaces and
  cgroup, its record, log and end; its network a namespace of its own on the microVM's
  switch, granted what it declares and nothing else (slice 3), `host` the command's own
  namespace where its client asks for it, `container:X` one of its own containers'. The
  microVM's boundary holds the host from all of them. It is named in the scope as the command named it, and on the
  host after its microVM's name (`PROV.NAME`), so that two microVMs' engines making the
  same name (two CI jobs of one project) never collide, where a shared dockerd's do. Its
  record keeps which microVM's engine made it (`engine_made`). It ends as its microVM's
  command does, as a nested engine's containers end with it: init kills each joiner its
  engine made as the command ends (`engine-made`), where a joiner made otherwise outlives
  it (D119); and it goes with its microVM, removed as that is.
- **Scoped, whatever is asked.** Through it, a command sees and acts on what its own
  engine made alone, by the names it gave: list, inspect, start, stop, kill, wait, logs,
  attach (`docker run`'s, before the start), resize, exec, remove; `_ping`, `version`, and
  an `info` of its own (its containers, its images, its microVM's CPUs and memory where
  its run limits them, its hostname; none of its host's name, directories, proxies or
  descriptors). Another microVM, its own included, and an exec of another's, are not there
  for it (404, as one that is not). What would reach past the microVM is refused with
  what asked for it (403): a named volume, another network, the host's GPUs, CDI and VFIO
  devices, a log driver that sends logs from the host past the microVM's grants, another
  runtime, an engine of its own for a joiner. A call it does not serve is answered 501
  before its body is read, naming what it serves; a registry login, 403.
- **A bind is of its microVM's own files**, as a bind on any engine is of that engine's
  host's, and the microVM is its host: `-v /work:/src` in the CI job binds the job's
  `/work`, where Docker's flag binds the host's path, which the job's files are not. The
  joiner's init copies the source from the workload's mount namespace while that is in
  reach (setns(2), open_tree(2) `OPEN_TREE_CLONE | AT_RECURSIVE`: a bind brings its
  submounts, which `-v`'s users rely on, Docker's binds being
  recursive), resolved from that namespace's root, the command's files, past none of them
  (`..` and links, absolute or not, stop there): its volumes and tmpfs mounts are in it,
  and a link to one resolves as the command's processes see it. Read-only binds are so
  with their submounts (mount_setattr(2) `AT_RECURSIVE`, Linux 5.12). `-v` makes a missing
  source, which scripts written for Docker rely on; `--mount` does not, and skips the host's check for
  it, the source being none of the host's. A propagation that would share mounts with the
  command's (`shared`, `slave`) is refused: a copy shares none.
- **Its images are its own.** A create runs its microVM's image, and those its engine
  pulled (`engine_images` in the microVM's record); another image the host's store holds
  is not there for it (404), so the docker CLI pulls, as on an engine without it, and a
  scope never reads an image it was not given. `images` and `image inspect` list its own
  alone; `info` counts them.
- **No credential enters the microVM.** A pull through it is the daemon's, with the
  registries' environment the run's client sent with the run (its `DOCKER_CONFIG` and the
  rest, `registry_env`), kept in the daemon's memory for the run's life alone, as a log
  driver's credentials are (D168), never written into the microVM, nor into the run's
  kept request; credentials a client in the microVM gives (`X-Registry-Auth`) go over
  them. A registry login asked from inside is refused.
- **The docker CLI's own flag, asked of shards' engine** (`docker run --use-api-socket`
  over `engine.sock`): its bind of its engine's socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`, bind
  options none set) is the microVM's own engine instead, and its `DOCKER_CONFIG` goes with
  it; the copy of its credentials it makes after the create (an archive whose first entry
  is `/run/secrets/docker/config.json`) is refused, which the CLI warns of: they never
  reach the microVM.
- **How a request travels, by no socket of the host's.** The command's connection is
  taken by a process of init's (outside the command's cgroup, as the DNS relay is, started
  before the command so that what keeps it from starting keeps the command from starting),
  which dials the host over vsock (`ENGINE_PORT`) for each, says a hello with its run's
  token first, and relays the bytes each way; the host's end ends the client's both ways,
  so that no relay outlives a connection the engine closed. The VM process registers the
  port only for a warm VM's run, and serves it only where its run has a token: its hello
  reader (exec's, review 8.8) checks each in constant time and hands the daemon those that
  say it, over the run's own link (`ENGINE_CONN`), holding its copy until the daemon says
  it has it (M24); any other is closed, and a run with no engine has no port (refused). A
  process of the microVM's that dials the port itself, past its seccomp filter, says no
  token its init was given. The daemon serves the connections of a run that has an engine
  alone, on the listener's threads, scoped to that run's microVM. A save keeps the token,
  which its restored guest's relay goes on saying (D176). No path on the host names the
  endpoint.
- **No microVM's engine takes the host's daemon.** Each of its connections holds a thread
  of the daemon's, and is counted as a client in hand (`busy`), of the clients the
  daemon's threads hold (`most_clients`: the process's thread limit past the daemon's own
  threads, at a client's two each; macOS gives 16,384 threads a process). A microVM's
  engine holds an equal share of them alone, among the host's own clients and each
  microVM whose engine holds any: one alone holds half, two a third each. Past its share,
  or where the daemon holds as many clients as its threads do, a connection is answered
  503 with why and closed; one of its own going makes room. Without it, a workload's
  1,023 idle connections (the vsock muxer's bound, Firecracker's) held as many of the
  daemon's threads, and sixteen microVMs held them all.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_command_reaches_its_own_microvms_engine`: made, started,
waited for, logged, listed, inspected and removed through it, the host's other microVM and
itself unseen, a named volume and a login refused, a call not served answered 501, one left running
ended with its command and removed with its microVM;
`the_docker_clis_use_api_socket_is_the_microvms_own_engine`; isolation's
`a_microvms_engine_port_answers_its_inits_token_alone`, a tmpfs over `/run` and a read-only
root among its cases, and the engine port among those a workload reaches none of), and in
the daemon (`an_engine_connection_is_served_for_a_run_with_its_own_engine_alone`) and the
scope (`a_scope_sees_its_own_containers_by_their_names_there`,
`a_create_stays_in_its_microvm`).

Slice 2 tested on real microVMs (`a_microvms_own_engine_runs_binds_execs_and_pulls`:
`docker run`'s calls, a create, an attach before the start and the start and wait on one
kept connection, its output from its first byte; binds of the command's file and of its
volume, read-only and written through, a link to its volume resolved as the command sees
it; an exec in its container, another microVM's exec unseen; a pull from a registry that
asks for credentials, which the run's client alone has, the image not its own before, its
own after; its images listed, none of the host's it never pulled), and in the scope
(`a_create_stays_in_its_microvm`).

Slices: (1) and (2) built, as above; (3), the containers its engine makes on networks of
their own and Compose through them, designed as follows and built in five parts. A first cut of
(3) (part 3a, b6083246) put each container on a bridge of its own in the command's
namespace, with every port open between them and their flows translated to the command's:
no part of the microVM's own network design (D59, D61), it is replaced.

- **The need.** A test suite, a CI job or an agent's tools in a microVM start services
  through its engine (Testcontainers' `docker run -p 0:PORT`, Compose's project of
  services), each listening on its own ports, two on one port among them, each reaching
  the others it needs by name; and they run under the microVM's own rule, default deny,
  beside its agents.
- **Each is a member of the microVM's switch.** A container its engine makes gets a
  network namespace of its own, linked to init's switch through a gate of its own (D59
  part three, D61), as each of the image's agents is: known by its link, never by an
  address it could claim; what it opens tracked in its gate's table alone; no state of it
  kept by the switch. Init makes the namespace, its gate and its link before the
  container starts, and its processes enter it (setns(2)); the switch and the gate are
  outside every namespace they have.
- **Its engine's networks are the switch's.** A network its engine makes (Compose's
  project networks, a test's own) is a network of the switch: a /24 of the switch's block
  (10.244.0.0/16) clear of eth0's subnet and of every network of the microVM's, the
  agents' among them, or the subnet its client gives where that is clear of them too; its
  gateway its first address, or the one given. Init holds them, and gives each member the
  lowest free address as it joins: a /32 routed through the gateway on its link, as an
  agent's is. The engine's default network, which its clients call `bridge`, is one; a
  container named onto no other is on it.
- **Joining grants nothing; what a container declares does.** Each flow is named
  (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §4.7): a container accepts, from each member of a network it shares,
  on the ports it declares, and on no other: its image's `EXPOSE`, its create's
  (`--expose`, Compose's `expose:`), and the container side of each port it publishes.
  That is the receiver naming what it accepts, as `CONNECT --port` names it for an agent:
  the network says who may ask, the receiver on what. The default network names no peers:
  a container on it is alone, as an agent with no `CONNECT` is. Nothing else crosses: no
  port a receiver did not declare, no member of a network the two do not share, no agent
  of the image, not the command.
- **Names, of granted peers alone.** A container resolves its own names and those of each
  peer it is granted a flow to, and no other (§4.7). Its names on a network are its name
  in its engine's scope and the aliases its client gives it there (Compose's service
  names, `--network-alias`); nothing else names it. Its `/etc/hosts`, a file of its own
  mounted read-only as an agent's is, names it alone: an agent's lists its granted peers
  too (D59 part seven), which its build fixes, but a member's peers come and go as it
  runs. The agents' resolver answers its peers' names, by the link the question comes up
  (`IP_PKTINFO`, D59 part seven), from a table init keeps for each member as peers join
  and leave; each answer's TTL is 0, which no cache keeps past the answer (RFC 1035
  §3.2.1), so a name goes with its grant. A granted peer's name is answered in the
  microVM, never asked past it.
- **Published ports, to the command alone.** A port it publishes (`-p HOST:PORT`, `-P`)
  reaches it from the command, its engine's host, at `localhost:HOST` in the command's
  namespace: init's proxy there passes each connection and datagram on to the container's
  port, and the switch and its gate let that port alone in, up the switch's link from
  init's namespace. Nothing past the microVM reaches it but through a port the run itself
  publishes. The command reaches no container on any port it did not publish.
- **Past the microVM, no more than the command.** A container acts for the command that
  asked its engine for it: what it reaches past the microVM is what the command reaches
  (the run's own grants, the network process holding the microVM to them; beside agents
  whose grants reach past it, eth0's own subnet alone, as `confine_eth0` keeps the
  command), its flows given eth0's address as the agents' egress is (D59 part four); on an
  internal network, nothing. Names past the microVM likewise: it asks the agents'
  resolver, which forwards what the command may resolve.
- **What it tells where a flow is refused.** A peer's connection to a port its receiver
  never declared ends at the receiver's gate, as any flow no grant names does.
  `shards read ports` of a container lists each port it listens on that no grant lets its
  peers reach, with what would declare it (`EXPOSE`, `expose:`, `--expose`), so the gap
  is seen at once rather than as a connection that hangs.
- **Its own values.** A container's link takes the hardware address its kernel gives it,
  as an agent's does. The proxy keeps a UDP client's mapping as long as the microVM's own
  connection tracking keeps a UDP flow (`nf_conntrack_udp_timeout`, and
  `nf_conntrack_udp_timeout_stream` once answered, read from the running guest), so that
  a published UDP port lasts as the microVM's translated flows do.
- **`--network host` is the command's own namespace**, as the client asks: the engine's
  host's network, the command's reach and no more. `none` is a namespace of its own with
  its loopback alone; `container:X` the namespace of X, one of its own containers.
- **The networks API** (create, list, inspect, remove, prune, connect, disconnect) takes
  what Compose and the SDKs send, and answers in the shapes they read, with the switch's
  values: its subnets, its members' addresses. A driver no microVM's switch can be
  (`overlay`, `macvlan`, `ipvlan`) and a setting it cannot hold are refused with why.
- **Named volumes it makes** are its own: the host's volume store's, named after its
  microVM's as its containers are (`PROV.NAME`), mounted through the join share (D119),
  removed with its microVM.

Each difference from Docker is deliberate: membership carries no flow, where Docker's
network carries every port both ways; the default network names no peers, where Docker's
carries every port between its containers; a container resolves its granted peers alone,
where Docker resolves every member by name, alias, short ID and hostname; the command
reaches a container through what it publishes alone, where Docker's host reaches every
container's address; and a container reaches past the microVM no more than the command.

Built in parts: (3a) members on the switch, the default network, published ports, `host`
and `none`, built; (3b) the networks its engine makes, their grants and names, and the
networks API, built; (3c) its
named volumes, one container in another's namespace (`container:X`, Compose's
`service:`), and Compose end to end, built; (3d) the undeclared listeners `shards read
ports` lists, built; (3e) connect and disconnect of a running member, built.

- **How 3a is built.** The daemon asks for a membership by network and name (`member=`,
  with `own-publish=` for each port it publishes), and nothing of addresses. Init holds
  the engine's networks (`members.rs`), each a /24 of the switch's block clear of eth0's
  subnet and of every subnet the switch carries (the agents', which the switch now keeps
  from its making); it gives each member the lowest free address, the lowest free link
  index past the domains', a namespace of its own with its loopback, and links it through
  a gate of its own (`Switch::attach_ns`, as `attach` links a domain by its process). The
  switch keeps what it carries (the domains' grants, its uplink once there is one, its
  subnets, each member's), and programs its rules and init's again from that, each chain
  emptied first in the same transaction, as members come and go (`admit`, `release`): the
  domains' rules come out as before, a member's are its own. A member's way up the
  switch's link is every TCP and UDP port, as far as the command goes (init's `forward`,
  marked and given eth0's address as the agents' egress is; to eth0's subnet alone beside
  agents with egress); the command reaches it on its published ports alone (init's `own`
  chain, before its drop, and the switch's and gate's rules for that port from the
  uplink). It asks the agents' resolver, which now takes askers as members join and leave
  over a control link of init's. The joiner's child enters the namespace (setns(2)) by
  init's descriptor, which it inherits as init's fork, and its `/etc/hosts` names it, its
  `/etc/resolv.conf` the switch's resolver. Init says the membership to the host before
  the joiner starts (`MEMBER`: its network, address and prefix, gateway and the kernel's
  hardware address), which the daemon keeps for inspect while it runs; its end lets the
  membership go. The proxy relays what is published, its UDP mappings kept as the guest's
  connection tracking keeps a UDP flow (read in a run of the pinned kernel, arm64,
  2026-10-17: 30 s, and 120 s once answered), and says a
  port it cannot bind in shards' words. `--add-host NAME:host-gateway` is refused: a
  member reaches nothing of the command's.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_each_container_a_member_of_its_switch`:
  two members serving one port, each at the port it was given on the command's loopback
  and at its own address on that port, from init's end of the switch's link; a port one
  declares but does not publish, dropped for the command; on the default network, a
  member reaching neither another's published port nor its declared one, and the other
  serving its next connection to the command; `--network none`'s loopback alone; its host
  name, and its name in its hosts file at its address; `host-gateway` refused; and its
  flows to a microVM on the host's network the command is on, from the command's address
  there. `an_engines_member_reaches_no_farther_than_the_command_beside_agents`: beside an
  agent granted a host's port, neither the command nor a member reaches it; with no
  agents, a member reaches what its command reaches. Every agent network test of D59 and
  D61 holds as before. Mutation-checked, each caught: a member beside agents reaching as
  far as the command of a run without them; the command's published ports not let
  through init's `own` chain; the default network carrying every port between members;
  members reaching nothing past the microVM.
- **How 3b is built.** Init makes and removes its engine's networks (`members::network`),
  asked by the daemon through a builtin (`NETWORK make NAME SUBNET GATEWAY RANGE FLAGS`,
  `remove NAME`, `default`) that init does itself before the builtin's fork, so that what
  it holds stays its own; the daemon keeps what its clients read of each (its ID, name,
  creation time, labels and options as given). A network's subnet is the lowest /24 of
  the switch's block clear of eth0's subnet and of every subnet the switch carries, or the
  one its client gives (a /8 to a /30, clear of the same), its gateway and range in it. A
  member on several networks has an address on each, routed on its one link
  (`Switch::routes`), and says each (`MEMBER`). Its grants are built again from every
  member whenever one joins or leaves (`members::grants`): for each two members of a
  network whose members are peers, the ports the receiver declares, held at two points
  that each hold them alone: the switch passes those only between the two links, and the
  receiver's gate accepts those only, from the opener's addresses. The opener's gate is a
  third that holds them alone: it opens those only to its peers, and what it opens past
  the microVM (every port, for a member that reaches past it) to none of the microVM's
  own subnets, its agents' networks' and its engine's, each gate made again as its engine
  makes or removes a network, as an agent's egress (D61). Each gate is programmed again
  in one transaction, the switch in one. A member's gate holds its declared ports from its start, before it has any peer,
  so that its own connections' ports are chosen clear of them (`local_ports`, D61). Its
  peers' names init gives the agents' resolver with its asker, over init's control link;
  the resolver answers a question that comes up the member's link from them first, and
  any other as that member's (forwarded where it reaches past the microVM, refused where
  it does not). The answerer is `shards-dns` (once `shards_net::dns`), a crate init and
  the network process share. Of the options its clients send, `enable_icc` false makes a
  network of no peers, `gateway_mode_ipv4` isolated an internal one, and
  `host_binding_ipv4` the address its members' published ports are bound at in the
  command's namespace where a binding names none. Refused, each with why: drivers other
  than bridge, IPv6, a network without IPv4, IPAM drivers, a second subnet, auxiliary
  addresses, ingress, configuration-only and configuration-from networks, a scope but
  `local`, gateway modes but `nat` and `isolated`, `enable_ip_masquerade`,
  `inhibit_ipv4`, a bridge's name, an MTU, an interface prefix; an endpoint's hardware
  address, link-local addresses and driver options; an alias on the default network,
  which names no peers. Connect and disconnect change a container's
  networks for its next start (the request it was made with), and refuse one that runs,
  with why, until 3e. Inspect's `NetworkSettings.Networks` has an entry for each of its
  networks (its address, prefix, gateway and hardware address as init said them, its
  aliases, and `DNSNames`, the names its peers resolve it by, none on the default
  network), and a network's inspect lists its running members.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_networks_whose_members_reach_what_each_declares`:
  two networks made, a third by a name taken refused, a `macvlan` one refused; listed
  with the engine's own, and by label; db, first on its network, declaring 7000 and
  40000, takes its own connections' ports clear of both; it is reached by its alias and by
  its name on 7000 from members of its network, its alias answered with a TTL of 0;
  stray, declaring 7000 and listening on 7001, is not reached on 7001; neither a member
  of the other network, by db's address or its name, nor the command reaches db, whose
  second connection is web2's; a network with a running member stays; a container that
  does not run joins one for its next start and resolves db there once started, and one
  that runs is refused; stray resolves db's alias while db runs and not once it has ended;
  a network naming 127.0.0.1 for its members' published ports binds one there, reached at
  the command's loopback and not at eth0's address; and the networks go once their
  members have, by name and by a prune. `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_each_container_a_member_of_its_switch`
  now has a member of an internal network alone reach nothing past the microVM, which a
  member of the default network then reaches. Mutation-checked: with the switch alone,
  the receiver's gate alone, or the opener's gate alone left holding a pair's ports, an
  undeclared port stays shut, and with every point opened (the opener's egress let onto
  the microVM's own subnets as well) the test catches it. Caught, each: grants
  past the networks two members share; peers' gates not built again as a member joins;
  the switch carrying no member's pairs; the resolver answering one member's question
  from another's table; grants not built again as a member goes; peers' names answered
  with the TTL the network process gives; a network's address for its members'
  published ports ignored; a member's own ports chosen before it has a peer; and, in the
  other test, the default network making peers of its members, and an internal
  network's member reaching past the microVM.
- **Found on the way.** A member first on its network had no peer as it was linked, so
  its gate then held none of the ports it declares, and its own connections took ports
  from the kernel's whole default range; once a peer joined, the gate left a declared
  port in that range untracked, and dropped the answers of the member's own connections
  that took it. The three-point check led to it: a receiver's gate made to accept every
  port left its member's own connections untracked too, which is what a declared port in
  the range its own connections take does. A gate now holds its member's declared ports
  from the start.
- **How its volumes are built (3c).** A volume a microVM's engine makes, through its API
  or as a container it makes names one (`-v NAME:DEST`, `--mount source=NAME`), is in the
  host's store, on disk rather than in the microVM's memory, where its writable layer
  is. The store's record says whose it is (`Of`, the microVM's ID) and what its engine
  calls it (`There`); on the host it is named after the microVM, as its containers are
  (`PROV.NAME`, or `PROV.NAME.N` where the host has a volume of that name: a host name is
  only how it is shown). Its engine finds its own by that record alone, so a renamed
  microVM keeps them, and no name of its reaches another microVM's or the host's own. A
