  container it makes mounts them through the microVM's join share (D119), a fresh one
  taking the image's files at its mount point and their owner as it is first mounted,
  and its anonymous ones are the microVM's too. Its engine lists, inspects, makes,
  removes and prunes them by its own names, with no path of the host's in what it says
  (`Mountpoint`, a mount's `Source`); a volume takes no driver and no driver options, the
  local driver's binding a directory of the host's (`o=bind,device=...`). One a container
  mounts stays; the rest go with their microVM, each as the last container that mounts it
  goes.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_volumes_of_its_own`: a volume
  made through the API by its name, at no host path, and none with driver options; a
  container writes to it by `-v`, another reads it through `--mount`, a third's named
  volume made as it is named; its engine lists its own alone, by their names, and a
  container's mount by that name at no path; the host lists them after the microVM's
  name; the host's own `prov.secret` neither taken nor seen by the microVM's `secret`,
  which is named `prov.secret.2`; renamed, the microVM keeps them and reads what it
  wrote; another microVM's engine finds none of them, its own `data` its own; one a
  container mounts stays, and goes once none does; and the rest go with the microVM,
  the host's and the other microVM's staying. Mutation-checked, each caught: its engine
  listing every volume; one found by its host name alone, which a rename lost; no free
  name taken, the host's `prov.secret` refusing its `secret`; no free name and another's
  volume taken, which read the host's file; its volumes left as it went; a host path in
  a volume's document, and in a container's mount; driver options taken. With a free
  name taken, the store's refusal of another's volume is a second guard the test does
  not reach.
- **One in another's namespace (3c).** `--network container:X` of a container its
  microVM's engine made, and Compose's `network_mode: service:X`, shares X's network
  namespace as it is: a member's (its link, address, gate, grants and names), one on
  `none` (its loopback alone), or the command's where X is on `host`. The daemon names the
  namespace to init by X's exec in its provider's guest (`net=joiner=ID`, as `pid=joiner=`
  names a PID namespace), following X to the one it shares where it shares another's; init
  enters it, and X's UTS namespace, before anything of the new container's runs. Its
  `hostname`, `hosts` and `resolv.conf` are X's, the same files read-only, copied from X's
  mount namespace (open_tree(2)), so that a link X put there resolves in X's files alone.
  It publishes and declares no ports of its own, refused as any joiner's are at create
  (D119), for it has no link to have them on. Found on the way: before, any such container
  but a member's was given its provider's namespace, the command's, so one beside a
  container on `none`, loopback alone, reached as far as the command; and one beside a
  member was refused.
- **Tested on real microVMs.**
  `a_container_in_anothers_namespace_shares_that_ones_as_it_is`: beside one on `none`, its
  loopback alone; beside a member, that member's server on their loopback, its host name
  and its hosts file at its address; ports of its own refused. Mutation-checked, each
  caught: init entering its provider's namespace (it saw the command's eth0 beside one on
  `none`); the daemon naming no namespace of the one it joins; X's files not shared; its
  provider's UTS namespace.
- **Compose end to end (3c).** `a_compose_project_runs_in_its_microvms_own_engine`: docker
  compose's own client for Linux (v5.6.0, pinned by its release's SHA-256), unchanged,
  run by a microVM's command against that microVM's own engine: `up -d` makes the
  project's network, volume and services; `ps` lists them running; `exec` in one reaches
  the other by its service's name on the port it declares (`expose:`); a file written to
  the project's named volume is read back, the volume on the host as `PROV.shp_data`;
  and `down -v` takes the containers, network and volume. What it relies on is
  mutation-checked in the tests above.
- **How 3d is built.** `shards read ports` of a container its microVM's engine made, a
  member of the switch, says each port it declares or listens on, where it is
  published, and who reaches it there (REACHED BY): the command where it publishes it;
  its peers on each of its networks that make peers of their members where it declares
  it; no one where its networks make no peers; and no one where it listens without
  declaring it, with what would (`EXPOSE`, `expose:`, `--expose`), so that a connection
  that would hang is seen at once instead. What it listens on init reads by a builtin
  (`LISTENS`) through its own `/proc` by the container's process (`/proc/PID/net/tcp`,
  `tcp6`, `udp`, `udp6`: TCP in LISTEN, UDP bound and unconnected), past the loopback,
  which nothing but itself reaches. Tested in the 3b test (stray's declared 7000 reached
  by its peers on app, its 7001 undeclared by no one, with what would declare it) and the
  3a test (one's published 7000 by the command, quiet's declared 7002 by no one, the
  default network making no peers); the socket tables' reading, IPv4 and IPv6, loopback
  and states, in init's unit tests. Mutation-checked, each caught: what it listens on
  ignored; what it declares ignored; a network of no peers taken for one; what it
  publishes ignored.
- **How 3e is built.** A container that runs is connected and disconnected at once, by
  init (`NETWORK connect ID NETWORK ADDR NAME...` and `disconnect ID NETWORK`, ID its exec's
  in the guest). Connect gives the member an address on the network, the one asked or the
  lowest free, routed on its one link as a member's addresses are: the switch's route to
  it through its gate, the gate's gateway on in0 and its route down to it, the member's
  address and its subnet's route through that gateway; then its reach as its networks now
  say, and every grant built again, its peers' names with them. Disconnect takes them
  back the other way round, and makes its way out of its namespace again through its next
  network where the one let go was its first (the kernel flushes an address's routes with
  it). Its last network stays, refused with why: it would be left a link with no address.
  The daemon records the address init gives, which inspect shows, and keeps the change for
  its next start. Its own hosts file stays as it started; its peers resolve its new names
  through the agents' resolver. A container that runs on `none`, or in another's
  namespace, gains no link as it runs, and is refused with why.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_running_member_is_connected_and_disconnected_at_once`:
  a member of a, connected to b as it runs, has its address there at once in its
  namespace, is resolved by its alias and reached on its declared port by a member of b;
  disconnected, it has none, is resolved and reached by none, and is still reached on a;
  its last network is refused; off its first network, it resolves its peers through its
  next. Mutation-checked, each caught: connected with no address of its own; connected,
  or disconnected, with no grants built again; disconnected keeping its address; its last
  network taken; no way out through its next network.

### D183. `--cgroup-parent`: a microVM's processes under a slice of the user's service manager (slices 1 and 3 built)

Decided by the user on 2026-10-14 ("so long as they apply appropriately to microvms").

- **The microVM need.** A host running many microVMs needs to cap and account groups of
  them with its own resource manager: a project's agents under one memory and CPU
  budget, a CI job's microVMs under its job's slice. A microVM's guest memory, vCPU
  threads and I/O are its VM process's, and its network process's, so `--cgroup-parent`
  (`run`, `create`, the Engine API's `HostConfig.CgroupParent`) names the group those
  processes go in. Inside the microVM, its cgroups stay its own.
- **On Linux, a slice of the user's own systemd manager.** `NAME.slice` (a `-` nesting
  it, `a-b.slice` under `a.slice`, systemd.slice(5)) is a slice of the user's manager,
  asked on the user's bus (`shards-bus`: the D-Bus Specification 0.43's EXTERNAL
  authentication as the user, `StartTransientUnit`, waited for to its `JobRemoved`, which
  systemd sends the client that started the job: src/core/dbus-job.c). Rootless, with
  nothing to configure: the manager is delegated the user's cgroups (on the GPU desktop
  `user@1000.service`, `Delegate=yes`, cpu cpuset io memory pids), and where the daemon
  was started from an ssh login, in a session scope the manager may not move a process
  out of, the manager has the system's manager move it (systemd's src/core/cgroup.c,
  `unit_attach_pids_to_cgroup`), which moves only a process of the uid that asks
  (src/core/dbus-unit.c). M248 placed 300 of 300 so, from a login and from inside the
  manager's tree.
- **Born there, charged there from its first page, never moved.** A process moved
  between cgroups keeps its memory charged where it was (cgroup-v2.rst, "Memory
  Ownership"; M248: a child that touched 64 MiB first left its scope 0 KiB), and each
  move waits out an RCU grace period (kernel/cgroup/cgroup.c, `cgroup_attach_lock`; M248:
  the manager's start of a scope 6.7 ms at p50 and 18.6 at p99 past its reply, a move by
  hand 8.4 and 16.7), past the whole start budget (§4, 5 ms). So no microVM is moved: the
  daemon keeps a spawner (D158's) for each parent, placed once by the user's manager as
  the one process of a scope of its own in that slice, and every process of a microVM
  under that parent, its VM process and its network process, is made by that spawner:
  in the scope from its first instruction (a child is born in its parent's cgroup, which
  takes no grace period), charged there from its first page. The first run under a
  parent pays the one placement (M248: 10 ms at p50 from a login); every one after, none.
- **Warm under its parent too.** A warm pool (D26) is kept per template and parent, its
  microVMs made by that parent's spawner: a warm microVM taken for a run has been its
  parent's from its first page, and none of another parent's is taken.
- **Refused before anything starts, each with why**: on Linux, a value that is no slice
  name (a path names a cgroup the user's manager owns, not the user), no user manager on
  the user's bus, a slice the manager refuses (its own words); on macOS and Windows, a name
  no group shards keeps may have (slice 3).
- **Shown as given**: inspect's `HostConfig.CgroupParent`.
- **Past a container's cgroup parent.** Rootless with nothing to set up, from an ssh login
  as from a desktop session; the microVM's whole host footprint, guest memory, vCPUs and
  its network process, under the parent and charged there from its first page, warm
  starts included; a run under a parent costs nothing past the first; and every refusal
  before anything starts.
- **How slice 1 is built.** The daemon's own spawner (D158) makes a spawner for each
  parent as its first run asks (`shards_ipc::start_group`), holding nothing the daemon
  lets go of, which the user's manager places before it makes anything
  (`shards_bus::place`: a match rule for `JobRemoved`, then `StartTransientUnit` of a scope
  `shards-PID-N.scope` in the slice with it as its one process, gone once its processes
  have, `CollectMode=inactive-or-failed`, its memory counted, `MemoryAccounting=yes`, which
  systemd turns on for its slices too, waited for to its job's end); one parent's
  placement keeps no run under another waiting (`daemon/parents.rs`). Every process of a
  microVM under that parent is made by it (`spawn_in_group`), in its scope from its first
  instruction: the VM process, its network process, its share process, a stopped
  container's visit's, and the join share of a microVM others join, under that microVM's
  own parent. Warm pools are kept per template and parent (`PoolKey`), and a template
  collected ends its pools under every parent. A spawner found ended as a run asks for it
  (its first connection, which it never writes, readable: one `poll(2)` that waits for
  nothing) is ended and another placed: one stopped with its slice is replaced by the next
  run. Each is the daemon's for its life, and goes with it, its scope once its processes
  have. Refused before anything is made, each saying why: any parent off Linux; a value
  that is no slice's name, as systemd's own check has it (src/basic/unit-name.c); a joiner
  (D119) naming a parent other than its provider's; and from a microVM's own engine (D181),
  not built yet (501). Inspect's `HostConfig.CgroupParent` says it, and the Engine API takes
  `HostConfig.CgroupParent` as the command line takes the flag (D170's create bodies, a
  case of it among them).
- **Tested.** On real microVMs on Linux, where CI's x86_64 runner has its user's manager
  (lingering, `SHARDS_REQUIRE_USER_MANAGER`): `a_microvm_is_made_under_the_slice_its_cgroup_parent_names`,
  a run under a slice made in a scope of it whose processes are its VM process, its
  network process and the spawner alone; all the VM process's own memory charged to the
  slice (its `RssAnon` within the slice's `anon`); a second run under it made in the same
  scope; a run without one, its template's pool warm, outside the slice; `inspect` saying
  it; a joiner naming another slice refused, its provider's taken; and the scope gone once
  the daemon has stopped. On macOS, the same test's refusals. Unit tests: slice names as
  systemd's check has them, the check before anything starts, the Engine API's create
  bodies, a microVM engine's refusal, a group's spawner making its children apart (their
  parent its process, watched, signalled and reaped through it; ended, signalled no more)
  and a killed one found ended; shards-bus against a bus of a test's own.
  Mutation-checked on macOS, each caught: a parent served off Linux; a path taken for a
  slice; the Engine API's `CgroupParent` dropped; a microVM engine's container given a
  parent; a group's children made by the process's own spawner; a killed group's spawner
  never found ended.
- **Where no user's manager is.** A `--cgroup-parent` there is refused before anything is
  made, naming the bus it looked for (its `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`'s, or `/run/user/UID`'s): a
  start would fail with it otherwise.
- **Slice 2, designed: a cgroup delegated to the user, where no user's manager is.** The
  kernel lets a process of the user place one in a cgroup only within a sub-hierarchy
  delegated to it, both of them in it (cgroup-v2.rst, "Model of Delegation", "Delegation
  Containment"): a cgroup namespace's root where the hierarchy is mounted `nsdelegate`
  (a container's own, the hosts of OpenRC, runit and s6 having no per-user delegation),
  or a directory an administrator gave the user, its `cgroup.procs`, `cgroup.threads` and
  `cgroup.subtree_control` theirs. There `--cgroup-parent PATH` would name a cgroup of
  that sub-hierarchy, the daemon's own cgroup in it, and the parent's spawner be moved
  into a leaf of its own there once (a move, PM M248's cost, once per parent), its
  children born there as slice 1's are. Built once a host needs it.
- **Slice 3, built on macOS and Windows: groups shards keeps, where its host has none a
  user's tools cap.**
  macOS has no group of processes a user may make and cap (its jetsam bands and
  coalitions are the system's own), and Windows' job objects are made by programs, none
  named by a tool of its user's. There `--cgroup-parent NAME` names a group shards keeps,
  a directory of the home, `groups/NAME`, made with the first run under it: its name a
  file's of letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_` alone (daemon/groups.rs); its budgets
  files in cgroup v2's own formats, as a Linux user writes a cgroup's (cgroup-v2.rst):
  `memory.high` and `memory.max`, bytes with the kernel's binary suffixes or `max`
  (mm/page_counter.c `page_counter_memparse`), and `cpu.max`, a quota and its period in
  microseconds, the period 100000 where left out, each at least 1 ms, the period at most
  1 s (kernel/sched/core.c `cpu_period_quota_parse`, `tg_set_cfs_bandwidth`). Each starts
  `max`. The daemon watches the files and holds the group's microVMs to them as they
  change:
  - **macOS** (built): what the group holds is its microVMs' VM processes' footprints
    (proc_pid_rusage's `ri_phys_footprint`), summed every pressure window while it has
    microVMs, its files read again then, so that a budget written is heard within one.
    Each microVM is told the room under the least of its budgets as D188 tells a slice's
    (init's `ROOM`), and where the group is short each gives back what it holds cold,
    then unplugs. Past `memory.max` with a pass that gave nothing back, the microVM of
    the group that holds the most is stopped, its container marked OOM-killed, as a
    cgroup's OOM killer takes its largest. Tested on real microVMs
    (`a_microvm_under_a_group_is_held_to_its_budget`, M355): 1,254 MiB held under a
    `memory.high` of 998 MiB, given back to 281; past a `memory.max` of 793 MiB, the
    microVM that held 679 MiB of 960 stopped, 137 and OOM-killed, the other running on.
    Mutation-checked: no give-back; no stop.
  - **Windows** (built): every process of a microVM under NAME is made in a job object of
    NAME's, nested above the VM process's own (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST, the
    group's first; Job Objects, "Nested Jobs", Windows 8 on), its warm VMs too: a VM
    process in a job of its own may join a group's job only while that holds nothing (the
    second was refused, M359), so a group's warm VMs are made in its job from their start,
    its pool its own. `memory.max` is the job's memory limit (JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_JOB_MEMORY,
    which refuses its processes' commits past it: 512 MiB alone, and 160 MiB beside
    another's 160, under 256, M359), set again as the file changes; `memory.high` the room
    its microVMs are told, as on macOS, whose give-backs on Windows are the platform parity
    plan's step 7. Tested on real microVMs on CI's windows-2022 and windows-2025
    (`a_groups_job_holds_its_microvms_to_its_memory_max`, budget-e2e run 40624202863):
    under a `memory.max` of 1 GiB, a run that allocates 2 GiB never holds it, where one
    that allocates 2 GiB under no group, and one that allocates 128 MiB under it, run to
    their ends. `cpu.max` is not the job's CPU rate (below).
  - **CPU, on both** (built): a group's microVMs hold themselves to its `cpu.max`
    together, as CFS bandwidth control holds a cgroup's threads
    (Documentation/scheduler/sched-bwc.rst), where macOS has no mechanism to cap a group
    of processes and Windows' job CPU rate holds no second: under a hard cap of one CPU,
    a 30 s spin's mean was 1.04 CPUs, and single seconds ran up to 1.88 (windows-2025)
    and 2.19 (windows-2022) (M361). The group's count is a file of its directory,
    `.cpu-budget`, the daemon's, mapped shared by the daemon, which writes the budget as
    the file says it (within a pressure window of a change), and by each of the group's
    VM processes, handed it with its run (`RunHead::group`, after its swap); a joiner's
    CPU is its microVM's. What it counts is the group's theoretical arrival time, the
    generic cell rate algorithm's (ITU-T I.371): each VM process's second governor
    (`vm::hold`, beside D191's own) reads its vCPU threads' CPU time as D191's does and
    charges it, at the budget's rate, to that one word by compare-and-swap, on the host's
    monotonic clock, one in every process (POSIX CLOCK_MONOTONIC; QueryPerformanceCounter,
    "consistent ... even when measured on different threads or processes", Microsoft
    Learn); while the group runs more than a period ahead of its rate, every microVM of
    it holds its vCPUs out of its guest, by D191's kick, until it is within it. Over any
    stretch the group uses at most its rate and a period's quota more, as a cgroup's
    periodic quota allows, and over a long one its rate: nothing of a period wraps, and no
    process waits on another. A budget of every CPU of the host's, or past what the word
    holds (a host of more than 4,295 CPUs), holds nothing. Tested: `vm::group`'s own
    (charges add up across mappings and threads, idle time no credit past a period),
    `vm::hold`'s `machines_of_a_group_are_held_to_its_budget_together` (two machines of
    two threads each under one CPU: 1.13 to 1.15 s of CPU in 1.14 to 1.15 s, three runs;
    with the hold off, 4.52 s in 1.13) and `a_group_whose_budget_goes_holds_nothing`; the
    groups' `cpu_budgets_read_as_the_kernel_reads_them`; and on real microVMs
    `a_groups_microvms_are_held_to_its_cpu_max_together` (two microVMs of a group of one
    CPU, four threads burning in each: on macOS 3.21 s of CPU in 3.02 s, with `max`
    23.9 s; on jupiter's WHP 3.08 s in 3.08 s, with `max` 23.97 s in 3.04; mutation-checked,
    the VM ignoring its group's budget, 23.85 s in 3.02 s, which fails it). Each second's
    hold, M370: under one CPU, p99 1.07 CPUs a second on macOS and 1.12 on Windows.
  - Shown as given (inspect's `HostConfig.CgroupParent`); the group's `memory.current`
    file the daemon writes as it sums it, as a cgroup's says what it holds.
- **Slices.** 1: Linux, a slice of the user's manager (built). 2: a delegated cgroup
  where no user's manager is (designed, above). 3: macOS and Windows, groups shards keeps
  (built, above). 4: the microVM's own engine's members (D181), a cgroup within the
  microVM, refused (501) until a need for it inside a microVM is shown.

### D184. A credential helper is asked at once and waited for only where its registry asks (built)

**Found.** `shards pull alpine:3.22` with a user's own Docker config (2026-10-17) waited
12 minutes and more on `docker-credential-desktop get`, Docker Desktop's backend not
answering: sampled, the daemon's thread read the helper's output (credentials.rs
`run_helper`). The client's Ctrl-C ended the client alone: the lookup took no cancel, so
the daemon's thread and the helper stayed. The lookup ran before the registry was asked
anything, so the pull waited on the helper whether or not the registry wanted
credentials, and said nothing of it. A docker client asks its helper before it sends a
pull too: the Engine API takes a pull's credentials in its request (`X-Registry-Auth`).

**The microVM need.** A pull is how a microVM gets its root, and a run that pulls is a
start: what an external holds of it must be only what it has to hold, isolated, said,
and ended with the pull.

**Decided.**
- A helper is started as the pull's registry is made (`credentials::find`): its key
  written and its input closed at once (a registry's key is far under a pipe's buffer, so
  the write never waits), and never waited for there. It runs while the registry's first
  round trip does: a pull that needs its answer waits for the longer of the two, not for
  both in turn.
- Its answer is read the first time the registry's own host challenges (`auth.rs`
  `Authorizer::credentials`, Basic or Bearer), never for another host's challenge, and
  never where the registry asks nothing: a registry that takes anonymous pulls is not
  held by a helper that never answers. It is read before the authorizer's lock of its
  hosts, so that no request to another host waits behind it; requests challenged
  meanwhile wait for the same answer (one read).
- Where the pull waits on it, it says so, once, as the wait begins: on a terminal a line
  of the pull's own, piped a line on stderr (`Waiting for docker-credential-desktop to
  answer for https://index.docker.io/v1/ (credsStore in ~/.docker/config.json)`), the
  helper, the key it was asked and where it was named, so that the user can answer it,
  mend it, or end the pull.
- No anonymous fallback and no deadline: a late answer is not a stuck one. osxkeychain
  asks the user to allow it, pass's gpg-agent asks for a passphrase, secretservice for a
  keyring's unlock, ecr-login goes to AWS. An anonymous pull in its place would race a
  user typing a password, and spend Docker Hub's anonymous allowance where the user is
  logged in: Docker Hub counts an unauthenticated pull against its IPv4 address or IPv6
  /64, 100 in 6 hours, and an authenticated one against the account, 200 for a personal
  one and no limit for a paid one (docs.docker.com/docker-hub/usage/pulls, read
  2026-10-18). The
  credentials the user configured are the ones used, whenever the registry asks.
- A cancel of the pull (its client gone or interrupted, the daemon stopping) ends the
  helper at once: started for a pull, it leads a process group of its own (a script's
  children with it, which hold its output open), which the cancel kills (`http::Cancel`,
  `watch_helper`); the read of its answer then ends, and the pull ends cancelled. A helper
  whose answer is never read is ended and reaped as its pull ends. None is left, process
  or thread.
- A registry token in the file wins over a helper's answer (dockerd's precedence), so
  with one the helper is not asked at all. A helper that cannot be started (not on
  `PATH`) fails only the pulls that need its answer.
- A build's base pulls, resolutions and cache imports say the wait among the build's
  plain lines, on stderr as they come (build/mod.rs `saying_waits`); the live display keeps
  its own frame, the step shown waiting.
- The eager callers (`shards login`'s check, a context's client sending credentials,
  `shards search`) read the answer at once, as before (`lookup` = `find` and `answer`),
  their helper in their terminal's process group, where a Ctrl-C reaches it.

**Tested.** `crates/registry`: a helper asked is ended and reaped as it drops unread; a
cancel ends a wait for one, its script's own child too; one that answers is read as its
registry challenges, a password and an identity token; another host's challenge waits on
none; a registry token asks none. `tests/login.rs`
`a_credential_helper_that_never_answers_holds_only_what_needs_its_answer`: with a helper
that never answers configured, a pull from a registry that asks for nothing completes
and leaves no helper; from one that asks for Basic credentials, the client says what it
waits on, and killing the client ends the helper. Mutation-checked, each caught: the
answer read as the helper is found; a helper dropped unread left running; a cancel that
ends no helper; one that ends the helper alone and not its group (its script's child
holds its output open); the answer waited for under the hosts' lock; a wait never said.

### D185. The client and its daemon meet through files in the home (built)

**Why.** shards is filesystem based (the user, repeatedly; 2026-10-18: `daemon.sock` was an
error). Its own interfaces are files in the home; a socket stays only where an outside
client's protocol demands one: the Engine API's `engine.sock` (D170), a context's
`e/ID.sock` (D180). The CLI's channel to its daemon, `daemon.sock`, is shards' own, and
goes.

**What crosses today.** A request (a run, an exec, an attach, a command of the catalog's:
`ps`, `inspect`, `rm`...), the client's stdin, stdout and stderr as descriptors
(`SCM_RIGHTS`), the streams of `save`, `export`, `import`, `load` and `cp`, answers (`OUT`,
`ERR`, `END`, progress), and, for a run, the client's connection itself, which the daemon
hands to the run's VM, which then sends `EXIT` and reads `RESIZE` and `SIGNAL`; a microVM
given a host's devices sends its process's pidfd with `EXIT` (D154). Files carry no
descriptors.

**Measured.**
- How each end of a FIFO learns the other has gone (PM M253): a blocking read(2) sees its
  writer's end at once on macOS and Linux, in every one of 5,000 trials each; on macOS
  poll(2) and kqueue(2) never do, and a writer learns of its reader's end only as it next
  writes (`EPIPE`). But on macOS a read that has just taken its writer's last data can
  sleep through the end that follows at once: 6 in 224,000, where select(2) saw all of
  192,000. So each side holds the read end of a FIFO the other writes, and waits on it in
  select(2) on macOS, in a read on Linux, never in poll or kqueue: but for the many clients
  of one list (M262, below).
- What a request costs (PM M254), against the socket's 23 to 30 µs at p50: a directory
  made for each request, 413 to 562 µs on macOS (APFS's metadata operations, with tails to
  21 ms under load) and 55 µs on Linux; a slot the daemon made ahead, which the client takes
  and opens, 83 to 112 µs on macOS (each open by path 10 to 28 µs) and 34 µs on Linux. A
  FIFO's round trip itself costs no more than the socket's. macOS refuses flock(2) on a
  FIFO.

**Decided.**
- **Slots, made ahead.** The daemon keeps requests' slots in `$SHARDS_HOME/requests/`,
  0700: each FIFOs named by its number, `N.say` and `N.answer`, and for a command with
  streams `N.in`, `N.out` and `N.err` too, made before any client asks, the daemon holding
  its own ends of each: `say`'s reader and a writer of its own until a client has written,
  `answer`'s writer. A slot is used once, then removed, and its number never again: no
  client can meet another's leavings in a FIFO.
- **Handed out by a FIFO.** The daemon writes each free slot's number to `requests/free`,
  or to `requests/free-streams` for a slot with streams, a record of fixed length, far
  under `PIPE_BUF`, so written whole; a client takes a slot by reading one record, which
  no other client can then read. No lock file, and no search: the client opens the list it
  needs, reads, opens its slot's `answer` to read and `say` to write, and writes its
  request. Where every slot is taken, the client's read waits until the daemon has made
  more. A slot a client took and never wrote to is removed
  after a minute, its wait ended through a pipe of its own, never a byte on its `say`,
  where a client may be writing; a client that finds its slot gone reads another.
- **Liveness, each way.** The daemon reads `say` (waiting in select(2) on macOS, then
  reading); once a client has
  written, the daemon drops its own writer, so the client's end, its exit or its kill, ends
  the read. The client reads `answer`; the daemon's end, or that of the VM it handed it to,
  ends the client's read. No timer, no process ID.
- **No daemon.** `free` with no writer reads its end at once: the client starts the daemon,
  as it does today where nothing listens, and waits for its first slot. One daemon a home:
  it takes `daemon.lock` with flock(2), exclusively, as it starts.
- **Streams.** A run's, an exec's and an attach's stdio, and `save`'s, `export`'s,
  `import`'s, `load`'s and `cp`'s streams go through the slot's `in`, `out` and `err`: the
  daemon gives the VM its ends, as it gave the client's descriptors, and the client copies
  between them and its own stdio. A microVM with a host's devices sends its process's ID
  with `EXIT`, and the client waits for that process's end itself (pidfd_open(2), as the
  same user).
- **Messages** are today's frames without descriptors, each FIFO of one writer at a time:
  the daemon's, until it hands `answer` to a run's VM.

**Built.**
- `shards_ipc::slots`: the slots, made, handed out, taken, read and written, each end seen.
  A slot is taken at its client's first byte, which says which streams it opened; the rest
  of its request says what each descriptor it stands for is (`slots::fds`), then the
  request itself.
- The daemon serves its clients through slots alone (`daemon/slots.rs`), each session
  bridged to its handling of a client: a connection of its own, taken as a socket's client
  was, the request's descriptors the slot's streams. The client's messages go on to the daemon, or
  to the run's VM it hands the connection to, and theirs come back, each side's end the
  other's. A device run's EXIT waits for its VM process's pidfd. So what serves a socket's
  client serves a slot's unchanged, the VM included.
- Two slots of each kind are kept offered, without streams and with (M255: making and
  removing a slot is 125 µs of the daemon's CPU on a loaded Mac, 317 with its streams, so
  none is made ahead that no client asked for; a hundred clients at once, each adding one,
  left the daemon making a hundred spares in a quiet 3 s). A client counts among those in
  hand from its first byte: past the daemon's most (`max_clients`), its slot is replaced
  at once but its request waits its turn, and no slot is offered, so that further clients
  wait on their list and cost the daemon nothing. A closing daemon unlinks its lists at
  once, so that a client looking for a slot asks the next daemon, and answers RESTART to a
  client that took a slot meanwhile; a client asks again as often as that can happen.
- The client asks through a slot for every command: the catalog's, its streams (`save`,
  `export`, `import`, `load`, `cp`) copied by the client to and from the slot's (`cli::Stream`:
  what the daemon writes, what it reads); a run's, an exec's and an attach's, its stdin
  filled into `in`, and `out` and `err` shown as they come, unbuffered, all of them before
  it ends; a detached run's none. Its signals and resizes go on its slot's `say` beside its
  request (`slots::Sender`, each message written whole). A daemon of an older build, which
  offers no slots, is still reached on its socket, so that it steps aside for this one's.
- On macOS every read of a FIFO waits first in select(2) (M253 part 3): the slots', the
  client's copies, and `shards_ipc::read` of a FIFO, a run's stdin in its VM among them;
  all but a client's wait on its list for a slot (M262, below).

- **No `daemon.sock`** (slice 4). The daemon makes its lists as soon as it holds the
  home's lock, so that a client that finds them waits on them for its slot rather than
  start a second daemon; an older build's socket left there goes. A home is served while
  its list `free` has a reader, the daemon's own (`slots::served`): a starting daemon
  waiting for the lock (`take_lock`) and a context's look at its machine ask that, or
  whether an older build's socket answers. `daemon stop` asks through a slot and waits for
  the slot's end, which comes as the daemon exits, at most 60 s (`Client::recv_within`); the
  requests a daemon puts to itself for a context's steps go through slots of its own home
  (`cli::ask_here`), which start no daemon. The default context's endpoint is the Engine
  API's socket, which Docker's clients take.
- **Lists made again.** Lists someone removes as the daemon serves are made again, the
  slots' numbers going on from the last, and what was offered on the old ones let go of:
  the waits of those no client took, read back from their lists, end through their own
  pipes. The maker looks as it is told to, never on a timer: by the listener, as a name of
  the home comes or goes (a removal of the home takes `requests/`), and, for lists removed
  by hand inside it, by the daemon the next client starts, which, finding the home's lock
  held and nothing offered, makes and removes a name in the home (`daemon.waiting`) once.
  Under `socket_at`, which `close` holds as it unoffers them, so that a daemon told to stop
  never offers again (PM M188, of the socket it replaces).
- **An idle daemon wakes for nothing.** The maker offers what its lists hold no client's
  of (their records counted where they wait, FIONREAD), so that a client dead after it
  took a slot holds no place; and sweeps only while a slot is taken with no request
  read: a minute after it is first seen so, and again a minute after, when a slot still
  unwritten goes. With none, it sleeps until it hears something (PM M260).
- **A request in time.** The rest of a request is read within 10 s of its first byte
  (`REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, a socket's first message's), and no longer once the daemon ends its
  clients (`requests_end`, a pipe written once): such a client hears RESTART, as one whose
  request no thread had read did, and asks the next daemon.
- **Out of descriptors**, the maker offers nothing, says so once, and looks again every
  250 ms (`RETRY`); no collection starts meanwhile, and clients wait on their lists. A slot
  is about 7 descriptors, 13 with streams, its FIFOs' ends and its stop pipe: four offered
  hold 40. At its most clients in hand it says so too, once a minute at most.
- **A request of any size.** The bridge starts the daemon's handling of its connection
  before it writes the request there: written first, a request past the socket pair's
  buffer (a run's labels; 8 KiB on macOS, 208 KiB on Linux) waited for ever for a reader
  that came only after (x86_64 CI's journald test, a request of 540 KB). Found on Linux CI,
  with the cap test's race: its silent clients now wait to be counted, which the daemon's
  log says, before the next asks.
- **Stdin after a restart.** A run's, an exec's and an attach's client fills its command's
  stdin only once its daemon has said the request is its own (`HEARD`, after the build's
  check): what went to the slot of a daemon that then asked for a restart went with it, and
  a piped stdin was lost, the next daemon's command waiting for ever. A client of an older
  build ignores the message.
- **What it said last** (PM M261). A daemon exits only once no slot holds it
  (`Daemon::live`, `slots_hold`): each slot is counted from its offer until its client has
  all the daemon will say to it, there in its FIFO whether or not the daemon is (pipe(7)),
  or until its serving ends. So what a closing daemon said last reaches each client still
  reading: a stepping-aside daemon's RESTART, and the RESTART a slot taken as the lists
  went is answered with by its own thread. Before, it exited once no client was in hand,
  and its exit cut off what its slots had yet to pass on: the client heard its slot end
  unanswered, "the command's microVM stopped before the command ended" (three tests on
  x86_64 CI, run 39191414199; 23 of 40 runs of them at 79caf2d7 on a loaded Fedora host,
  1 of 40 counting only the slots that pass a daemon's messages on). While it serves, a
  slot its client opened holds it; once it has closed, every slot does, but a client that
  takes nothing, stopped, or held by a pager that waits, holds it no longer than a
  request's time (`REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, 10 s) from the start of the piece of its answer it
  leaves untaken, or, its request not yet gone on, from its last step or the close, the
  later: the daemon says so, and exits, and the next daemon starts. A slot whose request
  went on, with nothing of its answer yet to take, holds it until the daemon has answered,
  its answer's last word (`EXIT`, `END`, `RESTART`) passed on, and a request's time at most
  after: an attached run its stop ended after a 35 s timeout said nothing meanwhile, and
  timed from the close, its slot let go of the daemon, which exited as the run's VM said
  DONE, before its slot passed on the EXIT the VM wrote next. The run's client said its
  microVM stopped before its command ended (125 where its SIGKILL's 137 was due), once in
  608 runs of the daemon suite on CI (PM M331). Held by
  `a_closed_daemon_waits_for_what_a_slot_it_passed_on_has_yet_to_hear`, mutation-checked. A FIFO takes 8 KiB on macOS and 64 KiB on Linux
  (M261), so an answer past that is what such a client leaves untaken. A slot writes an
  answer 64 KiB at a time, what a Linux FIFO holds, each piece a step on as its client
  takes it: a client taking a long answer slowly goes on (timed from the whole answer's
  write, one reading 16 KiB at a time, 60 ms apart, was let go of a request's time in, 3 s
  in the test, still reading). A stop's slot is not counted: the daemon holds that session
  until its exit, which is how `daemon stop` learns of it.
- **Many clients on one list** (PM M262). On macOS a client waiting in select(2) for its
  slot could stop waking at all while the others took theirs: 12 of 16 clients slept
  through 20 s of records others took, and one of an E2E test's 16 waited 60 s while its
  daemon served the rest. A waiting read(2), poll(2) and kqueue(2) saw every record, but
  only select(2) and a read see a FIFO's writer go there (M253). So a client waits on its
  list in kqueue(2), for its records, its name's removal (a closing daemon unoffers it; a
  new one makes its own), and its daemon's exit (the process `daemon.pid` names; a killed
  daemon leaves its list's name), and reads after each, not waiting; where `daemon.pid`
  names no live process, it looks again every 250 ms. On Linux a read waits, which sees
  both. Held by `clients_waiting_on_one_list_wake_for_its_records`, which failed in each
  of 6 runs with select(2) put back, 8 to 12 of its 16 clients asleep.
- **Measured** against slice 3 (build-ab, PM M259): what slots alone change costs a run
  nothing, within ±31 µs of none at every quiet round's p50 of 2.3 to 2.6 ms, and within
  the noise loaded; a request's own cost through a slot is M254's and M255's. Slice 4's
  first cut woke an idle daemon once a second, its maker looking at its lists on a timer
  (30 context switches in 30 s, where the daemon before had none, M259), which the looks
  above replaced.

### D186. How much of the disk shards keeps is its user's to set (`shards configure disk`, built)

**Found.** The audit of defaults taken from Docker (docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md):
the build cache's collection kept dockerd's default policy, 10% of the disk reserved, 80%
the most, 20% kept free (D114), and nothing changed it; a run's log kept Docker's `local`
driver's 5 segments of 20 MiB (D27), which only the daemon's environment changed, read once
as the daemon started.

**The user's calls (2026-10-18).** The build cache: dockerd's 10% to 80% kept, "but this
NEEDS to be user configurable". A log: 1 GiB, "but again, I expect this to be user
configurable".

**Decided.**
- `shards configure disk`, beside `configure guest` in shards' grammar (`disk configure`
  as the command it runs): `--build-cache-reserve`, `--build-cache-max` and
  `--build-cache-free`, each `N%` of the disk the image store is on (0 to 100) or a size
  (`50g`, `512m`: binary units, as `--memory` reads them); `--log-history SIZE`;
  `--events-history SIZE`, the home's events' journal's (D187); `--reset`.
  Alone, each setting and whether it is its default. Every flag is checked before any is
  kept, so a command that fails changes nothing; a reset sets aside what was there,
  whether it reads or not.
- **Files, as shards' own interfaces are.** The settings are the home's `disk`, a line a
  setting (`NAME VALUE`), written whole as a new file renamed over the last, so a reader
  finds the one or the other. They are read where they are used: as each run starts, by
  the daemon, and by each build's collection. A read where nothing is set costs what a
  stat does, and one with settings 7 to 12 µs at p50 on a loaded host (PM M252), so there
  is no cache, which a change could find stale; a change takes at the next run or build,
  whether the daemon runs or not.
- **A log's history** is the most of the disk a run's log takes, records' framing
  included (13 bytes a record), as written: equal segments of at most 20 MiB, two at
  least, so that it holds at most its history and, once its oldest segment has gone, its
  history less a segment at least (half of it below 40 MiB; for the default 1 GiB, 52
  segments of 20,648,881 bytes, 51/52 of it). Whole 20 MiB segments enough to hold it
  would hold up to 1,040 MiB where 1 GiB was asked, and a history in one segment would
  keep nothing just after each rotation. A run's own `--log-opt max-size` and
  `max-file` still bound its log (D161), and the daemon's environment
  (`SHARDS_LOG_MAX_SIZE`, `SHARDS_LOG_MAX_FILE`), where it is set, wins over the file.
- **The build cache's bounds.** A share is that much of the disk's bytes, exactly, 0% none,
  and a size is taken as it is; a reserve is at most the most. The defaults are the shares
  the user chose, and are now what they say: dockerd counts a share's whole GiB and one
  more in decimal gigabytes, which keeps 9.3%, 74.5% and 18.6% of a 2 TiB disk where it
  says 10%, 80% and 20%; shards took that from it (D114), and reserved 188.1 GiB of a
  2,014 GiB disk where its 10% is 201.4 GiB. Where the disk's
  size cannot be read, the sizes set apply, and a share is nothing to reckon, so the
  default holds: 2 GB reserved, no most. A changed cache setting is the next build's
  collection's, however recent the last: `configure disk` removes the throttle's stamp.
- **A file that does not read**, edited by hand: a run is refused, saying the file and its
  line; a build's collection collects nothing and says so at every build (`WARNING: the
  build cache was not collected: ...`), the build itself done; `--reset` mends it.
- With a context (D180), `configure disk` runs on the context's machine, whose disk it is.

**Tested.** On real microVMs: tests/containers.rs `a_logs_history_is_what_its_user_set`:
the default said; at 64k, a run's log is two segments on disk, 32 KiB (less a record's
head) to 64 KiB, the output's newest bytes; set to 128k as the daemon runs, the next run's is
128k's; a flag that does not read, before a reset, keeps nothing; a broken file refuses a
run, saying its file and line, and `--reset` mends it. tests/build.rs
`a_builds_cache_is_kept_as_its_user_set`: a broken file is said and collects nothing;
after `--reset --build-cache-max 1`, the next build's collection leaves no record, and the
step runs again. Unit tests: the settings read back as written; a history's segments; the
policy's bounds, set and unset. Mutation-checked, each caught: the daemon's logs ignoring
the settings; a short history in one segment; a reset reading what it resets; flags before
a reset unchecked; a run admitted past settings that do not read; a reserve past the most;
settings that do not read collected by the default policy; a set policy waiting out the
last collection; a failed collection unsaid; the collection ignoring the settings.

### D187. The home's events, kept for `--since` past their daemon (built)

**Found.** The audit of what was taken from Docker (docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md):
a home's events for `events --since` were the last 256, dockerd's `eventsLimit` (moby
daemon/events/events.go), in the daemon's memory and gone with it. A shards daemon exits
once idle (`SHARDS_DAEMON_IDLE`, 900 s), and `--since` then said nothing of what had
happened before, where Docker's daemon, which runs on, says its last 256.

**Decided.**
- **A journal in the home**, `events/`: segments of an event a line, each as `--format
  json` prints it (Docker's events.Message, the API's from 1.52), named by number. The
  daemon appends each event as it logs it, under the lock it tells its listeners under, so
  that a listener has each event once: read from the journal up to where it was written
  as the listener came, then heard. A segment that ends in a line cut short, by a crash
  mid-write, is let be and the next begun past it; a line that does not read is passed by.
- **Its history is a log's** (D186): `configure disk --events-history SIZE`, at most that
  many bytes of the newest events, in equal segments of at most 20 MiB, two at least, the
  oldest removed as the newest begins; by default a log's 1 GiB, the user's call for a log
  (2026-10-18), the home's events being the home's log. The setting is read as each
  segment begins, so a change takes at the next.
- **`--since` reads from the newest segment that begins no later than it**, each segment
  read whole, one at a time, its events filtered as before.
- An event costs a write(2) of its line to a file opened for appending, unsynced: a host
  that crashes may lose its last, as its page cache does a log's.

**Tested.** Unit (daemon/events.rs): events kept for the next daemon, read back whole; the
history kept and the oldest gone (two segments, at most the history's bytes); a line cut
short passed by; a listener reads what came before and hears what comes after, none
twice. Mutation-checked, each caught: no trimming; a line cut short written on. E2E
(tests/containers.rs): `events_outlive_their_daemon`, a run's life read back by the next
daemon after `daemon stop` (failed with the journal taken out); `events_tell_a_microvms_life`.

### D188. A host short of memory gets back what its microVMs hold cold of their files (built)

**Found.** The user's plan, item 4: memory that tracks the working set, reclaimed at the
host's pressure, not on a timer. A run's guest keeps what its workload reads in its page
cache, guest memory the host cannot drop, only swap: a 1 GiB file read from a volume left
944 MiB of page cache in the guest and 1,003 MiB more of the VM process's memory on the
host (PM M267), where a container's page cache is its host's to drop. Free page reporting
(D151) gives back what a guest frees, and nothing asked a guest to free.

**Decided.**
- **The daemon watches the host's memory pressure** (`platform::MemoryPressure`). On
  Linux, PSI triggers (Documentation/accounting/psi.rst): some task stalled on memory 140
  ms in 2 s, Android's lmkd's lowest level (70 ms in 1 s, lmkd.cpp `psi_thresholds`) over
  the shortest window an unprivileged process may watch (Linux 6.4, d82caa273565); on
  the host's memory, on the daemon's own cgroup, where its microVMs are made, and on each
  scope it makes microVMs in under a user's slice (D183), which may hold them to a budget:
  a cgroup's stall counts in the host's figure against every CPU busy elsewhere, so a
  budget is reached before the host says so. A kernel that arms none of its user's has
  the host's ten-second average read every ten seconds. On macOS, libdispatch's memory
  pressure source, said again every 2 s while the pressure stays raised, as a trigger is
  while its stall goes on. The daemon has no other platform yet.
- **Each time, every running microVM gives back what it holds cold of its files.** Its
  init (builtin `RECLAIM`) reclaims as much of its run's file pages as its memory.stat
  counts inactive, of its file pages alone (`memory.reclaim` with `swappiness=0`, Linux
  6.11, 68cd9050d871; a kernel without the key takes the amount alone), then reports what
  that freed at once (`page_reporting.flush`, D151's patch 0005), so that the host has it
  back before init answers. Each microVM through one of its runs, its own or else a
  joiner's (D119), each on a thread of its own, and one still giving back since a pass
  before asked nothing more until it has answered or been ended: passes that asked one
  microVM after another, each waiting up to 10 s for an answer and then for its end,
  waited on a guest whose own memory its host had taken for minutes, and gave back 3 times
  in 600 s (PM M308). One with no answer within 10 s is said to have had none, and is
  ended.
- **Held within what its budget leaves it** (PM M309). Where the cgroup a microVM's VM
  process is in, or one above it, holds it to a budget (`memory.high` or `memory.max`, a
  slice's `MemoryHigh` or `MemoryMax`, D183), the host can take back only page cache from
  it with no swap, and a guest's page cache is guest RAM, the host's anonymous memory: a
  guest that read past its budget filled it, and the host took back the one thing it
  could, the guest's own RAM as a template's file pages, which the guest read back as it
  ran, 400 to 600 s for a gigabyte its run read in 3 to 5 s with no budget, on CI's AMD
  and Intel runners alike. So each microVM's guest is told the room its budget leaves it,
  the least any cgroup over it may still take before its host must take back memory its
  processes map or hold: its budget less their anonymous, shared and kernel memory
  (memory.stat's `anon`, `shmem`, `kernel`, `sock`, `zswap`) and the file pages they map,
  wherever those are charged (each process's `Pss_File`, a page shared among them counted
  once), a restored guest's own RAM among them, which comes back charged to the budget as
  the guest reads it again once evicted; no less than its `memory.current` less its page
  cache no process maps, and of what is charged to it no more than its `memory.current`,
  which its kernel counts at once where its statistics may be behind it (just after a
  microVM ended they still counted it, a budget short by 577 MiB told the next); less the
  inactive page cache its kernel keeps beside the file pages the budget's processes map
  before it takes those (mm/vmscan.c, `inactive_is_low`: as many as the mapped under a GiB
  of them). A room of all its page cache no process mapped let one guest fill the budget
  to its last file page and read its own RAM back for 2,100 s, until its job was ended;
  statistics read just after the kernel reclaimed a gigabyte, still counting it, once gave
  a room of all the budget (PM M309). It is told as its run begins, each time a budget
  over it is set or changed (inotify on each cgroup's `memory.high` and `memory.max`) or
  met (its `memory.events`), and as another microVM the budget held ends. Init holds its
  run within it (builtin `ROOM`): the run's `memory.high` never past what it uses and that
  room, and its grower lifting no hold past it, nor plugging more than lets the run reach
  it beside its kernel's memory (with the page structures of what it plugs, a 64th of it:
  a grower that doubled its asks past the cap plugged 16 GiB, whose page structures took
  the budget), so that the guest's own kernel drops its run's page cache before its host
  must take anything, as a container's kernel drops its page cache within its cgroup.
  Where the room is short, the budget's warm microVMs end first, which are speculation;
  then the microVM gives back what it holds cold (`RECLAIM`; idle, it raises no pressure
  that would ask) and is told the room the budget has after, until the budget has room
  again (its `memory.events`, a give-back's end, another microVM's), when it is told so,
  and told again each window of the host's pressure while it is held short, as a guest
  held short asks for nothing its host hears. Its cap is the budget's alone: a give-back
  that held a run below it, at what the run used, once room had come back starved it, a 1
  GiB read crawling at 0.13 MiB/s for 100 minutes (PM M309). And never closer than the
  least room a run goes on in to what the run uses, however short the budget: what its
  kernel charges it ahead of the pages it takes, a batch of 64 pages for each CPU
  (mm/memcontrol.c, `refill_stock`), which no reclaim takes back; two windows of a read's
  read-ahead, 128 KiB each (`VM_READAHEAD_PAGES`); a reader's block as large as a
  share's request (`SHARE_MAX_PAGES`, 1 MiB), which with no swap no reclaim takes either;
  and the page cache that request fills on its way to the block, as many pages: 3.25 MiB
  on 4 CPUs, 6.75 on 18. Held within all but that page cache for the whole of a
  gigabyte's read through FUSE, alone in its slice under a budget a mebibyte short of what
  it held, a run on CI's runners read in 0.80 to 0.88 times its time with none at p50 on
  each of five runner CPUs, its slice refaulting none at p50 (PM M318), but its guest
  took its reads' own pages back and read them again, 2,899 times a read at the median on
  the EPYC 7763s and 16,327 at p90, its reader at times asleep at its run's
  `memory.high`, and 3 of 144 reads took over twice their CPU's time with none, 2.77
  times at most (an EPYC 9V74's); with it, 1 and 687 times, and of 288 reads on four
  runner CPUs none over 1.25 times its time with none (PM M321). Before the share kept its
  buffers, held within 2, 4, 8 or 16 times it, no faster than within it, 2.2 to 3.1 times
  its time with none (a Xeon's three reads at 8 times, 1.07), the share's fresh memory for
  each request holding it back (PM M314). Held at what it used, a run could not take a
  page past it: its reader slept in the kernel's throttle of a cgroup past its
  `memory.high` (`__mem_cgroup_handle_over_high`, up to 2 s each return to user space),
  and on CI read a gigabyte at 0.16 to 0.57 MiB/s for 190 to 672 s, each until its
  budget's own pressure brought room back (PM M309). A room short of the least raises no
  hold past what the run was held at, so that being told it again each window lets its run
  grow none, and lowers one its run no longer fills. Init answers what it holds the run
  within, which the daemon's log says where it is past the room the budget leaves. The cap
  is kept in whole pages, as the kernel keeps `memory.high` (`page_counter_memparse`): one
  past a page boundary read back short of itself, and the grower took a run held at it for
  one held short of it, writing its hold again at each of its run's events. A warm microVM
  restored under a budget copies its template's written pages ahead of its run as any
  does (64 MiB at most each, `hv::PREFETCH_PRIVATE`, which every warm microVM spends of
  the budget before any run comes: 65 MiB of a 384 MiB budget's anonymous memory for one
  such VM, 1 to 4 MiB for one without, PM M309). Restored with none, as from M309 to M333,
  each read of a budgeted slice's after its first, which met a warm VM restored before the
  budget, took 1.42 to 1.48 times its time with none at p50 against the first's 1.26 to
  1.28, each written page it touched copied as its run went; with them, 1.20 to 1.22, as
  the first (the test alone on CI's runners, 319 and 320 runs an arm; PM M333). On the Mac
  they bought no time (PM M62), where no budget holds a run. What they hold is a warm VM's,
  which the budget's room takes back first. None is made ahead of the runs that wait where
  its budget has no room.
- **What its host takes back of its guest's RAM is no room** (PM M318). A restored guest's
  RAM is its template's file pages as much as its anonymous memory, and a budget's host
  takes back file pages first. Counted as room as they went, with the inactive pages kept
  beside them, a lone microVM's 71 MiB of them told its guest 111 MiB of room where its
  budget was 23 MiB short; its page cache filled it in 3 s, its host then took back all of
  its RAM it could, and its vCPUs were throttled 68 s as its guest read it back, each
  give-back of a pressure pass telling it its room again. Each microVM's file pages are
  held at the most its VM process has held resident since its run began (its `RssFile`,
  which another VM sharing its template's pages leaves as it is), less those of them it
  let go as it gave back, read first as its run begins, before a budget set later takes
  any back: its host's taking them back makes no room, its own giving back does. Read
  first at a budget's word instead, a budget set a mebibyte short took a lone microVM's
  template's pages back as it was written, and 87 MiB of room was told where none was.
  Held a mebibyte short, alone in its slice, a gigabyte's read through FUSE took 0.80 to
  0.88 times its time with none at p50 on each of 5 runner CPUs (EPYC 7763, 9V45 and 9V74,
  Xeon 8573C and 8370C), 2.07 times at most, its slice refaulting none at p50; none of its
  336 ran away, where 7 of 126 did with the share's copy kept within its reads' room alone
  and 31 of 144 on the tree.
- **The share's copy of what its guest reads, kept only within its budgets' room** (PM
  M318). What a share reads for its guest its guest keeps in its own page cache, so the
  copy its host's page cache keeps beside it is a second one, under a budget charged to
  the run: as the tree's copy filled a lone microVM's slice, its host took back the
  guest's RAM, the slice's mapped files falling from 67 MiB to 15 while it held 213 MiB of
  the copy. The share process drops its copy of each range it reads (`posix_fadvise`
  `POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED`, which lets go of the range's clean pages no process maps, another
  program's of the same file among them) once keeping it would leave the budgets over its
  cgroups, each `memory.high` and `memory.max` short of `max` from its own up, less room
  past it than its own reads need: what its host's kernel charges ahead on each CPU, the
  read in flight and two read-ahead windows, as init's least room has them
  (`fs::headroom`, 2.25 MiB on 4 CPUs, looked at again a hundred looks' time after the
  last). Within that room it keeps its copy, for the run's next reader. Held so short, a
  lone microVM's reads took 0.81 times their time with none at p50 with the copy dropped,
  1.9 with the tree's, and 1.01 with it kept until its budgets had no room left, its slice
  then within half a mebibyte of its budget; under a budget with room, a run's later reads
  of a written gigabyte took 1.74 to 2.45 s at p50 as with the tree's, where dropped under
  every budget they took 2.91 to 3.94, read from its host's disk again.
- **The share's own memory held still** (PM M314). A share's process, and its VM process's
  queue workers, read each request into and build each reply in buffers each keeps from
  one request to the next (`Server::handle_into`, fs/mod.rs `Buffers`), a frame's size at
  most. A MiB read through the share had made 5 MiB of fresh memory, freed as its reply
  went, in processes whose memory a run's budget holds, their threads waiting in mmap and
  munmap: held short of its budget throughout, a gigabyte's read took 2.2 to 3.1 times its
  unbudgeted time at every least room from 1 to 16 times this one (a Xeon's three reads at
  8 times, 1.07), and with the buffers kept 1.19 to 1.31 times on the EPYCs and 1.86 on a
  Xeon 8573C, its unbudgeted reads 0.50 to 0.62 times as long.
- **File pages alone.** A clean page of the page cache the guest drops is one the host
  could only have swapped out, written and read back; dropping it reads none of its data.
  Anonymous memory and the tmpfs layer, the host's own reclaim takes as well as the guest
  would, and taking them would read memory the host may have compressed, which Apple's
  header warns against under pressure (dispatch/source.h, `DISPATCH_MEMORYPRESSURE_WARN`).
- **Then what it holds plugged past what it uses goes back too** (D148's unplug): init
  asks its device for twice what the run uses, past what the microVM booted with, in whole
  memory blocks, as the grower asks for twice what the run reaches, and holds the run at
  what it will have first, so that the grower hears it grow again however much the driver
  unplugs; the grower asks for no less than the device is asked for now. The driver
  unplugs what it can: a block the kernel holds part of stays (plugged memory comes online
  as the kernel's own, D133). Reporting gives back a block's free pages either way;
  unplugging gives back its page structures too, a 64th of it, which a session that once
  grew holds for as long as it lives otherwise.
- **Never from a run as it grows** (M275): a pass keeps no less than the run used at its
  peak since the pass before (its `memory.peak`, counted afresh through a descriptor PID 1
  holds, Linux 6.12), and gives back nothing while memory the grower asked for is still to
  come (the device's request a block or more past what is plugged). Passes seconds apart
  under a host's pressure had each cut back to twice the run's use at that moment the
  request the grower had just raised, the one register both write; a hold slows an
  allocation past it but cannot refuse one with no swap, and a run that grew faster than
  its memory came back took the kernel's own and met its OOM killer: 3 of 30 runs of the
  benchmark with DAX windows, whose guests hold no page cache of the files they map and so
  keep less; none of 60 since, the host as short of memory and as much given back.
- **No hold counts what goes** (PM M324): every hold init sets counts out the memory
  still plugged past its device's request, which goes as its driver unplugs it, free or
  not, as the give-back's own hold does; and what is plugged, for a run held at its cap or
  a grower lifting its hold once all its most is plugged, is what stays. The daemon tells
  a microVM its room again as it gives back, which came 10 to 15 ms after: worked out
  while the driver still unplugged, its hold counted the 128 MiB going as free, 261 to 274
  MB where its microVM would have 233 MiB, and its page cache filled its zones to their
  min watermarks, its guest's kernel throttling its own reclaim and its grower, woken
  only at the hold, plugging none: 5 of 384 past128 reads in the DAX budget job, and none
  of 288 since.
- **Said in the daemon's log** at most once a minute, with what was given back since.
- **Idle, it costs nothing**: with no microVM running it waits for one, hearing no
  pressure meanwhile, whose trigger fires each window while the host stays short (on a CI
  runner short of memory it woke an idle daemon's thread every 2 s: job 118535098642);
  then a thread blocked in poll(2) on Linux 6.4 and later and on macOS; on an older Linux,
  a read of the host's average every ten seconds.

**Measured against DAMON (PM M293).** DAMON_RECLAIM, built into the pinned kernel, does
nothing in a run's guest as the kernel has it (its watermarks, which run it only while a
guest's free memory is between a fifth and a half of it, kept it off in five rounds of
six); held active it gives back 53 MiB of a gigabyte
read in 180 s, or 568 MiB in 90 s with min_age 5 s, monitoring one range of the guest's
memory, at 1.5% of a CPU idle against 0.2. D188 gives back 875 MiB within 10 s, and nothing
until the host is short. DAMON stays off.

**Measured (PM M267, M268).** On the Mac, the guest's 944 MiB of a read file reclaimed in
33 ms (p50); with the flush, 946 MiB back to the host within 0.5 s (p50, the builtin 81
ms), where reporting at its own pace gave back 374 MiB by 2 s, 630 by 4 s and 952 by 8 s.
51 MiB of the read's stays: the page structures of the memory it plugged, and the
kernel's. On Linux (KVM) the same: 835 MiB back within 0.5 s (p50, 70 ms with the flush),
paced 357 by 1 s, 615 by 4 s, 866 by 8 s, 50 to 59 MiB staying. Unplugged after the
working set shrinks, all but 12 to 20 MiB of a gigabyte the guest plugged, used and freed,
on both.

**Measured (PM M309).** On CI's x86_64 runners (AMD EPYC 7763, 9V45 and 9V74, Intel Xeon
8370C, 8573C and 6973P, each a virtual machine its KVM is nested in), a gigabyte read
through FUSE under a slice held to 384 MiB with no swap took 355 to 604 s where it took 3
to 5 s with no budget; held within its budget's room and never closer than the least room
a run goes on in to what it uses, 4.79 s at the median sparse and 4.99 written, 8.38 and
9.14 at the most, where it took 4.65 and 4.95 with none (n 24 each, f0a68074): every read
within twice the median of none, where runs held at what they used had crawled for 190 to
672 s. On 12 more runners, each of those six CPUs among them, every read under the budget
took within 1.59 times its CPU's median under none (n 36 each). Its guest's own RAM, its template's pages, stayed: a read refaulted 1,634 file
pages at the median sparse and 3,016 written, where one read had refaulted 16.5 million;
counting only the files charged to the budget, 20,586 written at the median and 273,132 at
the most. On bare metal (an Intel Core i9-14900HX, Linux 6.19), 1.10 s sparse and 1.32
written at the median, 2.13 and 2.59 at the most, where it took 1.25 and 1.42 with none
(n 12 each), and no read refaulted a page.

**Tested.** Unit (platform): the host's memory pressure can be watched where the daemon
runs. Unit (daemon): a budget's room, the least any cgroup over a microVM leaves, its
unmapped page cache counted as room and its shared memory not, none with no budget and
none at the root (`a_budgets_room_is_the_least_any_cgroup_over_a_microvm_leaves`); the
files a budget's processes map held, past what its cgroup counts mapped, and the kernel's
inactive buffer beside them; a give-back saying what it gave or why it gave nothing, one
with no answer in time said so; and a microVM that does not answer its give-back keeping
no other's from the host, nor asked again until it has ended
(`a_microvm_that_does_not_give_back_keeps_no_other_waiting`, which passes asking one after
another hang on). Unit (init): a run held within its room, never closer to what it uses
than the least room a run goes on in, which a room short of it raises no hold past
(`a_run_is_held_within_its_budgets_room`), that room covering what a reader of 1 MiB
blocks needed on 4 and 18 CPUs (`a_run_held_short_keeps_the_room_its_reads_need`); a
microVM held to a budget plugging no more than its cap needs. E2E on Linux, real microVMs
under a slice of the user's manager, no swap (tests/containers.rs
`a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_gives_back_what_it_holds_cold`): a microVM that read 512 MiB
through FUSE into its guest's page cache (a file of a window's range or more is its host's
page cache, mapped into it: D189) gives back what it holds cold once a `MemoryHigh` of 384
MiB short of it is set, idle as it is, the daemon's log saying what it gave back and that
it holds it within its budget, in which it reads a gigabyte, in files of a MiB, to the
end. tests/daemon.rs
`a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_reads_through_fuse_within_twice_its_time_without_one`: runs
restored from their template, its warm microVMs in the slice, read a gigabyte through FUSE
under a `MemoryHigh` its idle microVMs leave 128 MiB of within twice the time runs under
none took (medians of 3), a run begun under no budget held to one set as it goes within it
too, and a run alone in the slice, its daemon keeping no warm microVM there, held under a
budget short of what the slice holds and its kernel's inactive buffer, by a mebibyte,
within the least room a run goes on in and reading within it too (where held at what
they used they read a gigabyte at 0.16 to 0.57 MiB/s, PM M309; with warm microVMs beside
it, the budget ended them for room, and room came back to every run, PM M314): dispatched
alone on CI, 32 of 32 copies passed on four runner CPUs (PM M318). Not on macOS, which has
no group of processes a budget holds. `an_idle_daemon_wakes_for_nothing` (tests/daemon.rs)
holds the idle daemon's threads still.

**Measured (PM M268, macOS).** Of a gigabyte a guest plugged, filled with its own pages
and the kernel's among them, and freed, the driver gave back 98% within 0.1 s, 18 MiB
staying (p50) in 3 of its 8 blocks; online as auto-movable, 14 MiB in one; all movable,
none. Plugged memory stays the kernel's own (D133).

**Not yet.** A budget below what a cold-booted microVM holds cannot be met: its guest's RAM
is all anonymous memory, which its host cannot take back without swap, and a read under
such a budget is throttled for as long as it runs (761 to 1,729 s a gigabyte, PM M318),
where one restored from its template holds that template's clean pages beside as much
anonymous memory, which its host may take back. Builders (D133) give back at their build's
word on their give-back port (`build::GIVE_PORT`, build/give.rs), a build running in `shards
build`'s own process, not the daemon's; on Windows too since 2026-10-28, free page reporting
(D151) theirs there as a run's: on jupiter's WHP a builder holding a step's 256 MiB file
gave back 253 MiB of it, its VM process from 350,516 KiB to 96,168
(`a_builder_gives_back_what_it_holds_cold_at_its_builds_word`). And they hold little a pass could take (PM M295): what a
builder's steps write it keeps in tmpfs layers, 148 MiB of Shmem after an npm install of 73
MiB of packages, against 1.4 MiB of file pages, so its memory comes back as its layers
leave memory, to its swap window or a layer on the host's disk as a run's (D190), not as
D188's file pages. M268 at larger sizes.

### D189. Volumes' file data once, in the host's page cache: virtio-fs DAX windows (built: every share's window as long as its host's memory, but on a virtual machine on an AMD CPU)

**Found.** The user's plan, item 5. A volume's file the guest reads is in the host's page
cache and again in the guest's (944 MiB of a 1 GiB file, PM M267), and every read and write
goes through the share process: two copies a request, on one queue (the benchmark's
trial, n 1: 1.1 GB/s of 1 MiB reads, where Cloud Hypervisor's virtiofsd gave 4.4). Linux's
virtiofs maps a file's ranges into a window of device memory that the host fills from the
file itself (DAX, fs/fuse/dax.c), with the pinned kernel's CONFIG_FUSE_DAX: the data then
lives once, in the host's page cache, and reads and writes are the guest's own loads and
stores.

**Built so far.**
- Each shared directory's device, the join share's too, may offer a DAX window
  (`MachineConfig::share_window_mib`, snapshot format 22): virtio-fs's cache, shared memory
  region 0 (VIRTIO_FS_SHMCAP_ID_CACHE), at a GiB boundary past the swap window, whole 2 MiB
  ranges as the guest maps files in them, within the addresses the guest's CPU has. The
  daemon gives every microVM's shares one, as long as its host's memory unless
  `SHARDS_SHARE_WINDOW_MIB` says another length (below), and keys its templates by it.
- The VM process answers FUSE_SETUPMAPPING and FUSE_REMOVEMAPPING itself
  (devices/virtio/fs/window.rs). Linux names a mapping's file by its node alone, its
  handle -1 (fs/fuse/dax.c, `fuse_setup_one_mapping`), so the VM process asks its share
  process for a descriptor of the node's file (a control frame; the descriptor by
  SCM_RIGHTS), which the server opens along the node's path, checked to be the node, as
  virtiofsd does (`setupmapping`): to read, and to write where the mapping is to be
  written, never in a volume the guest may not write. The ask says the range the mapping
  maps too, its offset and length (`descriptor_ask`), for a server that keeps a file's
  bytes in an object of its own (slates' shares answer each with a shared-memory object
  of the file, agreed 2026-10-24); shards' own reads the node and the flag alone. The
  range is mapped into the window shared: on KVM one memslot covers the window and its
  MMU notifiers follow each range placed in it; on HVF each range is mapped at stage 2
  as it is placed, readable and executable (a guest runs programs from its volumes), and
  writable where the guest may write it.
- HVF maps a shared range only from a descriptor opened to write too (M17), and a private
  one goes on showing the guest the bytes it first read after the host writes the file
  (M270): there every range's descriptor is opened to read and write, and the guest is
  told to map only files its server may write, in volumes it may write
  (`window::SHARED_NEEDS_WRITE`); a read-only volume's files go through FUSE.
- Which files: init mounts each volume `dax=inode` (a kernel without FUSE's DAX refuses the
  option, and the volume is mounted without it), and its server says which files to map
  (FUSE_HAS_INODE_DAX, FUSE_ATTR_DAX): regular files of 1 MiB or more that it may read
  (`DAX_SMALLEST`, PM M338). Measured from 4 KiB to 2 MiB through a window and through
  FUSE on the Mac and on Fedora's performance and efficient cores (first reads cold and
  warm, re-reads, overwrites, memory, a working tree's 66,357 files and 70,000 of 4 KiB),
  1 MiB is the smallest size from which the window is no worse on every host: from
  256 KiB on the Mac and Fedora's efficient cores, from 1 MiB on its performance cores,
  where a 256 KiB file's cold overwrite took 251 to 258 µs through a window (the host
  reads the page a guest's store lands in) and 202 to 209 through FUSE. A smaller file
  goes through FUSE: below 64 KiB a mapping's round trip to the share process and host
  mmap cost a first read more than it saves, and a 4 KiB file's mapping held 23 to 28 KiB
  more of its VM's memory than FUSE's page. Linux on arm64 is unmeasured: no host here
  runs KVM on it. FUSE_INIT says the host's page size (map_alignment).
- On Linux each of a VM's windows (its shares' and its join share's) is no longer than
  lets every range of them be mapped at once within the host's `vm.max_map_count`
  (`share_window_bound_mib`): a range of a file shorter than it takes two of its VM
  process's mappings (the file's and the zeros past it), a whole range one, a VM 385 of
  its own on 32 CPUs and a stack and its guard for each further vCPU (PM M338), and the
  guest maps every range when it must, the host refusing a mapping past the limit and the
  guest's access failing. Linux's default, 65,530, holds a VM of one volume to 31.8 GiB a
  window; Fedora's 1,048,576 to more than its host's memory.
- A range never holds a page of its file wholly past the file's end, which the host cannot
  give: HVF ends the vCPU's run at an access there (M271), and x86 KVM retries it without
  end, its vCPU spinning in KVM_RUN (M273). A range is the file's pages to the one that
  holds its end, and the window's anonymous zeros past it, from its mapping on; and before
  the device passes a reply that may tell the guest a file's size (its request's node's,
  and the entries a LOOKUP, CREATE, MKNOD, MKDIR, SYMLINK, LINK or READDIRPLUS gives), the
  window follows the file: its pages where it has grown, zeros where it was cut short.
- Another process cutting a file short under a mapping, which the guest reads past before
  it learns the size, never ends the microVM nor holds a vCPU. On Linux the VM names each
  file its windows begin to map to the daemon (`kind::WATCH`, the descriptor with it), and
  the daemon watches them with its one inotify instance, as an instance a microVM would run
  a user out of them (M257), and tells the VM of one cut short (`kind::CUT`): its window
  gives zeros there, and a vCPU that spun there runs on. HVF's abort and arm64 KVM's
  EFAULT have the window follow the file at once. Until the guest asks the file's size
  again it reads zeros there, as through FUSE it may read stale bytes from its page cache.
- An OPEN of a file the window maps, and a CREATE that opens one there already, is told
  to keep what the guest has of it (FOPEN_KEEP_CACHE): Linux drops a file's cached pages at
  each open, and for a mapped file those are DAX entries its processes may still map, which
  it lets go of first and unmaps after, its 2 MiB pages' counts going wrong, and every build
  of the benchmark's cargo workload ended in SIGBUS (M274). A mapped file has no page cache
  of the guest's to go stale. A size change another process makes, seen in the file's
  attributes, takes the same path in the guest kernel, which shards' kernel's patch 0007
  closes (resources/kernel/patches): a DAX file's entries left to its layouts' own
  breaking.
- A mapping is charged its file's bytes in its range against the microVM's I/O limits
  (D178) as it is made, once its file's size says them: a 5,000-byte file's range 5,000
  bytes, not the range's 2 MiB, which every file's last range was charged before, and a
  range past its file's end nothing (`a_dax_mapping_maps_the_file_of_its_node`). The
  guest's loads and stores through it are memory, which the host's page cache serves and
  writes back.
- A save (D176) keeps each mapping (snapshot format 23), and its restore maps each range
  again from its new share process, as the run gives the share its server, once that
  server has the tables the guest's node IDs are in, and before the guest runs; a range
  whose file that server no longer reaches is zeros, as past a file's end.
- **Each file's size looked at once a request** (PM M299). Each reply of the server's has
  the window follow the files it tells of first (`Window::reconcile`), the request's own
  among them; it looked at a file's size once for each range it mapped of it, so a request
  about a file mapped in 1,024 ranges took 1,024 fstat(2)s, and every write through such a
