  file's window paid for the guest's requests about it: on Fedora a 4 KiB write took 288
  µs where a FUSE_WRITE took 86. Each file is now looked at once a pass (`window::Sizes`),
  and a write through the window costs less than a FUSE_WRITE at p50 in every case
  measured: 4 KiB at random over 2 GiB 30.6 µs against 44.6, close together 23.4 against
  44.4, 1 MiB close together 74 against 855. Held by
  `a_file_mapped_in_many_ranges_is_looked_at_once` (mutation-checked: 8 looks for 8
  ranges).
- **Each window's page structures in its head, not its guest's memory** (PM M300). Linux
  describes a window's pages as it probes the device, with page structures (64 bytes for
  each 4 KiB page) it took from guest RAM: a 64th of the window (M269), from a guest that,
  given its memory as it needs it (virtio-mem, D133), boots with little. Each window's
  device now gives a head right before the window, shared memory region 0xfe (`fs::HEAD`):
  memory of the VM's own, sized so that head and window are whole sections, each
  section's page structures a 2 MiB block of the head (`head::window_head_len`: one 128
  MiB section for a window of 1 or 4 GiB), since a part section's would come from guest
  RAM on x86_64 (vmemmap_populate). The guest's kernel maps head and window as one range
  whose page structures are the head's, a vmem_altmap, as libnvdimm keeps a pmem
  namespace's (shards' kernel patch 0008); a kernel without the patch maps the window as
  before. A snapshot keeps the heads as it keeps a writable layer's (D190): each alike 2
  MiB block once, beside its memory (`window-heads`, format 25), mapped back after a
  template's save and privately by each restore. A microVM saved in format 24, as shards
  0.6.0 saves, restores where it has no windows. A window took a 64th of its length of its
  guest's free memory, 64.1 MiB for 4 GiB on Fedora, and 72.0 on the Mac with its linear
  map's page tables; with its head, none on Fedora (-0.2 to 0.1 MiB at every length, n 12)
  and those page tables alone on the Mac (8.3 MiB). Fedora's 4 GiB boot reached PID 1 20 ms
  sooner: its page structures go on the host's huge pages, not on a boot's base pages
  (D29). arm64 Linux maps memory it adds in base pages under rodata=full (arch_add_memory,
  force_pte_mapping), so that a page's permissions can change alone, which a DAX device's
  linear alias never does: shards' kernel patch 0010 maps a file system DAX device's memory
  in blocks, but where debug_pagealloc or a realm needs base pages, and an arm64 window
  takes none of its guest's memory either (0.0 to 0.1 MiB at every length to 4 GiB, n 12,
  M300). The pinned kernel carries both (since kernel-6.18.48-8df0015cca35); held by
  `a_dax_windows_page_structures_take_none_of_its_guests_memory`, its bound the spread of
  boots alone.
- **Whole pages a host does not hold written as FUSE_WRITEs** (PM M301). A store into a
  page its host does not hold waits for the host to read it, where a FUSE_WRITE's pwrite(2)
  of the whole page reads nothing (M283). Each window's device now keeps a record of which
  of the window's pages its host holds, one bit a 4 KiB page, in memory of its own right
  after the window, shared memory region 0xfd (`fs::HELD`, `head::window_held_len`): taken
  with `mincore(2)` as each range is mapped, cleared as it is unmapped, and taken again
  once a mapping after its first FUSE_WRITE, as the host reads around faults since
  (`Window::rerecord`). The guest's kernel (shards' patch 0009) maps, or upgrades from
  read alone, each range a write of whole pages meets, as a store would, then writes the
  host's whole pages its host does not hold as FUSE_WRITEs and the rest through the
  window, and records the pages it writes and reads. The host's page is FUSE_INIT's
  map_alignment, 16 KiB on Apple silicon: a FUSE_WRITE of part of one makes the host read
  the rest first, as a store does, so parts of host pages go through the window (on the
  Mac, 4 KiB FUSE_WRITEs into cold 16 KiB pages lost to the stores they replaced, M301). The record is advice: a page the host let go
  of since is read in as a store meets it, as before. Nothing keeps it: a restore takes it
  again as it maps each range (snapshot format 26, for the layout). The VM process's
  seccomp allowlist has `mincore`. On Fedora a cold file's scattered 4 KiB writes through
  the window took 315 to 319 µs at p99 where they took 1,604 to 1,905 (FUSE's 153 to 180),
  at twice the rate; 1 MiB into ranges not yet mapped a fifth to a third less at p50;
  nothing warm lost. Its first build sent a range's first write after a read as a FUSE_WRITE
  by a record taken before the read's fault read the range around, and the next store paid
  the upgrade after it (64 KiB writes 131.5 µs at p50 against 94.9): a read's mapping is
  upgraded as the write comes. A reply about a file the window maps in 1,024 ranges looks at
  that file's ranges alone, and its ranges follow it only where its size changed (`Table`,
  0.29 µs at p50 where walking every range took 8.54). Held by
  `a_ranges_held_pages_are_recorded_as_it_is_mapped`,
  `a_files_ranges_follow_it_only_where_it_changed`, and
  `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_its_dax_window` (whole pages written where the host
  holds none, read by host and guest). The pinned kernel carries the patch (since
  kernel-6.18.48-4970e0190ebe). On the Mac, evicted with msync(2) MS_INVALIDATE (M301: rewriting the
  file had timed the SSD's flush), cold 64 KiB writes into ranges mapped first took 306 µs
  at p50 where they took 2,459 (FUSE's 204 to 220), and 1 MiB into ranges not yet mapped
  1,310 where 2,811 (FUSE's 1,243 to 1,434); cold 4 KiB writes, parts of 16 KiB host
  pages, cost what they did.
- **One descriptor a file** (PM M302). The slowest write where ranges are mapped as
  writes come took 7.8 to 32.6 ms on every kernel (M301): the window kept each mapped
  range's descriptor, so its VM process's descriptor table grew as the run's mappings
  passed 128, 256, 512 and 1,024 descriptors, and Linux, growing a table other threads
  share, waits a grace period of RCU first (fs/file.c, expand_fdtable): 9 to 24 ms, once a
  growth. The window now keeps one descriptor a file (`Node::file`), which follows its size
  and maps more of it as it grows; each range's own, from its server, closes once the range
  is mapped, as virtiofsd's does: the slowest mapping took 0.25 to 0.5 ms. Mapping a
  file's ranges from one descriptor, which spares the server's open (6 to 19 µs), was
  measured and not taken: one open file's readahead stops reading around its faults after
  a hundred misses (mm/filemap.c, MMAP_LOTSAMISS), where each range's open begins anew
  (1,285 µs against 682 at p50 for kernel A's writes after a page of each range was
  written). A range mapped to be read alone keeps no record, which no guest reads: its
  mincore(2) took 51 to 53 µs of a warm mapping's 75 to 77. Held by
  `a_window_keeps_one_descriptor_of_a_file` (mutation-checked: 401 descriptors more for
  400 ranges where each range's was kept).

- **A device reaches the pages of the files its guest maps** (PM M304). A guest names its
  devices the pages a mapping of a file holds as any of its pages: an O_DIRECT read or
  write, and on a share a write that grows a file the window maps (fs/fuse/dax.c,
  `fuse_dax_direct_write`), whose user pages FUSE gives its device (fs/fuse/file.c,
  `fuse_get_user_pages`). A DAX file's are device memory, a pmem device's (the image's
  root, the writable layer) or a window's, which no device reached: in a microVM with a 64
  MiB window, an append to a file the window maps, from a mapping of another, was answered
  as done with 0 bytes written, and an O_DIRECT read into a mapping of one as done with its
  bytes missing; an O_DIRECT write from such a mapping was whole only because Linux's FUSE
  wrote it again, buffered, once the direct write wrote nothing (`direct_write_fallback`).
  Each device that gives its guest such memory now says so (`VirtioDevice::device_memory`:
  a pmem device's file, a layer's file system, a share's window), and its guest memory
  gives it to every device as RAM (`GuestMemory::give_devices`): system calls given its
  pages (`io_ptr`: a disk's transfers, vsock's), whose kernel answers EFAULT where one is
  gone, and an access's copies by `platform::copy_checked` (virtio-fs's requests and
  replies, a network frame), a copy whose fault its signal handler resumes as failed, as
  Linux resumes its own copies from user memory (its exception tables), never the end of
  the VM's process: a file cut short under its mapping by another process, which the window
  follows only as it learns (above), takes the request at it alone. It costs what the VMM's
  copy of RAM does on Fedora, and 1.2 times it for 1 MiB on the Mac, where a copy through a
  pipe cost 3.4 to 9 times memcpy (M304). A request whose bytes, or whose answer's, a
  device cannot reach is answered EIO (virtio-fs) or an I/O error (a disk), and a frame
  dropped (virtio-net), never served short. A GPU's renderer and a passed-through function
  are given RAM alone, as before. Held by
  `a_microvms_devices_reach_the_pages_of_the_files_it_maps` (mutation-checked: without
  device memory the append fails), and vmm's
  `device_memory_is_reached_as_ram_is_and_its_lost_pages_fail`,
  `a_requests_device_memory_goes_whole_and_its_lost_pages_fail_it`,
  `a_transfer_reaches_device_memory_and_its_lost_pages_fail_it`,
  `a_frame_from_device_memory_is_sent_and_one_whose_page_is_gone_dropped`,
  `a_checked_copy_fails_where_its_pages_are_gone` and
  `a_fault_outside_a_checked_copy_still_ends_its_process`.
- **What a window's guest makes of it, made as its guest uses it** (PM M306). A window's
  length cost its microVM what its guest's kernel made of the window at once, whatever it
  went on to map: its page structures, a 64th of it, written into its head as the guest
  probed the device (for 64 GiB, 1,044 MiB of its VM process's memory on the Mac and on
  Fedora, and 1.4 s of Fedora's boot), every one of which a template's save then read;
  the structures of its head's own pages, a 4,096th of it, each its own (each lists
  itself), so that every template kept them (18 MiB for 64 GiB); and FUSE DAX's mapping of
  each 2 MiB range, 128 bytes, made at every mount and freed at every unmount (a 64 GiB
  window's run in its microVM set up 3.0 ms slower and ran 4.2 ms longer at p50 on Fedora
  than with 0012 and 0013, n 40). shards' kernel makes each as its guest uses it: patch
  0011 a range's page structures as FUSE first sets the range up (`PGMAP_LAZY_MEMMAP`),
  0012 none of the head's own pages', its metadata, which no pfn of it hands out, and 0013
  a range's mapping as the range is first wanted. A head's save reads none of the blocks of its own memory its guest never touched
  (`Head::untouched`, by `platform::untouched`), where reading them gave each of their pages
  memory on macOS, and a block mapped from a snapshot's copy is read whole, its untouched
  pages the copy's; one its guest wrote zeros over is mapped back as fresh memory, where a
  discard (MADV_DONTNEED) brought the copy's bytes back on Linux. A 64 GiB window costs a
  boot 2.1 MiB of its VM process's memory on the Mac and 2.8 on Fedora, a template what one
  of 4 GiB costs, and a run with a volume nothing measured (Fedora, n 40: setup 2.69 ms at
  p50 against 2.84 with no window, 5.66 before 0013). The pinned kernel carries the three
  (since kernel-6.18.48-e39058b2b627). Held by
  `a_long_dax_window_costs_its_boot_next_to_nothing` (a 4,096th of the window, what the
  structures of the head's own pages take: 0011 alone took 20,544 KiB, the kernel before it
  1,069,184, an x86_64 CI runner 8,392 with all three while each boot wrote its whole held
  record, M307),
  `a_volumes_long_dax_window_takes_its_guest_no_mapping_for_each_range` (768 kmalloc-128
  objects in use with no window, 33,440 with a 64 GiB one before 0013), and vmm's
  `a_heads_save_reads_no_block_its_guest_never_touched` and
  `a_heads_blocks_from_its_copy_are_saved_whole_and_zeroed_ones_mapped_back_fresh`
  (mutation-checked on Linux and the Mac; the two above on the Mac).
- **Every share's window as long as its host's memory, by default** (PM M307). A window
  maps what its guest reads and writes of a volume's files from the host's page cache,
  which holds no more of them at once than the host has memory, and one shorter than what
  its guest maps churns its mappings (M276: 1 GiB under a 2 GiB file read slower than 4
  GiB). Its length now costs what its guest maps of it (above), so the daemon gives every
  share, the join share's too, a window as long as its host's memory, as it gives a run a
  swap window that long (D159); `SHARDS_SHARE_WINDOW_MIB` another length, 0 none. Where its
  guest's addresses cannot hold so many that long past its RAM, the memory it may plug and
  its swap window (each the host's memory too), its VM gives each the most whole ranges
  that fit and says so, as its swap window takes what the addresses leave
  (`share_windows`), and records the length its machine has: a restore, its heads kept for
  that length, has it or is refused. Eight volumes and the join share took 83,538 MiB each
  on the Mac (40-bit addresses, 128 GiB) and 41,202 on Fedora (39-bit, 62.5 GiB). APFS
  fills the holes a small file's writes leave as the file is synced, so a head's copy
  punches them (`platform::punch_hole`, F_PUNCHHOLE; ext4 keeps them): a window's heads
  file takes 12 KiB where 4 MiB, and a writable layer's head 6.5 MiB where 12. A device's
  reset, which every boot's driver makes, unmaps its whole window, and cleared the whole of
  its held record with it, writing every page of it (2 MiB for 64 GiB); it clears the
  record of the ranges it unmaps alone, the only ones whose bits are set. On the Mac, with
  a window of its host's 128 GiB, a template's boot takes 0.2 MiB more of its VM process's
  memory (4.2 before), its template is the size of one without (70 MB), its restored VMs'
  footprint is the same (19.2 MiB against 19.5), and a run with a volume sets up as fast
  (1.44 ms at p50 against 1.75, n 40); on Fedora a 64 GiB window's boot takes 0.3 MiB. A
  booted window's head is on the host's base pages, as a restored one is: where THP is
  always (x86_64 CI runners) its one page structure written at boot took a 2 MiB huge page
  (afa9b355), and with base pages the window's boot is within a huge page of guest RAM of
  none's (-1.9 to +2.1 MiB). Its held record is on base pages too: there the first range's
  words took a huge page, all 512 pages of a 64 GiB window's record (e1df33d4). A
  template's map-back gives a head's run of zero blocks back in one call (5.4 ms for nine
  83 GiB windows on the Mac, where 6.5; 187 µs on Fedora), and its save keeps the index it
  wrote and the blocks it found untouched for it: the map-back reads nothing back from the
  copy, whose index read back from APFS took 2.8 ms at the median and up to 22, leaves
  untouched blocks as they are, and takes from its guest, and gives back, only the blocks
  it changes (`Head::changing`), one a head where it took nine heads whole: 0.21 ms at the
  median and 0.35 at the most on the Mac, where 2.3 and 25 (n 30 each, PM M311). Held by
  `placed_window_heads_give_up_only_the_blocks_their_map_back_changes` (mutation-checked)
  and
  `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_a_dax_window_by_default` (a 4 MiB file mapped by
  default, through FUSE with 0), vmm's `share_windows_go_one_after_another` (fitted, none,
  a kept length refused), `a_kept_blocks_pages_of_zeros_are_holes_in_its_copy` (synced as
  a commit syncs it), `a_head_mapped_back_gives_back_its_blocks_of_zeros` and
  `a_cleared_window_leaves_the_record_of_ranges_it_never_mapped_untouched`, each
  mutation-checked on the Mac.
- **None by default on a virtual machine on an AMD CPU** (PM M308). There a guest's first
  touch of each 4 KiB page a window gives it is mapped twice, by the host's KVM and by the
  hypervisor beneath, which shadows the host's nested paging: on CI's x86_64 runners,
  Azure virtual machines, a 1 GiB read through a window took 41.2 to 138.4 s at p50 on AMD
  EPYC 7763 and 9V74 runners (139.9 to 178.9 s written out) where FUSE took 3.0 to 6.4,
  its pages landing in guest RAM already mapped on the host's 2 MiB pages; and under a 384
  MiB budget 23.2 to 134.0 s. The host's KVM took 1.4 exits a page, its vCPU threads busy
  half the run in guest mode, which is the hypervisor beneath's own time; Hyper-V's
  enlightened NPT TLB flush was in use, so no flush was the cost. Each range advised onto
  huge pages (`huge.patch`: 2 MiB folios, mapped whole, 58 times fewer faults and KVM's
  own 2 MiB entries) read no faster, and three times slower on the 9V74s (123.3 and 129.1
  s against 41.2 and 42.4): the hypervisor beneath shadows 4 KiB at a time whatever the
  host maps. So the daemon gives a share no window there unless `SHARDS_SHARE_WINDOW_MIB`
  asks for one, and says so as it starts (`share_window_default`, from `/proc/cpuinfo`'s
  vendor and `hypervisor` flag); an Intel runner there read 1 GiB through a window in 2.0
  s (3.5 written) against FUSE's 2.6 (2.9), 14 µs a fault, and under the budget in 2.6 s
  against 6.1, and Fedora's bare metal in 1.37 against 1.23, both with windows as before;
  there 2 MiB folios read five times faster sparse (0.39 s), and are not taken (below).
  Held by daemon's `a_shares_window_by_default_follows_its_host`,
  containers' `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_a_dax_window_by_default` (the host's
  default, none with 0, one given on any host) and
  `a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_reads_a_large_file_through_its_window_to_its_end` (512 MiB
  past a 384 MiB `MemoryHigh` through a window given, the budget met, to its end).
- **A range is mapped as its host's kernel faults it, not advised onto 2 MiB folios** (PM
  M339). Advised onto huge pages (`MADV_HUGEPAGE`, with `MADV_RANDOM` or without), a
  range's first touch reads a 2 MiB folio, two without `MADV_RANDOM` (mm/filemap.c
  `do_sync_mmap_readahead`), where its host's file system makes large folios (ext4 since
  6.16), and KVM maps it with one stage-2 entry. On three Intel CI runners (Xeon 8573C)
  that read 1 GiB sparse in 0.36 to 0.42 s against 1.91 to 2.15 and a range's second page
  in 2.2 to 2.4 µs against 313 to 337. But a range's first touch took 1.4 to 10.2 ms at p50
  against 0.52 to 0.55, and 10 to 38 ms at p99 against 1.0 to 1.1. A store into the folio
  dirtied all of it, 2 MiB written back where 6 KiB (ext4's `block_page_mkwrite`,
  `iomap_dirty_folio`). And 1,000 touches left 2.0 to 2.8 GiB of the file in the page cache
  where 240 MiB. On eight AMD runners (EPYC 9V45, 7763, 9V74) first touches took 1.6 to
  6.1 ms where 1.05 to 1.29; sparse reads were faster beyond the rounds' spread on two
  7763s and slower beyond it on the 9V74. On Fedora's Btrfs, which makes no large folios but
  in an experimental build, the advice made none, and its faults read 4 MiB around them
  already (fs/btrfs/disk-io.c).
  By the rule fixed before any number (docs/research/measurements/dax-huge/measure.py),
  neither arm passed on any host, so no class of host takes one. Linux on arm64 is
  unmeasured: no host here runs KVM on it. macOS's madvise(2) has no such advice.

**Measured (PM M269).** What a window costs a guest as it boots: its page structures, which
Linux makes of it as it probes the device (virtio_fs_setup_dax, devm_memremap_pages of
MEMORY_DEVICE_FS_DAX): 18.1 MiB of free memory for a 1 GiB window, 73.7 for 4 GiB, a 64th of
it and 15% and some 2 MiB more; a boot reached PID 1 no later for one up to 2 GiB. A
template pays it once; what its restores pay is to be measured with mappings.

**Next.**
- A window's ranges on 2 MiB folios: not taken, decided by measurement (above, PM M339).
- What a fault reads around it on Btrfs, 4 MiB (its read-ahead): on Fedora a range's
  first touch that read 2 MiB (`MADV_HUGEPAGE` with `MADV_RANDOM`) took 802 µs at p50
  against 1,076 and 1,698 at p99 against 2,284, but read 1 GiB written in 0.95 s against
  0.62 (PM M339). Whether a range's read-ahead should follow how its file is read is
  unmeasured.
- From what size a file is mapped: 1 MiB, decided by measurement (Which files, above, PM
  M338), as how long a window is (above, PM M306). Measured against FUSE (PM
  M276, the sustained-I/O benchmark, n = 10 a side): a window that holds what the guest
  reads through it (4 GiB under fio's 2 GiB file) reads 17 to 62 times as fast and writes
  whole MiBs 2 to 2.8 times as fast, the guest holding 28 MiB of memory where 2.1 GiB
  without, the host 43% less; one shorter (1 GiB) reads slower, its mappings churning.
  Random 4 KiB writes are 21 to 33% of FUSE's rate through either: a guest's store into a
  page its host's page cache does not hold waits for the host to read the page in, where a
  FUSE_WRITE's pwrite(2) of the whole page reads nothing (71 to 127 µs against 2 to 3 on
  Btrfs, PM M283), and M276's host, short of memory, held few of its file's pages.
  Reading each range ahead as it is mapped doubles the rate of a writer that writes a
  range about 20 times and halves that of one that writes it once, so it is not done.
  In the guest (PM M298, M299), what M276 and M298 took for a range's mapping was the
  device's own following of each file it maps, a look at its size for each range of it, as
  each request about it was answered: looked at once a request, a write through the window
  costs less than a FUSE_WRITE at p50 in every case measured (above). What stays is the
  page its host does not hold: a store there waits for the host to read it, which a
  FUSE_WRITE of the whole page does not, so a cold file's scattered writes have the worse
  tail (4 KiB, p99 1,483 µs against 206) and 1 MiB writes into ranges not yet mapped the
  worse middle (1,589 against 898 at p50). A guest's FUSE weighing each range's writes
  against its mapping (`dax-window-writes/fuse-writes-until-mapped.patch`, M299) was
  measured and not taken: its rationale was that cost. A whole page a host does not hold
  is written as a FUSE_WRITE now (above; M301), on Fedora and the Mac, and what a write into
  a range not yet mapped pays before it writes was measured part by part (M302): a cold
  file's 1 MiB writes into ranges not yet mapped cost 6% more than FUSE's, on Fedora's
  performance cores and on its efficient cores alike, their rounds' spread the cores the
  scheduler put a run on (M302). A window takes none of its guest's memory on either
  architecture (above: its page structures its head's, and arm64's linear map of it in
  blocks).

### D199. A run's log sent to macOS's own log: `oslog`, and syslog's local default there (built)

`--log-driver oslog` is served on macOS, the journal's counterpart there (D166, D198): a
run's lines go to macOS's unified log, which `log show` and Console read. Docker has no
driver of macOS's, whose engine runs in a Linux VM there. Sent as every driver's are, from
shards' store, by the daemon's shipper (D163).

- **Through os_log, in the daemon.** macOS keeps nothing sent to syslogd's socket,
  `/var/run/syslog`, at any level, while its syslog(3) and os_log reach the unified log
  (PM M374). So a line is an entry the daemon writes with os_log_with_type, through a shim
  of its macros that only a C compiler expands (daemon/ship/oslog.c, libSystem's, no launch
  cost). Its message is public: what a run wrote is no secret of shards' to redact.
- **Found as journald's are.** Its subsystem is `shards` and its category the run's tag
  (its short ID unless `tag` says), as journald's SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER is: `log show
  --predicate 'subsystem == "shards" AND category == "web"'`. stdout's lines are of the
  default type and stderr's of the error type, as journald's priorities 6 and 3.
- **Whole lines, in parts os_log keeps.** os_log keeps a line whole up to 1,015 bytes, and
  of a longer one its first 1,015 bytes and `<…>` (M374). A longer line goes in parts of at
  most 1,015 bytes, each cut at a character's boundary, none of it lost. Bytes that are no
  UTF-8, and a NUL, are U+FFFD.
- **syslog's local default, there.** `--log-driver syslog` with no `syslog-address` sends
  to the host's own syslog, which on macOS is its unified log: there it is sent as oslog's,
  the run's tag its category. Sent to syslogd's socket, as before, every line went nowhere.
- **Its options** are every driver's (tag, labels, env, mode, the local copy's).
- **macOS's.** Elsewhere it is refused as its run is made, in shards' words: the unified
  log is macOS's own.

Tested on real microVMs on macOS (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_macos_own_log_as_its_options_say`):
`log show` has a run's line on each stream with its type, a 3,000-byte line in parts of
1,015, 1,015 and 970 bytes, and syslog's local default's lines alike. Elsewhere it tests the
refusal. A unit test holds the parts to os_log's bound and to characters' boundaries.

### D198. A run's log sent to Event Tracing for Windows: `etwlogs` (built)

`--log-driver etwlogs` is served on Windows, the journal's counterpart there (D166): a run's
lines go to the host's own event tracing, as Docker's Windows driver sends them. Sent as
every driver's are, from shards' store, by the daemon's shipper (D163).

- **Docker's provider and words.** Each line, and each 16 KiB part of a longer one, is an
  event of moby's provider, `{a3693192-9ed6-46d2-a981-f8226c8363bd}`, written by
  EventWriteString at level 0 and keyword 0, its string moby's createLogMessage's:
  `container_name: NAME, image_name: IMAGE, container_id: ID, image_id: IMAGE_ID, source:
  STREAM, log: LINE` (daemon/logger/etwlogs/etwlogs_windows.go). A session listening for
  the provider has each, `logman start -ets NAME -p {a3693192-...}` and tracerpt among
  them, as for Docker's.
- **Registered once.** The daemon registers the provider with the first run that asks for
  it and keeps it for its life, as moby keeps one registration while any of its loggers
  lives; one that fails is asked for again by the next run.
- **Delivered as written.** An event is ETW's once written: a session that listens has it,
  and none that does not, for every sender alike. Its options are every driver's (tag,
  labels, env, mode, the local copy's); moby's reads none of its own.
- **Where Docker is wrong, shards is not.** A line holding a NUL fails Go's
  UTF16FromString, and moby's driver loses it; shards writes it, the NUL U+FFFD, as its bytes
  that are no UTF-8 are.
- **Windows'.** Elsewhere it is refused as its run is made, in shards' words: Event
  Tracing for Windows is Windows' own.

Tested on real microVMs on Windows (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_etw_as_its_options_say`): a
real-time ETW session of the test's own, its provider enabled, has a run's line on each
stream, word for word, and `logs` reads the run's own copy; an ETW session is an
administrator's or Performance Log Users', and a host whose user is neither says SKIP.
Elsewhere it tests the refusal. A unit test holds each event's words to moby's.

### D197. Host directories on Windows: a FUSE server over NTFS that keeps a Linux guest's files as WSL does (designed; slice 1 begun)

**Why.** Every feature on every host (the user, 2026-10-27; the platform parity plan's step 6,
docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md's host directories on Windows): a microVM's volumes
and binds reach it as virtio-fs shares (D38), whose device, FUSE wire and WHP DAX window
(D189, `fs/window_whp.rs`) Windows builds, but whose server (`fs/server.rs`), share process
and budgets are Unix's, so a run with `-v` or `--mount` is refused there.

**What a Linux guest's files need of NTFS, measured (PM M362, CI's windows-2022 and
windows-2025, as the runner's account and as a standard user, unelevated): every call below
did as asked.**

- **One server, its host behind a layer.** `fs/server.rs` answers FUSE requests in Linux's
  terms on every host; each call it makes of its host's file system is a function of its
  own (`host::Stat`, the `*_at` calls), Unix's the libc calls it makes now, Windows' the
  NT calls below. Its tests run on both.
- **Nothing past the share.** Each operation is relative to a handle of the shared tree, its
  name one component: NtCreateFile with that directory as its RootDirectory and
  FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, so a final reparse point is never followed, as `O_NOFOLLOW`
  holds Unix's server.
- **Owners, modes and device numbers** in WSL's extended attributes, `$LXUID`, `$LXGID`,
  `$LXMOD` and `$LXDEV` ("File Permissions for WSL", Microsoft Learn), set and read
  unelevated (M362), where Unix's server keeps them in Docker Desktop's
  `com.docker.grpcfuse.ownership` xattr: a file WSL made reads as WSL made it, and a file
  with none is root's, as Unix's.
- **Every other kind as WSL makes it.** Regular files and directories are NTFS's; a
  symlink, a FIFO, a character or block device and a Unix socket are reparse points of the
  LX tags, a symlink's buffer as MS-FSCC 2.1.2.7 lays it out, never an NTFS symlink, which
  "Developer Mode must first be enabled on the machine" to make unelevated
  (CreateSymbolicLinkW, Microsoft Learn).
- **Removal and rename as Linux's**: an open file's name gone at once
  (FILE_DISPOSITION_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS), a rename over a file held open
  (FILE_RENAME_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS), the holder reading what it held.
- **Names**: a directory the guest makes is case-sensitive (FileCaseSensitiveInformation),
  as WSL makes its own; a host directory keeps the flag its user gave it.
- **Inodes**: a file's ID (FileIdInfo), whose upper 8 bytes NTFS left unused (M362).
- **Its stream to the VM** a duplex named pipe, as a served share's on Windows (D38,
  `--slates-fs-handle`, PM M340).

**Slices.** 1: the server's host calls behind functions of their own, Unix unchanged
(begun: `host::Stat`, a8117424's `readlink_at`, `symlink_at`, `mknod_at`, `mkdir_at`,
`unlink_at`, `link_at`). 2: Windows' calls, the server's own tests on Windows. 3: the share
process and the daemon's shares on Windows, and the volume, bind and DAX tests on CI's
Windows runners.

### D196. Snapshots of WHP microVMs: a partition saved and restored (built)

**Why.** Every feature on every host (the user, 2026-10-27; docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md
row 2a): a microVM on Windows took no snapshot (D140), so `run --kernel --snapshot-dir`, `shards
restore` and everything built on them, templates (D25) and warm pools (D26), were Unix's alone.
What WHP keeps of a partition, and what a restore may set back, measured first (PM M345, a
probe on jupiter: a guest saved from one partition, restored into another, its memory a view of
its saved file); the order of the restore is OpenVMM's, Microsoft's own VMM over WHP (virt_whp's
`vp_state.rs`, `apic.rs` and `lib.rs`, at 429b72a9).

- **Each vCPU's state** (`hv::whp::state`): its registers as WHP names them, 69 every host reads
  (what it runs from, the MSRs a Linux guest writes, its APIC base, the VP assist page its
  Hyper-V setup gives it, its pending interruption, interrupt state, pending event and activity:
  an AP still held for its SIPI among it) and the optional ones its host reads (the variable
  MTRRs MtrrCap counts, XSS, the CET registers, SPEC_CTRL, TSX_CTRL, TSC_ADJUST, UMWAIT_CONTROL,
  XFD and XFD_ERR, the pending debug exception), asked once a process, each alone; its local
  APIC's page and its XSAVE area by WHvGetVirtualProcessorState (InterruptControllerState2,
  XsaveState), not the two functions it supersedes, which Microsoft's reference marks deprecated
  ("WHvGetVirtualProcessorXsaveState", "WHvGetVirtualProcessorInterruptControllerState2"). A
  restore sets the APIC base first, which the APIC page's mode follows, then the page, then the
  XSAVE area, then every register (XCR0 after the area, OpenVMM's order); a state naming a
  register no snapshot keeps is refused as it is read, as is one taken on another CPU (the
  leaves of its vendor, family, features, XSAVE components and address sizes, as WHP gives a
  guest: not its caches, which a hybrid host's cores describe apart, M258).
- **The partition's time, held.** A partition's TSCs and reference time stand still while it is
  suspended (WHvSuspendPartitionTime), and a partition never run keeps them where it was made
  (M345). A save holds them once every vCPU is parked, reads each vCPU's TSC there, at one
  instant, with the reference time and the Hyper-V MSRs the guest writes once for all its vCPUs
  (its OS ID before its hypercall page, then its reference TSC page), and resumes them: no
  vCPU's TSC comes back apart from another's by however far apart their captures were, and the
  guest's clocks run through the save as a KVM guest's do. A restore holds them before it sets
  them, and they stay held until a vCPU first runs (WHvSuspendPartitionTime's reference): the
  guest's clocks go on from the snapshot whenever its vCPUs are released, a held restore's wait
  (`--hold`) unseen, as KVM's restart their TSCs at the release. Its reference TSC page then
  reads the saved reference time, run on (M345).
- **The IOAPIC is the VMM's** (D140) and is saved with the partition: its registers and each
  pin's line; a level-triggered entry keeps its remote IRR, which the restored local APIC's
  EOI clears.
- **Memory.** A snapshot's memory file is sparse (FSCTL_SET_SPARSE): NTFS keeps no hole it is
  not told to, and writes the zeros of every page up to the last written (M345: a 2 MiB guest's
  four pages took 192 KiB, NTFS allocating sparse files 64 KiB at a time). A restore's RAM is the
  file's runs of data mapped copy-on-write (PAGE_WRITECOPY), a view each, and memory of its
  own between them, zeros (D151), placed at the address its RAM was reserved at:
  guest RAM is reserved as a placeholder that committed memory replaces at once
  (`platform::reserve_ram`), which the restore frees back to its placeholder, splits into one
  a part and replaces with each part's view or memory, leaving no moment in which another
  thread could take the range. WHP maps any view
  at stage 2 (copy-on-write, read-only, shared or of the pagefile, M345); the guest's stores
  land in the view and never in the file, and every restore shares the file's pages in the
  cache until it writes one. The file is made sparse as it is made, by whoever makes it: for a
  confined VM its spawner, since the VM process may make no FSCTL (D141). So is a run's
  swap kept by its save (D176), and every copy that skips zeros makes its file sparse
  before it ends it at its length (`platform::copy_ranges`), or is refused where it may
  not. Four saves of runs at once on windows-2025 took the 29.5 GB its temp disk had free
  within 20 s and failed as it filled, its memory and page file steady (budget-e2e run
  40627507997, its host sampled every 5 s); of a save's files only a run's swap was not
  sparse, which NTFS takes whole as a copy sets its length (M349).
- **Every VM's grants link kept, sealed, for its files' ranges** (M377). A copy reads only
  the ranges that hold data, which a confined VM asks its spawner (`RANGES`). A run's VM,
  given neither a snapshot to save nor a vsock path, let go of its link as it started, and
  saved later read its whole layer, having none to ask: on NTFS a sparse file's holes read
  through its handle while a writable view of it is mapped become allocated, so each save
  of a 10 GiB layer took 10.6 GB of its host's disk while its files held 104 MB, and
  saved.rs still ran windows-2025 out. Every VM now keeps the link and says `SEALED` once
  granted what it starts with: its spawner refuses every grant after, as after a vsock
  path's listen, and answers its ranges for its life (a save's copy then 1.5 MB, 107 MiB of
  the disk). Held by `a_sealed_vm_is_granted_nothing_more_and_its_ranges_are_read`.
- **One partition a process.** WHP maps no memory into a second partition of a process while
  another lives (STATUS_VID_PARTITION_ALREADY_EXISTS, until the first is deleted, M345). A VM
  process holds one; the partition that reads the host's vCPU limit is deleted before it.
- **Windows Server 2022 restores none.** Its WHP (build 20348) sets no vCPU's APIC page back
  through WHvSetVirtualProcessorState: the page as read is refused (ERROR_MORE_DATA), and its
  first 1 or 2 KiB too (E_INVALIDARG), where builds 26100 (windows-2025) and 26200 (jupiter)
  take it whole and in part (M345). The function it supersedes stays unused, deprecated as
  Microsoft marks it, so a snapshot taken there restores nowhere there, and a restore says
  why rather than an HRESULT alone; builds between 20348 and 26100 are unmeasured. Whether
  a host restores is asked of its hypervisor once a process, only where it is asked, so that
  no VM's start pays for it (`vm::restores_here`: the same page set back on a partition of
  one, and only that refusal says no): a daemon there keeps no template or warm pool and
  boots every run cold (D25, D26), and the tests of snapshots skip there, saying why.
- **A confined VM writes its snapshot through its spawner.** An AppContainer writes in no
  directory of its user's (D141), and a directory handle would give it every name in it: the
  spawner makes the snapshot's directory the VM asks to write in, stages each generation there
  on the VM's word (`kind::STAGE`), hands the VM the generation's files to fill, its memory
  and state and what its machine keeps beside them, its writable layer's head and file
  system (D190) and its DAX windows' heads (D189), as `STAGE`'s first byte asks
  (`platform::Kept`), and makes it durable and the one in use on its next (`kind::COMMIT`),
  as the daemon stages a run's save (D176), every file of the generation closed first: NTFS renames no
  directory a file in which is open (ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED, M345), so the VM's handed files go
  with its save, and a commit's own close before the rename that puts the generation in
  place, on every host. Once a generation is committed the spawner gives the directory
  up, as a Unix VM seals its own (vm_run.rs `seal`): a guest that took the VM's process over
  later cannot have every later restore of the template restore what it wrote. One staged and
  never committed goes with the VM. A template is saved by its image's first run, whose
  machine has a layer: staged with its memory and state alone, it was refused, and a Windows
  daemon's pools never filled (CI run 40602662393, 2026-10-27).
- **A restore reads its template through its grants**, as on macOS: the pointer, then the files
  of the generation it names (`granted_template`). A backing file's identity is its volume's
  serial number and its file index, as a Unix file's device and inode are: a file of the same
  bytes and times renamed over a disk is another (audit A18). An AppContainer may not even ask
  a file's metadata by its path (M201), so on Windows a restore first reads which backing files
  the snapshot's state names (`snapshot::backing_named`), has them granted, then reads the
  generation, and refuses one whose backing files changed between, a snapshot saved again as
  it was read. Its writable layer, where NTFS clones no file for it, it copies from the
  generation's into the empty file it is given: the ranges that hold data alone, which its
  spawner reads for it (`kind::RANGES`, FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES), as its save copied
  them, each layer's file sparse.
- **A rename over a file Windows will not yet let go of.** The store replaced its pointer and a
  generation's working set by renaming a new file over the old (`write_in`, a POSIX rename,
  M344). On jupiter Windows refused such renames (STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED): a single writer's once
  in 8,000, and eight writers' at once in episodes of a minute and more, Restart Manager naming
  no process holding the file (M345; Microsoft Defender's real-time protection was on, and
  logged nothing); in those holds it refused too the link and the move that might have
  stepped around one, while a rename of a file to a name no file had was never refused. So on
  Windows no write replaces a file: `write_in` lands each as its name's next version
  (`name.~N`, one past the highest listed, by a rename that replaces nothing; a writer that
  finds its version's name taken lists again), flushes the directory, then removes the
  versions before it, and a file at the name itself, where Windows lets them go. Versions
  count from those listed, never from a clock, which may step back. Readers take the newest
  (`platform::newest_in`): the store's pointer and working set, a template's record, and a
  confined VM's, through its spawner, which opens the newest for the path it asks
  (`grant::Access::ReadNewestIfThere`). The store's tidy removes the pointers a newer one
  superseded, and with no pointer to read keeps every generation; the daemon's sweep of
  templates takes every version of a record. Elsewhere `write_in` renames over the file, as
  rename(2) does. In five passes of the probe's writers on jupiter, 30,000 writes, none was
  refused (M345, 6). `point` writes the pointer by `write_in` on every host. A commit's rename
  of its generation's directory was never refused (M345: 2,000 commits, alone and beside
  churn).
- **What a restore costs** (M345, `benches/restore.rs`, jupiter, 256 MiB, n=100): a cold
  restore runs its guest again 69.8 ms after its process starts at p50, 84.8 at p99, a
  `shards restore` start to exit 171 ms; a warm one 59.6 ms after its release at p50, 71.6 at
  p99, its peak working set 10.1 MiB. Nearly all of it is the guest's first touches: a restore
  is ready to run 9 to 10 ms after its process starts, its vCPU entering the guest within 34
  µs of that, and from there to the guest's next store after its snapshot point took 79 to 95
  ms, and 3.4 ms with the whole of RAM populated at stage 2 beforehand (a populate that itself
  took 74 to 79 ms). The same at 1 GiB: what a guest touches, not what it has.
- **Not yet on WHP**: working sets (`vm::WORKING_SETS`), so a restore takes each page into
  stage 2 as its guest first touches it (M345: 6.4 µs a page read and 8.3 µs a page written
  at p50 on jupiter, where a populate maps a 2 MiB range at 0.4 to 0.7 µs a page, M341):
  what a working set recorded and populated ahead takes off a restore's path, with the
  daemon's templates and warm pools (D25, D26), which wait for the daemon on Windows (D195,
  the parity plan's step 4). Its recording is WHP's to find: no access bit is read back at
  stage 2, and a confined VM process may not ask its memory file's allocated ranges (an
  FSCTL, D141).

**Tested.** Unit: the states' round trips and damage, and a state naming any other register
refused (`hv::whp::state`); a restored IOAPIC going on as the saved one; a generation staged by
its spawner reading back once committed, and the store's every on-disk test, which run on
Windows now (`snapshot`), among them eight writers saving working sets into one generation at
once, which on jupiter failed in 3 runs of 10 with no fallback, in 3 of 10 with one retry
after a link, and in none of 25 with each refusal of another writer's file linked in turn; a
write landing as a version beside one held open that shares no delete, eight writers' at once
each landing whole, and a version one past the highest listed (`windows_files`); a spawner
granting a pointer written twice as its newest version (`grant_answer`); on Windows, a spawner
staging and committing a VM's snapshots over real pipes, refusing a stage elsewhere and a
commit of what is not staged, giving the directory up, and removing what is never committed
(`grant_answer`). On real WHP guests (jupiter and CI's windows-2025):
tests/snapshot.rs, every test, the storms of busy machines among them, which run on Windows
now, and the unwritable directory by an access list there; tests/restore.rs, cold restores of
one snapshot side by side and a held (warm) restore whose guest runs nothing until released.

### D195. The daemon and its client on Windows: request slots of named pipes (built)

**Why.** Every feature on every host (the user, 2026-10-27; docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md
row 1): on Windows `shards` had no daemon, so no `run IMAGE` and none of the commands of its
containers, images, volumes and networks. D185's slots are FIFOs in the home, their
streams handed by `SCM_RIGHTS`, its spawner a forked process: Windows has no FIFO in a
filesystem and passes no descriptor over a socket, and a process there is made, not
forked.

**Decided and built.**
- **Slots, named by files in the home** (`slots/named.rs`). Each list, without streams and
  with, is a named pipe whose name the file `requests/free` or `requests/free-streams`
  gives: a fresh random name each time the daemon makes its lists, the file written whole
  before it is renamed into place, so that a client reads a whole name or none. Its DACL
  grants the daemon's user alone, not an AppContainer of that user's (a VM process's) nor
  another user, and it refuses remote clients. A slot is an instance of its list's pipe: a
  client takes one by opening the name, which gives it an instance no client has opened,
  and no other client can then open that one (PM M340). The daemon's first word on it is
  its number; a slot with streams has three pipes more, `<list>-<N>.in`, `.out` and `.err`,
  each its name's first and only instance, so that no other process holds one first. Then,
  as on Unix, the client writes which streams it opened, what each descriptor its request
  stands for is, and its request. No socket of shards' own is made.
- **Liveness, each way**, as D185's: each side's end ends the other's reads after all it
  wrote (M340). A list's name lives while the daemon holds an instance of its own, as a
  Unix list has its daemon's reader. A client waits for a free slot in WaitNamedPipe, and
  hears of its daemon's end at once, its wait ending as the last instance closes (M348);
  it looks at the list's file again every quarter of a second, for a daemon that made its
  lists again under another name. A slot no client opened is stopped by an event of its
  own. Where the file names no pipe, or the pipe has no instance, the client starts the
  daemon. One daemon a home: it takes `daemon.lock` by LockFileEx (std's `try_lock`).
  A slot's `say` and `answer` being one instance, which its client hears end only once
  every handle of the daemon's has closed, the daemon reads what the client says only
  until its side has said all it will: a run whose microVM was killed left its client
  waiting for ever before (M348). Likewise a run's VM gives up its client's stdio at the
  run's end with its output first and without waiting on a read of its input, which an
  interactive client's open stdin never ends (M348).
- **Waits.** A read of no bytes on an overlapped pipe waits for what comes without taking
  it (M348): the daemon's followers wait on its runs' streams, and on processes' ends and
  events, through `pipe::Poller` (an I/O completion port, and a thread-pool wait on each
  process and event), and clients through `await_any`, where Unix has poll(2) and kqueue(2).
- **Handles where Unix passes descriptors.** A stream of `shards_ipc`'s carries handles:
  the sender duplicates each into its receiver's process (DuplicateHandle), and their
  values follow the message. A child's end takes them only from its spawner, its spawner
  none from it. So the daemon hands a run's VM the client's connection and the slot's
  streams as it does on Unix. A stream the daemon makes in pairs and gives one end of to a
  VM gives that VM its handles from the other: a joiner's connection, its provider's VM's
  (D119), whose run had reached the VM without them (M354). A VM's AppContainer opens no
  file by name, NUL included, which Windows Server refused it where Windows 11 let it open
  it (M351): the daemon opens NUL and gives it beside the VM's link, and the VM holds it
  for every client's stdio it lets go of, an `exec -d`'s among them.
- **A VM not ready says why** (M351). Its error closes its link as it returns, before the
  VM has written it, so the daemon gives a VM whose link closed a second to end of itself
  before it kills it, and says the status it ended with: its word of why reaches the
  daemon's log whole.
- **Cold boots held to the host's CPUs** (M357). Windows' daemon boots every run cold
  until the parity plan's step 4, and Server 2022's always, as it restores nothing (M345).
  Cold boots at once whose vCPUs pass the host's CPUs cost more than their work: eight of
  4 vCPUs at once on a 4-CPU runner took 52 to 55 s each on windows-2022, where one took
  1.6. On WHP the daemon holds the cold boots under way to their VMs' vCPUs of twice the
  host's CPUs, the most runs a second on both CI runners; a VM of more boots alone, and a
  restore takes no turn. Turns are taken in the order asked for (tickets, M357's hang: a
  boot asked for first waited out its client's minute as later ones went).
- **Not held across the host's daemons** (M376). Tried: a slot of the host's taken
  beside a daemon's turn, named mutexes every daemon on the host shared, two on CI's
  4-CPU runners. It tied each daemon to the slowest on its host: on windows-2025, where
  a boot alone takes 0.5 s quiet, 7 of containers.rs's 132 tests failed with it, their
  runs left Created as their boots waited on other tests' daemons' slots past their
  clients' minute, and all 132 passed without it (CI 40782667644 with it, 40796215375
  without it and with D196's sealed link besides, both quiet); on windows-2022 the one
  test that failed without it failed with it too, its daemon's one boot behind the
  others'. Each daemon
  counts its own boots alone: what a boot costs while others boot beside it is to be cut
  where it is spent (M376).
- **Lines and streams.** A slot's line holds 64 KiB, what a Linux FIFO holds (pipe(7)), so
  that what a client leaves untaken is what it leaves on Linux (D185, "What it said last");
  a stream's pipe holds 1 MiB, which moved more than 64 KiB in M340.
- **No spawner process** (D158). A Unix child is forked holding every descriptor its parent
  holds, so the daemon's children come from a process made before it held any. A Windows
  child is made by CreateProcess with the handles named for it alone
  (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST) and inherits nothing else, so the daemon makes its
  children itself. Having no console, it starts its confined VM processes detached: one
  started with CREATE_NO_WINDOW alone failed as it started (STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED, M348).
- **Another build's daemon steps aside**, `shards run daemon` serves and `shards stop daemon`
  ends it, as on Unix (D185).
- **Containers' directories** (M347). NTFS renames no directory while a file in it is open,
  and a run's VM or a reader of its log may hold one, so a removal marks its container's
  directory instead of renaming it: an empty file `.ID.removing` beside it, made durable by
  the containers' directory's sync as the rename is; the next start deletes a marked
  directory, then its mark. The directory is deleted where it is once no record of its
  container is being written (a write under way lands in it, which Windows leaves in
  place), and its mark only once that deletion is durable: removals completed together
  share that sync. A directory's entries are made durable by FlushFileBuffers of a handle
  to it that may write, in the VMM's platform and the image store, where Windows synced
  nothing before.
- **Files sized ahead are sparse** (M349). NTFS took every cluster of a file as it was
  sized, so each run's 10 GiB writable layer (D190) took 10 GiB of its disk at once, and
  eight runs filled jupiter's. A run's layer, its swap (D159) and a build's cache part
  (D134) are made sparse before they are sized, as a Unix file is: a running microVM's
  layer took 1.5 MiB.
- **Smaller things a daemon on Windows needed** (M348): guest RAM to plug (D133) reserved
  alone, its commit charge taken as each part is granted, since a host short of commit
  refused it whole; the daemon leaves its home before removing what is left of it, since
  Windows removes no directory a process stands in.

**Measured** (M347, M348, jupiter). A request through a slot costs 143 to 149 µs at p50 and
238 to 253 µs at p99, five times its two lines held open (28 µs), against 83 to 112 µs on
macOS and 34 µs on Linux (M254). A slot takes its daemon 7 µs to make and remove, 28 µs
with its streams, where macOS's FIFOs took 116 and 291 (M255): two are kept offered of each
kind, as on Unix. A removal costs 0.9 to 1.4 ms at p50 with its two syncs, against macOS's
4.3 (M46).

**Tested.** The slots' cases are one set that Unix's FIFOs and Windows' named pipes both
pass (`slots.rs`), beside each host's own (`fifo.rs`, `named.rs`, `pipe.rs`, `poll.rs`):
`shards_ipc`'s tests pass on jupiter, 58 of 58. A mutation run changed one line at each of
23 places of Windows' slots and pipes, among them a pipe's DACL granting Everyone and a
stream's pipe made without FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE, which another process could then
take first, and the tests caught every one: the last a client that read its list's name
just before its daemon made its lists anew (`take_listed`). On jupiter, 2026-10-27, the
daemon's and the containers' unit tests pass, 225 of 225, and tests/daemon.rs with real
microVMs, 37 of 37, `an_idle_daemon_wakes_for_nothing` among them, each thread's cycles
read there (QueryThreadCycleTime) where Linux reads its switches. Its eleven pool and
template tests, which the parity plan's step 4 takes up, skip there (`cannot_pool`), and so
do those of the other suites that reach a daemon's templates, warm pools and saves (images,
run, saved, warm): its daemon boots every run cold until then, though WHP takes snapshots
(D196). Those it leaves out on Windows are Unix's by nature (a terminal's job control,
descriptor limits, systemd's slices) or a later step's (the Engine API's stream, step 8;
FUSE under a budget, steps 6 and 7). Every command of the catalog was asked of a daemon
there once and answered; `pause` said a microVM was not paused on Windows yet, until a
pause became the VMM's own on every host (D191, step 2). On CI's Windows runners, nested in
Azure VMs of 4 CPUs, tests/daemon.rs passes too with real microVMs, 37 of 37 on each, the
same eleven skipping: on windows-2022 (Windows Server 2022, 10.0.20348) and windows-2025
(Windows Server 2025, 10.0.26100) at 61a07442 (CI 40618994939), and windows-2025 at
b7d8ee30 before (CI 40601221843). There it had first failed whole, every VM refused NUL
(M351); then, on windows-2022, two tests whose cold boots ran beside others' waited past
the daemon's 60 s, until cold boots waited their turn (M357). `shards_ipc`'s tests pass on
both, their pipe's DACL read by SID (M354).

**Not on Windows yet**, each refused with a message that says so, each a later step of the
parity plan: a host's network (step 5); a host's directories as volumes and binds (step 6);
memory given back under a budget (step 7); the Engine API, another machine's clients,
`--use-api-socket` and what log drivers wait on a TCP connection for (step 8). Templates,
warm pools and saves are served (step 4, on WHP's snapshots, D196), and published ports
(step 5, D142).

### D194. The registries Docker's daemon configuration names: an insecure one asked in plain HTTP too, Docker Hub's mirrors first (built)

**Found.** A registry off loopback that speaks plain HTTP, a `registry:2` on another
machine of a LAN, a CI job's, could be neither pulled from nor pushed to: shards asked
every registry in HTTPS but loopback's (containerd's defaults, `core/remotes/docker/
registry.go`), and nothing could say otherwise. dockerd takes such a registry from its
daemon.json's `insecure-registries`, and Docker Hub's mirrors from its `registry-mirrors`;
shards read neither, and its `info` left out the `Insecure Registries` lines docker/cli
prints.

**Decided.**
- **Read where Docker's daemons read it** (`shards_registry::registries`): Docker Desktop's
  `~/.docker/daemon.json` (docker/docs `desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings.md`), the
  rootless engine's `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/docker/daemon.json` or `~/.config/docker/daemon.json`,
  and the native one's `/etc/docker/daemon.json`, `%PROGRAMDATA%\docker\config\daemon.json`
  on Windows (`engine/daemon/_index.md`); what they name taken together, found through the
  environment of whoever asks, as `certs.d` is (D23). A missing file names nothing; one that
  cannot be read, or whose two keys hold what dockerd refuses, fails the pull, naming the
  file and why, as dockerd would not start with it. Checked as dockerd checks them (moby
  docker-v29.8.1 `daemon/pkg/registry/config.go`, `loadInsecureRegistries`,
  `ValidateMirror`).
- **Which registries are insecure**: one named by its `host[:port]` as a reference names it
  (dockerd's `IndexConfigs` keys), or one with an address in a network named in CIDR
  notation, its name looked up within a dial's time where any network is named
  (`isCIDRMatch`).
- **How one is asked**: in HTTPS first, then in plain HTTP once it answers HTTPS so or never
  finishes the handshake (containerd's `isTLSError`, as a loopback registry on a port is
  asked); one named without a port, once its HTTPS port refuses the connection too, then at
  HTTP's port, as dockerd tries its `https://` endpoint and then its `http://` one
  (`lookupV2Endpoints`). Pulls, pushes, logins and searches alike.
- **Better than dockerd**, three deliberate differences:
  - its certificate is verified where it answers in HTTPS, against `certs.d` and the
    system's roots, as every registry's is: dockerd skips verifying an insecure registry's
    (`newTLSConfig`, `InsecureSkipVerify = !isSecure`) and reads no `certs.d` for it. One
    whose CA no system trusts is refused; its CA in `certs.d` is the remedy, as D167
    refuses `splunk-insecureskipverify` and asks for its CA;
  - its credentials never go to it in plain HTTP: a registry off this machine that asks for
    them there is refused, saying so, where dockerd answers its Basic challenge with the
    password (`daemon/internal/distribution/registry.go`, `newRepository`: one credential
    store for every endpoint). A loopback registry is still given them, as containerd gives
    them (`dockerAuthorizer`);
  - no registry's name is looked up to decide whether it is loopback's: dockerd's networks
    always hold loopback's, so it looks up every registry's name at each pull, and takes one
    that resolves to loopback for insecure. shards takes `localhost` and loopback addresses
    alone, and looks a name up only where a network is named; a registry that resolves to
    loopback is named by its name.
- **Docker Hub's mirrors** (`registry-mirrors`, slice 2): a pull from Docker Hub asks each
  in order first, as dockerd does (`lookupV2Endpoints`, mirrors for pulls alone), then
  Docker Hub; pushes, deletes, logins and searches never ask a mirror. A mirror is a
  registry of its own (`Registry::mirror`): its host's certificates (`certs.d`) and its
  host's credentials, where its user logged in to it, never Docker Hub's, which dockerd
  gives a mirror (`newRepository`: one credential store for every endpoint); one in plain
  HTTP off this machine is asked with none. A request of the repository goes to the first
  mirror that has not failed; one that cannot give a manifest or a blob, or cannot be
  reached, is asked nothing more for the pull, as dockerd goes on to its next endpoint
  after any error of a mirror's (`continueOnError`); one with no list asked for
  (referrers, tags) is asked the next request still, where dockerd asks none. Tested:
  `registry`'s `a_pull_asks_its_mirrors_first_and_a_failed_one_nothing_more`
  (mutation-checked), and `images`' `a_mirror_daemon_json_names_serves_docker_hubs_pull`:
  `test/image:v1`, a Docker Hub name, pulled from a mirror on loopback, its digest the
  test image's.
- **`info` says them** as dockerd does: `RegistryConfig`'s `IndexConfigs` (Docker Hub's,
  with its mirrors, and each named insecure, not secure), its `InsecureRegistryCIDRs` (the
  networks named, then loopback's) and `Mirrors`; and in its text, as docker/cli lays them
  out (`prettyPrintServerInfo`), the `Insecure Registries` and `Registry Mirrors` lines,
  which it left out before.
- **Tested**: `registries`' (each key read and refused as dockerd reads and refuses it, a
  registry insecure by its name or its network, every file read together); `registry`'s
  (a registry at this host's address on its route out answering HTTPS in plain HTTP: asked
  in HTTPS alone unnamed, in HTTPS once and then in plain HTTP named, its credentials
  refused there and never sent; where each kind of registry is asked in plain HTTP);
  `info`'s text and JSON; and `images`' `a_registry_daemon_json_names_insecure_is_pulled_from_in_plain_http`:
  `shards pull` from such a registry fails, then pulls once the rootless engine's file
  names it, then fails again, naming the file, once it holds what dockerd refuses. The
  fallback and the credentials' refusal are mutation-checked.

**Next.** A mirror that answers but stalls a blob's body: the pull's resumes go on asking
it (fetch.rs), where dockerd's pull would fall to its next endpoint.

### D193. A run past its pids limit says so: a `pids-limit` event (built)

**Found** (kiln's harnesses, 2026-10-21). A run held to `--pids-limit` whose processes or
threads were refused, a fork or clone past its cgroup's `pids.max` failing with EAGAIN,
said nothing of it: its command failed as such a failure makes it, and nothing outside its
microVM said why. dockerd says nothing either: no event, and its State has no such field.
A harness that sorts its runs' failures could not tell a pids limit from any other.

**Decided.**
- **init reads the workload cgroup's `pids.events`** as the run ends, where its end is said
  alone and where its joiners go on past it (D119): a `max` count above 0 goes to the host
  before `EXIT` as `PIDS` (shards_abi::run::kind::PIDS, `pids_refused`), with the cgroup's
  `pids.max`, `pids.peak`, the count and `pids.events` whole, as `OOM` goes with memory's
  (D159). `max.imposed`, a newer kernel's count of an ancestor's limit, is not it.
- **The VM process passes it on** (shards_ipc::kind::PIDS), as it passes `OOM`; the daemon
  logs the facts and says a **`pids-limit` event** of the container's, shards' own action
  (dockerd has none): its attributes the name and image every event of a container's has,
  with `pids.max` and `refused`. Docker's typed State stays Docker's: inspect gains
  nothing.
- **A joiner's too** (D119): init reads its own cgroup's `pids.events` as its process is
  reaped, before its cgroup goes, as its OOM is read (D159), and sends `PIDS` before its
  `EXIT`; the VM process passes it on as it passes a joiner's `OOM`, and the event is the
  joiner's container's.
- **Tested** (containers.rs `a_run_past_its_pids_limit_says_so`, on real microVMs): a
  `--pids-limit 4` run starting eight threads at once says one `pids-limit` event, with
  `pids.max` 4 and a count of what was refused, and the daemon's log its facts; a run
  within its limit says none; a `--network container:` joiner held to `--pids-limit 4`
  says its own, by its own name (without init's read of its cgroup, the test fails).

### D192. A network's egress: its members' own commands reach the destinations it names, and nothing else (built)

**Found** (kiln's harnesses, 2026-10-21). A run's own command had three reaches past its
microVM: none (`--network none`, and every network by default), its network's own members,
or everything (`--network host`, D124). An Agentfile's egress and remote MCP grants are its
agents' (D59), never the command's (D115). So a sandboxed run could not be granted
"api.anthropic.com on 443, and its name": the one thing an agent harness needs, and
`--network host` gave it all of the host's reach instead.

**Decided.**
- **Where a grant lives: on a network**, as shards' own driver option `shards.egress`
  (`networks::EGRESS`): `docker network create --opt shards.egress=HOST:PORT[,...]`, which
  the Docker CLI, a Compose file's `driver_opts` and the Engine API's NetworkCreate all
  say, so no flag of `docker run`'s is added (its flags stay docker/cli's, held to them by
  the CLI's golden answers). Who is granted: the network's members, each joined by name;
  to whom: each destination, a host's name or an IPv4 address; which port: its TCP port;
  which way: out alone. A network without the option grants nothing past its microVMs,
  as before: default deny.
- **Held by the member's network process**, as a remote MCP server's grant is (D59 part
  seven): its policy the destinations alone (`encode_policy`, no ports, the names), a flow
  passed only to an address its own resolver answered for a destination's name, or the
  address a destination is, on that destination's port; and of names, only the
  destinations' asked of the host's resolver (`SHARDS_DNS` or its own), every other
  question REFUSED. A member asks through the network's relay at 127.0.0.11 (D46), which
  asks the gateway, where the network process answers its members' names and the granted
  ones.
- **Refused where it could not be held.** A destination that is no `HOST:PORT` (a port of 1
  to 65535; a host a name of DNS's letters, digits and hyphens, or an IPv4 address; no
  pattern, no IPv6 address yet), said as the network is made; on a driver but bridge, or
  an internal network, whose members reach nothing past their microVMs; and, as a run
  starts, beside its image's agents' grants past the microVM: its network process holds
  those for the whole microVM, and its command's flows and its agents' come to it alike,
  so the command would reach what the agents were granted (D115).
- **Tested** (containers.rs `a_networks_egress_is_a_grant_of_its_destinations_alone`, on
  real microVMs): a member reaches its destination by name; not another port of the same
  host, not a name the destinations do not name though the host's resolver has it, not
  the destination's address in a microVM that never asked its name; a run of the default
  bridge reaches none of it; and the option's refusals as the network is made. build.rs
  `a_remote_mcp_server_is_a_grant_of_that_server_alone`: beside an image's agents' grants,
  the start is refused. networks' `egress_names_each_destination_and_its_port` holds the
  option's reading.

**Next.** IPv6 destinations (the network process learns A records alone); a destination
on a network whose members' images have agents with grants of their own, held apart by
the address its flows come from; a run's own grant on the default bridge, if one is
asked for beside a network's.

### D191. A run's microVM has every CPU of its host, its workload the CPUs its limits give it (slices 1 and 2 built)

The user's plan, item 3 (2026-10-18): a run's `--cpus` as elastic as its memory (D148),
every microVM given the host's CPUs, init bringing the run's online and `update --cpus`
more or fewer. Bringing a CPU online as a run starts costs what no start has: 13 ms a CPU
on HVF and 45 on KVM where the microVM has the host's (PM M265: 31 brought online in 1.40
s), and taking one offline stops every other (kernel/cpu.c, `stop_machine`). So every CPU
stays online, in the template and in every run, and a run is held to what it is given
inside its microVM, as a Linux host holds a container's processes (decided 2026-10-20, and
the user told).

- **Its microVM: every CPU of the host's** (`resources::microvm_vcpus`), whatever its
  limits, as D125 gave a run without one. Every run of an image restores one template,
  as every `-m` does (D148), where each count had its own, booted and saved by its first
  run.
- **Its workload: the CPUs its limits give it**, its cgroup's `cpuset.cpus`
  (`resources::cgroup`): `--cpuset-cpus`'s; else its microVM's first N, N `--cpu-count`'s,
  else as many as `--cpus`, the quota or `--cpu-percent` needs (`resources::run_cpus`,
  D155), every one with none; `cpu.max` as before. Its processes see what a microVM of
  those CPUs alone showed them, `nproc` (sched_getaffinity) N; its guest's online CPUs are
  the host's, as a container's are.
- **The host holds its vCPUs to the same CPUs** (slice 2, `vm::hold`). Its workload is
  held inside its microVM; but a workload root of its own guest may leave its cgroup —
  with `--privileged --cgroupns host` it writes itself into the microVM's cgroup root,
  out of the run's cpuset, onto every CPU (PM M289). So the VM process holds its vCPU
  threads together to as many of the host's CPUs as the run's limits let its workload use
  at once (`resources::held_cpus`: the fewest of `--cpu-count`'s, the quota's rounded up,
  and the cpuset's; none where that is every CPU). A governor thread reads each vCPU
  thread's CPU time (`platform::ThreadClock`: Linux its CPU-time clock, which counts its
  time in the guest; macOS thread_info, PM M288; Windows GetThreadTimes), and once a 100
  ms period's share is spent holds every vCPU out of its guest, by the same kick a
  snapshot uses, until the period ends; what a period overran comes off the next. The
  governor runs as it wakes, however busy its vCPUs keep the CPUs they may use: on macOS
  at the vCPUs' real-time policy (M8, M10), on Windows at THREAD_PRIORITY_TIME_CRITICAL,
  above them, where at their priority three spinning threads of a process held to two CPUs
  kept it from running and used up to 1.58 s in a second held to one (PM M294). This
  bounds the whole guest — kernel threads, interrupts, and any escaped workload — to what
  a microVM of those CPUs alone could use, where the cpuset alone bounds only a workload
  that stays in its cgroup. It comes with the run (the `RUN` head's `cpus`), before the
  guest hears of the run, and `update` moves it (below).
- **A pause is the same hold, whole** (`Handle::pause`, the daemon's `PAUSE`, 2026-10-28):
  every vCPU kicked out of its guest and held there, whatever its share, until the microVM
  goes on; the daemon answers `pause` once its VM says each is held. It replaced a stop of
  the VM process (SIGSTOP), which Windows has no documented call for (NtSuspendProcess is
  ntdll's, undocumented), where WHP's kick is WHvCancelRunVirtualProcessor, documented,
  and holds for a run that has not begun (M198): one pause on every host. The VM process
  goes on answering its daemon and serving its devices as its guest is frozen, and a
  frozen microVM's VM process takes next to no CPU time, as
  `pause_freezes_a_microvm_until_unpause_or_stop` reads it from the host. A save of a
  paused microVM lets it go on for its guest to go quiet, as the stop's continue did.
- **`update` moves them, both ways.** A running run's `--cpus`, quota, `--cpu-count` or
  `--cpuset-cpus` changed writes its cpuset and quota at once (`builtin::CGROUP`, D40), a
  raise giving it CPUs it had not; before, a raise past its microVM's vCPUs bound at them.
  Where the CPUs its workload may use at once change, its VM is told the new hold first
  (`kind::CPUS`), on the link the cgroup write comes on after, as `update -m` tells it the
  new memory (D148).
- **Measured (PM M288; macOS on an Apple M5 Max, Linux on M258's i9-14900HX).** A count's
  first run 13.5 ms on macOS and 16.7 on Linux, where it booted and saved a template in
  216 and 694; one warm pool for every limit, three VM processes held where five and seven,
  22 MiB less footprint (macOS) and 63 MiB less Pss (Linux) in all; after `update --cpus 4`
  of a `--cpus 1` run, 4.01 and 4.04 CPUs used where 1.00 and 1.02. A run with a limit pays
  what one without pays: 5 MiB more of its VM process's footprint at `--cpus 1` (Linux 8.4
  of Pss), and its start, 2.5 ms more at p50 paced on macOS (12.73 against 10.23 ms), 2.6
  back to back on Linux; on a contended host 22 ms more (PM M292: 17.9 against 39.7 ms at
  p50, a `--cpus 1` run on 4 CPUs that 4 busy loops hold), slice 1's own. The host's hold
  (PM M289, n 10 a side): an escaped workload of a `--cpus 1` run uses 1.02 CPUs held, 3.99
  where only its microVM's cgroups hold it; on an idle host it costs a run nothing
  measurable.
- **Tested.** resources' `workload_limits_are_written` (a cpuset for every run: none given
  its microVM's every CPU, a quota's first N, `--cpu-count`'s); on real microVMs,
  `a_microvm_takes_its_cpus_real_time_isolation_and_annotations` (`--cpu-count 2` CPUs 0-1,
  every CPU of the host's online; `--cpu-percent 50` its share on half of them),
  `run_limits_a_microvms_resources` (`--cpus 1.5 --cpuset-cpus 0`: CPU 0, every CPU
  online) and `update_changes_limits_of_running_microvms` (`--cpus 1.5`, then the host's
  count: CPUs 0-1, then every one, and their quota). The host hold: resources'
  `microvms_are_held_to_their_runs_cpus` (the fewest of each limit's CPUs, none for every
  one); `vm::hold`'s own tests (threads held to one CPU use about the time passing, not
  every CPU's; a hold of every CPU holds nothing; the end lets a held vCPU go); on a real
  microVM `a_workload_past_its_cgroup_is_held_to_its_cpus_by_its_host` (a privileged
  guest-root workload that writes itself to the cgroup root, out of a `--cpus 1` cpuset,
  uses no more than one CPU's time, where without a limit four threads run free), and
  `platform`'s `a_threads_clock_counts_what_it_runs`. Mutation-checked: a run naming no
  cpuset given none fails resources' test, the CPUs test and the update test; a microVM of
  its run's CPUs alone fails the limits test and the CPUs test; the host hold removed, the
  escaped workload's four threads use four CPUs' time (11.41 s of CPU in 3.03 s, PM M289).
- **Next.**
  - A start on a contended host, this slice's regression (PM M292: 22 ms more at p50 on
    4 busy CPUs, 2 to 3 idle, M288): where a microVM's vCPUs, one for each host CPU, spend
    it, and taking off what is not its guest's own. Every run without a limit pays it
    too. Its timing line (`SHARDS_TIMING`) splits a start's phases.
  - What the hold costs a memory-heavy run on a contended host: fills 9 and 16% longer
    there (PM M292, n 8, its load rising). Repeated before it is read, and then why.

### D190. A run's writable layer on its host's disk: ext4 with DAX over pmem (slices 1 to 6 built)

A run's writable layer, the upper directory of its root's overlay, was a tmpfs in its
microVM's memory (D16, D156): what it wrote was memory, held to its memory limit, and gone
with its microVM unless packed as it stopped (D37). A test suite's build there ran its 8
GiB microVM out of memory every round of the sustained-I/O benchmark (PM M266). Now it is an
ext4 file system in a file of the run's own on its host's disk, on a virtio-pmem device of
its own, mounted with DAX: the guest's CPUs read and write its files as the host's page
cache of that file, which the host writes back and takes back as it would any file's, and
the guest keeps their metadata alone.

- **The device.** A head, then the file system, the run's file mapped shared and
  writable (vmm `pmem::Layer`). The head holds an NVDIMM pfn info block at 4 KiB
  (drivers/nvdimm/pfn.h, `nd_pfn_sb`, PFN_MODE_PMEM), which the host writes and the
  guest's libnvdimm finds as it probes the device: so its kernel keeps the device's page
  structures, which DAX needs, a 64th of the device, in the head itself (a vmem_altmap)
  rather than in its memory: a 64 GiB layer took none of an x86_64 guest's, where M264's
  page structures took a 64th of the device (PM M277). Each of the device's 128 MiB
  sections takes a 2 MiB block of them, at a 2 MiB boundary past the info block's 8 KiB
  (mm/sparse-vmemmap.c), so the head
  is two blocks more than a block a section, and the device starts at a section
  (`layer_head`). Init finds it by the address the control page gives (`control::LAYER`)
  and mounts its ext4 `dax=always,noinit_itable,no_prefetch_block_bitmaps` where it
  mounted the tmpfs. A machine without one, a joiner's root among them (D119), keeps its
  tmpfs. `no_prefetch_block_bitmaps`: ext4lazyinit reads every group's block bitmap and
  builds its buddy cache in the background after a mount (fs/ext4/super.c,
  `ext4_run_li_request`), so that a first allocation does not wait on a disk, where a DAX
  device's bitmap is memory; and as a template mounts its layer before its snapshot,
  every restored guest did that work again, which in a nested arm64 guest under load
  held a CPU 22 to 27 s (soft lockups in the logs of each of 5 failing rounds before, of
  none of 6 after; PM M346). What it saves a warm VM's memory is unmeasured.
- **Mounted in the template.** A mount took 0.4 to 0.65 ms at p50 and an overlay over it
  0.2 to 0.32 ms more on a guest that had mounted it before, 1 to 80 ms the first time (PM
  M277), where a run's whole start is 0.73 ms at p50 (M230): so the template mounts it
  as it boots, before its snapshot, and the snapshot keeps it, and every run restored
  from the template resumes with it mounted. A restore is given, in the home's `layers`,
  the file system its snapshot kept as a copy-on-write clone of it, where the home's file
  system clones files (APFS's fclonefileat(2), Btrfs's and XFS's FICLONE: slice 3), its
  blocks the snapshot's until its run writes them, so that nothing is copied as it
  restores and, on macOS, nothing written back (PM M278); else an empty file, which it
  fills with a copy. Either is the very generation's it resumes: the daemon names the
  generation it cloned (`--layer-cloned`), and a clone of another, a template saved again
  meanwhile, is filled as an empty file is (`copies_layer`), so that no run is paired with
  another generation's layer. Before any vCPU runs; off the request's path, as warm VMs
  are restored ahead of their runs (D26), but for a run's own snapshot (D176), whose
  `restore vm` it is on: one that holds 512 MiB restores in 34.7 ms at p50 from a clone,
  where from a copy it took 206.0 (Fedora's Btrfs; on the Mac's APFS 106.6 against
  350.6), a clone costing a restore the same whatever its layer holds, and nothing after
  it pays for one (PM M282).
- **Made by the host.** `shards-ext4` makes the file system a boot is given: what mke2fs
  1.47.0 makes for ext4 by default, less what a layer has no use for (no blocks kept to
  grow it, for root, or for an orphan file), its inode tables zeros as the sparse file
  reads, which neither mke2fs's lazy init nor the kernel's then writes. Held to e2fsck
  1.47.0, which finds nothing to fix in any of seven sizes from 8 MiB to 64 GiB
  (`scripts/ext4/generate`, `e2fsck_finds_nothing_to_fix`), and to mke2fs's own
  checksums of each structure (`checksums_agree_with_mke2fss`); every guest of M277's
  mounted one with DAX.
- **Its size.** It holds 10 GiB unless the run asks for another (`--storage-opt size`),
  Docker's device-mapper driver's default for a container's base device, a block
  device's writable layer as this is (dockerd's `dm.basesize`): what the file system's
  own metadata, its journal and the blocks the kernel keeps back (2% or 4096 clusters)
  take is added (`shards_ext4::size_for`). A size is a template of its own (its key holds
  it). One whose page structures, a 64th of it, would take more memory as its microVM
  boots than its host has is refused, as one past ext4's 16 TiB is.
- **Snapshots** (format 24) keep the layer's length in MiB, its head and its file system
  beside the memory: the head's 2 MiB blocks each once, after an index of them, since all
  but a few describe sections none of whose pages is in use, alike to the byte (a 10 GiB
  layer's head of 85 blocks kept in 5: 12 MiB where 170 MiB whole); a restore maps each
