  block privately where the head had it. A save of a running microVM (D176) keeps both
  as a template's snapshot does (`prepare` makes a run's five files).
- **A template's head mapped back** (slice 4). A booted microVM's head is memory of its
  own, written whole as its guest's kernel probes the device, and the template's microVM
  goes on as its image's first run, which held it for its life: with a 10 GiB layer 282.3
  MiB of physical footprint on the Mac and 257.1 MiB resident on Fedora, where a warm
  microVM restored from the template holds 13.9 and 37.3 (PM M277, M284). Once the
  template's snapshot is written, with every vCPU still parked, the VM maps its head back
  from the snapshot's copy as a restore maps one (`Layer::remap_head`): each block
  privately from the copy, the blocks alike one block's pages in the host's page cache,
  as the template's restores' are, and the blocks of zeros fresh memory. HVF's stage 2
  holds the pages it maps (PM M193), so the head is taken from the guest meanwhile and
  given back after, through the stage 2 the layer is given as it is mapped
  (`Layer::placed`); KVM's follows the host's mapping as it changes
  (KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION, Documentation/virt/kvm/api.rst). The first run then holds
  112.0 MiB (Mac) and 89.7 MiB (Fedora), 170 and 167 less; the mapping takes 4.97 and 1.65
  ms at p50, while the run's start waits for its template anyway, and a program the run
  then runs from its layer, whose page structures its guest writes, ran as quickly within
  the runs' spread (PM M284). One that fails partway leaves each block the copy's or the guest's own memory,
  which hold the same, and is said; one whose guest cannot be given its head back leaves
  the layer lost (`Layer::lost`), and the machine stops.
- **A save's copy asks what the file holds with nothing mapping it** (slice 5). A save
  copies the ranges of the layer's file that hold data, as lseek(2) SEEK_DATA and
  SEEK_HOLE say, but APFS says that a file mapped shared and writable, by the VM process
  or by its guest through Hypervisor.framework, holds data throughout, untouched or
  written, flushed or not, until neither mapping is left (PM M285): a template's copy of a
  10 GiB layer read all of it, 3 to 12 s of its image's first run as the host's load went
  (PM M284, M285). Where a mapping
  hides a file's holes (`platform::MAPPED_HIDES_HOLES`, macOS; a test holds it to what
  the host's file system does), the save takes the file system from the guest's stage 2
  and withholds the VM's own mapping while it asks, then maps both back
  (`Shared::data_ranges`); a run's swap is saved the same way. A template's writing then
  took 127 ms at p50 where it took 4,178, and the image's
  first run 707 ms where it took 5,152; a run's save that leaves
  it running 356 ms where it took 3,313 (PM M285).
  Linux's Btrfs and tmpfs answer as they would unmapped, and nothing is taken away there.
  One whose guest will not give its mapping up, or whose own cannot be withheld, copies
  the file whole, as before; one that cannot be put back leaves the layer lost, and the
  machine stops.
- **A guest's fsync is the host's** (slice 6). A guest's flush of the layer
  (VIRTIO_PMEM_REQ_TYPE_FLUSH), which its fsync waits for (drivers/nvdimm/nd_virtio.c,
  `virtio_pmem_flush`), was answered at once, and the run's root overlay was mounted
  `volatile`, which omits every sync of its upper (Documentation/filesystems/overlayfs.rst):
  a container's fsync made nothing durable on its host, where Docker's overlay2 passes it to
  the host's file system. The root is now `volatile` only over a tmpfs, which nothing
  outlives, and the device makes the layer durable before it answers (`Layer::flush`,
  `platform::sync_mapped`), outside guest memory's access, which other devices go on taking:
  fdatasync on Linux, which writes back what the guest wrote through the mapping; on macOS
  F_FULLFSYNC, the one call there whose data is persisted when it returns (fsync(2):
  without it a drive may lose or reorder what fsync gave it, "not a theoretical edge case"),
  and which writes back pages written through a mapping, which fsync leaves dirty (PM M286).
  As Firecracker's flush msyncs its device's file (docs/pmem.md) and QEMU's fsyncs it. ext4
  commits with two flushes, a pre-flush then its commit block's FUA (`journal_async_commit`,
  one, it refuses with `data=ordered`), so a guest's fsync costs two: 3.64 ms at p50 on
  Fedora's Btrfs and 26.6 on the Mac, F_FULLFSYNC 3 to 16 ms as the host's load went, where
  before it cost 0.68 ms and nothing it wrote was the host's to keep (PM M286). A run's
  swap and an image hold nothing past their run: their flushes are done at once.
- **Its file is its run's, then its container's.** A layer's file stays in the home's
  `layers` while its microVM serves its run, the daemon holding it with the microVM; what
  a daemon before left there is no run's by the next, which removes it as it starts. A
  container that stays keeps it once the microVM has gone (slice 2), in its directory as
  `layer.ext4`, in place of the layer it had; every other run's goes with its microVM.
- **Kept as it stops, not packed** (slice 2). As a run ends, its host asks the guest to
  keep its layer (`kind::KEEP`) where it asked it to pack one (`kind::SAVE`, D37): init says
  what the layer uses, writes beside its overlay's directories which directories its pack
  leaves out (`shards-made-only`: those holding nothing but init's own `/etc` files, as the
  image has them), syncs every file system (sync(2), its volumes' too), and writes the
  layer's journal in place (syncfs, then EXT4_IOC_CHECKPOINT, fs/ext4/ioctl.c, Linux 5.13:
  jbd2_journal_flush, every transaction written where its blocks are and the log emptied,
  `s_start` 0), so that its host reads it as it stands, with nothing to replay. A guest
  kernel without the ioctl leaves its journal committed, which its host replays (below).
  Then the VM process stops the machine, the guest having nothing left to write, rather
  than wait for its power-off (2 to 37 ms on the Mac), and says the layer is kept
  (`LAYER_KEPT`) only once nothing of the machine can write it: once no vCPU runs and the
  device workers are quiet, and on macOS once it has let go of the file too
  (`Running::wait_then`): there, whoever lets go of a file last after writing it through a
  shared mapping writes it back before the call returns, and whoever reads the file
  meanwhile waits (`platform::LET_GO_WRITES_BACK`). Until it says so the daemon reads
  nothing of the file: as the VM's link ended, its guest could still be powering off. A
  restore on macOS has its copy of its template's layer written back on a thread of its
  own as it restores (`platform::write_back_ahead`), so that what its VM lets go of at its
  end is its run's own writes. The guest's part took 0.50 ms (Mac) and 0.90 ms (Fedora) at
  p50, 1.9 at most, where a freeze (FIFREEZE: the same writes, and the file system then
  marked as needing no recovery, fs/ext4/super.c ext4_freeze) took 16 and 32 ms the first
  time in each microVM, 63 at most, and a read-only remount 3.6 and 7.3 (PM M278). A
  microVM whose run has containers joined to its network (D119) packs its layer as before:
  they go on in it, and its file with them.
- **Read on the host.** `shards-ext4`'s reader reads a kept layer as Linux 6.18 reads one
  (super.c, inode.c, extents.c, dir.c, namei.c, xattr.c, acl.c): its guest's bytes, which
  the host trusts no more than an image's, every structure that carries a checksum checked
  against it (metadata_csum), every number against the file system, a damaged one or one
  of a feature it does not read refused; held to e2fsprogs' own reader, debugfs, over a
  tree of every kind of file mke2fs -d copies into one, its directories indexed by e2fsck -D
  (`scripts/ext4/generate`, `a_volume_reads_as_debugfs_reads_it`), and read without panic
  however its bytes are changed. shards-archive packs it through `Files` as it packs the
  host's own files (`pack_from`), as go-archive packs a Linux host's, whatever the host:
  `commit` of a stopped container takes that pack, and its next run (`start`) and a visit
  to its files (`cp`, `diff`, `export`, D37) put it back as they put back a packed layer,
  the same bytes as its guest's pack of it (init's made-only rule now compares with the
  image's directory, where it compared with the root's own, which shows the copy: always
  alike).
- **Replayed where its microVM died.** A file system mounted is marked as needing recovery
  until its kernel unmounts or freezes it; one whose journal's log is empty, as a
  checkpoint leaves it, holds nothing to replay (jbd2_journal_recover: "No recovery
  required") and is read as it stands, the host writing nothing to it. A microVM killed
  before its guest wrote its journal in place leaves what its guest committed in its log,
  not yet in place. Its container keeps it all the same where its command had started (a
  run that never started leaves the layer it had), and its journal is replayed on the host
  before it is read (`shards_ext4::journal`), as jbd2 replays one as it mounts it
  (fs/jbd2/recovery.c, its three passes: the log's whole transactions found, its revoke
  records taken, each block it logged written in place but those a later transaction
  revoked, each checked against its tag's checksum first), then, once what it wrote is in
  the file (as jbd2 syncs its device first), the journal marked empty and the file system
  as needing none: a host stopped partway finds it to replay again, or replayed. Held
  block for block to debugfs's own replay
  (`journal_run`) of transactions debugfs wrote (`journal_write`: blocks, one escaped for
  jbd2's magic, a revoke, a later block over an earlier), but for two fields of debugfs's
  own (`s_lastcheck`, `s_kbytes_written`); a transaction whose commit block does not hold
  is not replayed; and replayed without panic however its log's bytes are changed.
- **Measured against packing** (PM M278, n = 20 a side, interleaved). A stop costs the
  same. `diff` of a stopped container is 25 to 84% quicker at 4 and 64 MiB written on both
  hosts and at 0 on the Mac (6.75 ms against 32.56), and on Fedora at 0 0.41 ms slower at
  p50; `start` quicker on the Mac at every size (64 MiB: 275 ms against 397) and on Fedora
  the same at 0 and 4 MiB and 4% quicker at 64; `commit` the same or quicker. Open: the
  Mac's `run` right after the same daemon's `rm -f` and `rmi`, its p90 at 0 B 24.76 ms
  against 6.68.
- **Tests.** `shards-ext4`'s, including the oracles'; `pmem`'s for the head's size, its
  info block's checksum, a layer saved and restored, a head's alike blocks kept once, a
  booted head mapped back from its saved copy, its own memory given back, taken from its
  guest meanwhile, a save that asks where the layer's file holds data with its mappings
  away, and a flush answered once what the guest wrote is its file's; `platform`'s that a
  mapping hides a file's holes where `MAPPED_HIDES_HOLES` says;
  the snapshot's for a run's five files; `layers`' for the files the daemon makes and
  removes; on real microVMs, `a_microvm_takes_its_ipc_hostname_cgroups_umask_and_writable_layer`:
  sizes held to, refusals, and 256 MiB written under `--memory 64m`; and
  `a_stopped_microvms_layer_stays_in_its_file`: a stopped container's `layer.ext4`, its
  journal written in place, holding its file and its whiteout, put back as it starts
  again; a microVM killed after its guest committed a file, its layer kept with its
  journal to replay, replayed as `diff` visits it, and the file found.

- **Read at random until its command runs** (PM M297). A run's first write into its root
  landed in a hole of its layer's file, a clone made for its warm microVM of whose pages its
  host held none, and the host read 4 MiB around it (Btrfs's readahead): 2.4 ms of a 5 ms
  start, every run. The layer's mapping is advised MADV_RANDOM as it is made
  (`platform::reads_at_random`), and to read ahead again as its command runs
  (`Layer::read_ahead`, as the guest says STARTED; a resumed microVM's at once): a
  sequential read of what the layer holds, cold, reads 5,089 MiB/s with readahead and 86
  without. A start on Fedora, its host busy, takes 2.6 to 3.5 ms at p50 where it took 8.1
  to 9.4, and on 4 contended CPUs 18.9 where it took 31.9; on the Mac, where no write paid
  it, a start stays about 1.2 ms. Held by vmm's
  `a_layer_reads_ahead_once_its_command_runs` (its mapping's VmFlags; mutation-checked both
  ways).

- **Its linear map in blocks on arm64** (PM M300, shards' kernel patch 0010). arm64 Linux
  mapped the device memory it added 4 KiB at a time under `rodata=full`, its default
  (arch_add_memory, force_pte_mapping), so that a page's permissions could change alone,
  which a DAX device's linear alias never does: a 512th of the layer in page tables, 133
  MiB of a guest's memory for a 64 GiB layer (M277). 0010 maps a file system DAX device's
  memory in blocks, but where debug_pagealloc or a realm needs base pages: a layer of 4 to
  64 GiB takes none of its guest's memory (-0.7 to 0.3 MiB at p50), and its probe is done
  11 ms (16 GiB) to 41 ms (64 GiB) sooner. The pinned kernel carries it (since
  kernel-6.18.48-8df0015cca35).

**Next** (the slices after these).
- A restart that goes on over the kept file itself: today its files are put back, packed
  on the host, into the warm microVM's own layer, which its template mounted as its root's
  (a copy, as long as the layer's changes are); a template's root mounted where a run can
  swap the file under it would make a restart's cost the layer's mount alone.
- Blocks the guest frees go back to the host: pmem takes no discard
  (drivers/nvdimm/pmem.c), so a layer's file only grows while its microVM lives; its
  microVM gone, the host could punch out what its bitmaps say is free.
- Joiners' layers (D119) on the microVM's own, rather than tmpfs.
- The head's boot: a 2 MiB block a section for the guest to write as it probes, on KVM
  1.9 ms a GiB when the host has huge pages free and up to 19 ms a GiB when it compacts
  for them (M277): a 10 GiB layer's template boot is 19 to 190 ms longer.
- Hosts whose runs restore no template yet (Windows, whose daemon is yet to come: D195,
  D196) boot every run, so each run pays the head's probe and the layer's first mount: not
  measured there yet.
- APFS fills a hole shorter than 16 MiB between written blocks of a sparse file (PM
  M277): a layer's file, as a swap file and a template's memory, takes more of a Mac's disk
  than it was written.

### D179. Other CPUs' images, emulated in their microVM (parts 1 to 3 built)

Images built on an arm64 Mac usually ship to x86_64 hosts, and the other way round, and a
build for both (`--platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, D87) runs each platform's RUN steps.
shards refused a step for a platform its microVMs do not run: "shards runs steps for
linux/arm64 only, the platform its microVMs run, not linux/amd64". Docker runs one under
qemu-user, which its binfmt tool registers with the host kernel's binfmt_misc
(`docker run --privileged tonistiigi/binfmt --install all`: every architecture the host
does not run, for every process on the host, until it reboots), and BuildKit runs the
step under whatever the kernel finds for its programs; Docker Desktop's VM registers its
own, Rosetta's for x86_64 on a Mac where it is on (M241: 4.66.1's VM has both, and
Rosetta runs x86_64).

A microVM has a kernel of its own, so the emulator is its kernel's to register: a builder
registers the emulators of the platforms its build's steps run, and nothing outside it
changes. That beats Docker in isolation and in what a build depends on: no privileged
container, no host-wide state that every process inherits and a reboot loses, no step of
one build reaching another's emulators (binfmt_misc is the kernel's: a privileged step
there changes the host's); the emulator is one pinned by digest, the same on every host,
where Docker's is whatever the host has installed, or Docker Desktop's own. It does not
beat Docker Desktop's speed on a Mac:

- **Measured (PM M241).** Docker's builds of qemu-user (`tonistiigi/binfmt`, BuildKit's,
  pinned) registered in a microVM as its tool registers them run another CPU's programs.
  From the host's side, an emulated run costs 4.6 and 5.5 times the cycles of a native one
  for sha256 and gzip at p50, and each program started about 5.5 ms more (15.5 times the
  cycles); a guest has no steal clock (the VMM answers SMCCC's PV_TIME_FEATURES with not
  supported), so its own CPU times count the time its vCPU waited for the host, and the
  host's figures are what a run cost. Docker Desktop on the same Mac runs x86_64 through
  Rosetta at 1.3 to 1.4 times native for compute and 12 to 13 for starts: compute 3.3 to
  7.6 times faster than qemu in a microVM, starts at much the same cost.
- **Rosetta is not shards' to use.** Apple gives Rosetta to a Linux VM through
  Virtualization.framework's `VZLinuxRosettaDirectoryShare`; shared into a shards microVM
  and registered as Apple documents it, its binary refuses to run: "Rosetta is only
  intended to run on Apple Silicon with a macOS host using Virtualization.framework with
  Rosetta mode enabled" (M241). shards drives Hypervisor.framework itself (D1), and does
  not get round Apple's check. Rosetta would mean a second kind of microVM on Macs,
  Virtualization.framework's, for other CPUs' work: the user's decision, open.

So emulation is for steps that cannot be cross-compiled, at qemu's cost; a native host of
the platform builds faster, reached as a context (the next item).

- **The emulators.** `tonistiigi/binfmt@sha256:400a4873…` (binfmt e29e7d7, QEMU 10.2.3),
  this host's platform's image of it, fetched as a base the first time a build needs it
  and kept as the build cache keeps what it made, until `builder prune`; never in the
  shards binary (QEMU is GPL-2.0). Its root is one more of the builder's pmem devices,
  which init mounts where no step reaches it, and registers each emulator the build needs
  (`shards_abi::emulate`: the binfmt tool's table, QEMU's magic and masks, flags
  CFP: the program's credentials, the emulator opened as it is registered so that every
  root and mount namespace reaches it, argv[0] kept, which the image's builds expect).
  Measured: written through printf's format, a register line's `\x` escapes are printf's
  to read, its mask comes out matching every ELF, the emulator's own included, and every
  program fails with ELOOP; init writes the line as it is.
- **What runs natively.** A platform a builder runs itself needs no emulator: its own, and
  linux/386 on an x86_64 host (the guest kernel's `IA32_EMULATION`; BuildKit's util/archutil
  probes a host kernel for the same). Apple's CPUs run no 32-bit Arm, so linux/arm is
  emulated on arm64 hosts. A platform without an emulator is refused at its step's turn.
- **A build's steps** (part 1, built): each RUN step for another platform runs in the
  builder as any step does, its programs under their CPU's emulator: the builder boots with
  the emulator image's root as one more pmem device, and before any step is asked
  (`EMULATE`) for the architectures the build's steps need, which init registers, or
  says why not (`EMULATED`). `tests/build.rs`
  `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator` builds `uname -m` for the other
  64-bit CPU, for linux/386 and linux/arm/v7, and for both 64-bit platforms at once, each
  step seeing its own CPU; with the registration left out, the step fails with the
  kernel's "exec format error".
- **A run of another platform's image** (part 2, built): a run of an image no guest runs,
  asked for by `--platform` or named by its lone manifest or by an image here, runs under
  its CPU's emulator. The daemon gives its microVM the emulator image's root after its
  other devices, and names it on the kernel's command line (`shards_emulate=DEVICE:ARCH`);
  init registers it in the initramfs before the image's root moves over it, which then
  keeps the emulator's mounts out of every process's reach (the workload's mount table
  starts at its own root). Its template, saved with the device, keeps it registered in
  every restore, the daemon's record of it naming the device it gives a restore. A run
  that names no platform is warned of, in dockerd's words (PM M250), exactly when it runs emulated:
  when no guest runs its image's platform itself (the host's platform, as the warning
  names it, arm64's `v8` or an amd64 host's level as go-archvariant v1.0.0 reads the
  CPU). dockerd's matcher counts 32-bit Arm as an arm64 host's own, for a CPU that runs
  it; no guest of shards' does (PM M250), so its runs, emulated, were not warned of, and
  now are. And a pull or a run that names no platform takes a lone manifest whatever its
  platform, and runs it under its CPU's emulator, where shards refused it (measured: Docker
  29.3.1 pulled `alpine@sha256:3e9b4b68…`, amd64's, on arm64, warned of it, and ran it). Of
  an index, a pull or run that names no platform takes, after the guests' own platforms,
  those a guest runs emulated, as it runs a lone manifest of them: the other 64-bit CPU's,
  then 32-bit Arm's v8 to v5 (on arm64: arm64, amd64, 32-bit Arm's; on x86_64: amd64 and
  386, arm64, 32-bit Arm's). containerd's order put 32-bit Arm first on arm64, for a CPU
  that runs it itself; a microVM's here does not (PM M250: its guest refuses an armv7
  program's exec), and emulated the two cost alike (M250: 32-bit Arm 11% less for sha256,
  amd64 6% less for gzip and starts). What decides is what a run can use: a 32-bit process
  addresses 4 GiB at most, where a microVM's memory can be the host's (D148). An index of
  the other CPU's alone, which shards refused, runs emulated and warned of, as its lone
  manifest did. Tested: `crates/image`
  `a_pull_of_no_platform_takes_the_other_64_bit_cpus_before_32_bit_arms`. A commit of
  another CPU's image is that CPU's, its base's variant kept (moby NewChildImage).
  `tests/images.rs` `a_run_of_another_cpus_image_runs_under_its_emulator` boots one,
  restores its template (without the emulator's device in the restore, it boots instead),
  and runs with no platform a lone manifest, an index of the other CPU's alone
  (`amd64/alpine:3.22`'s on arm64, `arm64v8/alpine:3.22`'s on x86_64) and one of 32-bit
  Arm's (`arm32v7/alpine:3.22`), each emulated and warned of.
- **An image's platforms** (part 2, built): an image keeps each platform pulled of its
  index (dockerd's keeps them too, PM M243), where shards' kept one, the last pulled: a run of
  another platform made a plain run of the image take that one, emulated and warned of.
  Its name names this host's best of its platforms here, which a run that asks no
  platform takes, and a pull of another platform leaves it so; the collector keeps each
  platform here unpacked. A name a load gives an index none of whose platforms is this
  host's names the index itself; a run of it takes its platforms here, where shards refused
  it ("its record names an index"), and one with none of them here is refused, with the
  words a `docker` script reads ("… does not provide any platform"). A run of a platform not
  here pulls it ("Unable to find image", then "Image is up to date", its name resolving to
  the index it did), and pull and run
  say whether it is up to date, the name resolved here to what it resolves to now, a
  digest's by a name of its repository (moby image_pull.go, resolveImage, answers a script
  the same). A run that may not pull refuses it, with the words a `docker` script reads
  ("image with reference … was found but
  does not provide the specified platform (…)"), as does a run for another platform of a
  lone manifest, which a pull takes whatever its platform. Deliberately unlike Docker:
  - a platform is here when all of it is, its config and layers with its manifest, where
    dockerd takes one whose manifest alone is, which a pull cut short leaves: shards pulls
    it whole again rather than fail the run;
  - an image named by its ID, for a platform not here, is refused, naming the image, where
    Docker's CLI reads a short ID as a repository's name and pulls that ("pull access
    denied for 11a3eb1597e8", M243).

  A build's base, for its guests' platform, is pulled for it where another platform's alone
  is here. `crates/registry`
  `an_image_keeps_each_platform_pulled_and_names_this_hosts` (mutation-checked: the name
  naming what was pulled last, a lookup taking its name's platform alone, a platform taken
  without its layers, a collection keeping its name's platform's root filesystem alone) and `a_lone_manifest_is_pulled_for_any_platform_and_found_for_its_own`;
  `tests/images.rs` as above, with this host's pulled first, then each refusal and status
  (mutation-checked: a lone manifest run for another platform than its own, an ID pulled
  as a repository's name, a digest's status by its own name's record alone).
- **A build on another CPU's base** (part 3, built): a build takes a base's lone manifest
  whatever its platform (containerd v2.2.1 core/images/image.go, `Manifest`, checks a
  platform of an index's manifests alone), where shards refused it, its steps run under the
  base's CPU's emulator (build.rs `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator`), and warns of it in BuildKit's check's words (InvalidBaseImagePlatform:
  "Base image … was pulled with platform "linux/amd64", expected "linux/arm64" for current
  build"). Asked for no platform, the image is its base's platform, as Dockerfile2LLB
  leaves an implicit target's; its stage keeps the build's platform, as dockerui gives
  the frontend the worker's first platform alone to detect a stage's by (v0.28.1
  dockerui/config.go), so no emulated platform is ever detected (measured: Docker
  29.3.1's BuildKit v0.28.1 on linux/arm64, its worker listing seven platforms, warned,
  ran the step emulated and made an amd64 image). BuildKit's step runs the base's programs
  under whatever emulators the host's kernel has, whatever the step's platform says: a
  builder registers, beside each step's platform's emulator, the one of the CPU of the
  base its root comes from, down the step's first inputs to its stage's FROM, so that a
  base of another CPU only copied from fetches no emulator. What a policy reads of a base
  (D101) is the manifest the build takes, its root filesystem left unbuilt. The planner's
  oracle gains a build that asks no platform (`scripts/agentfile/generate`,
  `implicit_target`), and `corpus/plan/base-platform.Dockerfile` and
  `base-platform-implicit.Dockerfile` hold the warning, the stage's platform and the
  image's to BuildKit's, asked for and not; `tests/build.rs`
  `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator` builds on the other CPU's lone alpine
  manifest asking no platform: the step runs emulated, the warning is BuildKit's, the
  image the other CPU's (mutation-checked: without the base's CPU's emulator the step
  fails with the kernel's "exec format error"; a lone
  manifest refused by a build's lookup, or by a policy's; the oracle planning every build
  with a platform asked).

**An emulated command is never PID 1 (2026-10-18).** A run of another CPU's image runs
its command under shards' reaper (`--init`'s), and a build step for another CPU runs its
command as its namespace's first process's child (`shards_abi::build::Step::emulated`, set
from the step's platform or its base's), where each was PID 1 of its PID namespace. The
emulator ends a program that dies of a signal by sending that signal to itself, its
default action restored, and waiting for it; a PID namespace's init is sent only the
signals it has a handler for (pid_namespaces(7)), so the wait never ended: every emulated
run or step whose program crashed, aborted or met an instruction the emulator lacks hung
for ever (PM M251), where a native one's fault ends it, the kernel's own signal reaching
init too. Now it ends as the native one does, 128 and the signal's number. What differs
from a native PID 1: a signal the command sends itself takes its default action, where a
native PID 1 is not sent it. Tested: `tests/images.rs`
`a_run_of_another_cpus_image_runs_under_its_emulator` (a program meeting an undefined
instruction, emulated: 132) and `tests/build.rs` `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator`
(an emulated exec-form step's crash fails its step, `exit code: 132`). Mutation-checked,
each caught: an emulated run's command left PID 1; no step marked emulated; the guest
ignoring the mark; the reaper ending 0 for a signal's end.

**amd64's levels (2026-10-18).** A guest runs its host's x86-64 level: KVM's supported
CPUID and a WHP partition keep the host's feature bits (vmm `cpuid.rs` rewrites only
topology), which `tests/images.rs` `a_guest_runs_its_hosts_x86_64_level` pins on every
x86_64 host CI boots guests on (the guest kernel's own flags reach the host's level). So an
x86_64 host's guests take amd64's levelled builds, `v2` up to the CPU's, as their own, the
highest first, then the level-less amd64 and 386; where shards ran every levelled build
emulated (no guest listed one), and an index of levelled builds alone not at all. The
emulator runs amd64's v2 and v3 and none of v4's AVX-512 (PM M251): an arm64 host's pull
takes amd64's v2 and v3 builds after its level-less one, and a run of a v4 image on a host
whose CPU lacks it is refused, saying why, where it would end at its first such
instruction. A pull that names no platform and finds none says the guest's level-less
platform (`linux/amd64`), as a script reading the refusal expects. Tested: `crates/image`
`a_guest_runs_its_cpus_x86_64_levels_best_first`,
`a_pull_of_no_platform_takes_the_other_64_bit_cpus_before_32_bit_arms` (v3 before 32-bit
Arm on arm64, the level-less first, v4 never) and
`the_emulator_runs_amd64_up_to_its_own_level`. Mutation-checked, each caught: arm64's pull
without amd64's levels; the emulator taken to run v4.

**The platform a user prefers (2026-10-16).** Docker's CLI takes `--platform`'s default
from `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` for `pull`, `import`, `run`, `create` and the classic
builder (docker/cli v29.8.1 cli/command/image/pull.go:61, import.go:53, build.go:159,
container/create.go:84, run.go:73), and buildx for `build` (v0.37.1 commands/build.go,
platformsDefault); shards took it, `SHARDS_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` first (D157), for `run`,
`create` and `import`, and not for `pull` or `build`, so `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64
shards pull alpine` stored this host's where Docker stores amd64's. Both take it now: a
pull as the flag said first, so that one named after it is the one kept, as pflag keeps
the last given; a build where the flag is not given, as pflag's first value given
replaces a string array's default whole (a build that names `--platform` builds that alone,
not an index of it and the default). Tests no longer inherit a default the host's user
prefers (`common::command`). Tested: `a_pulls_platform_defaults_to_the_default_platforms`
and `a_builds_platform_defaults_to_the_default_platforms` (an index of two platforms: the
default's stored and built, shards' variable before Docker's, a named platform over both).
Mutation-checked: pull's default not taken, Docker's variable read first, build's default
not taken, build's default kept with a platform named.

### D178. A microVM's I/O limits, kept outside it

`--io-maxbandwidth BYTES` and `--io-maxiops N`, on `shards run` and `create` and in the
Engine API's `HostConfig.IOMaximumBandwidth` and `IOMaximumIOps`, are the most bytes and
requests a second of a microVM's I/O to the host's storage: its volumes (virtio-fs) and its
disks (virtio-blk). Docker takes them for its Windows containers' system drive alone:
dockerd on Linux refuses them (`Invalid QoS settings: linux does not support Maximum IO
Bandwidth or Maximum IO IOps`, moby 464cd50c daemon/daemon_unix.go), and docker/cli hides
them from a Linux daemon (their `ostype` annotation, cli/command/container/opts.go). A
microVM's limits per device (`--device-read-bps` and the rest, D44) are written in its
guest's cgroup, which the guest keeps; these the VMM keeps, outside the guest, where no
process in the microVM, its root among them, can lift them. A microVM's image (read through
memory, DAX) and its swap window (D159) are memory to it, not device I/O, and are not
limited.

Every request its devices serve is charged before it is served (devices/virtio/limit.rs):
a volume's READ by the bytes it asks for and its WRITE by those it gives, every request as
one request (the high-priority queue's FORGETs and INTERRUPTs, no I/O, not at all), a
disk's read or write by its data. Each measure keeps its theoretical arrival time (ITU-T
I.371's generic cell rate algorithm): when what it charged so far would have been done at
its rate. A request waits for that, then moves it on by its own cost: a microVM left idle
is served at once, a busy one is paced at the limit, and no window of time holds more than
its rate's worth and one request; one larger than a second's worth is served whole, and
the next waits it out. Two things a busy host does would cost the rate, and do not (PM
M240, where each was found by counting the device's requests and the limiter's waits): a
request that costs a measure nothing neither waits on it nor moves it, so that the zero-
byte GETXATTR the kernel asks with each write takes its time within the write's wait; and
a wait that runs past its deadline, as a loaded host's timers leave it, lets the next
request that measure charges keep its place in the schedule, which it would otherwise start
over, never going before it.

One budget a microVM, its VM process's, which each of its devices charges, one VM a
process; its rates come with its run's request, so that a warm VM restored ahead of its run
takes the run's. A wait is on a device's worker thread, never a vCPU's. While a snapshot
pauses the devices (D176), none waits: the request a worker has in hand is served at once,
its cost kept, so that a save waits for no limit. A run joining a microVM (D119)
does its I/O through that microVM's devices and takes no limits of its own: refused,
saying so. `inspect` reports them in its HostConfig.

Measured (PM M240, M5 Max, release build): the limit is a ceiling, kept: 16 MiB under 4
MiB a second achieved 0.844 of it at p50 and 0.894 at most quiet, 0.841 and 0.931 loaded,
never over it; where the host's storage answers within a write's place in the schedule
the rate is the limit's to 0.4% (4.001 s where its time is 3.98), and where it stalls past
that the writer gets the less it can take, catching nothing up, which would take a burst
past the limit. A limit that holds nothing back costs nothing measurable: 64 MiB with none
and with one of 1 GiB a second agree at p50 within 4%, either faster. Held by
`requests_are_paced_at_their_rates`, `a_late_request_keeps_its_place` and
`a_pause_lets_a_waiting_request_go` (limit.rs), and on real microVMs by
`a_microvms_io_is_paced_at_its_limits` (tests/containers.rs: 3 MiB under 1 MiB a second
takes two seconds and more, thirty synced writes under 20 requests a second three; the
limits in `inspect`; a joiner's refused; mutation-checked); the CLI's flags by docker/cli's
oracle (`MICROVM_FLAGS`), the API's by its create bodies.

### D177. `build --squash`: a build's layers as one

`shards build --squash`, and the Engine API's `POST /build?squash=1` (docker-py's
`build(squash=True)`, the docker CLI's legacy builder's `--squash`), make the layers a
build adds past its base's one layer: the base's layers as they were, then one that makes
the build's tree of the base's. What a later step removed is in no layer, so it is neither
pushed, pulled nor kept; a file of the base's that the build removed is a whiteout. Its
history is moby's squash's (moby 464cd50c `daemon/images/image_squash.go`): the entries as
the unsquashed image has them, times and all, each past those of the base's layers an
empty layer's, then the merge's, `merge sha256:<unsquashed> to sha256:<base>`, at the
image's creation (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH where given, which moby's does not take); built FROM
scratch, every layer is the one, `create new from sha256:<unsquashed>`. moby keeps the
base's entries by index, which leaves the merge's layer without an entry of its own
wherever the base's history names fewer layers than it has (the test image's names none):
`docker history`, which pairs entries with layers in order (`daemon/images/image_history.go`),
then gives the merge's entry a layer of the base's. shards keeps, for
each of the base's layers, the entry the image pairs with it, so every layer has one and
the merge's is the merge's (`squash_makes_a_builds_layers_one`, mutation-checked against
moby's rule).

What it does not change is a microVM: shards flattens every image's layers into one EROFS
filesystem (crates/image), so a squashed image runs as the unsquashed one does. It changes
what a registry and the store hold.

Docker's own: BuildKit has no squash, and buildx warns it removed (`experimental flag
squash is removed with BuildKit`) and builds unsquashed. dockerd squashes an experimental
daemon's builds once they are done (`daemon/builder/backend/backend.go`), and only in its
graph-driver image store: the containerd image store, "now the default for fresh installs"
(Docker Engine 29 release notes), answers `error squashing image: not implemented` after
the whole build has run (`daemon/containerd/image_squash.go`). shards squashes in its one
store, and leaves no unsquashed image behind, where moby's squash leaves it untagged.
Before this, shards accepted the flag and ignored it (buildx still does): a client of the API
that asked for a squashed image got an unsquashed one, which only a warning said.

A step's layer is what its own step stamped in the tree (`diff::write_layer`, BuildKit's
overlay differ); a squash spans every step, so its layer is continuity's doubleWalkDiff of
the two trees from the root (`diff::write_squash`), which reads a file's bytes only where
its metadata matches and its data is not the same node's: a file no step touched is the
base's own. The steps run and are cached as ever, a build without `--squash` reusing them;
`mode=max` provenance names the layers the image holds, which the steps' of a squashed
image are not. Held by `a_squash_writes_every_step_between_two_trees` (diff.rs), and on
real microVMs by `squash_makes_a_builds_layers_one` (tests/build.rs) and
`images_are_built_from_a_context_in_the_body` and
`the_docker_cli_runs_microvms_through_the_engine` (tests/engine.rs: the API's `squash=1`,
and the docker CLI's own legacy `build --squash`, which it offers an experimental engine).

### D176. A running microVM saved whole, and resumed (in progress)

`shards save vm NAME`, and Docker's `checkpoint`, save a running microVM whole: its
memory, vCPUs and devices as they are, every process, pty, pipe, socket within it and file
in its writable layer with them; `shards restore vm NAME` resumes it from there. Docker's
checkpoint is experimental and Linux's alone (docker/cli: `experimental`, `ostype`
`linux`), and needs CRIU 2.0 or later (docs.docker.com, `docker checkpoint`), which dumps a
container's processes one by one and refuses what it cannot: a `docker run -t` terminal,
device files, files sent over Unix sockets, locks held unless told to, processes joined
to anything outside the set it dumps (criu.org, "What cannot be checkpointed"). A
microVM's state is its memory and its devices', which shards' VMM already saves and
restores for templates (D25): HVF and KVM, on x86_64 and arm64 (D154), and WHP (D196). What
lies outside the microVM goes as with CRIU by default, and is said: connections to the
world beyond it, exec sessions and attached clients.

Templates are saved before their guest has plugged any memory or swapped (D148, D159). A
running microVM has done both, so a save keeps them:

- **Memory plugged** (part 1). The memory file holds the RAM, then each run of the blocks
  a virtio-mem device plugged, in the order of their addresses, all-zero pages as holes;
  the state lists the runs (snapshot format 17), and virtio-mem keeps what it asks for and
  what is plugged. A restore remakes the region as boot made it, plugs the same runs
  again through the hypervisor's stage 2, as a plug does, and reads them back before any
  vCPU runs. Held by `memory_plugged_is_saved_and_plugged_back` and, on real microVMs,
  `a_snapshot_keeps_the_memory_its_guest_plugged`: a guest plugs 512 MiB, writes 448 MiB,
  more than it booted with, and only then asks for a snapshot; the VM that booted and two
  restores find all it wrote. Mutation-checked: without the plug again, the restored guest
  faults at the first address of the region it reads.
- **Swap** (part 2). A run's swap file is unlinked once its microVM maps it (D159), so the
  VM process copies it, the guest's writes flushed to it first (msync(2)), into the
  generation's `swap`: the ranges the file holds data in (lseek(2) SEEK_DATA, SEEK_HOLE),
  of them the 4 KiB blocks not all zeros, asked, on macOS, with the guest's mapping and
  the VM's taken away for the moment: APFS says a file mapped shared and writable holds
  data throughout (D190, PM M285). The swap window's state keeps the length, and a
  restore maps a copy of its own back at that length before any vCPU runs (snapshot format
  18). Held by
  `a_runs_swap_is_kept_by_a_save_and_mapped_back_by_its_restore`. ext4 and XFS count a
  page written through the mapping as data before it is written back, reserving its
  block as it is dirtied (`ext4_da_get_block_prep`, `xfs_buffered_write_iomap_begin`), as
  Btrfs and tmpfs do (PM M285); the flush is for a file system that gives a page its block
  only at write-back.

A save is the host's to ask for (part 2), where a template's is the guest's. The daemon
prepares a generation in the microVM's directory, `snapshots/NAME/`: its memory, state
and swap files, empty, created there, since the VM process opens no path of its own (D30).
It hands them to the VM process with `SAVE`. The VM process parks the vCPUs, quiets the
devices, fills the files and answers `SAVED`, then goes on or stops; the daemon commits
the generation, synced, renamed into place, its pointer moved, as the VMM commits a
template. One save at a time, and none while a template is still to save, whose
coordinator would take the request for its own. The machine is taken apart only once a
save has let go of it: the save holds the VM and its devices by weak references, which
`Running` alone owns. What a save cannot keep whole refuses it, and the microVM goes on as
it was, with nothing of the save left: a host's devices (VFIO), a GPU's contexts, a
container joined to it (D119), and files it holds open in its volumes after removing them
that hold more than a snapshot's state keeps (part 5).

Runs joined to a microVM (`--network container:NAME`, D119) run in it, each a run of its
own: a snapshot would keep their processes, and a restore bring them back without their
runs. So a
microVM is saved while none runs in it, which its VM process, which takes the daemon's
messages in order, knows as no other can: a JOIN before a SAVE counts its joiner as it is
taken, and the save refuses while one counts; a JOIN after it is refused until the save is
done, its joiner's start failing with why. Once they end it is saved, its join disk with
the ranges their images had, each let go (snapshot format 19): its restored guest knows the
disk's capacity, and a container that joins the restored microVM takes the next range, no
place given twice (D119). Before this, a microVM saved with joiners running kept them, and
one any container had ever joined was never saved again. Held by
`a_save_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_and_nothing_behind` (refused while a joiner runs,
saved once it ends, restored and joined again) and `a_join_disk_reads_each_image_at_its_range`
(the ranges kept, mutation-checked).

Saved with `--leave-running`, the microVM goes on. Otherwise its save stops it, and it is
told as stopped, not ended: its attached client says it was saved and as which snapshot,
and exits 148, the status a shell gives a job it stopped (128 + SIGTSTP); its run records
that status. The save answers once its run's record says it has stopped, so that a
`restore vm` asked at once finds it stopped: answered at its VM's word alone, a restore
straight after found it running, 2 of 10 back to back on a Fedora host (none of 20
since). Docker takes a checkpoint's stop for an exit like any other (moby
daemon/monitor.go, handleContainerExit): a restart policy restarts it, and `--rm` removes
it with its checkpoints, what was saved lost. A saved microVM is
neither restarted nor removed: what it is saved as is there to resume. Held, on real
microVMs, by `a_running_microvm_is_saved_whole_left_running_or_stopped` and
`a_save_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_and_nothing_behind` (tests/saved.rs).
Mutation-checked: removed with `--rm`, and saved with its volume mounted.

`shards restore vm NAME [SNAPSHOT]` resumes a stopped microVM from a snapshot of its own,
its newest unless named (part 3). It is a start of the microVM again, whose VM restores the
snapshot rather than a template: its run's
log, ports, events and end are a start's. Three things a start does not have make it whole:

- **A cut with nothing in flight.** What the guest's init wrote to the host and the host
  had not yet read when the vCPUs parked is in neither the host's log nor the guest's
  memory: lost from every copy restored, and, for a microVM its save stops, from the
  microVM. So the VM process first asks init to QUIESCE, on the run's connection: init
  sends all it holds, then QUIESCED, then nothing until RESUME, and the VM process saves
  once it has read QUIESCED, all before it in the log. What the host sends meanwhile, its
  stdin and signals, comes after the cut in a restored copy, where it is not, as anything
  sent after the cut is. Held by `a_microvm_saved_as_it_writes_loses_none_of_its_output`,
  a guest writing as fast as it can through its save: every count once, up to the save
  and on from it. Mutation-checked: saved without waiting for QUIESCED, a restored copy's
  log went from 56,812 to 57,686, the 873 counts between them lost.
- **Its connections, dialed again, and only by init.** A restore resets the streams the
  snapshot held (D12). The VM process's run and signal ports take one connection each, so
  that a workload dialing one finds it taken (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §9.7); in a restored copy
  the workload runs already, and would find a fresh port first. So a restored VM process
  has no run or signal port: the daemon gives each save two tokens, which init holds from
  QUIESCE on and the generation keeps (`resume`), and a restored init, finding its
  connection reset and its lineage's generation past the relay's (control::GENERATION),
  dials the exec port twice, each HELLO one token, as an exec's connection is checked:
  compared whole, in constant time, by the exec port's one reader. The VM process waits
  for them before its vCPUs run, and only where the restored init speaks this build's
  protocol (control::ABI). An exec's connection is its client's, which went with the
  microVM saved: init lets go of each as it redials, ending the exec's stdin as its
  client's going does, and what the exec writes after has nowhere to go and is dropped as
  it is read, as anything whose connection is gone is.
  Waited on, a connection the restore reset as it held what init had not read stayed
  established, readable to its end and never writable, the reset taking its credit
  (Linux's vsock, `virtio_transport_space_update`): init, which reads an exec's connection
  no more once its stdin has ended, never wrote the exec's end, and the run outlived its
  stop until its VM was killed, a give-back the save cut short once in 608 CI runs. Held
  by `a_microvm_saved_as_an_execs_stdin_waits_ends_with_its_run_once_restored`, the
  connection full of an exec's unread stdin as the save is taken, mutation-checked: without
  the release, the stop took 40.03 s and the run ended with its VM (PM M330). It had read an exec's
  output only while less than BUFFERED of it waited, so an exec that wrote that much more
  was read no more: killed with the run, it was never seen to end, and its run outlived
  its stop's SIGTERM and SIGKILL until its VM was killed. Held by
  `a_microvm_saved_as_an_exec_writes_on_ends_with_its_run_once_restored`, an exec writing
  as fast as it can through the save, its run stopped once restored: ended by the stop's
  SIGTERM (143). Mutation-checked: without the drop, the stop took 40.0 s, its 30 s
  timeout and the 10 s past its SIGKILL, and the run ended with its VM (255) (PM M328).
- **Its interface, as its guest holds it.** Its MAC, and its address on a network of its
  own (D46), are kept with the snapshot, and asked for again as `--mac-address` and `--ip`
  ask: a member that took the address meanwhile keeps it, and the restore fails, naming
  the snapshot's address. Its swap, a copy of the one the save kept,
  as sparse, is mapped back before its vCPUs run. Held by
  `a_saved_microvm_on_a_network_is_restored_at_its_address`, its peers reaching it at its
  name and that address, mutation-checked (restored at the lowest address free), and by
  `a_saved_microvm_keeps_what_it_swapped`: 96 MiB of a pattern under a 64 MiB limit, read
  back whole after the restore.

A microVM restored resumes where it was saved, as often as its snapshot is restored: its
log goes on from the save, once for each restore. Measured (PM M239, a 256 MiB microVM on
the M5 Max): a save left running parks the guest's vCPUs for 17 ms at p50 and 46 ms at
most on a loaded host, its going quiet first under 0.2 ms at p90; its caller waits 92 ms
at p50 quiet, the commit's sync among it, and a restore 18 ms at p50. `shards list snapshots NAME` lists a
microVM's snapshots, newest first, when each was saved and the disk it takes; `shards
remove snapshot NAME SNAPSHOT...` removes them, and `shards rm` with the microVM. A run on
the host's network (D124) is not saved: its guest's sockets are the host's, which no
snapshot keeps.

**Volumes** (part 5). A volume is served to the guest by its run's share process (D38),
whose FUSE server holds what the guest's kernel holds of it: each node by an ID the server
drew, with its parent, its name and its count of lookups, and each open handle. A snapshot
keeps those tables. As the devices are paused, each share's device asks its server for
them by a control frame of the VM process's own, marked by its length word's top bit,
which no guest's request sets (a guest's frame is at most a write's data and headers), and
the save keeps them in the device's state (snapshot format 20). A restored run has a share
process of its own, as every run has, and the restored device gives its new server the
tables before it asks anything, before the guest's vCPUs run. The server opens each node
and handle along its path as the guest uses it, checked to be the same file by its device
and inode, as it opens one it let go of; the guest's open files, its working directory in
the volume and its cached names go on as they were. A directory whose device numbers
changed, as a host's boot may change them, is taken as of the new ones; one that is
another directory, its root not the saved root's inode, refuses the restore, as every file
the guest held of it would be stale. A file the guest holds open after removing its last
name no path reaches, and its server holds it by a descriptor alone: its bytes go with
the tables, as CRIU's images carry such a "ghost" file's (Documentation/criu.txt, up to
`--ghost-limit`, 1 MiB unless told otherwise), within what a snapshot's state holds, 64
MiB, which a save now checks it is under as a restore does. A restored server holds each
in a file of its own, made in the home's private directory (`tmp`, 0700), which the
daemon hands each share process, and removed from it at once; one a crash left there
before its removal, the next daemon's start removes. A directory or special file removed
while open, and a removed file the server had no descriptor left to keep (past its
budget), still refuse the save. Held by
`a_saved_share_is_served_again_by_a_restored_server` (fs/server.rs: an open handle read on,
a directory's node, another directory refused, the device renumbered, mutation-checked),
`a_shares_tables_go_to_the_server_its_restored_slot_is_given` (fs/mod.rs), and on real
microVMs by `a_saved_microvm_writes_on_through_its_volume`, a guest appending to a file it
holds open, from the volume's directory, through a save and a restore: each count once, in
order (mutation-checked: without the tables, the restored guest writes nothing more), and
its guest writing and reading on through a file it removed (mutation-checked: restored
without its bytes, the file's next write fails); and by
`a_save_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_and_nothing_behind` for removed files past what a
snapshot keeps.

**Docker's command lines for it** (part 4). A `checkpoint create [--leave-running] CONTAINER
CHECKPOINT`, `checkpoint ls`, `checkpoint rm` or `start --checkpoint CHECKPOINT` command
line, a `docker` script's, is read as `save vm`, `list snapshots`, `remove snapshot` or
`restore vm`, on shards' command line and through the Engine API (`POST` and `GET /containers/{id}/checkpoints`, `DELETE
/containers/{id}/checkpoints/{name}`, `POST /containers/{id}/start?checkpoint=`). docker/cli
shows them only to a daemon that says it is experimental (docker/cli v29.8.1
`checkpoint/cmd.go`, `container/start.go`: the `experimental` annotation, read from
`/_ping`'s `Docker-Experimental`), so the engine says so, as `info` and `version` do. What
it means for Docker, a daemon started with `--experimental`, CRIU installed and Linux, a
microVM needs none of. Their answers are dockerd's (moby 464cd50c `daemon/checkpoint.go`,
`daemon/start.go`), in its order: a name that is not `[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+`, or ends
in `.`, refused before anything is looked up (`invalid checkpoint ID "../x", only … are
allowed`, quoted as Go's `%q` quotes it), then the container, its state, a name taken.
`start --checkpoint` prints nothing, which is what a `docker` script reads of it, and
restores one microVM at a time. A paused microVM is not started, by `start` with a
checkpoint or without, where shards had answered it as one running already: it is refused
(409, `cannot start a paused container, try unpause instead`, the words a `docker` script
reads, validateState), before the 304 for one running.

Better than dockerd, a checkpoint's name is taken as its directory is made (mkdir(2)'s
EEXIST), where dockerd looks for it and then makes it (getCheckpointDir: os.Stat, then
os.MkdirAll): two creates of one name at once both go on, into one directory, and one that
fails removes it (os.RemoveAll), the other's dump with it. In shards the second is refused,
and a save that fails removes only the directory it made. Before this, shards looked and
then made it too: a second save of the name passed, waited for the first's lock, and then
saved over it, or, finding the microVM stopped by the first, failed and removed the
snapshot the first had saved, the stopped microVM's only copy. What a daemon's end cuts
short, a save or a removal, leaves a snapshot with no generation in place, whose name the
claim would hold, and whose files `list snapshots` would not show: the next daemon's start
removes it before it serves (`a_start_removes_snapshots_cut_short`, and on a real daemon
restarted, `checkpoint_command_lines_save_list_and_restore_microvms`, mutation-checked), and
a removal takes the pointer first, so that one cut short is never a snapshot a restore
would take.

A checkpoint directory of the client's (`--checkpoint-dir`, the API's `CheckpointDir`) is
refused, saying why: dockerd writes and lists checkpoints wherever its caller names, but
restores from none of them (`custom checkpointdir is not supported`, 403, which shards'
start answers too), so that its checkpoints move between containers and hosts only by
being copied into the one's own directory by hand. A microVM's snapshot is its devices as
they were, its disks and its interface's identity among them, which another microVM can
resume only with the same devices: a snapshot restored in another microVM, or on another
host, is part 6, which checks them. Held, on real microVMs, by
`checkpoint_command_lines_save_list_and_restore_microvms` (tests/saved.rs) and
`the_docker_cli_checkpoints_and_restores_microvms` (tests/engine.rs, the docker CLI
itself), and by docker/cli's own answers to the command lines (oracle_test.go).

### D175. Sockets read in poll(2) on macOS, and streams ended one way at a time

On macOS a read waiting on a Unix stream socket can sleep through its peer's half-close,
and SHUT_RDWR after one shuts nothing (PM M236). Together they hung `docker compose exec`
long after its command had ended:

1. Compose shut its writing once its stdin ended, as a Docker client does on every
   attached stream (docker/cli hijack.go, `CloseWrite`).
2. The daemon's copy of that stdin slept on in recv(2).
3. The shutdown(SHUT_RDWR) that was to end the client's stream said ENOTCONN, and the
   stream stayed open.

Others half-close as well: the guest's init as a run ends, and the VMM, passing on a
guest's half-close (vsock `Shutdown::Write`).

- **On macOS a socket's read waits in poll(2), never in the read** (`shards_ipc::read`,
  and `Polled` for what takes a reader).
  - It reads with MSG_DONTWAIT, and waits in poll(2) where nothing has come, as a read
    would wait: not at all where the descriptor is set not to block, and no longer than
    its receive timeout. Messages (`shards_ipc::recv`) wait the same way.
  - A read that finds data is the one recv(2) it was. One that waits makes a failed
    recv(2), an fcntl(2) and a getsockopt(2) first: over three runs a round trip whose
    two ends both waited took 2.0 to 5.8 µs more at p50 than with recv(2), and 3.3 to
    3.9 µs more where each reply came 50 µs on (M236).
  - Linux's read looks for the end under the lock its waker takes and missed none, and
    a pipe or a terminal is no socket: those are read as they were.
  - Read through it: the Engine API's connections and the stdin they attach; the VM
    process's guest streams and the stdins it copies to them; the CLI's stdin; the
    builder's connection, its ssh agent's and its proxy's; the local image store's
    answers; a log shipper's Unix endpoint.
- **A stream ends one way at a time** (`shards_ipc::end`): SHUT_WR, so that its peer
  reads the end, then SHUT_RD, so that readers here read theirs. On Windows the build's
  connections end as they did.
- **TCP** lost no end in M236 and keeps its reads. Its SHUT_RDWR is XNU's too, so the
  registry client and the tests' registry end a connection one way at a time.

Held by shards_ipc's tests, each mutation-checked on macOS:
- `a_read_sees_its_peers_end_that_lands_as_it_starts`: 20,000 races, reads and messages.
  A recv(2) that may sleep, in either, missed an end by round 1,722.
- `a_read_waits_as_a_read_would`.
- `ending_a_stream_reaches_a_peer_that_ended_its_side_first`: with SHUT_RDWR, the peer
  read no end.

### D174. Overlays on volumes: runtimes nested in a microVM

A runtime nested in a microVM keeps its images' layers as overlays on a volume: buildx's
own builder (BuildKit, its docker-container driver), Docker in Docker, Podman. shards'
volumes reach a microVM as virtiofs from its run's share process (D38), unprivileged on
the host, and overlayfs refused them as an upper layer. Measured in buildx's builder and
in tests/containers.rs, by the guest kernel's log:

1. Its work directory, made with mode 0 (fs/overlayfs/super.c, ovl_workdir_create), was
   the guest root's to write in and not the share process's (EACCES), so the overlay
   mounted read-only.
2. Past that, an upper filesystem it takes for a remote one must give it RENAME_WHITEOUT,
   xattrs and `d_type` ("upper fs missing required features", EINVAL). Neither host gives
   an unprivileged process RENAME_WHITEOUT: macOS has none, and Linux's asks CAP_MKNOD.

Now, each held by the server's unit tests and by an overlay on a volume in a microVM:

- **What the host cannot hold is kept beside it**, in the owner's attribute Docker
  Desktop's file sharing writes (D38).
  - A mode that would lock the share process out of its own file keeps the host file's
    owner access (`rwx` for a directory, `rw` for a file, a FIFO or a socket). The guest's
    exact mode is kept in the attribute where the two differ, and the guest's kernel
    checks it (`default_permissions`). A device node takes the guest's mode as it is: the
    share process never opens one, and none can hold the attribute (on Linux, which makes
    an unprivileged process the whiteout, the owner's access showed as the guest's).
  - A device node the host makes only for a privileged process (overlayfs's whiteout is
    one, of 0:0) is an empty regular file whose kind and number the attribute holds. The
    guest sees, lists and looks it up as the node it made; its kernel opens a device
    itself, never through the share.
  - The attribute gains `kind` and `rdev`; its `mode` stays Docker Desktop's.
- **RENAME_WHITEOUT**, as Linux makes it: the rename, then a whiteout in its place, the
  rename undone where the whiteout cannot be made.
- **`trusted.` and `security.` attributes on a Linux host**, which only a privileged
  process sets there (xattr(7)), are kept under `user.shards.` and read and listed back
  under their own names; a guest's own `user.shards.` names are refused. macOS keeps no
  namespaces, so names stay as they are.
- **A file is reached by any name the guest knows it by.** The server knew a file by the
  name the guest last looked it up by. overlayfs links its one shared whiteout for each
  removal and unlinks the links as it cleans a directory, so the file went stale (ENOENT
  for GETATTR and LINK) until the guest looked another of its names up. Each node keeps
  the names it was looked up by, and is reached by one that still leads to it.
- **O_CREAT never changes what it finds.** A CREATE that finds its file opens it as it
  is, where its owner was rewritten before.

So `docker buildx build`, with buildx's own builder on the host's network (`docker buildx
create --driver docker-container --driver-opt network=host`, D124), builds in a microVM:
its daemon nests its cgroups (D173), keeps its snapshots on its state volume, runs each
RUN step in a container of its own runc, and its image is loaded into shards and runs as
a microVM (tests/buildx.rs, BuildKit v0.33.0). On the default bridge, default deny gives
the builder no way out: the host's network, asked for and warned of, is what gives it
its registries. Not yet: O_TMPFILE (FUSE_TMPFILE), which overlayfs does without.

Held by the virtiofs server's unit tests (`what_the_host_cannot_hold_is_kept_beside_it`),
tests/containers.rs (an overlay on a volume, its kernel's log clean) and tests/buildx.rs.

### D173. Compose projects through the Engine API

Agent stacks are written as Compose files: an agent, its MCP servers, a database, a
store. With `DOCKER_HOST` at shards' socket, `docker compose` (Docker's own client,
unchanged; v5.1.0 tested) makes each service a microVM. Most of it is a control surface,
given by D170's calls. What a project gains, each for the microVM:

- **Each service its own kernel.** A service is a microVM, never a process on a kernel it
  shares with the rest of the project and the host. Its project's networks are closed to
  all but their members, who reach each other by service name (D46), where Docker's
  reach the internet unless `internal`. Its volumes are served by its run's share process
  (D38). Its secrets and configs are written as Compose writes them, packed into the
  microVM by its init (D170).
- **What Compose asks, kept.** Held by tests/compose.rs with Compose's own client:
  - `up -d --wait` with `service_healthy` and `service_completed_successfully`;
    `up --exit-code-from`, attached;
  - `ps`, `exec` by service name, `logs`, `cp` in and out of a named volume, `port` (the
    host reaches it there), `run --rm` and its status, `stop`, `start`, `restart`,
    `pause`, `unpause`, `top`;
  - profiles, replicas, `network_mode: service:`, `environment` and `env_file`, secrets
    from a file and from the environment, configs of their own content, `read_only` with
    a `tmpfs`, `init`, `hostname`;
  - `build` with the API's first builder (where buildx is absent, or with
    `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0`), and `down -v --rmi local`.
- **A container's events carry its labels**, as dockerd's do (daemon/events.go,
  LogContainerEventWithAttributes: copyAttributes, then image and name). They carried
  none, so `docker compose up`, attached, never heard its services end (its monitor
  follows its project's label: `label=com.docker.compose.project=P`) and waited for
  ever, and `docker events --filter label=…` matched nothing.
- **An exec joins a workload that nests its own cgroups.** A nested runtime (BuildKit's
  buildkitd, Docker-in-Docker) moves itself into a cgroup below its own and enables
  controllers for that one's children. cgroup v2 then keeps every process out of its own
  (no internal processes), and an exec failed with EBUSY. It now joins the cgroup the
  workload's process is in, as runc's exec joins container init's
  (libcontainer/process_linux.go, addIntoCgroupV2; runc#2356), within the workload's own
  alone.
- **Builds through buildx.** Where buildx is installed, Compose builds with `buildx
  bake`, and buildx gives a non-dockerd engine a BuildKit of its own: moby/buildkit as a
  privileged container (its docker-container driver), which in shards is a microVM. On
  the default bridge, default deny gives it no way out. With `--driver-opt network=host`
  (D124) it builds, since D174 gave its snapshots overlays on its state volume. The
  engine's own BuildKit API (buildx's docker driver: `/session` and `/grpc`), which
  would need no builder of buildx's, is a slice of its own.

Held by tests/compose.rs (three projects), tests/engine.rs (a container's events by its
label) and tests/containers.rs (an exec into a workload that nests its cgroups).

### D172. Images found in registries: `shards search image`, and `GET /images/search`

An agent's sandbox starts from an image that someone, or the agent itself, chose. A
microVM boots this machine's architecture, so an image with no build for it does not run
here, and its size is what its first pull downloads before the first start. docker
search says neither, and searches Docker Hub alone: a term that names another registry
asks it for an index's search, which no registry serves now (a 404). `shards search image
TERM` (`shards search TERM` too, the docker CLI's form, for its scripts; crates/cmdline/tests/search.rs) finds images through what each registry
documents, and says of each whether it runs here and what its pull takes. `GET
/images/search` answers SDKs and the docker CLI in the shape they parse (engine.rs
`images_are_pushed_saved_loaded_and_imported`).

- **Whether it runs here, and what it pulls** (the microVM's need). Each result's
  `latest` is looked up, as a run that names no tag pulls it, and chosen as a pull
  chooses (`shards_image::platform`: arm64 alone; amd64, then 386).
  - Docker Hub's comes from its API's tag (`/v2/namespaces/NS/repositories/REPO/tags/TAG`,
    https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/hub/latest/): every platform's image and compressed size in one
    answer. Attestations (`unknown/unknown`) name no platform.
  - Any other registry's comes from the tag's index or manifest, and a lone manifest's from
    its config.
  - A repository without `latest` says so. 11 of the 25 results of a search for `python`
    had none (PM M234), and a `shards run` of one would fail.
  - Lookups go four at once, the most measured with none throttled by Docker Hub; 25 at
    once was throttled (PM M234). Each is its own, so a slow one holds up no other.
- **Across registries, through what each documents.**
  - Docker Hub: its index's search (`/v1/search`), the one its API describes. A password login
    goes as Basic credentials, an identity token as the bearer token for
    `registry:catalog:search`, which distribution's authorizer takes from the challenges
    of the index's `/v2/` (registry/client/auth/session.go).
  - quay.io: its own search (`/api/v1/find/repositories`, in its API description), each
    result described by its README's first paragraph.
  - Any other registry: its catalog (`/v2/_catalog`, followed by its `Link`), the
    repositories whose names hold the term, with the credentials a pull finds for it. A
    registry that serves no catalog says so; one that refuses is named.
  - ECR Public and Artifact Registry document no search: none of ECR Public's 23 API
    actions searches (its gallery's search is its website's own), and Artifact Registry
    implements OCI distribution alone. They are searched as any registry with a catalog
    is. Their listing APIs (ECR's DescribeRepositories, Artifact Registry's
    dockerImages.list) list the repositories a user owns: a later slice.
- **On a terminal, at once** (UX). The page is drawn with every result found, and each
  lookup's answer is filled in as it comes. Piped, it is Docker's exact table, held to
  docker/cli v29.8.1's formatter by 44 recorded cases. A template may name shards' fields
  (`{{.RunsHere}}`, `{{.Platform}}`, `{{.Platforms}}`, `{{.Size}}`, `{{.PullCount}}`),
  which are looked up only when it does; `{{json .}}` says what docker's says. Docker
  Hub's pull counts, which its index gives and the Engine API's result has no field for,
  are kept for `{{.PullCount}}`.
- **The CLI's own** (efficiency): a search starts no daemon. Its credentials,
  certificates and proxies are those a pull finds.
- **dockerd's terms, without two of its flaws.** Its limit (25 when none, 1 to 100), its
  filters (`is-official`, `stars`, `is-automated`, true of which finds nothing) and its
  refusals are in its words. A negative limit is refused, where dockerd answers 200 with
  no body (an `errors.Wrap` of no error). A registry's refusal carries what the registry
  said, which dockerd leaves out ("unexpected status code N", its own TODO).

Held by crates/registry's unit tests (each source, its pages and credentials; what runs
here from Docker Hub's tags and from manifests), crates/cmdline/tests/search.rs (docker/cli's
formatter, 44 cases), tests/search.rs (a catalog searched; what runs here; limits, filters
and refusals; credentials), tests/engine.rs (`GET /images/search` with and without the
client's credentials; `docker search` through the engine) and the docker CLI oracle. Every
command a test starts is given the tests' own docker config, so that no test, nor a daemon
one starts, reads this host's docker config or its credential helpers.

### D171. Registry logins: `shards login registry`, and `POST /auth`

A microVM's image often comes from a private registry: a team's agents on GHCR, ECR,
Artifact Registry or private Docker Hub repositories, pulled for a run or a build's
`FROM`, pushed once committed. Pulls and pushes find the credentials `docker login`
keeps (D23). `shards login registry` and `shards logout registry` (`shards login` and
`logout`, as Docker says them) keep and forget them, and `POST /auth` checks them for
the programs that make sandboxes through the Engine API (docker-py's `login`, the docker
CLI's `docker login` with `DOCKER_HOST` at engine.sock). Mostly a control surface. What
it holds, and where it differs:

- **One store, docker's** (control surface). Kept as docker/cli v29.8.1 keeps them
  (login.go, storeCredentials): by the registry's credential helper, the config's
  `credsStore`, or the platform's helper where the config holds no credentials
  (DetectDefaultStore), else in the config's `auths`, an identity token in the
  password's place. A login made by either works for both: no second login, and no
  second copy of a secret.
- **No microVM and no daemon holds a credential.** `shards login` checks them from its
  own process, with the certificates (`certs.d`) and proxies a pull uses, and starts no
  daemon. `POST /auth` checks them in the daemon's memory and keeps them nowhere, as
  dockerd keeps none: its client keeps them. A microVM is given layers, never the
  credentials that fetched them. Docker's is the same; it is said because the agent in
  the microVM is the party least trusted with them.
- **Checked as dockerd checks them** (daemon/pkg/registry/auth.go, loginV2): the
  registry's `/v2/` asked with them, a bearer challenge answered asking for a refresh
  token as well (containerd's FetchRefreshToken: `access_type=offline` posted,
  `offline_token=true` got). A refresh token given is the identity token kept in the
  password's place. With nothing given, what a login kept for the server is tried
  first: its user logged in to be known there.
- **A refusal is 401, with the registry's word** (correctness). dockerd answers a
  registry's own refusal of Basic credentials 500: loginV2's untyped "login attempt to …
  failed with status: 401 Unauthorized" (its TODO says so); only a token server's
  refusal is typed Unauthorized. A client cannot tell wrong credentials from a failing
  server by it. shards answers both 401, the status the API's description gives an auth
  error (docker-py's `APIError.is_client_error`), its text naming the URL that answered
  (`http://` once a loopback registry's fallback took it). The answer is otherwise
  moby's `AuthResponse`, `IdentityToken` left out where there is none.
- **A config that is a link stays one, and is never found half written** (robustness).
  The config is written whole beside where it leads, synced, and renamed over it, its
  other keys as they were; a new one is the user's alone (0600, in a 0700 directory),
  and the staged file is opened `O_EXCL`, never through a link at its name. docker/cli's
  Save follows the link too (EvalSymlinks), but stages its file beside the link, so its
  rename fails where the link leads to another file system (`EXDEV`), and renames a file
  it never synced.
- **Passwords taken as docker/cli v29.8.1 takes them:** `--password-stdin` and `-p -`
  read stdin, one line end cut; `-p` is warned of as insecure; at a terminal, asked
  without echo; without one, refused. `shards logout registry` forgets every key a login
  may have used (the server as given, its host, its `http://` and `https://` forms;
  Docker Hub's key alone), from its helper and the file.

Held by crates/registry's unit tests (a challenge answered and its refresh token kept;
the file, a helper and a linked config), tests/login.rs (refused, kept, tried first, used
by a push, forgotten, the grammar's form, no terminal), tests/engine.rs (`/auth` raw, and
the docker CLI's login then push through the engine) and the docker CLI oracle. Tests
that log in give their commands a `PATH` of an empty directory: found on `PATH`, the
platform's helper kept a test's credentials in this host's keychain once.

### D170. The Engine API, on a socket file in the home

The programs that make agents' sandboxes speak the Engine API: Docker's SDKs,
Testcontainers, the agent frameworks built on them, the docker CLI. Served by shards,
every sandbox they make is a microVM, made as `shards create vm` makes one, their code
unchanged (`DOCKER_HOST=unix://HOME/engine.sock`). What they gain, each for the microVM:

- **Reach: a file in the home, its user's alone.** `engine.sock` sits in the home beside
  its request slots (D185), a Unix socket file whose peer's user is checked: no root daemon's
  socket, whose group Docker's own post-install guide calls root-level, and no TCP
  listener. Remote use is shards' own, over QUIC (hyper-raft's `hyper-quic` and
  `hyper-tls`).
- **On Windows, a named pipe** (`npipe`), as Docker's clients reach their engine there
  (`DOCKER_HOST=npipe:////./pipe/NAME`): its name a fresh one each daemon makes, which the
  home's `engine.pipe` names once it listens, as Unix's socket is renamed into place.
  - Its DACL admits this user alone, and it refuses remote clients. Each client takes an
    instance of its own, one always waiting, whose connect the daemon's loop waits on with
    its others (`shards_ipc::Listener`). Its clients' streams carry bytes alone, no handle
    either way.
  - **Written in messages, as dockerd's is**: moby makes its pipe with `MessageMode:
    true`, "so that CloseWrite() is supported" (daemon/listeners/listeners_windows.go).
    go-winio, which Docker's clients dial with, ends a side's writes with a message of no
    bytes, which reaches a reader only on a pipe written in messages
    (`PipeConfig.MessageMode`): on a pipe in bytes `docker run -i`'s end of stdin would
    never come.
  - **Read in messages on shards' side**, a message at most each read. Read in bytes,
    one read took a client's last bytes and its end together, and the end was lost (jupiter,
    `a_listeners_clients_end_their_writes_and_read_on`): go-winio flushes before it writes
    the end, waiting for its reader to have read all before it, and a flush that waits
    cannot be cut short by a close from another thread. A wait for something to read (a
    read of no bytes) that takes the end keeps it as the stream's end, which every read
    after it reads.
- **Isolation as shards' runs have it.** Each call is put to the daemon as shards' CLI
  puts the same thing (a run, an attach, an exec, a command), on a socket pair of the
  engine's, taken as any client's request is: each sandbox a microVM of its own, its
  network default deny (its grants the ports it publishes and the networks it joins),
  its log and drivers shards'. No path exists through the API that the CLI does not
  have. A pull's credentials (X-Registry-Auth) stay in memory, never written.
- **What is asked is kept, or refused with why.** A create's body becomes the run
  `shards create vm` makes of the command line that made it (daemon/engine/create.rs),
  held to docker/cli v29.8.1's own `parse` by 72 recorded command lines of every flag,
  each making the same run (the I/O maxima since D178, `--cgroup-parent` since D183).
  Two things a command line cannot
  say are kept as given, and inspect gives them back: the streams a client attaches
  (none for a detached run) and GPU requests whole (Compose's `capabilities: [gpu,
  utility]`, which `--gpus` would reorder). `Entrypoint: []` takes the image's command,
  `[""]` none (moby's merge, daemon/commit.go). What a microVM cannot hold is refused,
  the field named, never dropped: OnBuild, Shell, legacy Links (default deny names each
  grant), Cgroup, custom masked and read-only paths, tmpfs
  mount flags (HostConfig.Tmpfs takes them), one mount type's options on another, a `=`
  in a map's key, a `:` in a tmpfs path. `NetworkDisabled` is network none.
- **Output from its first byte.** A client that attaches before it starts a sandbox (the
  SDKs and the docker CLI do) has its output from the start: the attach is held, and
  the start is an attached one (`shards start vm -a`'s), its stdio pipes to the
  attaches, the first that asked for it the command's stdin. An attach and a wait are
  registered before their heads are written, as clients start once they have them, so
  no first byte and no end goes unseen. A wait is for a microVM not running, its next
