  end though it has yet to start, or its removal.
- **Its output before its end.** A run's end (its container stopped, its waiters
  answered, `die` logged) and an exec's `exec_die` wait for what the daemon relays of
  their output to their attaches, up to 2 s from the end, as dockerd waits for its streams
  before it stops a container or an exec (moby v28.5.1 daemon/monitor.go, `StreamConfig.Wait`
  at lines 74 and 210; daemon/engine.rs `Relaying`). Without it a built service's one line
  reached Compose's attach 25.6 ms after its `die`, and Compose v2.38.2, which stops
  printing at the first exit it hears when it stops on one, dropped it (1 of 80 runs on
  CI, PM M352). Tested by `a_runs_end_waits_for_the_relays_of_its_output`,
  mutation-checked. An Engine API exec's events carry the ID its client was given:
  `exec_create` as it is made, then `exec_start` and `exec_die` (moby daemon/exec.go),
  where each had another, the daemon's own, before.
- **An answer given before the body is read, never lost.** A call answered before its
  body is read whole (an upload its handler refuses, a build's context sent through a
  session; a call refused before it is routed, an API version not served; a body past
  what a call may carry, 413) is answered as one whose connection is kept, and the rest
  of its body is then read and dropped, however large, as a server that answers first may
  (RFC 9110 §10.1.1; daemon/engine.rs `answered_first`). Before, a refused upload's
  connection was closed with none of the rest read, and a client still sending got a
  broken pipe, its answer unread (CI saw a refused build's context cut short once, on
  x86_64 musl); a call refused before routing dropped 256 KiB first and closed past it,
  as Go's server, dockerd's, does (net/http server.go, maxPostHandlerReadBytes), which
  loses a larger body's answer the same way. Tested
  (`a_call_answered_first_keeps_its_connection`: each refusal's answer read before any
  of its 4 MiB is sent, then the body, the 413 once 9 MiB is sent, then another call on
  the same connection), mutation-checked: an early answer closing; a drained body
  closing; Go's 256 KiB; the 413's rest counted again.
- **Files, packed and unpacked in the microVM.** `shards copy vm` (the archive calls),
  `export vm` and `diff vm`: archives are packed and unpacked by the microVM's own init,
  so a hostile archive, or a path swapped as it is copied (the class of CVE-2018-15664,
  a race in a host-side copy), stays behind the hypervisor. What a guest packs it writes
  onto the client's connection itself, never through the daemon (no length; the
  connection closes at its end); an upload is taken as it comes, never staged. A stopped
  microVM's files are read by a VM visiting them; a paused one's are in its frozen guest,
  and that is said.
- **A visit's namespaces whole before anything enters them.** A stopped microVM's visit
  gives its standby orders without a command: it sets up the copy's view in its own
  namespaces, as a run's standby does, says it is done by its error channel, and holds.
  Before, nothing waited for a standby that had just isolated itself, and a copy could
  enter its mount namespace half made (`umount2` EINVAL on x86_64 CI). A visit that
  fails now says why, as its microVM told its client.
- **A copy lands where the command will find it.** A running microVM's copies are made in
  its command's mount namespace, its volumes and tmpfs mounts in it: a file copied into
  a volume is in the volume, and one copied into a tmpfs is what its command reads. A
  stopped microVM's visit, for a copy, serves and mounts its volumes and binds where its
  runs mount them (a tmpfs is a run's own, a directory only its agents mount none of its
  root's), makes its root read-only where theirs is, and holds what is copied in to its
  writable layer's size (`--storage-opt size`, D156). This slice's volume test found
  that copies were made in init's own namespace, under the volumes' mount points, into
  the root; fixed in init (`builtin`, `hold_mounts`). dockerd's copies write a tmpfs of
  their own, which the container never sees, and read none of its (moby
  daemon/containerfs_linux.go, containerFSView).
- **A read-only refusal as the command's mounts have it.** Whether a copy may write is
  decided in the guest, on its destination with its links followed, by the mount it is
  on: a writable volume or tmpfs over a read-only root takes files; a link from a volume
  back into the root does not. dockerd decides by its records of mount points
  (checkWritablePath), in which a `--tmpfs` is none, so it refuses a copy into one over a
  read-only root as the root's. The refusal is the 403 the API's own description gives
  it (PutContainerArchive, v1.56); dockerd answers 400 (checkWritablePath's
  InvalidParameter, v28.5.2 to v29.4.0).
- **Volumes: data that outlives a sandbox.** Created, listed, inspected, removed and
  pruned as `shards create volume`, `list volumes`, `inspect volume`, `remove volume`
  and `prune volumes` do them. Each microVM that mounts one is served it by a share
  process of its own run, which takes every request of its guest as one the guest could
  forge, and its VM process reaches no host directory (D38), where a container's volume
  is a mount in the host's own kernel. One a microVM mounts is not removed (409). A
  cluster volume is a swarm's, refused.
- **Networks: sandboxes that work together.** MicroVMs on one network reach each other by
  name, answered at 127.0.0.11, where programs written for Docker ask, and reach nothing
  else through it: every network is closed to all but its members, who reach one
  another past default deny (D46), where Docker's reach the internet unless `Internal`.
  A create that does not ask `Internal` is answered with a warning that says so, so a
  program that expected more learns why. A created or stopped microVM joins and leaves
  one for its next start; legacy links are refused (default deny names each grant).
  Not yet: a running microVM joining another network, as a running microVM keeps the one
  network device it started with; and a MAC given on a join, which the CLI's join has no
  way to say, and the API reaches nothing the CLI does not. Both are refused with that
  reason.
- **What a microVM costs.** `shards stats vm`: its workload's use from its guest's
  cgroup, its system time the host's clock times its vCPUs, so that a client's share of
  two samples is its share of its vCPUs (the guest's own `/proc/stat` is not kept on a
  loaded host: measured 329% and 2503% for one spinning vCPU). Beside it, `microvm`:
  its VM process's own footprint (as PM M30 counts memory per VM), its resident memory
  and its CPU time, what it costs the host, which no guest's cgroup holds.
- **A stream ends with its client.** An events stream and a followed log end as their
  client goes, or sends anything more, which a client that waits for a stream sends none
  of: a stream no one reads holds the daemon for nothing (moby's end with their request,
  Go's server cancelling a request's context as its connection's read ends, net/http
  `backgroundRead`). They waited for their next message
  first, which a quiet microVM's log, or a host where nothing happens, may never send, and
  the daemon, kept by each such stream, never went idle (`tests/daemon.rs`,
  `an_engine_stream_ends_with_its_client`, mutation-checked; a stats stream and a wait
  looked already).
- **Its processes as its guest has them.** `shards top vm`: its own PIDs, its users named
  by its own `/etc/passwd`, no `ps` in its image.
- **Managed whole.** `pause vm` freezes the whole microVM, its kernel with it. `restart
  vm` is now said as a `restart` event too once it has started, for what follows
  microVMs by their events (it was kill, die, stop and start alone). `update vm` changes
  what a running microVM's guest cgroup can take, and refuses the rest by name. `prune
  vm` answers the bytes it reclaimed, counted, not rounded for a reader.
- **Terminals and execs.** A terminal's output is raw, its detach keys found as the
  escape proxy finds them, and a client that detaches leaves the command's stdin open;
  a terminal is resized through its attached client's connection. An exec's status is
  kept before its stream ends; a detached exec's VM now tells its client its end after
  its start (workload.rs).
- **Images named, traced, removed and pruned** as `tag image`, `history image`,
  `remove image` and `prune image` do them: control surfaces tools call. A tag that
  names no repository is refused, where dockerd answers 200 and tags nothing
  (httputils.RepoTagReference's nil). An image that goes takes the microVM templates made
  of it, and their warm microVMs, with the store's next collection (`collect_garbage`).
- **Images pushed, saved, loaded and imported, and microVMs committed**, as `push image`,
  `save image`, `load image`, import and `commit vm` do them. A push's credentials
  (X-Registry-Auth) stay in memory, as a pull's; each layer is said by its ID, its digest
  and size an `aux` message, and our platform's manifest pushed alone, where an index was
  not all here, the `aux` (manifestPushedInsteadOfIndex) the docker CLI tells of it by,
  as dockerd's are (daemon/containerd/image_push.go). An archive saved is written onto
  the connection as it is made, each image found before its head so that one not here
  is 404; one loaded, and a root filesystem imported, are read as they come, never
  staged. An import reads the call's body or an http or https URL, `http://` where none
  is named, as moby does; any other scheme is refused, and the daemon opens no path it
  is given. A commit's config is the microVM's, changed by its Dockerfile `changes`: a
  body that gives another is refused (changes say each field a config has), and an
  empty one, `{}`, which docker-py sends when given none, is none, where dockerd's merge
  of it drops the microVM's Shell and OnBuild (daemon/commit.go, merge).
- **Images built** as `shards build image` builds them, from a context in the call's body
  or `remote`'s: what docker-py's and docker-java's builds send (Testcontainers' images
  from Dockerfiles among them), and the docker CLI's legacy builder. Each RUN step runs
  in a microVM, never a container on the host's kernel, by BuildKit's plan and cache,
  where dockerd answers the API's first version, which those clients ask for, with its
  legacy builder. The build is a `shards build` process of its own, each option the flag
  it takes it by; each line it says is a `stream` message, then the image's ID (`aux`,
  from API 1.30) and the "Successfully built" and "tagged" lines docker-py finds an
  image by; with `q`, the ID alone. Its client's registry credentials
  (X-Registry-Config) stay in memory; a client that goes ends the build. A context sent
  through a BuildKit session, as `docker build` sends one where buildx is installed, is
  refused, saying so: BuildKit's session and control API on the engine's socket is a
  slice of its own.
- **A pull or push refused before it says anything is answered by its status**, as
  dockerd answers one whose stream it has not flushed; SDKs read that as the call's error
  (a 404 as not found; engine.rs `images_are_pushed_saved_loaded_and_imported`). `pull -a`'s trailing `:` is taken as Docker's clients send it, and `scratch`
  is refused before any registry is asked (403), the empty base a Dockerfile builds
  FROM, which no registry holds; shards' CLI refuses it so too now.
- **What shards takes on disk** (`inspect disk`): each kind's usage as API 1.52 gives it
  (ImageUsage, ContainerUsage, VolumeUsage, BuildCacheUsage), the fields of clients
  before it read unless `verbose`, both as Docker's clients parse them (engine.rs
  `images_are_tagged_traced_removed_and_pruned`); and `TemplateUsage`, the microVMs'
  templates, the snapshots each image's runs restore: what the cache behind a start in
  milliseconds costs the disk, which no Docker client is told otherwise.
- **Prunes said as events.** Pruning microVMs, volumes or networks is said as a `prune`
  event with what it reclaimed, as dockerd says each (daemon/prune.go; the volume
  service's Prune); none was before. Its containerd store says none for images, and
  neither does shards.
- **The build cache stays** through `prune vm` and `prune image`: every prune cleared it
  before, a shards bug this slice found; `prune system` clears it, as `docker system
  prune`'s users expect, and so does `builder prune`.
- **Errors in shards' words**, their status the one dockerd's error kind for the same
  refusal gives (engine.rs, `STATUSES`, each with its source): 404 for what is not there,
  a network removed among them (it was 500); 409 for a conflict (anything in use, a
  running microVM removed, an image a microVM was made of or more names refer to); 403
  for a read-only refusal, a predefined network removed, one with members, or one others
  take their settings from (500 before; libnetwork's ActiveEndpointsError is Forbidden);
  400 for a network more than one answers to; 503 for a daemon stopping.
- **Version and platform.** 1.56, docker/cli v29.8.1's (its moby/moby/api v1.56.0), from
  1.40, paths with or without `/v1.NN`; the platform said is the sandboxes': linux and
  the guests' kernel, which clients choose by. `shards version` says the API it serves.
- **The daemon stays while it is asked:** a call, or an open connection (SDKs pool
  theirs), is its work, as a run is; `shards stop daemon` ends API connections too.
- **Out of scope**, as decided (2026-10-13): swarm, plugins and trust.

Served now: `_ping`, `version`, `info`, events; microVMs' create, list, inspect, start,
attach, wait, logs, resize, stop, kill, removal, copy in and out, export, changes,
processes, stats, pause and unpause, restart, rename, update and prune; exec's create,
start, inspect and resize; images' pull, list, inspect, tag, history, removal, prune,
push, save, load, import and search (D172); commit; build; logins (`/auth`, D171);
volumes' create, list, inspect, removal and prune; networks' create, list, inspect,
removal, join, leave and prune; what is on disk. Held on real microVMs by
tests/engine.rs, raw and through the docker CLI, copies into tmpfs mounts over a
read-only root by tests/containers.rs, and the build cache kept through other prunes by
tests/build.rs. Any other call answers 404, naming itself.

### D169. A run's log sent to Cloud Logging

`--log-driver gcplogs` is served, sent as syslog's is (D163): from shards' store, by the
daemon's shipper, never by the microVM, to Cloud Logging's `entries:write` (its REST
form; moby's client sends the same request over gRPC, WriteLogEntries).

- **Credentials are the client's**, as awslogs' are (D168): the client gives its
  Google variables with the run (`GOOGLE_*`, `CLOUDSDK_*`, `GCE_METADATA_*`, beside AWS's,
  `crate::cloud_environment`), kept in the daemon's memory alone. An access token for
  `logging.write` (the client's WriteScope) is found as FindDefaultCredentials finds one
  (crate::google, now for any environment given): Application Default Credentials'
  JSON (a service account's key, a user's refresh token, an impersonated service account,
  workload identity federation), else GCE's metadata server, asked for that scope. A token
  is asked for again 5 minutes before it expires, and as soon as Cloud Logging refuses
  it. A user's quota project goes with each write (`x-goog-user-project`, or
  `GOOGLE_CLOUD_QUOTA_PROJECT`).
- **The metadata server is reached directly**, never through a proxy: Google's metadata
  client has none, so an instance's token reaches no proxy. Keyless signing's Google
  providers (D126) sent theirs through the environment's proxy; they no longer do.
- **Entries.** Each line is an entry at its output's time, its JSON payload moby's
  dockerLogEntry as Go's encoding/json writes it (daemon/logger/gcplogs/gcplogging.go):
  `instance` (zone, name and ID) where there is one; `container`, the run's name (`/`
  first), ID, image, image ID, `created` always, `command` with `gcp-log-cmd=true`, and its
  attributes as `metadata`; `message`, none for an empty line, a byte that is not UTF-8 a
  U+FFFD of its own. Its stream is a label (`stream: stdout|stderr`): moby's leaves it
  out, so the two cannot be told apart there.
- **Project and resource.** The project is `gcp-project`'s, else GCE's metadata server's,
  else the credentials' JSON's `project_id`, else `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`'s; moby's asks the
  option and the metadata server alone, and refuses the run without them. On GCE the
  resource is its instance (`gce_instance`, its zone and ID) and the payload its instance;
  off it, the instance `gcp-meta-zone`, `-name` and `-id` name, where given; else the
  project's `global`.
- **shards' own log name.** Entries are written to `projects/P/logs/shards`, unless
  `gcp-log-name` (shards' own option) names another. moby's driver writes to
  `gcplogs-docker-driver`, which `gcp-log-name` gives to keep a query, a metric or a sink
  written for it.
- **Writes.** A batch goes once it holds 1,000 entries or 8 MiB (the client's bundle) and
  whenever the shipper has caught up with its log, where moby's waits up to a second. A
  write is delivered once Cloud Logging answers 200; one that fails is written again,
  never dropped, where moby's client drops what overflows its buffer and what a write fails
  with. Each asks partial success, so that an entry Cloud Logging refuses holds up none of
  the others; those it refuses are said in the daemon's log. No entry is written as the
  run starts to see that the service answers (moby's Ping, whose failure refuses the run);
  shards' run starts regardless, its log sent once the service takes it.
- **Options checked as the run is made.** `tag` is refused: an entry is named by the run's
  details and its log (moby refuses it too). `gcp-project` is to be a project's ID,
  `gcp-log-name` a log's name, `gcp-endpoint` (shards' own: a private endpoint, a
  restricted VIP's) a URL. `gcp-log-cmd` says so with `true` alone, the value its users give.
- **Not yet.** etwlogs, Event Tracing for Windows' own, waits for shards' daemon on Windows.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_cloud_logging_as_its_options_say`),
against Google in the test:

- a user's credentials: their refresh token's access token, their quota project with each
  write; the options' project and its `global` resource; each line an entry of the run's
  details, at its `logs -t` time, its stream a label;
- GCE's metadata server: its project, instance and token, asked for `logging.write`, the
  `Metadata-Flavor` asked; the log name the options give;
- the refusals.

Unit tests cover the entries as Go writes them, HTML's characters escaped; the resource
and the log name; the options; bytes that are not UTF-8; and a partial success's
refusals read.

### D168. A run's log sent to CloudWatch Logs, signed with its client's credentials

`--log-driver awslogs` is served, sent as syslog's is (D163): from shards' store, by the
daemon's shipper, never by the microVM, to CloudWatch Logs' JSON 1.1 API
(`X-Amz-Target: Logs_20140328.*`), signed for `logs` with Signature Version 4
(crates/shards/src/aws/sigv4.rs, the S3 cache's signer, D88).

- **Credentials are the client's.** A run's credentials are found with the environment of
  the client that started it: its `AWS_*` variables, its home, `PATH` and proxies, sent
  with the run (`Run::cloud_env`), so they are what that client's shell would find. One
  daemon serves every run of its home, started by whichever client came first; finding
  credentials in its own environment, dockerd's way, would sign one shell's runs with
  another shell's account. The daemon keeps the environment in memory alone. The request a
  container keeps on disk holds neither it nor, any longer, the client's registry
  environment, `DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG`'s credentials among it. A container started again is
  signed with the credentials of the client that starts it; a daemon that restarts before
  a run's log is sent sends the rest once a client starts the run again.
- **The whole default chain** (crates/shards/src/aws/credentials.rs), in the order
  aws-sdk-go-v2 v1.41 resolves one (config/resolve_credentials.go):
  - the environment's keys, then its web identity (STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity);
  - then the profile, one `AWS_PROFILE` names and no file has refused: its source profile
    and role (STS AssumeRole, signed, its session name, external ID and duration as the
    profile says; an MFA code refused, as no one is there to give it), its keys, its
    `credential_source`, SSO (the token cache by the SHA-1 of the session's name,
    refreshed through SSO OIDC once a session's expires, written back whole), an `aws
    login` session (refreshed through sign-in with an ES256 DPoP proof), its
    `credential_process` (`sh -c` in the client's environment, a minute at most, 1 MiB of
    output at most);
  - else the container's endpoint (a relative URI at the ECS agent's address; a full one
    over HTTP only to loopback or the ECS or EKS agent's), its token file read each time;
  - else EC2's instance metadata: an IMDSv2 token of 300 s, IMDSv1 where the token is
    refused unless that is disabled, 250 ms to connect and 500 ms for an answer's head, as
    the SDK gives it (the HTTP client's `Patience` now bounds a connect too).

  `AWS_CA_BUNDLE`, or the profile's `ca_bundle`, takes the platform's roots' place, as the
  SDK trusts the bundle alone. Credentials are found again 5 minutes before they expire,
  and as soon as CloudWatch refuses them. Where shards does better: a DPoP proof's key
  coordinates are 32 bytes each, as RFC 7518 §6.2.1.2 has them, where the SDK drops their
  leading zero bytes; a token file's trailing line ending is left out, where the SDK
  refuses the token.
- **The S3 build cache uses the same chain** (D88). It took keys alone before, and refused
  profiles that assume a role or sign in with SSO, a process or a web identity, as CI on
  AWS does. Its region falls back to `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` and the profile's, where
  BuildKit refuses the cache.
- **Region and address.** The region is `awslogs-region`'s, else `AWS_REGION`'s,
  `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`'s, the profile's, else EC2's instance metadata's; dockerd skips the
  two in the middle, so off EC2 it refuses a run whose profile names a region. The
  address is `awslogs-endpoint`, else the configured endpoint (`AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_CLOUDWATCH_LOGS`,
  `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`, the profile's services section), which dockerd's client discards,
  else the partition's own by the SDK's endpoint rules, FIPS's and dual-stack's where asked.
- **Events.** Each line is an event at its output's time in milliseconds. A line of up to
  262,118 bytes, as CloudWatch counts them (a byte that is not UTF-8 counted as U+FFFD's
  three), is whole: the shipper cuts this driver's lines in parts of that length
  (`Driver::part`), not 16 KiB. A longer one is cut where no character is. With
  `awslogs-multiline-pattern`, or `awslogs-datetime-format` made a pattern by its strftime
  table, lines are joined, each followed by a newline, until one matches. Lines held wait
  `awslogs-force-flush-interval-seconds` (5 s) for more, the shipper woken for them
  (`Driver::due`). A joined event's time is its first line's: moby's keeps an older one
  after its tick flushes the buffer. An empty line is no event, as CloudWatch takes no
  empty message. The JSON is written as smithy-go's encoder writes it. The bodies are
  held byte for byte to Docker 29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`, its capture a fake
  CloudWatch Logs, its credentials an ECS endpoint's): 7 cases (each stream, a named
  stream, a tag, a group made, multiline, datetime, EMF) and 15 of which options it takes.
  The recorded requests' signatures are made again.
- **Puts.** A put holds at most 10,000 events and 1 MiB, each counted 26 bytes more,
  sorted by time; and they lie less than 24 hours apart, which CloudWatch requires of one
  put and moby does not check, so a shipper catching up on an old log never makes a put
  CloudWatch refuses forever. A put goes once full, and whenever the shipper has caught
  up with its log. One CloudWatch refuses is put again, never dropped; moby logs the
  failure and drops it. One whose stream or group was deleted since makes them again
  first. Events CloudWatch takes and does not keep (too old for it or the group, too far
  ahead) are said in the daemon's log.
- **Its stream** (`awslogs-stream`, else the run's tag, by default its container's whole
  ID) is made as the shipper starts, one already there taken as made, its group first
  where CloudWatch says it is not there and `awslogs-create-group` says to make it. The run
  starts regardless; dockerd refuses to start a container whose stream it cannot make.
- **Options checked as the run is made.** moby's checks, then what CloudWatch would refuse
  of every put: a group's name (1 to 512 of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . - _ / #`), a stream's (no `:`
  or `*`), the region a host's label, the endpoint a URL, the pattern compiled. Docker
  29.8's entity (`awslogs-entity-service-name`, `-environment`, `-attributes`), newer
  than the recording, is taken as its source takes it. `awslogs-max-buffered-events` is
  taken and holds nothing back: the log is on disk until sent, and no event waits in a
  queue to be dropped from.
- **Not yet.** gcplogs and etwlogs; gcplogs came with D169.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_cloudwatch_logs_as_its_options_say`),
against CloudWatch Logs in the test:

- a line on each stream: its stream made first, named for its container's whole ID; each
  line an event at its `logs -t` time to the millisecond; signed with the client's keys
  and token;
- a second client's keys, its run's own, the daemon having been started by another;
- a credential process the daemon runs in its client's environment;
- a group not there, made as asked, then its stream;
- lines joined by a pattern;
- a line put while its run still runs;
- nothing of the client's keys, token or registry credentials in the request the
  container keeps;
- the refusals.

Mutation-checked: with the client's registry environment kept in the request, its
credentials are found on disk; with the daemon's environment in the client's place, no
put is ever made.

Unit tests cover:

- every recorded request's body, byte for byte but for the run's stream name, and its
  signature;
- the options;
- cutting, joining, the strftime table, entity attributes as one CSV record, the batch
  bounds, smithy-go's string escaping, CloudWatch's names;
- the chain against a fake STS, SSO, SSO OIDC, sign-in, IMDS and container endpoint: its
  order, roles assumed with their source's keys and form, web identity, the container's
  token file, IMDSv2 and its IMDSv1 fallback, SSO's cache and refresh, a login session's
  refresh and its DPoP proof verified, a credential process; mutation-checked on the role
  duration's rule and `AWS_PROFILE`'s refusal.

### D167. A run's log sent to Splunk

`--log-driver splunk` is served, sent as syslog's is (D163): from shards' store, by the
daemon's shipper, to a Splunk HTTP Event Collector.

- **Events as Docker's driver sends them** (logging/testdata/splunk.json), so that a Splunk index fed by Docker's runs reads
  shards' alike. Each line is an event, byte for byte moby's splunkMessage as Go's
  encoding/json writes it: `{"event":…,"time":"…","host":"…"}`, then `source`, `sourcetype` and
  `index` where given. Its event, as its format says:
  - `inline`, the default: `{"line":…,"source":"stdout","tag":…,"attrs":{…}}`, its tag
    and attributes where it has them, `tag` given empty taking the tag away;
  - `json`: the same, a line that is JSON written as Go writes a json.RawMessage,
    compacted with HTML's characters escaped (`shards_image::json::compact_escaped`);
  - `raw`: the tag, the attributes as `KEY=VALUE`, each followed by a space, then the
    line; no event for a line of whitespace alone, which HEC takes none of.

  Its time is its output's, as Go's `%f` writes the float64 of its nanoseconds over a
  second's. A batch's events go in one post to `/services/collector/event/1.0`, with
  `Authorization: Splunk TOKEN`, gzipped where asked. All are held byte for byte to Docker
  29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`, its capture a fake HEC over HTTP and HTTPS): 7
  cases of formats, gzip, TLS, fields and tag, and 17 cases of which options Docker takes.
- **Batches posted as the log is caught up with.** A batch goes once full, 1,000 events or
  `SPLUNK_LOGGING_DRIVER_POST_MESSAGES_BATCH_SIZE` (moby's default and variable: the default
  open in docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md, to derive from what a batch costs). It also goes whenever the
  shipper has caught up with its log (`Driver::flush`). moby waits for a 5 s tick instead,
  so a quiet run's last lines waited up to 5 s; shards' wait no longer than the log does.
- **Delivered once HEC has it.** A post is delivered once HEC answers 200. A batch takes a
  message only when it has room, so a refused post leaves the message for the next try,
  and none is lost or doubled. moby drops what it cannot post once 10,000 messages wait.
  Each post is given 30 s, moby's `batchSendTimeout`.
- **Indexer acknowledgment, kept.** With `splunk-index-acknowledgment`, a post is
  delivered once HEC says its events are indexed. Its ack is asked for on the driver's own
  channel, a GUID, as the shipper catches up and as its run ends. One not acknowledged
  within 5 minutes is posted again, as Splunk's documentation asks of a client ("About
  HTTP Event Collector Indexer Acknowledgment"). moby sends each post on a new channel,
  whose acks no one can ask for, and never asks.
- **Where Docker is wrong, shards is not.**
  - `splunk-insecureskipverify` is refused, its CA asked for instead: shards posts a log
    only to a Splunk whose certificate it verifies.
  - `splunk-capath`'s file is read as the run is made, so one that is not there is
    refused then. Docker fails the container as it starts.
  - `splunk-verify-connection` is taken, and moot. Docker's driver asks HEC (OPTIONS)
    as its container starts, and a HEC that is down keeps the container from starting;
    shards' run starts regardless.
  - `raw`'s attributes go in name order, where Docker's go in a Go map's random one.
- **`splunk-caname`** names the server its certificate is verified for, and SNI's name,
  as Go's tls.Config.ServerName does: the registry client's `with_server_name`.
- **Not yet.** awslogs, gcplogs and etwlogs.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_splunk_as_its_options_say`), against a
HEC in the test:

- a line on each stream: its event, tag, attributes and host, its time `logs -t`'s to
  the microsecond, its token;
- a line posted while its run still runs;
- indexer acknowledgment: posts and ack queries on one channel;
- the refusals.

Unit tests cover:

- every oracle event, byte for byte but for the run's own time, host and tag;
- the options;
- the times as Go writes them;
- the batches: full, flushed, and a refused post's messages given again
  (mutation-checked: a message taken before its batch has room fails it);
- indexer acknowledgment: delivered once indexed, the close waiting, a post not acked in
  time posted again.

### D166. A run's log sent to the journal; a container's own fields its own

`--log-driver journald` is served on Linux, and sent as syslog's is (D163): from shards'
store, by the daemon's shipper.

- **Entries in systemd's native protocol** (systemd.io, "Native Journal Protocol"), with
  the fields Docker's driver gives them, so that a journal query written for Docker's runs
  finds shards'. Each is written as go-systemd's journal.Send writes one. A field is
  `NAME=value` and a newline; a value with a newline in it is its name, its length as a
  little-endian u64, and itself. Its fields:
  - PRIORITY (6 for stdout, 3 for stderr) and MESSAGE, the line;
  - moby's:
    - CONTAINER_ID (the short ID) and CONTAINER_ID_FULL;
    - CONTAINER_NAME and IMAGE_NAME;
    - CONTAINER_TAG and SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER (the tag: the short ID unless given);
    - CONTAINER_LOG_EPOCH, an ID each shipper makes as it starts;
    - CONTAINER_LOG_ORDINAL, the entry's place from 1;
  - SYSLOG_TIMESTAMP, its output's time, RFC 3339 to the nanosecond;
  - a part's place where a line is longer than 16 KiB: CONTAINER_PARTIAL_ID, _ORDINAL
    and _LAST, and before the last, CONTAINER_PARTIAL_MESSAGE;
  - the attributes asked for, named as journal queries for Docker's runs name them (moby's
    sanitizeKeyMod): letters in
    upper case, every other character but a digit `_`, none leading.

  All are held field for field to Docker 29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`, its
  capture taking the journal's socket in the probe container):
  - each stream's lines, and a 40,000-byte line's parts;
  - a tag and attributes;
  - an entry longer than a datagram;
  - 7 cases of which options Docker takes.

  Docker writes the fields in a Go map's random order; journald keeps them in none.
- **An entry longer than a datagram** goes in a sealed memfd, passed with an empty
  datagram, as systemd's own sd_journal_sendv passes one; journald takes that from any
  sender. go-systemd writes a file in /dev/shm instead, which journald takes from there,
  /tmp or /var/tmp alone.
- **The journal's socket** is systemd's, /run/systemd/journal/socket, or the one
  `SHARDS_JOURNAL_SOCKET` names. A datagram is in the journal's queue as it is sent:
  delivered.
- **Linux's.** macOS keeps no journal, and refuses the driver in shards' words. Docker
  refuses it as its container starts on a host whose journal is not running ("journald is
  not enabled on this host"). shards' run starts, and its shipper waits for the journal.
- **Where Docker is wrong, shards is not.**
  - An attribute whose field journald would drop (a digit first, or past 64 characters)
    is left out, and the daemon's log says so. Docker sends it, and journald drops it
    without a word.
  - An attribute named as a field of the driver's own is left out. Docker's lets it
    replace the container's own: a label `container.name` its CONTAINER_NAME, or
    `container.id` its CONTAINER_ID, so an image's labels could say another container
    wrote its lines. It can also stand beside the driver's, as a second MESSAGE or
    PRIORITY.
  - gelf's and fluentd's own fields win alike. A label `container_id` no longer replaces
    gelf's `_container_id`, nor a label `log` fluentd's line.
  - An entry that fails keeps its ordinal, and is sent again. Docker counts it, and
    drops it.
- **fluentd's record has no `tag`.** D165 sent the tag asked for as a member of the
  record, as json-file's `--details` shows it. moby's fluentd sends its attributes from
  logger.Info.ExtraAttributes, which leave the tag out. shards' now does too, as do its
  gelf and journald.
- **Not yet.** awslogs, gcplogs and etwlogs; splunk came with D167.

Tested on real microVMs on Linux (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_journald_as_its_options_say`),
against a journal socket in the test:

- a line on each stream: its priority, the container's fields, its time `logs -t`'s, and
  its ordinal; an attribute asked for, and those left out;
- a 40,000-byte line in three parts;
- an entry past twice `wmem_max` (Linux doubles a send buffer) in a memfd, sealed against
  every change.

On macOS it tests the refusal.

The fluentd test now asks for a tag. Mutation-checked: a record with the tag in it fails
it.

Unit tests cover:

- every oracle entry against Docker's, but for the three recorded differences;
- the options;
- the fields' writing;
- the names journald keeps;
- gelf's and fluentd's own fields winning.

### D165. A run's log sent to fluentd

`--log-driver fluentd` is served, sent as syslog's is (D163): from shards' store by the
daemon's shipper.

- **Events in Fluentd's forward protocol**, as Docker's driver sends them (logging/testdata/fluentd.json), so that a
  Fluentd pipeline built for Docker's runs takes shards' alike. Each line is an event in
  Message mode, MessagePack written as fluent-logger-golang's EncodeData writes it: an array of
  the tag (the short ID unless given), the time, the record and the options.
  - The time is whole seconds, as msgp's AppendInt64 writes them, or with
    `fluentd-sub-second-precision` an EventTime (extension 0: seconds and nanoseconds).
  - The record is moby's: `container_id`, `container_name` (Docker's, with its `/`),
    `source`, `log`, the attributes asked for (an attribute named as one of those is
    left out: D166), and a part's place over all
    (`partial_message`, `partial_id`, `partial_ordinal`, `partial_last`) where a line is
    longer than 16 KiB. Its members are sorted, where Go writes a map in no order.
  - Held to Docker 29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`): over TCP in whole seconds
    and to the nanosecond, over a unix socket, and 26 cases of which options Docker
    takes.
- **Acks.** With `fluentd-request-ack` each event's options name its chunk, fluent-logger-
  golang's ID (its seconds and a random number, base64), and the server's ack is read back
  and matched.
- **Transports.** `tcp` (the default, 127.0.0.1:24224), `tls` (verified against the
  platform's roots, as fluent-logger-golang's tls.Dial is), `unix`.
- **Retries.** A failed send is tried again after `fluentd-retry-wait`, half as long again
  each time up to a minute, `fluentd-max-retries` times, as fluent-logger-golang tries it.
  Then the shipper's own waits take over, where fluent-logger-golang gives the event up.
  `fluentd-write-timeout` and `fluentd-read-timeout` bound a write and an ack. Without
  acks, an event is delivered once its receiver's TCP has it; what a connection had not
  delivered goes on the next (D163). With acks, an event's ack says it is delivered.
- **Taken, and moot.** `fluentd-async`, `fluentd-async-reconnect-interval` and
  `fluentd-buffer-limit` are taken and checked as Docker takes them (logging/testdata/fluentd.json). They change nothing:
  every log is sent off its run's path, with the store as its buffer. Docker's driver
  without `fluentd-async` dials as its container starts, so a server that is down keeps
  the container from starting.
- **Lines' parts.** A line the run left unfinished goes whole, or as its last part. moby's
  copier sends it as a part never the last, which leaves consumers that join parts
  waiting.
- **Not yet.** awslogs, gcplogs and etwlogs; journald and splunk came with D166 and D167.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_fluentd_as_its_options_say`), against a
server in the test that acks as fluentd does:

- TCP to the nanosecond with acks: each event's tag, record (the label asked for) and
  chunk, its time `logs -t`'s exactly;
- a unix socket in whole seconds, a 40,000-byte line in three parts, one ID, its places
  and its last;
- the refusals.

Mutation-checked: an ack never asked for fails it. Unit tests cover every oracle event
decoded against Docker's, the options against Docker's, an ack's chunk, and the cutter's
parts.

### D164. A run's log sent to a GELF server

`--log-driver gelf` is served, sent as syslog's is (D163): from shards' store, by the
daemon, on the shipper's thread, so the microVM reaches no network for its log, a run
starts whether or not its server is up, and nothing is lost to a server that is down.

- **Messages as Docker's driver sends them** (logging/testdata/gelf.json), so that a Graylog
  stream of Docker's runs takes shards' alike. Each line is a GELF 1.1 message, as go-gelf's
  MarshalJSONBuf writes it:
  - first its own fields in their order: the version, this host's name, the line, the
    time in seconds to the millisecond (GELF 1.1's), and the level, 6 for stdout and 3 for
    stderr;
  - then the container's own, the fields such a stream is searched by (gelf.json): `_container_id`,
    `_container_name`, `_image_id`, `_image_name`, `_command`, `_tag` and `_created`;
  - then the attributes asked for (`labels`, `env`, their regexes), each named with a `_`
    first, all sorted by name and HTML-escaped, as Go's encoding/json writes a map.

  Held byte for byte to Docker 29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`: UDP gzipped, zlib'd
  and uncompressed, TCP, and 17 cases of which options Docker takes).
- **UDP.** gzip unless told, at go-gelf's level 1 unless `gelf-compression-level` says;
  zlib, or none. A message past 1,420 bytes goes in chunks of 1,420, each with its magic,
  a random 8-byte ID, its number and how many, 128 at most.
- **TCP.** Each message is followed by a NUL. A write that fails is tried again on new
  connections `gelf-tcp-max-reconnect` times, `gelf-tcp-reconnect-delay` seconds apart,
  as go-gelf tries it. After that the shipper's own waits take over, where go-gelf drops
  the message. What a connection had not delivered goes on the next (D163). Docker's
  driver dials as its container starts, so a server that is down keeps the container
  from starting; shards' run starts regardless.
- **Not yet.** awslogs, gcplogs and etwlogs; fluentd, journald and splunk came with D165
  to D167.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_gelf_as_its_options_say`):

- UDP gzipped: every field checked against `inspect`, a label asked for, and the time
  `logs -t`'s to the millisecond;
- uncompressed, a 40,000-byte line in 16,384 + 16,384 + 7,232, each its own message in
  chunks;
- TCP, each message ended by a NUL;
- the refusals.

Mutation-checked: the attributes left out fail it. Unit tests cover every oracle message
byte for byte (with its chunk count and compression), the options against Docker's, and
chunking.

### D163. A run's log sent to syslog, by the daemon, from shards' store

`--log-driver syslog` is served, the first of Docker's drivers that send a log elsewhere,
and the way every later one sends.

- **From the store, by the daemon.** The run's VM keeps its output in shards' store as
  every run's does (D161). The daemon follows the log of each container whose driver
  sends it elsewhere, on a thread of its own (`daemon/ship.rs`), as `logs -f` follows
  one, and sends each line. So:
  - the VM, its guest and its run reach no network for their log;
  - a server that is slow or down holds up nothing but its own sending, retried after
    1 s, half as long again each time, at most 60 s (fluent-logger-golang's waits, through
    which moby's fluentd driver sends);
  - a run starts whether or not its server is up, where Docker's would not start;
  - what is not yet sent waits in the store, bounded as the store is, and survives the
    daemon's restarts: the shipper keeps its place beside the log (`ship`), and the next
    daemon sends what is left. Docker sends from the run's copier and loses what it had
    not sent.
- **Lines cut where Docker's are** (logging/testdata/gelf.json), so that a receiver that joins
  Docker's parts joins shards'. Each line is a message, cut as moby's copier cuts it (the size
  open in docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md): past
  16 KiB, in parts of 16 KiB, then the rest.
- **Delivered, not written** (`daemon/ship/stream.rs`, PM M233). Over TCP, TLS or a unix
  stream socket, a message counts as sent only once its receiver has it.
  - Over TCP, that is once its receiver's TCP has acknowledged its last byte, as the
    kernel counts them: Linux's SIOCOUTQ, macOS's TCP_CONNECTION_INFO, Windows'
    SIO_TCP_INFO, whose BytesOut counts the bytes sent again too (PM M373): there the
    bytes written less `BytesOut − BytesRetrans − BytesInFlight`, BytesRetrans's 32 bits
    counted past their wraps, the FIN while FIN_WAIT_1, CLOSING or LAST_ACK. A unix
    socket's bytes are in its receiver's buffer as they are written; on Windows an AF_UNIX
    stream's (afunix), Windows having no AF_UNIX datagrams: a `unixgram` address is
    refused there as its run is made, in shards' words.
  - The shipper keeps its place only as far as what is delivered. So a daemon that stops
    or dies costs sending again what was not yet delivered, and loses no line.
  - What a connection had not delivered when it ended (a reset, a receiver that
    restarts, a timeout after a partition) is held, and written again, in order, on the
    next. srslog, go-gelf and fluent-logger-golang lose it.
  - A connection ends only once its receiver has all of it:
    - TLS's close_notify is sent;
    - its write side is shut;
    - what the receiver still sends is read and let go;
    - the socket closes once all is acknowledged.

    A socket closed with bytes unread resets its connection, and what is not yet sent
    goes with it. TLS 1.3's session tickets are such bytes: no sender that only writes
    reads them. D163's first CI lost a run's last line this way, held back by Nagle's
    algorithm behind the line before it, on every x86_64 Linux run; the probe loses it in
    200 of 200 rounds on Linux and 90 of 200 on macOS. Docker's drivers close their
    sockets this way.
  - A receiver's TCP having a message is as far as TCP can say. fluentd's acks (D165)
    say its receiver has it.
- **Messages as Docker's driver sends them** (logging/testdata/syslog.json). Its formats (srslog's Unix format, rfc3164, rfc5424,
  rfc5424micro), its facilities, info for stdout and err for stderr, the tag (the short ID
  unless given), its framing (newlines, octet counting over TLS for RFC 5424), and udp,
  tcp, tcp+tls, unix, unixgram and the host's own syslog. All are held byte for byte to
  Docker 29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`: 25 transport, format and facility
  cases, recorded in shards-dind, and which options Docker takes).
- **Where Docker is wrong, shards is not.** Each difference is recorded, in the oracle's
  test where it has one:
  - a message is stamped with when its output came; srslog stamps when it sends;
  - it names this host; srslog names its socket's local address and port, which no RFC
    5424 HOSTNAME is;
  - its tag fills its fields: RFC 5424's APP-NAME and MSGID are printable ASCII of at most
    48 and 32 characters, and a space would end either format's tag early;
  - a datagram socket's send buffer grows to each message, since macOS takes none longer
    than it (PM M232). A line whose datagram its receiver refuses for its size goes in
    halves, down to RFC 5426's 480 octets. moby drops it;
  - nothing is dropped: a send that fails is sent again, and what a connection had not
    delivered goes on the next;
  - `syslog-tls-skip-verify` is refused, its CA asked for instead: shards sends only to a
    server whose certificate it verifies;
  - `unix://host/path` is refused. Go's parser takes `host` for a host, and moby's driver
    drops it.
- **The local copy.** A driver that sends its log elsewhere keeps it in the store too, as
  Docker's dual logging does.
  - `cache-max-size`, `cache-max-file` and `cache-compress` bound it. Docker takes them and
    applies none: its cache is the local driver with its defaults
    (loggerutils/cache.WithLocalCache passes the options unchanged).
  - `cache-disabled=true` keeps it from `logs`, which says so. The segments wholly sent go.
  - Every driver takes the `cache-*` options, as Docker's do; D161 refused them.
- **`inspect`'s LogPath** is empty, as dockerd leaves its local driver's: shards' store is
  its own, no file a reader of Docker's json-file logs could read.
- **Segments filled.** A record fills the room its segment has, the rest going on in the
  next. D161's rule moved a record that did not fit whole into the next segment. On CI's
  x86_64 Linux, whose guest's records are 32 KiB, that left segments of 64,000 bytes half
  full and a log half its retention; D162's test caught it there.
- **Not yet.** awslogs, gcplogs and etwlogs, each refused with a word that says so; gelf,
  fluentd, journald and splunk came with D164 to D167.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_syslog_as_its_options_say`):

- UDP in srslog's format;
- TCP in rfc5424micro and local0, its time `logs -t`'s to the microsecond and its host a
  name;
- TLS with a CA made for the test, octet-counted, its connection ended cleanly with
  close_notify;
- a unix datagram socket, a 40,000-byte line in 16,384 + 16,384 + 7,232;
- a server that comes up only after the run, and one up only after the daemon restarted;
- `cache-disabled`, `logs` refusing it;
- the refusals, and an empty LogPath.

Unit tests cover:

- every message of the oracle, byte for byte;
- the options, against what Docker takes;
- addresses, ports and tag fields;
- the copier's cuts;
- the shipper's place, kept only as far as its receiver has the messages before it, and a
  reader resumed from it showing every line once;
- a TLS stream closed at once after its last writes, its receiver's session tickets
  unread, delivering all of them and ending with close_notify (mutation-checked: closed
  at once, its receiver sees a reset);
- what a connection reset by its receiver had not delivered, written again on the next,
  in order, before what comes after (mutation-checked: what is held dropped fails it);
- the segments wholly sent going.

### D162. A run's rotated log segments compressed, seekably; a log that never holds up its run

D162 serves two of Docker's log options that D161 refused, `compress` and
`mode=non-blocking`, and serves both better than Docker does.

- **`compress`: rotated segments, seekable.** The daemon's packer thread compresses each
  segment once it has rotated. That thread is off every run's path, and off the files'
  thread that makes the segments runs wait for (D161).
  - Each segment becomes zstd frames of 1 MiB of it, each compressed alone at
    klauspost's best level. Their seek table follows, as zstd's seekable format lays it
    out (facebook/zstd contrib/seekable_format, v0.1.0). The file is `log.N.zst`, beside
    the segment's index, which stays as written.
  - Real logs come to 7.63% of their size, against 9.20% for Docker's gzip of each whole
    rotated file (PM M231).
  - A reader (`logs`, and its `--tail`) reads any record by decompressing its frame
    alone, 1.7 ms at most, its checksum checked. Docker decompresses a whole rotated file
    into a temporary file to read any of it. `zstd -d` reads the file whole.
- **Whole on every path.**
  - The compressed file is made durable before the segment as written goes, so a reader
    finds one or the other whole. It looks for the one as written first.
  - Retention removes either. A segment removed as it is compressed leaves nothing, and
    a container being removed is left to its removal.
  - As a daemon starts, it compresses what one before it left as written, including a
    file a crash left half compressed. The container's record says which logs compress
    (`log_compress`).
- **Which logs.**
  - `shards`, shards' own driver, compresses by default: 13 times less disk, for at most
    184 ms of a thread a 20 MB segment (PM M231). So does `local`, as Docker's default
    does.
  - json-file compresses only when asked: uncompressed is what the name means to its users. Its `compress=true` without
    `max-size` is taken: Docker refuses it for want of a bound, and shards' store always
    has one.
  - One file (`max-file 1`) never rotates, so it is never compressed. Asking for that is
    refused in shards' words.
- **`mode=non-blocking`.** The run's output is queued in its VM for the log's own thread,
  so a log that falls behind never holds up the run's output.
  - The queue holds at most `max-buffer-size` bytes (go-units' RAMInBytes, binary units),
    or moby's 1,000,000 when none is given (open in docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md).
    Output that comes while it is full is dropped: non-blocking mode is chosen to drop rather
    than hold its run (moby's ring logger drops so too). Output that would pass the size goes only
    into an empty queue.
  - Docker drops in silence. shards counts what it drops (`LOST`'s second count, the
    record's `log_dropped`), and `logs` says it on stderr: `N bytes of NAME's output were
    dropped, as they came while its log's queue was full (--log-opt mode=non-blocking)`.
    `logs` still exits 0, since dropping is what the run asked for.
  - All that is queued is kept before the run's end is told.
- **Not yet.** The drivers that send a log elsewhere (D161's list), of which D163 serves
  syslog.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_compressed_and_queued_as_its_options_say`):

- 30,000 lines through segments of 64,000 bytes, four kept: three compressed, `logs` the
  output's newest, and `--tail 12000` read from the middle of compressed segments.
- json-file: none compressed by default, three with `compress=true`.
- `max-buffer-size=0`: what was kept and what was dropped add up to the output exactly,
  with 36 to 51% dropped in three runs, and the drop said. 4 MiB: all of it kept, nothing
  said.
- The refusals.

Mutation-checked: drops left uncounted, and shards' own driver not compressing, each fail
it. Unit tests cover:

- the format, read back across frames and as one stream;
- damage refused, in the seek table and in a frame's checksum;
- a segment removed as it is compressed, and retention;
- what a daemon compresses as it starts;
- every read of a log in compressed segments, against the plain way;
- the queue's drops, and the options.

### D161. A run's log, as `--log-driver` and `--log-opt` keep it

`run` and `create` take `--log-driver` and `--log-opt` as docker/cli takes them (scripts/docker-cli/oracle_test.go; served,
held to the CLI by the docker-cli oracle; options with `none` refused as the CLI refuses
them). A run's log is shards' own store (D27's segments), which `shards`, the default,
`json-file` and `local` name; `none` keeps none. `inspect` says the driver given, shards'
own where none was, and the options as a map (`HostConfig.LogConfig`).

- **Its bound, its own.** `max-size` (go-units' FromHumanSize, decimal, as both of
  Docker's file drivers read it) is each segment's most bytes, `max-file` how many it
  keeps, the newest written; they go to the run's VM with its request, and the daemon
  rotates by the run's count. A record fills what room the segment written has, the rest
  going on in the next, each saying whether it ends a line, so no segment is longer than
  asked, each is as long as it may be, and a line so cut is read whole. Before, a segment
  took a whole frame past its size (12 KB a segment where 1 KB was asked); then, until
  D163, a record that did not fit went whole into the next segment, which left segments
  of 64,000 bytes half full of a Linux guest's 32 KiB records. json-file
  keeps one file where only `max-size` is given, what the option means to its users (D161); where neither is, every
  driver keeps the home's bound, its user's (`shards configure disk --log-history`, 1 GiB
  by default, D186), or the daemon's environment's (`SHARDS_LOG_MAX_SIZE`,
  `SHARDS_LOG_MAX_FILE`), where Docker's json-file keeps one file that grows without end.
- **None.** No `RUN_LOG`, no segments sent: a detached run's output goes nowhere, an
  attached one's to its client alone, and `logs` is refused (`NAME keeps no log: it was
  run with --log-driver none`).
- **Details.** `labels`, `labels-regex`, `env`, `env-regex` and `tag` (a Go template of the
  container: `{{.Name}}`, `{{.ID}}`, `{{.ImageName}}`, `{{.Command}}`, ...) are what `logs
  --details` shows before each line, in the form `docker logs --details` prints, which scripts read: sorted by name, each
  `NAME=VALUE` query-escaped, joined by commas (moby logger.Info.ExtraAttributes,
  loggerutils.ParseLogTag), from what `inspect` says of the container's environment,
  labels and command.
- **Refused, in shards' words.** An unknown driver or option; values that do not read
  (`max-size`, `max-file`, `compress`, `mode`, the regexes); `max-buffer-size` without
  non-blocking mode.
- **Not yet.** The drivers that send a log elsewhere (`syslog`, `journald`, `gelf`,
  `fluentd`, `awslogs`, `splunk`, `gcplogs`, `etwlogs`), each refused with a word that
  says so. `compress` and `mode=non-blocking` came with D162.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_kept_as_its_driver_and_options_say`): 10,000
lines through `max-size=1k` and `max-file=2`, the log the output's newest lines, two
segments; `none`: its client's output, nothing written, `logs` refused; `--details` with a
label, a variable (escaped) and a tag; the refusals; `inspect`. Mutation-checked: a run
logged whatever its driver fails it. Unit tests: each option's reading and refusal, the
attributes and the tag.

### D160. The streams a run's client attaches (`-a`)

`run -a` and `create -a` take `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr`, in any case, as docker/cli takes them (scripts/docker-cli/oracle_test.go)
reads them (validateAttach, its refusal held to the CLI by the docker-cli oracle). A
run's client shows the streams it attaches and passes `/dev/null` for the others; its
log keeps every stream, as every run's does, so `logs` shows what the client did not.
None given, stdout and stderr; stdin is the command's with `-i` alone (Docker's
`OpenStdin`, which its clients set). A run attached to stdin alone shows nothing and ends with its command's
status. `-a` with `-d` is refused: a detached run's streams go to its log alone.

`inspect`'s `Config.AttachStdin`, `AttachStdout`, `AttachStderr` and `StdinOnce` say what
the command line gave: a created container's as the CLI's create sends them, which clients read back (stdout
and stderr without `-a`), which shards showed as detached before, its kept request losing
that it was a create; `run -d`'s none.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_run_attaches_the_streams_it_asks_for`): stdout alone, stderr
alone, each run's log holding both; stdin alone, its status 3; `-d` refused; `create
-a stdout` and plain `create` as `inspect` says them. Mutation-checked: the client
attaching every stream; a create's request kept detached: each fails.

### D159. A run's swap, written to its host's memory at the guest's own speed

`-m` with `--memory-swap` (by default as much swap again as memory), `--memory-swappiness`
and `--oom-kill-disable` are the run's microVM's own. Docker's swap is its host's swap
device, which a host may not have; on a cgroup v2 host it discards swappiness and
`--oom-kill-disable` with a warning. A microVM is its own kernel, and its host's memory
and disk are its swap.

- **The swap window.** Every run's microVM has one: a virtio-pmem device as long as the
  host's memory, the most a run may have and so its default swap, past everything else
  the guest is given and within the addresses the host allows (a window cut short holds
  less, as a host's swap device smaller than a container's allowance does). A run with
  swap gets a sparse file of its own, made anew each run in its container's directory and
  unlinked there once its microVM holds it, off the run's path: what it swapped out is
  nowhere once the microVM has ended. Its VM writes the file's first 64 KiB through the
  file's own path, then maps it at the window's start, shared and writable; init writes
  the swap header there (past the page cache) and swaps on before the command starts. The
  guest's CPUs write swapped pages as memory, into the host's page cache of the file:
  pmem completes each write as reclaim makes it (BLK_FEAT_SYNCHRONOUS), so reclaim frees
  each page at once (mm/vmscan.c, shrink_folio_list) and never waits on a host thread.
  The first page is the host's to write: the guest's first write to a page of the sparse
  file, through the mapping, takes the host's fault path to make the page, 3.4 ms at
  p90 and 80 ms at worst for the header, where written first by the host it is 23 µs at
  p50 and 31 µs at p99 (PM M230). The rest stays sparse: reserving the file's disk
  (`F_PREALLOCATE`) cost 5.3 ms at p50 for 424 MiB on APFS, 29 ms for 4.4 GiB (M230).
- **Why not a block device.** Swap was first a writable range of the join disk (D119),
  through a loop device, buffered and then direct. A workload within its swap was killed:
  under `-m 64m`, allocating 96 MiB, one run in four ended 137. Reclaim under a cgroup v2
  limit passes over anonymous folios under writeback rather than wait for them (mm/vmscan.c,
  folio_check_dirty_writeback and shrink_folio_list's second case), and 16 rounds without
  progress call the OOM killer (mm/memcontrol.c, try_charge_memcg). The VMM's worker
  completing the writes, on its own host thread, was too late under load (PM M230).
- **Hidden as the kernel boots.** Probed then, libnvdimm would give the window page
  structures, a 64th of it (2 GiB of a 128 GiB window: drivers/nvdimm/pmem.c,
  pmem_should_map_pages); swap needs none. Its transport reads as no device (DeviceID 0,
  virtio 1.3 §4.2.3.1.1) until init shows it (the control page's `SWAP`), with
  libnvdimm's drivers kept from binding of themselves meanwhile, and has its namespace
  probed raw (`force_raw`): mapped, never described. Before the template's snapshot, so
  a restore pays nothing for it. Its head reads as zeros until a run's file is mapped
  over it, what the kernel's partition scan reads; a snapshot keeps the window and never
  a run's file.
- **Sizes.** The device is the allowance and 20 MiB a vCPU (the clusters each CPU keeps,
  PM M229), whole 2 MiB, which the run's cgroup holds to the allowance
  (`memory.swap.max`); unlimited (`-1`) is as much again as the memory: a device as large
  as the host's memory would cost the guest's kernel 0.8 KiB a MiB of it (M229). The
  kernel's bookkeeping is in the microVM's memory, beside the limit (`swap_kernel_bytes`).
  A run without `-m` has none: its microVM grows to the host's memory (D148).
- **Swappiness** is the microVM's (`vm.swappiness`): the run's kernel is its own.
  **`--oom-kill-disable`** makes the limit a throttle (`memory.high`): past it the
  workload is slowed under reclaim and never killed, as cgroup v1's OOM control held a
  container's tasks, which cgroup v2 has no control for. `inspect` says both as given.
- **Agents take none.** An Agentfile's agents and harnesses (D59) have the memory their
  Agentfile grants and no swap (`memory.swap.max` 0 over their domains' cgroups): given
  the run's microVM's swap, an agent past its limit swapped rather than ended
  (`agents_out_of_memory_end_whole_and_spare_the_run`, which holds it).
- **A kill says why.** Where the kernel ends a run's or a joiner's process for want of
  memory, its init sends with the `OOM` what the run's cgroup held and was allowed then
  (`memory.max`, `memory.peak`, `memory.swap.max`, `memory.swap.peak`, `memory.events`,
  `memory.swap.events`) and the kernel's report of it (its lines that say why, among them
  the cgroup's `memory: usage ... limit` and `swap: usage ... limit`, read with syslog(2)
  where the run's /dev has no kmsg), which the daemon writes to its log. A joiner's kill
  was said nowhere: init removed its cgroup as it reaped its process, before its end was
  said, and the VM process's reader of a joiner's frames took no `OOM`. Now it is read at
  the reap, and a joiner is `OOMKilled` as a run is (D119). Found chasing a joiner killed
  within its swap on x86_64 CI (job 117491995198, run 39245355471): the next such kill's
  log says what its cgroup held of its swap.
- **Members share.** A run joining another's microVM (D119) swaps to that microVM's swap:
  the first member with an allowance maps its file, and the rest share it, each held to
  its own allowance by its cgroup, as a host's containers share its swap. Joiners had
  none of their own limits before: the daemon set them where it named a run's guest,
  which a joiner skips, its names its provider's; every run's are now set apart.
- **Costs** (PM M230, n=100 a side, interleaved). A run's start: +170 µs [+148, +182] from
  request to answer (p50 731 µs without, 889 with), of which the guest's header write is
  23 µs and swapon 25 µs (p50; 31 and 44 at p99), the rest the file's first page and its
  mapping. A workload 32 MiB past `-m 64m`: +12.6 ms [+12.1, +13.1], its pages swapped
  out at memory's speed where the block device's took seconds, or killed it. A template's
  boot, its window shown and probed: +0.6 ms [+0.4, +1.0]. The guest's address space, 40
  bits with a 64 GiB window where 36 without: a page-strided walk, every step a
  translation's miss, −0.1 ns [−1.3, +2.2] in one pass and +2.3 [+0.1, +4.2] in another,
  of 98 to 124 ns a step: at most about 2% of such a load, on the hosts whose microVMs the
  window takes past 36 bits (on this one, every microVM has 40 without it).
- **Not yet.** `update --memory-swap` past the swap a run started with, which its device
  holds; a build's `--memory-swap` (D64), whose builder has no swap window; what a host
  whose disk is full does to a microVM writing a new page of its sparse swap file, which
  is not measured.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_microvm_swaps_and_throttles_as_its_limits_say`): under `-m
64m`, 96 MiB allocated, five runs in a row; no swap with `--memory-swap 64m` (137) or
without `-m`; `memory.swap.max` for each allowance; unlimited; swappiness 10;
`--oom-kill-disable` past the limit; the refusals; `inspect`; a joiner held to its own
`memory.max`, killed without swap and swapping to its provider's microVM, twice.
Mutation-checked: without swapon; with `--oom-kill-disable` a hard limit; a joiner's swap
not mapped; a joiner's limits not set: each fails.

### D158. What shards refuses, in its own words

A refusal says what shards does with its microVMs and how to get what was asked; it does
not repeat what dockerd's or the Docker CLI's code says. An error reads `shards: MESSAGE`,
as Unix tools name themselves; the Docker client's `Error response from daemon:` is gone
(on a terminal the panel showed the message alone already). What scripts match is kept in
each message: `No such container: NAME`, `No such image: NAME`, `is not running`,
`port is already allocated`, `address already in use`, `executable file not found`; exit
statuses are unchanged. Compose and the Docker CLI decide by the API's status codes, not
by these texts: Compose matches its own "no such service" (cmd/compose/run.go), the CLI
the API's own words where it tries kinds of object (cli/command/system/inspect.go).

- **Reworded.** The microVMs' lifecycle (exec, pause, unpause, rm, stop, restart, kill,
  rename, logs, top, update); a run's network checks (what a joiner takes of its
  provider, the host's and no network, addresses, link-local addresses, endpoint
  sysctls); the network commands (connect, disconnect, create, rm, inspect, and the subnet
  checks, which leaked Go's netip errors); port publishing (another run's port, or another
  program's); image tags and removals (which microVM uses an image, and whether `-f`
  would remove it); volumes; the time windows of logs and events; signals; flags given
  together; a run's limits (`resources::verify`, with D159) and what `update` refuses of
  them (the CPU time set one way, updated another; memory past the swap already set). An exec that does not start says `shards: cannot start the command: WHY`.
  Each names the flag, or the run as it was given, never a 64-digit ID.
- **Not yet.** The build's texts, which its oracles hold byte for byte to BuildKit's; the
  CLI's usage and help texts and its checks of flags' values (crates/cmdline), byte for
  byte docker/cli's when piped; filters' and
  `inspect`'s validation; the Go errors of an image config that does not read; the
  guest's network setup errors.

### D157. shards' own names first; Docker's and buildx's still read

What a user writes or sets for shards carries shards' own name, as its build file is an
Agentfile before a Dockerfile (D35). The name Docker's or buildx's tools read for the same
is read after it, so that what a user has keeps working.

- **Ignore files.** A build's context is sent without what `.agentignore` excludes, else
  `.dockerignore`; one beside the build file, `NAME.agentignore`, else `NAME.dockerignore`,
  takes the context's place, as an ignore file beside a Dockerfile does for BuildKit's users (frontend/dockerui).
  The progress and a copy's warning (`CopyIgnoredFile`) name the file read; a build's
  `mode=max` provenance lists the one beside the build file it read. Verified
  (`the_agentignore_is_read_before_the_dockerignore`, mutation-checked: Docker's name
  looked for first; the warning naming `.dockerignore` whichever was read). The frontend
  image, which runs in another builder and reads what that builder's client sends, asks
  for `.dockerignore`, the file docker/dockerfile reads; it takes `.agentignore` with its own work,
  which comes last.
- **Environment.** `SHARDS_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` before `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM`,
  `SHARDS_BUILDER` before `BUILDX_BUILDER`, `SHARDS_DEFAULT_POLICY` before
  `BUILDX_DEFAULT_POLICY`, `SHARDS_NO_DEFAULT_ATTESTATIONS` before
  `BUILDX_NO_DEFAULT_ATTESTATIONS`, `SHARDS_AUTH_CONFIG` before `DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG`, each
  where set and not empty; a value one of them gets wrong is said of it by its name.
  `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONFIG` and `DOCKER_CONTEXT` stay where shards finds the user's
  Docker engine to read images from it: they are that engine's settings.
- **The policies' builtin module** is `builtin/defaults.rego`; a policy written for buildx
  imports it as `data.builtin.buildx_defaults` and gets it too
  (`the_builtin_is_imported_by_either_name`).
- **Code.** The crate that reads Agentfiles and Dockerfiles is `crates/agentfile`, its
  recorder `scripts/agentfile`. Functions, tests and files say what shards does, never
  that it is another tool: what a recording holds shards to is named as a recording
  (`plans_match_their_recorded_answers`), the recordings named for what they record.

### D156. A run's IPC, hostname, cgroups, umask and writable layer, as its microVM has them

A run's flags for the namespaces it has, its umask and its writable layer are taken as
Docker's CLI takes them, and mean what they can for a microVM: a run shares no kernel
with its host, so "host" is the microVM's, and what one run shares with another it shares
inside the microVM the other runs in (D119).

- **IPC: a namespace and a /dev/shm of the run's own.** A run's standby enters an IPC
  namespace of its own and mounts its own /dev/shm before the template's snapshot, and its
  execs enter both. Before, a workload shared init's IPC namespace and /dev/shm. No restore
  time resolved, and memory per VM within one 16 KiB step of what two templates of one
  machine differ by (PM M228).
- **Every /dev/shm of a microVM is half the memory it may have.** A microVM's /dev/shm is
  its own kernel's tmpfs, bounded by the microVM's memory alone, and what agents run share
  memory through: a browser's renderers, a data loader's workers (Playwright's docs and
  PyTorch's README tell containers' users to raise Docker's 64 MiB, which a container takes
  of its host's). The microVM's own, each run's, each joiner's and a builder's steps' are
  all half the memory the microVM may have in all (`run::sizes`, D148: a run without a
  limit, the host's), as Linux sizes a tmpfs by default (Documentation/filesystems/
  tmpfs.rst). The daemon tells each run its bytes with the run (its `shm=` setup entry,
  `run::shm_bytes` of the most of the run whose microVM it is: its own, a joiner's
  provider's), as every limit's runs restore one template (D148), whose own is sized by
  half all its guest may plug; a builder's are on its kernel's command line (`shards_shm`).
  The entry comes before any of the run's mounts, so that what the run mounts at or under
  /dev/shm (a volume, `--tmpfs /dev/shm:size=8m`) goes over the /dev/shm it was given, as
  a container's mounts go over its default one, and is never resized itself: told after
  them (32df9efc), a run's 8 MiB tmpfs there was made the microVM's 64 GiB.
  `inspect`'s `ShmSize` says them, held to what the guest's statfs says. A run's
  memory limit still holds what it writes there, as memory. A run wrote 128 MiB there,
  where 64 MiB refused it (`a_microvm_takes_its_ipc_hostname_cgroups_umask_and_writable_layer`).
  Each of an image's agents (D139) has a /dev/shm of its own, mode 0700, as large as its
  run's (`domains::shm_of`, the run's `shm=` entry): it kept Docker's 64 MiB, which a
  browser an agent drives outgrows (`agents_run_in_their_domains`: past 64 MiB, which the
  64 MiB mount fails).
  - `--ipc private` (the default) and `shareable`: its own; another run may share a
    `shareable` run's alone, as Docker's daemon allows (moby
    daemon/container_operations_unix.go, getIPCContainer). `--shm-size` sizes its own.
  - `--ipc none`: its own namespace, and no /dev/shm at all.
  - `--ipc host`: the microVM's, init's namespace and /dev/shm, which no run has unless it
    asks, of the same size as its own.
  - `--ipc container:NAME`: NAME's namespace and /dev/shm, inside the microVM this run
    joins (`--network container:` of a run in NAME's microVM, D119), NAME `shareable` (or
    `host`, the microVM's); a run sharing a third's is followed to it. A joiner's own is
    shared as the workload's is: init copies the other run's /dev/shm mount from that
    run's mount namespace with open_tree(2) and attaches the copy with move_mount(2) (no
    bind reaches another namespace's mount; its copy, an anonymous namespace's root, moves
    into any: fs/namespace.c, may_copy_tree and do_move_mount). `--pid container:NAME`
    takes the same rule: any run of the microVM it joins.
  - A /dev/shm a run does not own is not its to size: `--shm-size` with `none`, `host` or
    `container:` is refused in shards' words, where Docker ignores it.
- **`--uts host`: its host's hostname.** The microVM's hostname is the host's, as a run on
  the host's network has it (D124), inspect's and the guest's the same (dockerd gives
  `--uts host` a configured hostname its processes do not have). A joiner with it shares
  its microVM's UTS namespace. `--hostname` with it is refused: each names the host.
- **`--userns`**: a run's users are its microVM's own, unmapped, either way; `host` and
  none are both taken and shown.
- **`--cgroupns host`: the microVM's cgroup tree**, read-only, where by default a run sees
  its own cgroup as the root. Beside an Agentfile's agents it is refused, by the daemon and
  again by init, in shards' words (`beside::cgroupns_host`): their cgroups are in that
  tree.
- **`--umask`**: its command's and its execs', as the workload's limits are (Docker's
  daemon keeps the container's for an exec too: moby daemon/exec_linux.go). At most 0777,
  the bits a umask clears.
- **`--storage-opt size=`: its writable layer's size.** A run's writable layer is an ext4
  file system on its host's disk (D190), made to hold the size asked: its microVM restores
  a template of that size. A joiner's is a tmpfs in its microVM's memory, made at it, and
  unsized it holds what the workload's tmpfs does, all the memory its microVM may have
  (D148): the kernel's default, half the memory at its mount, held a joiner of a microVM
  that plugs its memory as it needs it to half of what it booted with, and a 256 MiB file
  failed with ENOSPC (`a_joiners_layer_is_kept_whole_as_its_provider_ends` writes one).
  Docker serves `size` only on overlay over XFS with project quotas; every run here takes
  it.
  `size` is the one key; above 0; for a joiner no more than the memory its layer is held in
  (`--memory`, or the host's, which the microVM may grow to), and for a microVM's own no
  more than the memory its page structures take as it boots, a 64th of it, of all its host
  has, nor than ext4 holds: each refused in shards' words.
- **A joiner beside an Agentfile's agents.** A run joining a microVM was held to its own
  image's rules alone, and the microVM's agents' went unchecked: a joiner could run
  `--privileged` beside them. It is now held to that microVM's (D115), by the daemon and
  again by init, either alone enough (`a_run_reaches_none_of_its_images_agents`,
  mutation-checked: with neither, a privileged joiner ran).
- Each refusal in shards' words; `inspect` says each mode as given (`private` where none).
  Verified on real microVMs
  (`a_microvm_takes_its_ipc_hostname_cgroups_umask_and_writable_layer`, mutation-checked,
  each caught: execs outside the workload's IPC namespace; no /dev/shm of the run's own;
  `none` leaving the microVM's; umask not applied, or not to execs; the layer not sized;
  `--cgroupns host` not entered; a joiner not entering the workload's IPC namespace; a
  joiner's donor's /dev/shm not copied from its namespace; sharing without the donor's
  leave; `--uts host` not naming the run by its host; a joiner's writable layer not
  sized; a joiner not in the microVM's cgroup namespace with `--cgroupns host`).

### D155. A run's CPUs, real-time time, isolation and runtime, as its microVM has them

Every run is a microVM: its own kernel, its vCPUs host threads the VMM schedules. A run's
flags are taken as Docker's CLI takes them (crates/cmdline/tests/docker-cli.json), and do what they mean for a microVM, not what
Docker on Linux does, which refuses several of them for want of a VM.

- **`--cpu-count N`: its vCPUs.** Docker defines it for its VM-isolated containers as the
  VM's processors (moby daemon/oci_windows.go, setResourcesInSpec), and its CLI refuses it
  against a Linux daemon (cmd/docker/docker.go, areFlagsSupported). From 1 to the host's
  CPUs, past which a vCPU gives no more time; `--cpuset-cpus` names CPUs it has.
- **`--cpu-percent P`: the share of the host's CPU time its workload may use.** P% of all
  the host's CPUs' time each period, as the workload's `cpu.max`, on vCPUs enough for it
  (rounded up). One cap of CPU time at most: with `--cpus` or `--cpu-quota`, refused.
- **Real-time time, which runs did not have.** The guest kernel (Firecracker's base
  config: `CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED=y`) gave a workload's cgroup no real-time time, which
  cgroup v2 has no files to give (they are cgroup v1's: kernel/sched/core.c,
  cpu_rt_group_init), so `sched_setscheduler` refused SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR with EPERM
  even to root with CAP_SYS_NICE (kernel/sched/syscalls.c), where Docker on a typical host
  allows them. Runs and builders now boot with `rt_group_sched=0` (Linux 6.16; shards'
  kernels are 6.18): real-time time is the guest's own budget. `--cpu-rt-period` and
  `--cpu-rt-runtime` set it (`sched_rt_period_us`, `sched_rt_runtime_us`), the run's alone
  in its microVM, where Docker on a cgroup v2 host refuses them ("kernel does not support
  CPU real-time scheduler"). Checked as the kernel takes them, the runtime within the
  period where both are given; what the guest keeps of the other is its kernel's own
  (950000 of 1000000 µs on 6.18; Linux 7 gives all of it, c2e390197ad1), which init reads
  and checks as the run starts, refusing in shards' words. No runtime without a limit
  (-1): init and the run's agents share its CPUs. Verified on real microVMs
  (`a_microvm_takes_its_cpus_real_time_isolation_and_annotations`, mutation-checked:
  without `rt_group_sched=0` root with CAP_SYS_NICE is refused; without init's write the
  budget stays the kernel's): root with CAP_SYS_NICE and the image's user within
  `--ulimit rtprio` run SCHED_FIFO, the rest are refused (EPERM).
- **`--isolation`: its microVM's.** `default` and `hyperv` (a VM's) are what every run
  has, in any case; `process`, a kernel shared with the host, is refused in shards'
  words. Docker on Linux refuses all but `default`.
