- **`--runtime`: its microVM.** `shards`, runc's names (the default runtime's) and Kata
  Containers' (whose runs are VMs too) ask for what it is; any other is refused in
  shards' words. `inspect` names it `shards`.
- **`--annotation`**: kept, shown as `HostConfig.Annotations` and matched by `ps --filter
  annotation`, each with a key.
- **`--io-maxbandwidth` and `--io-maxiops`: its microVM's (D178).** A run's root is its
  image read through memory (DAX) and its writes in its memory: no drive of its own to
  cap. Its I/O to the host's storage goes through its virtio-fs shares and virtio-blk
  disks, which the VMM paces at them, outside the guest.
- `--help` lists `--cpu-count` and `--cpu-percent` as the microVM's; the CLI's oracle
  (scripts/docker-cli, against a CLI that knows its daemon is Linux's) holds every other
  answer byte for byte, and its test names each difference (MICROVM_FLAGS).

### D154. KVM on arm64, and a host's PCI function passed through (VFIO)

D13 planned KVM on arm64 Linux hosts, and none ran a VM: the KVM backend was x86_64's.
D153's test path for VFIO is a guest given the test function, passing it to a guest of
its own, on an arm64 Mac (D132): shards' VM process inside that guest is an arm64 Linux
one. So both, in that order.

- **One KVM backend for both architectures.** What is KVM's everywhere is shared (hv/kvm):
  /dev/kvm opened and checked once, guest memory's slots, the run loop, the kick. Each
  architecture's VM and vCPUs are its own module's, and so are its ioctls.
- **arm64's VM is the arm64 machine's** (vm/aarch64.rs), as Hypervisor.framework's is,
  with KVM's semantics behind the same names. Its GICv3 is KVM's
  (KVM_DEV_TYPE_ARM_VGIC_V3, Documentation/virt/kvm/devices/arm-vgic-v3.rst): the
  distributor and redistributors at the machine's places; 96 interrupts, 32 private and
  then the SPIs the machine's devices use, in KVM's steps of 32; initialized once every
  vCPU exists, before any runs (KVM_DEV_ARM_VGIC_CTRL_INIT), as the machine's `finish`
  now asks of every backend. PSCI is KVM's (KVM_ARM_VCPU_PSCI_0_2, api.rst 4.82): the boot
  vCPU enters at the kernel with X0 the devicetree, the others start powered off, CPU_ON
  and CPU_OFF are the kernel's, SYSTEM_OFF and SYSTEM_RESET come back as system events.
  Each vCPU's MPIDR, which KVM derives from its id, is checked against the devicetree's
  (`arch::aarch64::mpidr`). The address width is asked of KVM
  (KVM_CAP_ARM_VM_IPA_SIZE); pointer authentication is on where KVM gives both kinds, as
  the guest has it under Hypervisor.framework; EL2 where KVM gives it (KVM_CAP_ARM_EL2: a
  CPU with FEAT_NV2 and a host booted with kvm-arm.mode=nested, arch/arm64/kernel/
  cpufeature.c has_nested_virt_support), its maintenance interrupt the devicetree's,
  INTID 25, which KVM reads from the attribute's `addr` (arm64/kvm/vgic/
  vgic-kvm-device.c), where arm-vgic-v3.rst says its `attr`.
- **Confined as on x86_64** (D30): Landlock, and the seccomp filter, whose system calls
  are x86_64's but those the generic ABI has none of (open, stat, access, mkdir, rename,
  unlink, readlink, poll, dup2), whose `*at` forms musl and glibc make there instead.
- **VFIO** (`run --kernel … --vfio NAME`, Linux): VFIO's container, group and device
  (include/uapi/linux/vfio.h; Documentation/driver-api/vfio.rst). The function's group is
  found by its `iommu_group` before the VM process is confined, and the container and the
  group are the only devices Landlock then lets it reach (IOCTL_DEV); VFIO's requests are
  in the seccomp filter, of no use without them. A group with an IOMMU takes type 1 with
  all of guest RAM mapped for the function's DMA, pinned; a no-IOMMU group
  (vfio.enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode) maps none, for a function that makes no DMA. The
  configuration space is vfio-pci's, which keeps from a user what it must not touch, but
  for the BARs, the expansion ROM and the interrupt line and pin, which the VMM keeps
  (D153's header); the memory BARs are placed in the bus's window, each at the next
  multiple of its size, and each access goes to the device's region at its offset; an
  I/O BAR is left out, as the machine has no I/O window. Each group is added to KVM's
  VFIO device (Documentation/virt/kvm/devices/vfio.rst) before its device is opened, as
  drivers that need the VM to open one ask; through it KVM learns whether the function's
  DMA snoops the CPU's caches, and on x86 honours the guest's memory types where it does
  not (virt/kvm/vfio.c, kvm_vfio_update_coherency). The VM keeps that device as long as
  it lives: KVM forgets its groups as its descriptor closes (kvm_vfio_release). A machine
  given a function has no memory to plug, no balloon (its DMA mappings pinned; QEMU's
  `ram_block_discard_disable`) and no snapshot.
- **Where no OS passes one through, refused with its OS's own limit** (the parity plan's
  step 13, M356). macOS: Hypervisor.framework assigns no device to a VM, Virtualization's
  passthrough is USB's alone, and a PCI function reaches a process only through a
  DriverKit driver Apple entitles to it (`com.apple.developer.driverkit.transport.pci`).
  Windows: a partition is given one only once its administrator dismounts it from the
  host (Discrete Device Assignment; WHP's `WHvCreateVpciDevice`), which Microsoft supports
  on Windows Server alone, not on Windows 10 or 11; Windows Server's, on a host with a
  function to give, is not built. Each refusal says so (`vm::NO_PASSTHROUGH`), held by
  `a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_with_its_oss_own_limit`.
- **BARs in the guest's memory.** Each BAR vfio-pci lets a user map
  (VFIO_REGION_INFO_FLAG_MMAP: a memory BAR of a page or more, vfio_pci_probe_mmaps) is
  mapped into the VM process, and its pages, but for those of the MSI-X table and pending
  bits, which the VMM keeps, are memory slots of the function's own, which the guest
  reaches without an exit. They are in the guest while it enables the function's memory
  space, and leave before it disables it: vfio-pci then takes its mappings away
  (vfio_basic_config_write) and a vCPU touching one would fail its run (EFAULT); out,
  the BAR is trapped again, and a read with memory space off is all ones, as an access
  no function claims (PCI 3.0 §6.2.2, §2.3.2), which the test function now does too. A
  BAR of less than a page stays trapped whole, as its page in the guest holds others.
- **An IOMMU for the functions the VMM emulates** (virtio-iommu, virtio 1.3 §5.13;
  include/uapi/linux/virtio_iommu.h): a machine with the test function has one, last of
  its virtio devices, which translates the test function's requester ID alone: the
  devicetree's `iommu-map` on the host bridge (Documentation/devicetree/bindings/pci/
  pci-iommu.txt) and, on x86_64, ACPI's VIOT (ACPICA's actbl3.h; Linux
  drivers/acpi/viot.c). A passed-through function stays out of it unless it is given
  behind it (`--vfio-iommu`, below): its DMA reaches guest RAM through the host's
  mappings of all of it. The guest's driver attaches each endpoint to a domain and maps I/O addresses
  in it to guest-physical ones, a domain going with its mappings once its last endpoint
  leaves it, as Linux's driver expects (virtio-iommu.c, viommu_attach_dev); MAP refuses
  what is not whole pages or overlaps a mapping, UNMAP what would split one. On x86_64,
  PROBE gives each endpoint the local APICs' window, 0xfee00000 to 0xfeefffff, as a
  reserved region of subtype MSI (virtio 1.3 §5.13.3), so that MSIs need no mapping. On
  arm64 it gives none: Linux's MSI parents, GICv2m's and the ITS's, have the IOMMU map
  their doorbell for the device's domain (iommu.c, iommu_dma_prepare_msi), which VFIO's
  type 1 can do only in the software MSI window Linux's driver adds where the device
  reports no MSI region, mapped as device memory (IOMMU_MMIO), which the driver maps only
  where the device offers VIRTIO_IOMMU_F_MMIO; with a bypassed region instead, VFIO's
  MSIs failed (ENOSPC, msi_handle_pci_fail). The test function's MSIs are writes to an
  I/O address there, translated as its DMA is; on x86_64 an MSI into the window lands
  untranslated, as Linux takes a reserved region of subtype MSI (IOMMU_RESV_MSI), where
  the test function's had been translated through its domain, which maps nothing there,
  and dropped (`Translation::msi_target`). An endpoint attached to no domain bypasses
  translation until the driver says otherwise (the configuration's `bypass`, 1 from the
  start, as QEMU's `boot-bypass`): a guest without the driver keeps DMA by guest-physical
  address. Where only functions passed through are behind it, it offers no bypass at all
  (no VIRTIO_IOMMU_F_BYPASS_CONFIG, so no bypass domains, and a bypass flag refused as one
  it does not recognize): they are blocked, and pin nothing of the host's, until the
  guest's driver attaches them, as a guest needs the driver to give them to a process
  anyway (virtio 1.3 §5.13.4.2: the device MAY initialize bypass to 1). A device reset
  leaves `bypass` as it was, as the same section asks, where it had been set to 1 again. Linux defers probing a
  function behind an IOMMU it has no driver for, ten seconds where it has modules
  (driver_deferred_probe_check_state), so the `kvm` kernel has the driver.
- **A passed-through function behind the guest's own IOMMU** (`run --kernel …
  --vfio-iommu NAME`): what a guest's own VFIO needs to give the function to a process
  of its, as a workload's `--device /dev/vfio/N` does. A type 1 container maps one set of
  I/O addresses for all its groups, so the function's group gets a container of its own,
  as Cloud Hypervisor gives each VFIO device attached to its virtio-iommu (vmm/src/
  device_manager.rs, add_vfio_device: "a limitation of the legacy VFIO interface using
  container/group"; iommufd's address spaces lift it, a later layer). The container maps
  what the function's endpoint sees ([`iommu::Follower`]): all of guest RAM while it
  bypasses translation, from reset or in a bypass domain, as virtio 1.3 §5.13 has a
  bypassing endpoint's DMA go untranslated (Cloud Hypervisor's maps nothing there, so its
  device cannot DMA); nothing while it is blocked; and its domain's mappings of guest RAM
  otherwise, replayed as it attaches, then each MAP and UNMAP as they come. A mapping of
  device memory, an MSI doorbell's, is not the container's: the function's MSIs are
  VFIO's interrupts, which the VMM routes, each to where the endpoint's domain maps its
  address for a write, or into the MSI window untranslated (`vfio::Translated`). A request
  the host cannot carry out (no memory to pin: S_NOMEM; a mapping of what is not RAM:
  S_RANGE) is refused and changes nothing; an UNMAP the host could not make keeps the
  mapping here too, as the device can still reach it. The guest's kernel needs the
  driver, VIRTIO_IOMMU, as the `kvm` kernel has. Offering no bypass there, the IOMMU
  never shows a function all of RAM, which memory plugged later would outgrow: so memory
  to plug and free page reporting (D148, D151) work beside it. The host's IOMMU keeps
  the pages it pinned, so guest memory keeps each range a function's DMA holds pinned
  (`GuestMemory::pin`) from being given back under it: a report of it free keeps it, and
  an unplug of a block it meets is refused (virtio-mem's BUSY, which the driver retries)
  until it is unpinned. A function outside the guest's IOMMU (`--vfio`) reaches all of
  RAM, pinned, which neither may take from under it, so a machine given one has neither.
- **A host IOMMU group's functions in one device** (`vm::vfio_places`): the functions of
  one host IOMMU group, which the host cannot keep from each other's DMA (that is what
  makes them one group: Linux iommu.c, pci_device_group; peer-to-peer through a switch
  without ACS), share a device on the guest's bus 0, eight at most, so that the guest
  takes them as one group too and its IOMMU core keeps them in one domain, as the host's
  container does; and a workload given `/dev/vfio/N` finds all of them in it. Where they
  are one host slot's with its function 0, each keeps its function number; else they are
  numbered from 0 in their addresses' order, as a guest scans a device's other functions
  only where it has function 0. Each function of such a device reads as a multi-function
  device's (the header type's bit 7, PCIe 6.0 §7.5.1.1.9), and one of a device of one
  function as a single function's, whatever its own device says: Linux groups a
  multi-function device's functions by each one's own bit (get_pci_function_alias_group).
  And a function of a device of several reads as having no ACS, its extended capability
  taken out of the list (its predecessor's next pointer past it, or a header of ID 0 in
  its place at 0x100, which a guest passes over, as QEMU's vfio-pci hides one): ACS
  controls the host set would have the guest take it for isolated from the others
  (pci_acs_enabled), which it is not. Placed by slot alone, as at first, the functions of
  a group of several slots would have been groups of the guest's, whose domains one host
  container could not keep apart; and two functions of one group behind the guest's IOMMU
  each opened the group in a container of its own, which VFIO refuses (a group opens
  once): so a GPU with its audio function, the commonest passthrough, failed.
- **A group's endpoints share their follower** (`iommu::Follows`): one container for each
  host group behind the guest's IOMMU, which a type 1 container maps one set of I/O
  addresses for (vfio.rst). It shows the view of the last of the group's endpoints
  attached or detached, as the guest's IOMMU core attaches a group's devices one after
  another (__iommu_group_set_domain), and each MAP and UNMAP of the domain it shows
  reaches it once. A guest that kept the endpoints in domains apart would have the last
  one's view for all of them: of its own RAM still, all a container is given.
- **A run given a host's VFIO group** (`shards run --device /dev/vfio/N`, Linux, as
  Docker's is given a VFIO group's node; `/dev/vfio` gives each group in it, as
  DevicesFromPath walks it). The daemon finds the group's functions the host gave
  vfio-pci or another of VFIO's PCI drivers (/sys/kernel/iommu_groups/N/devices; its PCI
  bridges, which VFIO gives no guest, and what no driver holds stay the host's), as the
  run starts, a group it cannot give failing the start rather than running without it
  (`run::vfio_groups`), and boots the run's microVM for it, of no template, as a host's
  device is no snapshot's: the functions behind the microVM's own IOMMU, so that its
  guest's VFIO can give them to a process, with the pinned kernel's `kvm` variant
  (`KERNEL_KVM`), which has VFIO and virtio-iommu, or the kernel given. Its guest's init
  gives each function to vfio-pci, through a sysfs of its own attached nowhere (the run's
  root's is read-only), as the host's was, and the workload is given the group's node
  where the guest's sysfs puts the group, `/dev/vfio/G`, G the guest's number, unless the
  run named a path of its own for it: a VFIO user finds a function's group by its
  address's `iommu_group` in sysfs (DPDK's rte_vfio_get_group_num), which in the microVM
  is the guest's; Kata's agent does the same (vfio_device_handler.rs: the guest's group
  path for the container's, its numbers the guest's). Linux's sysfs is one superblock for
  each network namespace (kernfs, sysfs_init_fs_context), read-only where its first mount
  is, as the run's root's is: so a microVM booted for VFIO has its init keep a sysfs of
  its own from boot (`shards_vfio`), attached nowhere, through which it binds them. A
  no-IOMMU group is refused: its DMA reaches all of the host's memory. The VM process
  raises its locked-memory limit to its hard limit, as far as it may unprivileged,
  against which type 1 pins what it maps (vfio_lock_acct), and says what type 1's EPERM
  means where it refuses a group: no isolated MSIs on the host, its administrator's to
  allow. A CDI device whose node is a host's VFIO group (D146) is the group's too, its
  spec's mode and owner on the guest's node: the daemon declares each group to the
  guest's init (`v`), which binds it, and a device that names the group's host path, by
  `--device` or a CDI node, is the group's node in the guest. The run is over for its
  client once the group is free, as `docker run` returns once its container's processes,
  which held its devices, have gone: its VM process sends its own pidfd with the run's
  status, and the client waits for it to poll readable (pidfd_open(2)), the process's
  files closed before it can (exit_files before exit_notify); without, the next run given
  the group found it open still (VFIO opens a group for one process at a time,
  vfio_group_fops_open). Verified on real VMs (`a_run_is_given_a_hosts_vfio_group`,
  mutation-checked): a nested arm64 guest given test functions (`--pci-tests
  01.0,02.0,02.1`) runs shards as a Linux host does, and a run of it given the group of
  the device of two, its group 1, by its node, by a CDI device and by the directory
  `/dev/vfio`, has them as one device and its own group 0, whose node is its
  `/dev/vfio/0`, and moves a page through each by DMA, its workload finding the group as
  DPDK does.
- **A function by its VFIO device node, and iommufd** (`--device /dev/vfio/devices/vfioN`
  and `/dev/iommu`, or each node in `/dev/vfio/devices`; `run --kernel --vfio[-iommu]
  /dev/vfio/devices/vfioN`): the other way Linux hands a process a function (vfio.rst,
  "VFIO Device cdev"; Documentation/userspace-api/iommufd.rst), as hosts that give a user
  a device but not its group do. The VM process opens the node, tells KVM's VFIO device of
  it before binding it, as a driver that needs the VM finds it then (KVM_DEV_VFIO_FILE_ADD
  takes a group's file or a device's), binds it to /dev/iommu and attaches it to an I/O
  address space (IOMMU_IOAS_ALLOC, VFIO_DEVICE_BIND_IOMMUFD,
  VFIO_DEVICE_ATTACH_IOMMUFD_PT), each struct as Linux 6.6 first had it, its `argsz`
  saying so, which every host since takes: one address space for each group behind the
  guest's IOMMU, which the group's follower maps into (IOMMU_IOAS_MAP and UNMAP), as
  iommufd attaches a group's devices to one; and one that maps all of guest RAM for those
  outside it, once the first is attached. iommufd pins what it maps for an attached device
  then (iopt_area_fill_domains), and counts what it pins for all of a user's processes
  together against the pinning process's locked-memory limit (incr_user_locked_vm;
  /dev/iommu's default, which only CAP_SYS_RESOURCE changes), where type 1 counts each
  process's alone: a user's microVMs given functions so share that limit, as its refusal
  says. iommufd, like type 1, binds a function whose MSIs its host isolates, or where its
  administrator allows them (`iommufd.allow_unsafe_interrupts`; iommufd/device.c,
  iommufd_device_bind): a microVM whose MSIs are not isolated (`ISOLATED_MSIS`) has its
  guest's iommufd told so too, as its VFIO is. A group's functions are each taken one way,
  by the group's node or by their own, and all behind the guest's IOMMU or none, as VFIO
  gives a group one way at a time (vfio_device_block_group) and its functions share the
  host's mappings (`vm::vfio_given`); a run that names a group and a node of one of its
  functions takes the group by its node, which gives all of them, its guest still giving
  the workload each node named (`run::vfio_functions`). Each refusal of the kernel's at
  the bind says which holder it means: the group's node open elsewhere (EBUSY), the device
  open elsewhere (EINVAL), MSIs not isolated or the group's DMA another's (EPERM), a VF
  whose PF is vfio-pci's (EACCES). The function's group is still the group the bus places
  it by; a no-IOMMU function has no device node ("cdev does not support noiommu device",
  vfio.h). The guest's kernel, the `kvm` variant, makes VFIO's device nodes too (IOMMUFD,
  VFIO_DEVICE_CDEV), and a device that names the host's node is the guest's node of the
  function (sysfs's `vfio-dev`), there in the container too where its path there is the
  host's; `/dev/iommu` is the guest's. Verified on real VMs (mutation-checked: the guest's
  node of the function, the follower's maps, guest RAM's address space): the daemon's runs
  given the two functions' nodes and /dev/iommu, and the directory of the nodes, whose
  workload takes them so, binding both to one iommufd and one address space
  (`a_run_is_given_a_hosts_vfio_group`); and the VM process given a function by its node,
  outside the guest's IOMMU, its interrupts and its DMA by guest-physical address
  (`a_nested_guest_runs_vms_of_its_own`).
- **MSIs isolated on arm64 KVM, by an ITS.** A guest's VFIO refuses a group whose MSIs
  nothing isolates, unless told it may take one (vfio_iommu_type1.c,
  `allow_unsafe_interrupts`): a function's MSIs could forge another's. An arm64 KVM
  machine with a PCI bus takes its MSIs at its GIC's ITS (KVM_DEV_TYPE_ARM_VGIC_ITS,
  devices/arm-vgic-its.rst; its frame at QEMU virt's place, 0x08080000), which
  translates each by the ID of the function that wrote it, and which Linux marks so
  (irq-gic-v3-its.c, IRQ_DOMAIN_FLAG_ISOLATED_MSI): the devicetree's `arm,gic-v3-its`
  node, and the bridge's `msi-map`, each requester ID its device ID; a function the VMM
  emulates sends its MSIs by KVM_SIGNAL_MSI with its ID (KVM_MSI_VALID_DEVID), and a
  passed-through function's go by irqfds on GSIs routed to the ITS with it, the routing
  table KVM's defaults, each SPI on its own number's GSI (vgic-irqfd.c), and the MSIs
  routed (`Gic::route_msi`). Its guests are told nothing, and take groups (`vm::
  ISOLATED_MSIS`). Hypervisor.framework's GIC has a GICv2m frame of its own and no ITS,
  and x86_64's guests have no interrupt remapping yet: theirs are told they may
  (`vfio_iommu_type1.allow_unsafe_interrupts=1`), as a function's MSIs reach the
  microVM's own interrupt controller alone, the host's own remapping keeping them from
  the host's. Verified on real VMs: the nested tests' inner guests, KVM's, take their
  groups through type 1 told nothing, the daemon's run's among them; mutation-checked,
  with the routes' device IDs left out, no MSI comes in 10 s. To do: interrupt remapping
  on x86_64.
- **Its addresses are the guest's.** A function sits at a place on the microVM's bus 0,
  not at the host's address, and its group has the guest's number: a workload told the
  host's address (DPDK's `-a 0000:3b:00.0`) finds no such function. Docker's container
  sees the host's own sysfs; Kata's rewrites the SR-IOV device plugin's variables
  (`PCIDEVICE_*`) instead. To do: the host's addresses kept, a host bridge of the guest's
  for each host domain and bus, which Linux allows one of per domain on a devicetree
  (pci.c, of_pci_bus_find_domain_nr) and whose buses behind bridges it renumbers but where
  told not to (`linux,pci-probe-only`, pci-host-common.c).
- **The test function's DMA** is edu's engine (edu.rst: source, destination, length and
  command at 0x80 of BAR 0, its 4 KiB buffer at 0x40000 of its DMA addresses), run at once
  rather than on edu's timer: guest memory is reached at what its endpoint's domain maps,
  each part read or written as the mapping allows, and a transfer to what it does not map
  moves nothing, as an IOMMU's fault ends a device's DMA.
- **A 64-bit window.** 64-bit BARs, a GPU's of tens of GiB among them, take a window of
  their own above 4 GiB, past the rest of the guest's address map, as long as they need:
  each placed at a multiple of its size, the test function's and then each
  passed-through function's in order, from a start aligned to the largest. The window is
  sized before the VM exists, as arm64's address width follows the map's top: a
  function's 64-bit BARs are read from sysfs (`resource`: IORESOURCE_MEM_64) while it is
  found, before the VM process is confined. It is not prefetchable, so BARs of either
  kind fit it: the devicetree's second range, 64-bit memory (0x03000000), and on x86_64
  the host bridge's QWordMemory (ACPI 6.5 §6.4.3.5.1). On x86_64, the guest's whole
  address map, RAM, memory to plug, pmem and the window, must now lie within the
  physical address width its CPUID gives it (0x80000008), on KVM and WHP alike, where
  before nothing checked it. The test function has a 64-bit BAR 4 of its own, 1 MiB, its
  first page a scratch.
- **Interrupts.** A PCI bus's functions interrupt as PCI's do. On arm64, each device's
  INTx on an SPI of its own, level-triggered (the devicetree's `interrupt-map`): KVM's
  GICv3 keeps one level a line, so a line the VMM drives and an irqfd must not share one.
  MSIs go to a GICv2m frame (Linux's GICv3 driver takes one where the distributor has no
  LPIs, irq-gic-v3.c; its SPIs in the devicetree, irq-gic-v2m.c): Hypervisor.framework's
  own; on KVM, to the GIC's ITS (below). On x86_64, every device's INTx on GSI 22, wired-OR
  as PCI's may be, by the DSDT's `_PRT` (ACPI 6.5 §6.2.13), so that a machine with a PCI
  bus has one virtio device fewer (KVM's IOAPIC has 24 pins); MSIs to the local APICs,
  delivered by KVM_SIGNAL_MSI, or on WHP decoded as the IOAPIC's messages are (Intel SDM
  Vol. 3A §11.11). The test function raises INTA# and MSIs as edu does, its status
  register's Interrupt Status set while its interrupt is pending whether or not INTx is
  disabled (PCI 3.0 §6.2.3): with it clear while disabled, a guest's vfio-pci, which masks
  INTx by disabling it, took the next for another device's and the kernel shut the line
  ("irq 15: nobody cared").
- **A passed-through function's interrupts** reach the guest in the kernel, the VMM never
  seeing them: VFIO signals an eventfd (VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS) that a KVM irqfd raises a
  line by. INTx level-triggered: VFIO masks it as it fires, and KVM's resample eventfd,
  written as the guest ends the interrupt, unmasks it in vfio-pci, which takes that
  eventfd only for INTx it already signals (vfio_pci_set_intx_unmask). INTx is routed as
  the guest first reaches the function, as KVM takes no irqfd before its interrupt
  controller is initialized, after every vCPU exists (kvm_irqfd_assign: EAGAIN). The VMM
  keeps the function's MSI capability, at the device's place and of its length, as
  vfio-pci leaves MSI's enable to VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS (vfio_msi_config_write): as the
  guest enables it, INTx goes off and the message is routed: on arm64 to the frame's SPI
  it names (KVM's default routes, GSI n to SPI n), on x86_64 to a GSI past the IOAPIC's
  by KVM_SET_GSI_ROUTING, the table KVM's defaults and every route, whole each time.
  irqfds with resampling are among what KVM must offer.
- **MSI-X** (PCI 3.0 §6.8.2): one table, `pci::MsixTable`, for the functions the VMM
  emulates and those it passes through: each vector's message and mask, masked from
  reset, reached a dword or an aligned qword at a time, and its pending bit, set as a
  masked vector would have been sent and cleared as it is sent unmasked. The test function
  has an MSI-X capability of shards' own beside edu's MSI, as edu has none: two vectors,
  a raise of bit k sending vector k, the table and pending bits in BAR 2. A passed-through
  function's table is the VMM's, as vfio-pci keeps a user from the device's
  (vfio_pci_rdwr.c, vfio_pci_bar_rw), and so is its capability, as vfio-pci enables MSI-X
  only through VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS. As the guest enables MSI-X, INTx and MSI go off and
  VFIO enables MSI-X with no vector signalled (eventfd -1). Where VFIO cannot add a vector
  later (VFIO_IRQ_INFO_NORESIZE: a host whose MSI domain allocates no vectors on demand,
  MSI_FLAG_PCI_MSIX_ALLOC_DYN, which x86's does and arm64's GICv2m and ITS do not:
  arch/x86/include/asm/msi.h, irq-gic-v2m.c, irq-gic-its-msi-parent.c), every vector at
  once, as one added by disabling MSI-X and enabling it again, which vfio.h leaves to a
  user, would lose the interrupts between; else vector 0 alone, and each other as the
  guest first unmasks it, so the host allocates only vectors in use. A vector gets its
  eventfd as the guest first unmasks it, routed by its message through an irqfd. Masked,
  by itself or by the function, it loses only its irqfd: VFIO keeps signalling, and the
  eventfd counts, where a new eventfd would cost a host interrupt freed and requested
  again (vfio_msi_set_vector_signal). A read of the pending bits takes each masked
  vector's count as its pending bit, with the device's own bits, set for vectors VFIO
  signals on nothing, which the host leaves masked at the device; an unmasked vector
  sends what pended, by the machine's MSIs. KVM injects what an eventfd counted as its
  irqfd is assigned but leaves the count (virt/kvm/eventfd.c, kvm_irqfd_assign), so the
  VMM takes the count before assigning, to send it once, and after, so that it is not
  sent again at the next mask. The host's pending bit trails the device by the host's
  interrupt: a guest polls it as it would a device's.
- **Verified on real VMs** (`a_pci_functions_interrupts_reach_the_guest`,
  `a_nested_guest_runs_vms_of_its_own`), on an M5 Max, macOS 26.4.1. The test guest takes
  the test function through vfio-pci in its own userspace and waits on eventfds: INTA#
  twice, acknowledged and unmasked between, then one MSI, then MSI-X: its two vectors
  enabled with no eventfd, so masked, a raise of vector 0 held, its pending bit read,
  and sent as VFIO is given its eventfd; vector 1 sent at once, then held while VFIO
  has freed it, and sent as given its eventfd again ("interrupts: INTx 2, MSI 1, MSI-X
  3, 2 of them held"), on Hypervisor.framework. Nested: shards boots the `kvm` kernel at EL2 with an initramfs
  of the test guest, shards' VM process for arm64 Linux and the `kvm` kernel again. In it, shards' KVM backend boots a
  guest of its own, under its seccomp filter and Landlock: "smp: Brought up 1 node, 2
  CPUs", its second vCPU's redistributor found, its test passed. Given `--pci-test`, the
  inner guest's PCI bus reaches the test function. Given the outer guest's test function,
  bound to vfio-pci there in a no-IOMMU group, the inner guest finds 1234:11e8 at 00:01.0
  and reads the identification register and the liveness check's inverse through BAR 0,
  which the outer VM process maps into the inner guest (its log): the inner guest's access
  reaches the outermost VMM's function with no exit to the outer VM process. With its
  memory space off, BAR 0 leaves the inner guest and reads all ones through the outer VM
  process and vfio-pci, and comes back as it is on again. BAR 4 lies past 4 GiB in each
  guest's 64-bit window, its scratch reading back what each wrote, in the inner guest
  through the window the outer VM process sized from sysfs and mapped. DMA: the test
  guest takes the test function through vfio-pci in a group with the IOMMU (its INTx, MSI
  and MSI-X as before, the MSIs through the domain to the doorbell), maps two pages at
  I/O addresses of its own (type 1), and the function moves a page of a pattern
  from one into its buffer and back to the other, then to an address never mapped,
  which moves nothing. Nested, the inner guest does the same behind the outer VM
  process's IOMMU; and given the outer guest's function, its group now with an IOMMU,
  so that the outer VM process maps all of the inner guest's RAM for it through the
  outer guest's IOMMU (type 1), the inner guest, which has none, gives the function its
  pages' guest-physical addresses (pagemap), and the outermost VMM's function reaches
  them through the outer guest's mappings. Given the function behind its own IOMMU
  (`--vfio-iommu`), the inner guest's VFIO maps its pages at I/O addresses of its own
  (0x10_0000 and 0x20_0000, where the inner guest has no RAM), the outer VM process's
  container maps what the inner IOMMU maps, and the outermost function moves the page
  through them; its MSI and MSI-X land through the inner guest's mapping of its ITS's
  doorbell. Mutation-checked: with the container's map left out, the page comes back
  zero; with MSIs routed by their I/O address, no interrupt comes in 10 s. The inner guest takes INTx, MSI and MSI-X, both of the VMM's
  own test function, through its ITS, and of the function passed through, by
  the outer VM process's irqfds: its vector 1 held while masked is the outer VM process's
  count, as the outermost function sends it at once. CI's arm64 runners give no KVM: the nested test runs where a
  Mac gives a guest EL2. x86_64's interrupts are held to their encodings by unit tests
  (the `_PRT` as iasl compiles it, an MSI's decoding), and run on CI's KVM runner once its
  `kvm` kernel, built now for x86_64 too, is pinned.
- **A cache maintenance instruction KVM cannot take is skipped** (hv/kvm, `skip_cmo`).
  A Linux arm64 guest cleans and invalidates each page it maps for execution to the point
  of unification, line by line, where its CPU has neither CTR_EL0.IDC nor DIC (arm64
  mm/flush.c, __sync_icache_dcache; cache.S, caches_clean_inval_pou): with its root on
  DAX, a page of the read-only pmem slot. KVM maps a slot's pages as the guest first
  touches them, takes a cache maintenance fault for a write (its WnR is 1), which a
  read-only slot refuses, skips one only outside every slot (mmu.c,
  kvm_handle_guest_abort; "Handle out-of-RAM cache maintenance as a NOP", 2016), and so
  fails KVM_RUN with ENOSYS, an access with no syndrome it cannot emulate (api.rst 4.10):
  every run of an image on such a host failed. KVM returns such an access to the VMM
  instead (KVM_CAP_ARM_NISV_TO_USER, KVM_EXIT_ARM_NISV), which skips one of cache
  maintenance (ISS.CM) as KVM skips its own, PC past it and PSTATE's BTYPE and SS cleared
  (kvm_skip_instr): skipped, it changes nothing the guest could see, as the guest cannot
  have written memory it may not write and KVM cleans and invalidates what the host wrote
  there as it maps the page; and gives the guest an external data abort for any other,
  as QEMU does (target/arm/kvm.c, kvm_arm_handle_dabt_nisv), or, where KVM cannot, ends
  the VM saying where. Found nested, where KVM's guest's CPU, Apple's, has neither: a run
  of the test image skipped 2,048 to 4,095, all at one PC, 64 to a page, about 40 µs
  each nested (shards' debug log). Not yet measured: what the skips cost on a bare-metal
  host whose CPU has neither; CI's arm64 Linux runners' runs never met one, and pass.
- **Snapshots on arm64 KVM** (the parity plan's step 9, 2026-10-26): a microVM on an arm64
  Linux host is saved and restored, cold and from warm pools, and templates, their working
  sets and pools serve its runs, as on x86_64's KVM and Hypervisor.framework.
  - **A vCPU's state is every register KVM lists** (KVM_GET_REG_LIST, api.rst 4.84; each
    by KVM_GET_ONE_REG, 4.68): the core registers, KVM's firmware pseudo-registers (PSCI's
    version, the SMCCC workarounds, the hypercall bitmaps), the system registers, the
    timers' among them, and the caches' geometry; with its power state (KVM_GET_MP_STATE,
    PSCI's, which KVM's own PSCI keeps) and a virtual SError pending in it, which no
    register shows (KVM_GET_VCPU_EVENTS). As Firecracker and QEMU keep one
    (vmm/src/arch/aarch64/vcpu.rs, save_state; target/arm/kvm.c): what KVM lists is what
    a user may read and write back (its get-reg-list self-test), and a register a later
    KVM adds is in it unasked. A PSCI CPU_ON owed to a vCPU not yet run is finished before
    any of its registers is read (arm.c, KVM_GET_ONE_REG: "We could owe a reset due to
    PSCI"). Restored into a vCPU initialized with the same features, in KVM's order; a
    register this KVM has not, or a value it refuses, fails the restore, as a snapshot of
    another CPU or KVM should. HVF's state keeps its own encoding byte for byte
    (`arch::aarch64::state::VcpuCodec`).
  - **The counter, once, for the VM.** KVM keeps one offset of the guest's virtual counter
    for a VM, which a write of KVM_REG_ARM_TIMER_CNT through any vCPU sets as of the write
    (sys_regs.c, arch_timer_set_user; Linux 5.x set it on every vCPU at once,
    update_vtimer_cntvoff): so the restore writes it once, through vCPU 0, as the vCPUs
    are released (`hv::Counter`), where each vCPU writing its own, as under HVF, would
    step a running vCPU's counter back by the next write's lag. The counter goes on from
    the snapshot's; the physical counter stays the host's, as under HVF, and neither
    counter is written with the rest of the registers.
  - **The GIC through its registers** (KVM_DEV_ARM_VGIC_GRP_*, arm-vgic-v3.rst), kept as
    the writes that make a new VM's GIC, initialized and with every vCPU, the one saved,
    in QEMU's order (hw/intc/arm_gicv3_kvm.c, kvm_arm_gicv3_put): the distributor's
    implementation revision first, as the document asks, and its control; each
    redistributor's private interrupts; the SPIs', each interrupt's configuration before
    its line's level and its routing and enable before its pending state; then each CPU
    interface's, its active priority registers as many as its priority bits make. A
    set-enable and a set-active register follow all-ones written to their clear twins, as
    a new GIC's SGIs are enabled; the pending registers set the latched state themselves,
    and the line levels (KVM_DEV_ARM_VGIC_GRP_LEVEL_INFO) the rest of a level interrupt's.
    KVM takes every vCPU for each access, and fails one while any vCPU is in a call of its
    own (EBUSY): the GIC is read once every vCPU has parked and written as the machine
    finishes, its vCPUs' threads waiting. A machine with an ITS (a PCI bus) saves none.
  - **Working sets as on x86_64's KVM** (`vm::mapped`): recorded from the pages the host
    maps of the first warm restore, its fault-around held off; the pages it wrote copied
    ahead at a restore. **Mapped ahead by a program on vCPU 0**: arm64's KVM has no
    KVM_PRE_FAULT_MEMORY (x86's and s390's alone, virt/kvm/Kconfig, to Linux 7.2), so
    vCPU 0 runs the prefetch program Hypervisor.framework's does
    (`arch::aarch64::prefetch`). KVM runs no vCPU before the GIC is initialized
    (vgic_v3_map_resources: EBUSY) nor makes one after (kvm_arch_vcpu_precreate), so it
    runs as the machine finishes, from that thread, its own waiting; then vCPU 0's state
    is restored again. KVM takes a guest's HVC for itself (SMCCC), so the program ends
    with a write KVM returns as MMIO, which a run with `immediate_exit` then retires, as
    KVM_RUN completes the last exit's access first (mmio.c, kvm_handle_mmio_return), lest
    it advance the restored PC; its exception vectors end it the same way. Its memory slot
    is read-only and deleted after, which unmaps it at stage 2 and flushes the VM's stage
    1 translations with it.
  - **A guest with virtualization of its own is shown the host's widest addresses**
    (`--nested`, D132): Hypervisor.framework's guest is shown the PARange its memory map
    needs (D10), and arm64's KVM sizes the VMs it runs by its CPU's PARange (kvm_ipa_limit),
    so a nested guest's own microVMs had no room past their memory for a share's DAX
    window or a run's swap window ("the guest's addresses leave none a 2 MiB range").
  - **Tested on arm64 Linux by the snapshot tests themselves**, where no arm64 Linux host
    of ours has KVM (CI's arm64 runners have no /dev/kvm): boot.rs's
    `snapshot_tests_pass_on_a_kvm_host_of_this_architecture` builds tests/snapshot.rs,
    warm.rs, saved.rs and daemon.rs whole, and the snapshot tests of run.rs, vsock.rs,
    pmem.rs and boot.rs, for arm64 Linux (static musl, `common::linux_tests`), and runs
    them in a guest with EL2 on an M3 or later Mac, the `kvm` kernel's, as such a host runs
    them, every VM test required (SHARDS_REQUIRE_VMS), one at a time: two of the daemon's
    tests together, some 20 VMs of eight vCPUs on the guest's eight, its KVM nVHE, stalled
    restored guests 20 to 31 s in 11 of 24 rounds (PM M346). The guest is a host as Linux
    has one: the test guest's `e2e` mode, PID 1, mounts its pseudo-terminals, cgroups and
    debugfs, brings its loopback up, holds the host's CA certificates, reaps every process
    orphaned to it as an init does (a daemon that detached and ended was a zombie its test
    took for alive), and ends what each binary left running before the next.
    Found and fixed on the way: a Linux host without /dev/fd (made by an init or udev) had
    no share start (`platform::open_descriptors` reads /proc/self/fd); the nested width
    above; two daemon tests that needed a shell for `ulimit` and one `cp` now need neither;
    a host with no CA certificates reached no registry over plain HTTP (registry `tls.rs`);
    and, as loaded restored guests showed them, a guest's dial of its host that gave up
    after Linux's 2 s though its host had answered (D12), a pool's keep-alive counted from
    its claims, past which its runs went on (D26), and ext4's bitmap prefetch in every
    restored guest (D190). A restored guest faults back in what it holds there at 0.9 ms a
    fault: the swap test now waits for its rounds as long as its guest makes them or its VM
    process faults pages in.
- **Not yet:** more vCPUs than one redistributor region holds (123). For
  VFIO: MSI of more than one message, and its per-vector masking; isolated MSIs on x86_64
  and the host's addresses (above); a VF whose PF is bound to vfio-pci, which VFIO gives
  only with the PF's VF token (vfio_pci_core_match_token_uuid); then `--gpus` on Linux.

### D153. A PCI bus, for the devices a microVM is given (VFIO's first step)

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11 row 978: Linux's VFIO is the last gap of `--device` and `--gpus`.
A Docker container on Linux is given a host's device by its node; a microVM's guest
kernel drives a device only as a device on a bus of its own, and VFIO (Linux
Documentation/driver-api/vfio.rst) hands a process a PCI device: its configuration space,
its BARs and its interrupts, its DMA confined to what the process maps. Every shards
machine had virtio-mmio alone, and x86_64's kernel was told `pci=off`. First, the bus.

- **One segment, bus 0**, each function's configuration space reached through an ECAM
  window (PCI Express Base 6.0 §7.2.2, 1 MiB for 32 devices of 8 functions); an access a
  function does not claim reads as all ones (§2.3.2). An arm64 guest finds it by a
  `pci-host-ecam-generic` node (Linux Documentation/devicetree/bindings/pci/
  host-generic-pci.yaml), its window at QEMU virt's places, 0x3f000000, and one 32-bit
  memory range below it from 0x10000000; an x86_64 guest by ACPI, an MCFG table (PCI
  Firmware 3.3 §4.1.2) and a PNP0A08 host bridge whose _CRS is bus 0 and a 32-bit memory
  window from 0xc1000000, the ECAM window at 0xe0000000 reserved in the e820 map, without
  which Linux takes no MMCONFIG (arch/x86/pci/mmconfig-shared.c), and no `pci=off`.
- **BARs where the VMM places them.** A function's type 0 header (PCI Local Bus 3.0
  §6.1) is the VMM's: its BARs sized as §6.2.5.1 asks and otherwise kept, which the guest
  is told to keep (`/chosen/linux,pci-probe-only`; x86_64's Linux keeps firmware's
  placement inside the bridge's windows), the command register's enables, the interrupt
  line.
- **A test function**, for the bus's tests and VFIO's to come (`run --kernel …
  --pci-test`): QEMU's edu device's IDs, 1234:11e8, and its identification and liveness
  registers in its BAR 0 (QEMU docs/specs/edu.rst), reached with no driver, through sysfs.
- **No snapshot** of a machine with a PCI bus: its functions' state is their devices'
  own, a passed-through device's above all.
- **Verified on real VMs** (`a_pci_bus_reaches_its_function`): an arm64 guest on
  Hypervisor.framework says "pci-host-generic 3f000000.pcie: ECAM at [mem
  0x3f000000-0x3f0fffff] for [bus 00]" and "pci 0000:00:01.0: [1234:11e8] type 00 class
  0xff0000", BAR 0 kept at 0x10000000, and the test guest maps it from sysfs and reads
  0x010000ed and the liveness check's inverse; unit tests hold the ECAM decode, BAR
  sizing, the devicetree node and the ACPI tables to their specs' encodings. x86_64's
  guests on KVM and WHP, by CI.
- **To build:** VFIO (Linux): the container, group and device; a passed-through
  function's configuration space read from the device but for its BARs and MSI/MSI-X
  capabilities, which the VMM keeps; its memory BARs mapped into the guest, the MSI-X
  table's pages trapped; INTx and MSI through irqfds; all of guest RAM mapped for its
  DMA, pinned, so that a machine with one boots with all its memory and no balloon. Then
  `--device /dev/vfio/N`, `--gpus` and CDI's VFIO nodes. Its tests: a shards microVM on
  an M3 or later, with KVM inside (`--nested`), given the test function, binding it to
  vfio-pci and passing it to a microVM of its own.

### D152. A run's devices found by name in the VM's devtmpfs

D44 found a run's `--device` among the VM's devices by reading the uevent of each device
`/sys/dev` lists, 104 of them: 582 µs at the median in a microVM just restored, and every
run given a device paid it, the GPU's render node among them, 1.2 ms of its command in
all (PM M223).

- **Found where the microVM's kernel made them.** Boot keeps the devtmpfs it mounts at `/dev` open
  (O_PATH), before any template is saved, as it keeps `/proc/sys`. A run's device is the
  node at its path there (fstatat(2), 1.5 µs), or each node beneath a directory there,
  in WalkDir's order, as DevicesFromPath walks a host's `/dev` and runc's DeviceFromPath
  stats each node. A node has the numbers, mode and owner devtmpfs made it with, from the
  device's own name, mode and owner, which its uevent said, with udev's modes over them
  as before. `--privileged` walks all of it: a privileged run is given every device its
  microVM has.
- **Nothing more for the workload.** The descriptor is init's and close-on-exec, and
  every process init starts closes all it holds past stdio before a workload runs. A
  path outside `/dev`, or with a `.`, `..` or empty name, finds nothing, as before, so
  that no lookup leaves the devtmpfs.
- **Measured (PM M223):** a run given `--device /dev/fuse`, 774 µs sooner in its command
  [−796, −761] and 954 µs in all [−1,124, −780], paired over 200; a device now costs a
  run 106 µs [+90, +115] of its command: its filter compiled, loaded and attached, and
  its node made. Loading a GPU's filter before its template is saved, where every GPU
  run's filter is known, took 100 µs off init's work but nothing off the run's
  (−1 µs [−19, +15]): the load is off a GPU run's path, and is not done.

Tested: `devices_are_found_in_dev_by_name` (shards-init, in a guest): a node by its path,
with a trailing `/` too, a directory's each in WalkDir's order, and nothing at
`/dev/./null`, `/dev/../dev/null`, `/dev//null`, `/devnull`, `/etc/passwd`, a link or a
missing name; on real microVMs, the tests of `--device`, joiners', CDI's, `--privileged`
and the GPU's devices. Mutation-checked: finding nothing fails the first three; a
privileged run's walk finding nothing fails `devices_are_given_and_confined`.

### D151. What a run frees goes back to the host (free page reporting)

D148 plugs memory into a run as its workload needs it, and nothing gave any back: a
workload that touched 512 MiB and freed it held it to its end, 562 MiB of footprint where an
idle run as long held 90 (`a_runs_memory_freed_goes_back_to_the_host`, mutated), where a
container's memory freed is its host's at once.

- **The guest reports, the host gives back.** Linux's free page reporting
  (mm/page_reporting.c; the pinned kernel has CONFIG_PAGE_REPORTING and
  CONFIG_VIRTIO_BALLOON) hands a virtio-balloon device the blocks of its free lists of its
  pageblock and up (2 MiB with 4 KiB pages), two seconds after one is freed, paced to some
  64 blocks of each free list a pass, a pass each two seconds ("all pages on an idle
  system in about 30 seconds"). shards' device offers that feature alone
  (VIRTIO_BALLOON_F_REPORTING), its queues inflate, deflate and reporting, as Linux gives
  indexes only to the queues it names; the balloon never inflates (`num_pages` 0).
- **A reported range stays the guest's.** Each range, those that meet joined, is given back
  under guest memory's lock, as unplug and plug in turn (`memory::Access::discard`): taken
  from the guest at stage 2 where the hypervisor holds what it maps (Hypervisor.framework,
  WHP; M193: replaced in the host alone, the guest kept the old pages), its pages given
  back (`platform::discard`: on Linux MADV_DONTNEED, which keeps the mapping, its advice,
  and frees a private mapping's copies; on macOS fresh anonymous memory mapped over it,
  as MADV_FREE_REUSABLE gave nothing back, M193), and mapped to the guest again, before
  the report is answered, after which the guest may use the pages, zero-filled as first
  touched. Only the host's whole pages of guest RAM in a range are given back; one the
  host could not give back is kept, and said once.
- **Where.** Every run's microVM, last of its devices, so that no other device's window
  moves; its templates with it (snapshot format 14). Builders on every host: a build's
  peak is not held to its end. On Windows a cold-booted microVM's RAM, private memory, is
  given back as decommitted and committed again (PM M371: its private working set 64 MiB
  less of 64), and a restored one's too. Windows gives back a copy-on-write view's written
  pages only as the whole view is unmapped (M371: decommit refused,
  ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER; DiscardVirtualMemory and MEM_RESET refused,
  ERROR_USER_MAPPED_FILE), so a restore maps from its template's file only the runs of
  2 MiB blocks its state says hold data (snapshot format 27, `memory::DATA_BLOCK`, the
  least a guest reports), a view each, and the stretches between them, zeros in the file,
  as memory of the guest's own (`platform::map_file_views`). What its workload allocates
  and frees comes from those, and goes back at its pages' grain; a run of data goes back
  only whole, its view unmapped and mapped again from the file (M375: the guest then reads
  the file's bytes), and a part of one is kept. A template of 280 MiB on the M5 Max held
  data in 36 of its 140 blocks, in 2 runs: three parts to map (M378), where a view of every
  block took 307.7 µs for 256 MiB at p50 (M372). A state of a format before 27 says no runs, and
  its RAM is mapped from the file whole, one view.
- **What the host holds none of is left alone.** A range none of whose pages the host
  holds (`platform::untouched`: never touched, or a restored guest's that is still its
  template's file's) is answered as it is, no stage 2 touched.
- **A template is saved with nothing left to report.** Registering the device schedules a
  first pass over every zone two seconds on (mm/page_reporting.c
  `page_reporting_register`), and a template, saved some 150 ms into its boot, was saved
  with it to run: every restore then reported what its template's boot freed, 208 MiB,
  two seconds into its life, and runs paid for that state, 50 to 79 µs of a 1 ms command
  at the median, though no report came during them (PM M222). Kernel patch 0005 adds
  `page_reporting.flush`, which reports at once what waits, pass after pass until
  nothing does; a template's init writes it before the template is saved (6 ms), through
  a sysfs of its own opened as it boots, its container's being read-only. A guest kernel
  without it reports as before.
- **What a pass holds is free memory (patch 0006).** A pass holds up to 32 free blocks
  of at most 4 MiB, 128 MiB, until the host answers, and the zones count them gone:
  readings of the guest's free memory dipped by as much, and an allocation needing them
  found nothing to reclaim, and the OOM killer ended a task in a guest whose memory was
  free. A growing run was ended as a restore's pass came (4 of 8 asked at that moment), a
  run of fixed size with three agents as its first pass came (6 of 8 runs of
  `agents_out_of_memory_end_whole_and_spare_the_run`), and agents were given a share of
  none, read during a pass (PM M224). Patch 0006 counts what a pass holds as free in
  sysinfo(2) and /proc/meminfo, and has an allocation that would otherwise give up wait a
  tick and try again while a pass holds any (`should_reclaim_retry`); the zones' own counts,
  by which the allocator's watermarks see the pages gone until they are back, are as they
  were. With it, `MemAvailable` moved 8 to 12 MiB as a pass held 128 MiB, as without
  reporting, and the agents' test none of 24 times as it had: once, after its run was
  spared and y ended, z was ended too, its memory read as 65,679,360 bytes where it holds
  16 MiB, which is not yet explained.
- **A guest kernel without it reports nothing.** shards-init reads `page_reporting.held`,
  which 0006 adds, as it boots, before any template is saved: where its kernel has none,
  it lets the virtio-balloon device's driver go (sysfs `unbind`), and the guest keeps what
  it frees, as before D151.
- **Measured (PM M222):** with the flush, runs cost what they did, wall time −5 µs
  [−94, +98] and the command's −11 µs [−22, +0], paired over 400; a run that touched
  512 MiB and freed it held 57 to 132 MiB at its end where an idle one held 94, and with
  none given back 562.

Tested: in crates/vmm, `reported_memory_comes_back_empty` (ranges that meet joined, each
unmapped and mapped again around its pages, the rest of RAM as it was),
`a_range_the_host_holds_nothing_of_is_left_alone`,
`a_range_past_ram_or_in_part_of_a_page_keeps_what_is_not_wholly_its` and
`the_device_asks_for_nothing_and_keeps_actual`; on real microVMs,
`a_runs_memory_freed_goes_back_to_the_host`: restores of a template reporting nothing in
their first seconds, where the kernel has the flush (a VM's timing line says what its
guest reported, `reported_kib`), and 512 MiB touched and freed given back, where its kernel
has 0006, and nothing reported where it has not; and
`agents_out_of_memory_end_whole_and_spare_the_run`, which a pass ended 6 times in 8 on a
kernel whose allocations did not wait. Mutation-checked: runs without the device hold 562
MiB; a template saved without the flush has its restores report 212,992 KiB. What a pass
does to readings and to growing runs is shown by `reporting-dip` and
`run-plug/report-race.py` (PM M224).

### D150. A GPU's runs restore templates of their own

D144 booted every run given the GPU and saved no template: a GPU's state is its host
driver's, which no snapshot holds, and the renderer's threads reach guest memory without
the VMM's access. Each such run paid a whole boot, 98.8 ms at the median where a restore
took 7.6 (PM M223).

- **Saved before the guest has anything of the GPU's.** A template is saved once its root
  is mounted, before any workload runs. By then the guest's driver has negotiated its
  features and asked for the capsets, and has made no context and no resource: the
  device has no scanout, so DRM makes no framebuffer either. All the device holds of the
  guest then is its rings' places, which a snapshot keeps as it keeps every virtio
  device's. The renderer's threads reach guest memory only through a context's blobs and
  fences, and there are none. A snapshot is refused once the guest has a context or a
  resource, or while a request waits on a fence, and says how many (`Gpu::unsaved`),
  as D148 refuses one while memory has been asked for and not plugged.
- **A restore makes its renderer anew**, in the GPU's VM process (`shards restore --gpu`).
  Its window has the place and the length its template's guest saw: snapshot format 15
  records the length. A host whose renderer offers less refuses the restore, since the
  guest would be told of memory its host cannot map. One that offers more maps only what
  the guest was told of.
- **Its own template.** A GPU run's template is keyed apart from the same image's runs
  without the GPU: by "gpu", and by the pinned gpu kernel's digest whatever guest is
  recorded. Its origin says so. A run without the GPU never restores one with it, and the
  daemon gives a GPU template's restores the GPU's VM process.
- **Measured (PM M223):** a GPU run restored is 90.6 ms sooner than one booted, wall
  time paired over 200 [−91.6, −89.5] (p50 98.8 → 7.6 ms, p99 129.8 → 31.7), and holds
  18.4 MiB of footprint where one booted holds 94.8. Restored, the GPU costs a run
  0.19 ms of its command against a run without it, its device's cost found and taken
  down to 0.1 ms (D152) and the gpu kernel and the GPU's VM process the rest; restoring
  itself costs the same, with the GPU or without.

Tested: in crates/vmm, `a_gpu_is_saved_only_with_nothing_of_its_host_drivers`. On real
microVMs, in tests/gpu.rs: with the gpu kernel recorded as the guest, a run without the
GPU saves a template first, and the GPU run after it still boots and saves its own. The
next GPU run restores that template, and so does one with the usual kernel recorded;
each finds "Virtio-GPU Venus (". Mutation-checked: keyed without "gpu", the GPU run
restores the template saved without the GPU, which has no render node; restored in the
VM process without the renderer, the restore is refused and the run boots; keyed by the
recorded guest's kernel, the usual one boots, without virtio-gpu; and a GPU that never
refuses a snapshot fails the unit test.

### D149. A guest reports the memory it may still plug

A run without a limit grows to its host's memory (D148), but its guest reported only what
had been plugged: 243 MiB as it boots, where a container's is its host's, by which Node.js
sized its heap at 259 MiB where Docker's is 4,144 (PM M220). sysinfo(2) and /proc/meminfo
take total and free memory from `si_meminfo()`, which counts what the kernel has. A
builder, booted with 512 MiB and grown to half its host's, was the same: a step's Node.js
sized its heap at 259 MiB, where `docker build`'s sizes it at 4,144. And the kernel's
overcommit heuristic (`overcommit_memory` 0, mm/util.c `__vm_enough_memory`) refuses any
one allocation larger than the memory it has: `dd bs=1G` failed in a run and in a step
("memory exhausted"), where Docker's makes it (its VM's `overcommit_memory` is 1, and a
Linux host's heuristic counts the host's memory).

- **The kernel's report** (resources/kernel/patches/0004): `vm.pluggable_kbytes`. Written,
  the memory the host may plug from then on; the kernel keeps what the guest has with
  all of it plugged, and sysinfo(2) and /proc/meminfo add what is still to be plugged,
  that less the memory each read, to the total, free and available memory they report.
  Memory plugged lowers what they add as it raises what they read, in the same read, so
  the total reported is what the guest may reach at every moment; read, the sysctl gives
  what the reports add then. The overcommit heuristic and the commit limit
  (`vm_commit_limit`) count it too, read once with the memory it is measured against
  (`si_reachable_pages`): an allocation a guest could hold once its memory is plugged is
  made, as on a host of that memory, and one past all of it is refused. Nothing in the
  kernel's own accounting of the memory it has counts it: `si_meminfo()` and
  `totalram_pages()` are as they were.
- **Init** opens it before /proc/sys is masked, where the kernel has it, and writes it
  once as a template boots (its host's) and once as each run comes (the run's own most
  less what is plugged), before anything of the run grows its memory; a builder's, once,
  as it boots (its most). A first draft had
  init lower it as its grower plugged memory: the total reported then overstated what
  the guest may reach for as long as each block took to be seen, and two processes
  wrote it.
- **Init's own view is the kernel's:** what it reads to hold and grow its runs' memory
  (`memory.high`, what is plugged, what the domains may take) is sysinfo(2) and
  `MemAvailable` less the report, read before and after: the report changes only as
  memory is plugged, one way at a time, so the same report on both sides is the one
  added, and where memory came between, init reads again. With the report counted, the
  grower saw the memory it was to plug as had and a workload was ended at 1 GiB (137).
- **An extra layer:** a guest kernel without it reports what it has, as before, and its
  runs grow all the same.
- **Result (PM M221):** a run without `-m` reports its host's memory less the 37 MiB its
  kernel keeps (`MemTotal` 134,179,892 kB of the host's 134,217,728), and Node.js sizes
  its heap at 4,144 MiB; with `-m 8g` and `-m 1g`, at 2,096 and 524; in a build step, at
  4,144: each what the same run or step sizes under Docker (PM M221). `dd bs=1G` copies
  its gigabytes in a run and in a step, which under Docker it does too.

Tested: in crates/init, on Linux, `memory_is_read_without_the_kernels_report` (the report
read again where memory came between); on real microVMs,
`a_runs_memory_grows_as_its_workload_needs_it` (with the report: a gigabyte allocated where
the first draft's grower, counting the report as memory had, let it be ended; a run's
`MemTotal` its host's, what may still be plugged free and available too, and a run with
`-m`'s none; and a gigabyte in one allocation) and `a_builders_steps_see_the_memory_it_may_have`
(a step's `MemTotal` its builder's most, and 1.5 GiB in one allocation, of a builder
booted with 512 MiB). Mutation-checked: init counting the report as memory it has (the
workload ended, 137); a run not lowering its template's report as it begins (a run with
`-m 1g` reporting its host's memory); a builder not reporting (a step's `MemTotal` 483,556
kB); and the kernel's overcommit heuristic not counting the report (the first draft's
kernel: each one allocation refused): each fails a test.

### D148. A run's memory, plugged as its workload needs it (virtio-mem)

A run's microVM was sized at boot: without `-m`, 256 MiB less what its kernel keeps
(`MemTotal` 248,820 kB), so a workload past it was ended (test-backend-ops, 137, M218),
where a Docker container without `-m` may hold its host's memory (`memory.max` "max",
`MemTotal` its host's: shards-dind, docker 29.3.1); with `-m`, booted with all of it, its
page structures paid at boot (21 MiB and 4 ms per GiB, PM M82). D133's virtio-mem gives a
builder memory as its build needs it; runs now have it too.

- **A run without a limit** boots as before, with a region to plug of the host's memory
  less that, and is given memory as its processes reach what it has, up to the host's
  memory, as a container without one may have. **A run with `-m`** boots as one without
  a limit does (the user's plan, item 3, 2026-10-19), its most to plug what its limit
  needs, and `-m` ends a workload past it (`memory.max`, 137), as Docker's does. Its guest
  reports what it may plug (D149), so Node.js sizes its heap by its limit as under Docker
  (PM M220, M221: 2,096 MiB at `-m 8g`), where booted small before D149 it sized it at
  259. Every limit's runs restore one template, where each limit had its own, and a run
  of a large limit pays page structures as it plugs what it uses, not for all of it as it
  boots (21 MiB and 4 ms per GiB, PM M82).
- **Templates.** A snapshot keeps the region to plug, none of it plugged (format 13: the
  machine's `hotplug_mib`); a restore remakes it as boot made it, withheld. Every run
  shares one template, its limit or none its own most, and since D191 its CPU limit too. What is plugged or asked for is not saved: a device says why
  (`VirtioDevice::unsaved`), and the snapshot is refused, not written without it. A run's
  most comes with the run (the `RUN` request) and the VM sets it before its guest hears
  of the run (`Handle::set_plug_most`): the host keeps the bound, never the guest.
- **Init** holds every process past it, the workload's, each joiner's (D119) and the
  domains' (D109), in one cgroup (`/sys/fs/cgroup/run`; each keeps its own namespace's
  view), at a `memory.high` of the memory plugged so far, and a process of its own in the
  root cgroup grows it, D133's grower, reading the run's most again as it grows; it says
  what it sees in the kernel's log. It starts before the template's snapshot and goes on
  in each restore, and through the workload's end, where joiners go on. The template's kernel limits sized by memory are those of all of it
  (D133's `raise_limits`), and its root's writes hold as much (the writable layer's
  tmpfs), as a container's are its host's; the domains count what may still be plugged.
- **Verified on real VMs** (containers.rs `a_runs_memory_grows_as_its_workload_needs_it`):
  without `-m`, 1 GiB in a microVM booted with 256 MiB, in the one that saved the
  template and in a restore; `-m 256m` ended at 137; `-m 1g` holding 512 MiB.
  `update_moves_a_microvms_memory_both_ways`: raised from `-m 256m` to `1g` and
  allocating 512 MiB, plugged as it grows, 600 of 600 alone on 8 CI runners (EPYC 7763
  ×4, 9V45 ×2, 9V74, Xeon 8573C), none killed (PM M325).
  `run_limits_a_microvms_resources`: each limit, at 1 vCPU and at every one, held
  to within 16 MiB of it. boot.rs `a_snapshot_keeps_memory_to_plug`: a guest snapshotted with memory to
  plug, the booted VM and two restores each plugging 512 MiB. Mutation-checked: without
  the grower, the 1 GiB run is ended (137); without the restored region, a restore fails.
- **What it costs** (PM M219): a run's start and end within 0.1 ms of before (paired
  A/B, median +36 µs, 95% [-14, +100]), an idle run 0.2 MiB more of footprint; a region
  of 128 GiB costs a cold boot 0.8 ms. Found on the way: `SHARDS_TIMING`'s count of held
  pages asked the OS of the whole region, 7.75 ms a run; it asks of blocks ever plugged.
- **Not yet:** what a guest without a limit reports of its memory: what it has, 243 MiB
  as it boots, where a container's is its host's, by which Node.js sizes its heap at 259
  MiB where Docker's is 4,144 (PM M220): it must report what it may plug. Memory given
  back as a long-lived run's workload frees it (D133's device can unplug; a guest must ask
  for less).

### D147. Mounting a pmem root once libnvdimm has made it

- **What:** init mounts an image's EROFS on its pmem device (a run's root, a builder's
  base images) once; where the mount fails with ENOENT (no node yet) or ENXIO (a node
  whose disk is not there yet), it waits for libnvdimm's probing to end, reading each nd
  bus's `wait_probe` as ndctl does, and mounts again. Before the root is mounted, sysfs is
  mounted for the wait alone.
- **Why:** libnvdimm registers pmem regions and namespaces in an exclusive asynchronous
  domain, which the kernel does not wait for before init runs (drivers/nvdimm/bus.c,
  include/linux/async.h, init/main.c). A 2.1 GB root, whose region takes longest to
  probe, was not there yet as init mounted it, and its runs failed every time (M217).
- **No deadline:** the wait ends when the kernel says probing is done; a mount that fails
  again says why. Where the first mount succeeds, it is the one call it always was.
- **Verified:** `an_image_of_gigabytes_boots` (a 2 GiB root of random bytes); 200 of 200
  cold boots of 108 MB and 2.1 GB roots (M217). Mutation-checked: without the retry, the
  test fails 3 of 3 with ENOENT.

### D146. A run's `--device` by CDI name

- **What:** `--device VENDOR/CLASS=NAME` gives a run what the device's CDI spec says, as
  dockerd's CDI driver gives it as a container starts (moby daemon/cdi.go,
  injectCDIDevices; CDI v1.1.0 Cache.InjectDevices, ContainerEdits.Apply): each name the
  device of that name in the specs of the daemon's CDI directories (SHARDS_CDI_SPEC_DIRS,
  else /etc/cdi and /var/run/cdi, read as builds read them, D96), the spec's edits once,
  then each device's.
  - Its variables over the workload's whole environment (AddMultipleProcessEnv).
  - Its groups, but root's, once each (AddProcessAdditionalGid).
  - Its nodes from the guest's own device at the host path, a host's numbers meaning
    nothing in a guest, checked against the kind the spec says; the spec's mode, else the
    device's (udev's); the spec's owner, else the process's user and group but root's,
    which init resolves from the image's user database; the spec's cgroup access, else
    `rwm`. A FIFO is made as one, outside the device filter.
  - Its mounts as binds of the host path, read-only with `ro`, of the propagation its
    options name, with `nosuid`, `nodev` and `noexec` on the guest's mount; a container's
    record keeps none of them, as dockerd's keeps none.
  - A node of the GPU's render node gives the run this Mac's GPU (D144, D145).
- **As dockerd fails:** a name no spec has fails the start, not the making, in dockerd's
  words (`CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices …`); a hook, a host's
  network interface or an Intel RDT class, which only a container's host has, is refused
  by name, as a build's step refuses it.
- **Verified on real VMs** (containers.rs `cdi_devices_are_given_to_microvms`,
  gpu.rs): variables, groups, a node's owner, mode and access, a read-only nosuid nodev
  bind, a name refused at start, a hook refused; `--device test.example/gpu=0` finds
  Venus. Mutation-checked: without `nosuid` on the guest's mount, or with root as a
  node's owner, the test fails.
- **A joiner's nodes** (D119) are owned once its root is built: its user by name is
  resolved by its own image's users, as a run's is; verified (`-u app`).

### D145. A build's steps given the GPU by CDI name

- **What:** a step given a CDI device whose edits bring the render node
  `/dev/dri/renderD128`, the node Linux's virtio-gpu driver makes for a guest's first
  GPU, has this Mac's GPU: the build's builder boots in `shards-vm-gpu` with `--gpu`, on
  the gpu kernel where SHARDS_KERNEL names none (D144), and the step's node is made from
  the guest's own, as each CDI node is (D96).
- **Why by the node:** `RUN` asks for devices by CDI name alone (`--device`, BuildKit
  v0.28.1, CDI v1.1.0), never for GPUs by count as `--gpus` does, and a CDI spec says
  which nodes each device brings: a spec of the user's own (SHARDS_CDI_SPEC_DIRS, else
  /etc/cdi and /var/run/cdi) names the GPU with nothing new to learn. A build's steps share
  one builder, so all of them run in the GPU's VM process where any is given the GPU.
- **Elsewhere:** a host without a GPU for microVMs (Linux and Windows, until VFIO) makes
  the node from the guest's own device as before, which it has not.
- **Verified on this Mac** (tests/gpu.rs): `RUN --device=test.example/gpu=0 vulkaninfo
  --summary`, the device a spec of the test's brings the render node by (auto-allowed),
  finds "Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)"; mutation-checked: with the builder never given
  the GPU, the step fails.

### D144. GPUs: macOS first, Venus in a VM process of its own build

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11 row 978: a GPU given a run or a build's step (`--gpus`, `--device`'s
CDI names, `RUN --device`), which shards creates rather than refuses (the user, 2026-10-10:
"Then we create it"). The research set its shape (gpu-accelerators.md): a GPU costs nothing
where it is not used (R1); on Linux, VFIO through iommufd, a GPU VM a class of its own
assigned from a warm pool, as a device passed through pins all of a guest's memory and
breaks copy-on-write restores (R2, R3); on macOS, virtio-gpu with Venus over MoltenVK,
Vulkan compute in the guest, as libkrun gives it (R6). macOS is first: its hardware is here
to test on, where no CI runner has a GPU behind an IOMMU.

- **A VM process of its own build** (PM M214): MoltenVK links Metal, QuartzCore, IOSurface
  and Foundation, which dyld loads as a process launches: 1.3 ms more at p50 and 480 KB
  more footprint for every VM that linked them, a GPU's or not. A GPU VM runs
  `shards-vm-gpu`, the VM process built with the renderer and MoltenVK in it, carried and
  written out as `shards-vm` is (D36); every other VM's links neither. Its Metal device
  costs it 19 ms as it boots, in its pool's refill.
- **Rendering in that process**, as krunkit does: on macOS the renderer (virglrenderer's
  Venus, in the 0.10.4e-krunkit fork libkrun's Homebrew formula builds) maps a blob's
  device memory and hands its address (`virgl_renderer_resource_get_map_ptr`), which the
  VMM maps into the device's shared memory window (hv_vm_map). A renderer in a process of
  its own would need that memory shared between processes, which the fork does not export
  on macOS.
- **The transport's shared memory regions** (virtio 1.3 §4.2.2): the region a driver
  selects reads its length and base; one a device has not, all-ones, as every one read
  before.
- **The device** (`devices::virtio::gpu`): what the Linux driver needs for Vulkan through
  Venus (virtgpu_kms.c; Mesa's vn_renderer_virtgpu.c asks for 3D, blobs, contexts and the
  host-visible region): VIRGL, RESOURCE_BLOB, CONTEXT_INIT and BLOB_ALIGNMENT offered, no
  scanout, the renderer's capsets alone (Venus). A request is read once, copied, its
  lengths held to what it holds and the whole to the guest's RAM. A blob of guest memory
  is given to the renderer as its RAM's host addresses; one of host memory is mapped into
  the window at the place the guest chose, of whole host pages, over nothing else mapped,
  within the window. A fenced request's answer waits for its fence, after those before it
  on its ring, as the driver signals a timeline's fences in order; one refused waits only
  for those; one of no ring is answered as it is done. The renderer runs on the device's
  worker; its threads signal fences to it. A request the driver made available again while
  the device held it is a malformed ring.
- **The window** is placed after RAM, the memory to plug and pmem, at a GiB boundary, as
  long as the host's GPU says it has memory the host can map (Vulkan's host-visible heaps,
  which Venus tells the guest): the most a guest can have mapped at once. On this Mac,
  128 GiB (PM M216); the IPA's width grows to hold it. Blobs are mapped read and write,
  never executed.
- **Blobs held from their making** (PM M216): the renderer frees a blob's memory when the
  guest frees it, blob or not, and the fork keeps only its address, which MoltenVK's next
  allocation takes: mapped from it, a blob freed and then mapped would have given the guest
  another context's memory. The device remaps each blob's pages as it is made
  (`mach_vm_remap`, shared) and maps those, which no other allocation is given while held;
  a blob said to be larger than its memory is refused, its region ending first.
- **Blob alignment.** Host pages are 16 KiB, and a blob's place in the window must be
  whole pages. The driver of Linux 7.2 aligns them where the device asks
  (VIRTIO_GPU_F_BLOB_ALIGNMENT, commits 7b5121c3374e, 47248e0d8264, 6bd7e82e2653, for
  libkrun on macOS), and Mesa's Venus rounds its blobs' sizes to it
  (vn_renderer_virtgpu.c); an unaligned place is refused, said once.
- **No snapshot of what the GPU holds.** A GPU's state is its host driver's, and the
  renderer's threads reach guest memory without the VMM's access: a snapshot is refused
  once the guest has made a context or a resource, and a template is saved before it has
  (D150).
- **The gpu kernel variant** (resources/kernel/gpu.config): DRM's virtio-gpu driver without
  modesetting, apart from every other guest's kernel; patch 0003 backports the blob
  alignment to 6.18.48 and rounds a host blob's size up to it where upstream refuses it,
  so that Mesa that aligns nothing, Debian trixie's 25.0.7 among them, maps its blobs too.
- **`shards-vm-gpu`**, the VM process built with the renderer (`--features gpu`), built
  and signed by build.rs where SHARDS_GPU_LIBS names the libraries scripts/gpu-libs builds
  from pinned sources, carried in `shards` and written out the first time a GPU VM needs
  it. MoltenVK says its errors alone (MVK_CONFIG_LOG_LEVEL 1).
- **`--gpus`**, read as docker/cli reads it (crates/cmdline/tests/docker-cli.json), gives a run this Mac's GPU where it asks for
  any or for device 0: its microVM is `shards-vm-gpu`'s, on the gpu kernel, restored from
  a template of its own (D150), and the run has the render node as `--device` gives one;
  inspect shows the requests as the CLI makes them. More GPUs, another device or a driver
  of its own are refused. `run --kernel … --gpu` does the same for a kernel booted
  directly.
- **The render node's mode is a host's:** udev's 0666 (systemd v257
  50-udev-default.rules.in, `KERNEL=="renderD*"`, group-render-mode's default), where the
  guest's devtmpfs gives 0600, so a run's user other than root has the GPU, and a step's
  node where its CDI spec gives no mode; verified (`--user 1000`), mutation-checked.
- **Verified on this Mac** (tests/gpu.rs): `shards run --rm --gpus all` of an image with
  Mesa's Venus finds "Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)", conformance 1.3; the guest's
  driver negotiates VIRGL, RESOURCE_BLOB, CONTEXT_INIT and BLOB_ALIGNMENT.
- **Built by CI and releases:** the macOS arm64 jobs run scripts/gpu-libs, so `shards`
  carries `shards-vm-gpu`; CI lints vmm's `gpu` feature, which no workspace lint compiles,
  and runs the renderer's tests, which skip where Metal finds no GPU (a virtual Mac). The
  renderer links compiler-rt (`libclang_rt.osx.a`) for MoltenVK's `@available` checks
  (`__isPlatformVersionAtLeast`), which clang links into every Darwin program and rustc
  does not: std's weak copy is gone under release's fat LTO, and the release build failed
  to link without it. A link-lib, as a library's build script's link-arg reaches no
  binary.
- **The gpu kernel is pinned** (`KERNEL_GPU`): kernel-6.18.48-7ccc39cf716b's
  `Image-6.18.48-aarch64-gpu`, whose release rebuilt the other kernels byte for byte; a
  GPU run downloads it as the pinned kernel is. tests/gpu.rs boots it in the GPU's VM
  process that `shards` carries, as a user's run does.
- **E6 measured** (PM M218): matrix multiplication at the GPU's speed through Venus
  (guest time over host time, geometric mean 1.003 over 218 cases); llama.cpp ahead in
  the guest on a busy host, by its vCPUs' scheduling and Venus's asynchronous submits;
  a blob's first map about 0.1 ms; the renderer some 3 MiB of a VM's footprint.
- **To build:** Linux's VFIO (R2). A build's `RUN` steps: D145; a run's `--device` by
  CDI name: D146; a GPU's templates: D150.

### D143. `RUN` on Windows hosts: the builder

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11 row 975: a Windows host runs a build's `RUN` steps in a builder
microVM as Linux and macOS hosts do (D34), its VM process confined as D141 confines one,
its network the network process's (D142).

- **One builder, every host.** Its code is the Unix builder's: the same frames over the
  same build port, layers sent once, caches attached to its join disk (D134), SSH agents
  relayed, the build's proxy (D110). Its sockets are AF_UNIX on Windows too
  (`shards-afunix`: M199, made overlapped, M207), and a wait on two of them is WSAPoll's
  where Unix polls (`platform::wait_readable`).
- **Started in order.** Its VM process is made suspended in its AppContainer; its network
  process starts next in one of its own, given a handle to the VM's process that may only
  wait for its end (PROCESS_SYNCHRONIZE); then the VM runs. A thread answers what the VM
  asks for (its base images, its vsock socket, its dials to the build port) with a handle
  to it that may only give it handles (PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE), and ends with it.
- **Its caches' files** go to the VM by handle: duplicated into it, each one's value in its
  attach message, as a message on Windows carries no handle (shards_ipc).
- **Its sockets' directory** is in the user's own temporary directory, its lock a file
  shared with no one, which no other process opens while its owner holds it; a later
