  build's sweep removes one whose lock opens (D137).
- **A child's environment** is `SHARDS_LOG` and `SHARDS_TIMING`, as on Unix, and this
  process's `LOCALAPPDATA` and `SystemRoot` (PM M208): without `LOCALAPPDATA` Windows makes
  no child in an AppContainer, and points it at the container's own folder, the child's
  `TEMP` at the `Temp` there; without `SystemRoot` Winsock makes no socket
  (WSAEPROVIDERFAILEDINIT). A Windows child had its spawner's whole environment until now
  (D141).

### D142. The network process on Windows

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11 row 975: a VM's flows go through a network process of its own (D31)
on Windows as on Linux and macOS.

- **Its ring** is a pagefile-backed section, the doorbell its VM sleeps on an auto-reset
  event, 23-35 µs a round trip (PM M204), and the one it sleeps on an AF_UNIX socket its
  VM rings a byte on, 29-34 µs (PM M213); a socket pair takes 0.6 ms to make (M199).
- **It waits on a completion port** its sockets and that doorbell are registered with
  (ProcessSocketNotifications, Windows 11 and Server 2022 on), which names those ready: a
  round trip beside 10,000 idle connections costs what one beside none does, 37-41 µs,
  where one event every socket set and a look at every socket after each wake cost
  39-54 ms (PM M213). One event to wake on with the port asked which sockets are ready
  lost wakes, and is not used.
- **One-shot registrations** (PM M215): a notice disarms its socket's, and the next wait
  arms it again, in the call that waits, for what the socket then waits for; one that
  waits for nothing (its guest's window full, nothing for its host) is left as it is, and
  its one notice let go of. A registration removed could not be made again until its
  removal's notice came, and one filtering nothing is refused (WSAEINVAL): a connection
  that waited for nothing for a while was reset either way (net costs runs 38303389671,
  38308200096, 256 KiB each way).
- **Confined** in an AppContainer that holds `internetClient`, `internetClientServer` and
  `privateNetworkClientServer` (M204): it reaches the networks and never this host's
  loopback or own addresses, nor a file or socket by its path. Its spawner dials those for
  it, as on macOS a build's proxy is (D31): a build's proxy's socket, and a TCP flow to
  the loopback or to one of the host's own addresses, each up adapter's unicast ones,
  which it is told as it starts. Each ask is numbered and answered once its connect has
  ended, the connection shared with it (WSADuplicateSocketW, M203), as Windows documents a
  shared socket's use: one process makes the connection, another exchanges data on it.
  The spawner waits on all its connects at once, and the network process asks without
  waiting, its guest's SYN waiting for the answer as for a far end's SYN-ACK and nothing
  else with it (`dials_are_answered_as_they_end_and_hold_up_nothing`). An earlier dialer
  that shared connects still under way and was waited on in the network process's loop
  left a build's 178th connection to its host unanswered for 137 s (M212). The spawner
  connects from the address asked for, which binding to it proves the host holds as it
  dials, and to no other. A step reaches its host's own services as Docker's do
  (build.rs `run_steps_reach_the_network_unless_it_is_none`, which failed without it, PM M204's
  finding).
- **Its VM's end** it learns as its doorbell's socket hangs up, as a pipe's does on Unix,
  and from the VM's process, a handle it may only wait on, which a thread-pool wait posts
  to its port once it ends. Its spawner gives it that handle before the VM runs (D143).
- **Published ports and peers** (the platform parity plan's step 5): bound by the daemon
  as on Unix (D31) and handed to the network process on its control, an AF_UNIX socket it
  waits on with its own, as its doorbell is. Each socket goes shared with that process
  (WSADuplicateSocketW), its protocol info before the message's payload, where Unix passes
  descriptors beside it (`shards_ipc::with_sockets`, `kind::hands_sockets`): a listener its
  spawner bound and shared takes its spawner's connection, with or without capabilities
  (M204). Each listener holds its address alone (SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE): Windows lets a
  process of the same user bind the port at one address over a listener at every address
  and take what comes to it there, where Linux refuses that bind ("Using SO_REUSEADDR and
  SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE", Microsoft Learn: "All server applications must set
  SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE"); Windows' SO_REUSEADDR, which a Unix listener sets to bind over
  connections left in TIME_WAIT, binds over a listener in use, and is not set. A run's
  ports close as it ends on its VM's release, an AF_UNIX socket too, before its end is
  told. A peer's link on a network (D46) is an AF_UNIX pair, an end shared with each
  network process. A builder publishes none, and drops both.

### D141. The Windows VM process confined

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11 row 975, after D140: a VM process on Windows reaches no more of its
host than one on macOS or Linux does (D30). Windows' own primitives, each measured before it
was built on [PM M200-M203]:

- **An AppContainer of its own**, as macOS's App Sandbox: no file or socket of its user's,
  but what its spawner hands it. A profile per VM, not a SID derived from a name, which
  CreateProcessW refuses an AppContainer without (ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND) [PM M201]; holding
  the capabilities `\\?\VidExo`'s DACL grants, read from the device as it starts, without
  which WHP sets up no partition in it [PM M200].
- **Grants as macOS's, over a pipe each way.** Files by DuplicateHandle, each with the path
  its spawner found it at (GetFinalPathNameByHandleW refuses an AppContainer [PM M203]);
  sockets by WSADuplicateSocketW, as Winsock documents, 6-10 µs more a dial than
  DuplicateHandle at p50 [PM M203]. The spawner of `shards run --kernel` answers in its own
  process, since Windows has no exec: the VM is its child, which shares its console, one
  with a window or one without, as a CI runner's is (counted by GetConsoleProcessList, where
  GetConsoleWindow answers none for one without: its VM was made detached there, and heard
  no interrupt), and gives the console's Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Break to its guest as SIGINT;
  the spawner takes both and waits on, where ignoring Ctrl+C alone (a null handler) left a
  process group's Ctrl+Break to end it (run.rs `signals_reach_the_command`, CI's
  windows-2022 and windows-2025, 2026-10-28). Nothing more is granted once its vsock path
  is, and without one the link closes.
- **A Job and Windows' mitigations**, given as the process is made, suspended, its handles
  duplicated into it and their values told it through a pipe, its one inherited handle:
  none is made inheritable where another child could take it [PM M201]. Dynamic code it
  forbids itself once its partition is set up (SetProcessMitigationPolicy), since
  windows-2022 sets no partition up without it, while every call a VM makes after its
  setup works [PM M202]; the library never does, as a test's process sets up many.
- **No profile left behind.** Each lives with a record its spawner holds open
  (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\shards\containers`); the next spawner deletes the profile of each record
  no process holds.
- **The partition that reads WHP's vCPU limit is made as a VM's** (D140 fixed): offered the
  synthetic features without its APICs emulated, WHP refused it (HV_STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER),
  and with it every VM (CI run 38222358454).

Tested on real VMs (`the_vm_process_is_confined`): the VM process's token is an
AppContainer's, it is in a Job, each mitigation is on, dynamic code forbidden once its guest
runs; killed with its spawner; and the profile its killed spawner left is deleted by the next.
The `vsock` tests run through the spawner's grants on Windows: both directions, eight streams
at once, refusals.

### D140. microVMs on Windows hosts: the WHP backend

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11 row 975 (`RUN` on Windows hosts) starts here: shards' VMM drives the
Windows Hypervisor Platform on x86_64 Windows, as it drives KVM and Hypervisor.framework
(D13), and a Windows host boots shards' guests. Its VM process's confinement (D141), its
network process (D142) and its builder (D143) follow.

- **The backend (`hv::whp`).** WinHvPlatform.dll's functions are bound as first called, as
  HVF's are (PM M113): a `shards` without the optional feature "Windows Hypervisor
  Platform" starts, and says why it runs no VM. A partition per VM, its local APICs
  emulated by the hypervisor (XApic), which runs HLT itself; its application processors
  held in wait-for-SIPI as created, and started by the boot vCPU's INIT and SIPI (PM M198).
  Its guest is offered, of the host's synthetic features, those it keeps time by (the
  reference counter and TSC page, the frequency MSRs) and those Linux's Hyper-V setup
  writes (hypercalls, the VP index, the APIC's synthetic MSRs and VP assist page), with the
  TLB-flush and cluster-IPI hypercalls its hints recommend; not synthetic timers, which the
  host refuses without the SynIC, nor anything of VMBus's (M198). As many vCPUs as the
  hypervisor tells a partition's guest it supports (leaf 0x40000005, read once a process
  from a partition of one made as a VM's is, without whose synthetic features the leaf
  reads 0 (M202): 240 on GitHub's runners, fewer than the host's own CPUID says), and at
  most 254.
- **One package of cores, and invariant TSC** (M206). Each vCPU's CPUID is a KVM guest's
  (`cpuid::for_vcpu`: one package of single-thread cores, private L1 and L2 caches, a
  shared L3), told WHP as results masked to the bits they change (CpuidResultList2,
  `cpuid::masked`), so that the hypervisor keeps each vCPU's APIC id and the bits it
  changes as the guest runs; with invariant TSC where the host's processor has it, which
  Windows Server 2025 leaves out of its partitions' CPUID though their TSC keeps the
  host's one rate (within 0.02 ppm of the partition's clock over 3 s, idle and loaded) and
  a partition never moves to another host. One list, set as the last vCPU is made: WHP
  refuses per-vCPU results before setup (HV_STATUS_INVALID_VP_INDEX), a second list
  replaces the first, and no vCPU runs before all are made (D5); 0.7-0.9 ms for 64 vCPUs,
  2.9-3.7 ms for 240. Without them each AP timed the boot CPU's ticks for its own delay
  loop (Linux's `calibrate_delay_direct`), the ticks late on a busy host: 63 APs took a
  240-vCPU boot past a minute on a 4-CPU runner, starving every VM beside it (CI run
  38240024887).
- **The IOAPIC is the VMM's** (`arch::x86_64::ioapic`), as KVM's in-kernel one presents
  itself (82093AA, version 0x11, 24 pins): its pins driven by the machine's devices, each
  interrupt it sends asked of the hypervisor (WHvRequestInterrupt, 3.8-6.3 µs a call),
  each level-triggered EOI taken back from its exit to clear the pin's remote IRR (M198).
- **MMIO decoded by the VMM** (`arch::x86_64::mmio`). WHP hands the VMM an MMIO exit's
  instruction bytes, not its length or its effect (M198). The VMM decodes the instructions
  Linux's own decoder takes for its TDX and SEV-ES guests (`insn_decode_mmio`: MOV to and
  from memory and of an immediate, MOVZX, MOVSX), and shards-init's control-page loads and
  stores; at two register calls of 0.1 µs, where WinHvEmulation spends 8-11 µs (M197).
  Anything else is refused, its bytes named, rather than its effect guessed. Port I/O is
  completed from the exit's own registers and length.
- **No doorbells.** A notification port's round trip was no shorter than an MMIO exit's
  (M198): virtio's notifications are exits.
- **A kick is a cancel**, which a run about to start takes too (M198).
- **A console nobody reads is told `quiet`** (vm `kernel_cmdline`, M376), on every host: a
  VM whose console is discarded, every daemon's, boots its kernel writing it errors and
  worse alone, unless its command line names a level. Each byte a kernel writes there is
  an exit or two, and a boot writes some 18 KB: of a cold boot's kernel to its panic with no
  root, quiet took 0.50 s of 2.14 on windows-2022, 0.50 of 1.49 on windows-2025, and on an
  M5 Max's HVF 27.9 ms of 65.2 (n=20 each, interleaved). What it says stays in its ring
  buffer, which `dmesg` reads; a VM whose console is shown (`run --kernel`) boots as told.
- **Its CPUs brought up one at a time.** Its kernel is told `cpuhp.parallel=0`: brought up
  in parallel past the host's CPUs, each AP started spins in its turn while the next waits
  for a host CPU, which Windows Server 2022's WHP gives no other vCPU, and 32 vCPUs took 39 s
  where one at a time took 96 ms, never slower, at 4 vCPUs as at 240 (M353).
- **Its CPUs past the first brought online by its init, on a nested Hyper-V**
  (`vm::late_cpus_cmdline`, M379). Where the host's Hyper-V is nested in another's
  partition, a Windows host that is itself a virtual machine (CPUID 0x40000004's bit 12,
  Linux's HV_X64_HYPERV_NESTED), a guest of shards-init's of more than one vCPU boots its
  kernel with its boot CPU alone (`maxcpus=1`), and init, told `shards_online`, brings the
  rest online before anything runs. A boot's initcalls patch its kernel's text as they set
  static calls and keys (the crypto and CRC libraries', SELinux's netfilter hooks) and
  switch its clocksource by stop_machine, each waiting for every CPU online, and on CI's
  runners, nested in Azure, a vCPU waited on had no host CPU while the one waiting spun:
  eight guests of 4 vCPUs booting at once on windows-2022's 4 CPUs spent 75.7% of their
  kernels' ticks so and took 46.20 s, with their boot CPUs alone at boot 5.37 s; on
  windows-2025 11.61 s and 3.84 s; a guest alone 0.09 to 0.19 s slower. Bare metal, every
  CPU at boot: on jupiter a guest of 32 vCPUs came up in 0.32 s alone and 0.68 to 1.16 s
  eight at once, and its CPUs brought online after took it to 2.28 s and 3.89 to 4.24 s,
  31 CPUs in 2.1 s. RCU's grace periods stay normal: expedited for the CPUs brought online,
  they took longer eight at once on windows-2022, each an IPI to every CPU online. HVF and
  KVM boot every CPU at boot (on the M5 Max a guest of 18 vCPUs came up in 0.11 s so, and
  in 0.35 s with its CPUs brought online after; KVM unmeasured so).
- **The guest kernel's `hyperv` variant** (resources/kernel/hyperv.config): Linux 6.18
  marks the TSC unstable on a Hyper-V that does not offer TSC invariance, as no runner did,
  and keeps time by Hyper-V's reference TSC page only with CONFIG_HYPERV (M197). No VMBus,
  nor its drivers. Windows hosts boot it (`kernel::KERNEL`); KVM and HVF guests boot the
  kernel without its code. Release kernel-6.18.48-4062e616c93a, which rebuilt the other
  kernels byte for byte.
- **pmem on Windows**: the image's view and the zeros after it in one range, a placeholder
  split in two (VirtualAlloc2, MapViewOfFile3 with MEM_REPLACE_PLACEHOLDER). A view may not
  run past its section's end, the file's size, so it holds the file's whole pages, and the
  file's last partial page is copied into the read-only zeros after it.
- **vsock on Windows**: AF_UNIX sockets (afunix.sys), 3.4-3.7 times loopback TCP's
  throughput (M199), made overlapped, as std makes its sockets: Windows serializes the I/O
  of a socket made otherwise, so that a send waits out another thread's read of the same
  connection (M207); its worker sleeps on WSAEventSelect's events and reads each socket's
  state with a WSAPoll that does not wait, as WSAPoll alone reports a peer's half-close as
  a hangup whatever is asked, which would wake a writer without end (M199). Its waker is an
  event, not a socket pair. An ended connection's host socket is held, its writing shut
  down, reading and dropping what comes, until its peer ends its side: an AF_UNIX socket
  closed holding any of its peer's data unread, or written to by its peer after its close,
  loses the peer all it had not read, as a reset (M358).
- **Carried on Windows too**: shards-init and the in-VM server, built for the guest as on
  every other host.
- **Snapshots** came after (D196); templates and warm pools wait for the daemon on Windows
  (D195).
- **Recorded differences** from a KVM guest's machine: its clock is Hyper-V's reference TSC
  page where KVM's is kvm-clock; its APICs are xAPIC alone, offering neither x2APIC nor
  TSC-deadline (M198).

### D139. Files handed across, through the in-VM server

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §9.4, §9.10 and §11 row 1001: what one domain produces reaches another only
through what a directive declares, and the reader never trusts its shape; a harness drives
an agent through the in-VM server and reads nothing of the agent's directory (§12 answer
11). Until now a harness had an agent's output only as the texts of its messages (D60).

- **The scratch, the server's too.** A domain's `/tmp` is no longer a tmpfs it mounts
  itself: init makes it, where the image has a `/tmp`, attached nowhere (`fsopen`,
  `fsmount`), `nosuid` and `nodev`, the domain's own (its uid and gid) and its group's to
  read (0750); the domain attaches it at `/tmp`, and its server instance, of the domain's
  group (D60), holds the same mount.
- **`hand`.** A caller hands a peer a file of its scratch: as a request, where it may send
  the peer requests, or, with `id`, as the answer to the peer's request (`ATTACH`: an agent
  answers its harness's). The grant is checked first: nothing is read where nothing may
  go. Its server opens the path beneath the scratch as the kernel resolves it (openat2(2),
  `RESOLVE_BENEATH | RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_XDEV`),
  without waiting (`O_NONBLOCK`: a FIFO's open waits on no writer), refuses any but a
  regular file, and reads it whole within what a message to a peer holds (1 MiB less the
  file's name and its length), else refuses, naming why. So a link the caller planted (to
  its server's own key), a FIFO, a giant file or a path above the scratch redirects,
  stalls and exhausts nothing.
- **On the channel**, a file is a message of kinds of its own, a request or an answer with
  the file's name and bytes, held by the receiving instance under the same grants as a
  text; `receive` shows it as `"file":{"name","size","data"}`, its bytes in Base64 (RFC
  4648). Code mode's programs hand files too (`shards.hand`, D136).
- **Recorded difference**: a file handed is one its server may read, the caller's group's
  (mode 0640 or wider); one of mode 0600 is refused, its server owning no file of the
  caller's.

Tested: in crates/server, on Linux, `only_a_regular_file_of_the_scratch_is_handed` (a link, a
FIFO, a directory, a file past the bound, a path above the scratch and one outside it
refused; none without a scratch), `a_peers_file_is_heard_as_granted`, `base64_is_rfc_4648s`;
on real microVMs, `a_harness_is_handed_files_and_no_link_fifo_or_giant`: an agent plants a
link to its server's key, a FIFO and a 2 MiB file in its scratch, its harness asks it once,
and its tries to hand each, a path above its scratch and one outside it are refused by its
server, which stalls on none; the regular file it hands is the one thing the harness
receives. Mutation-checked: links followed, a path above the scratch reached, a FIFO waited
on (the server stalls), any kind of file read, a giant file not refused, a file heard
without its grant, Base64 unpadded, the scratch not given to its instance, and the scratch
closed to its instance: each fails a test.

### D138. The in-VM server speaks MCP 2026-07-28, and the revisions before it

The in-VM server spoke MCP 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26 (D60). The current revision is
2026-07-28 (modelcontextprotocol.io, "Versioning", read 2026-10-11): stateless, with no
`initialize`, no session and no stream of the server's own; each request says its
revision, its client's capabilities and who the client is in its `_meta`, and its HTTP
headers say again what its body says. A client of it alone fails against a server of the
revisions before it; one of those alone fails against a server of it alone. The server
now speaks both, as the revision allows a server to ("dual-era"), each request by its own.

- **The current revision**, a request whose `_meta` names its revision:
  - its headers checked against its body, as its transport asks: `MCP-Protocol-Version`
    the revision, `Mcp-Method` the method, `Mcp-Name` the tool a `tools/call` names
    (plain, or Base64 between `=?base64?` and `?=`); any missing or other, 400 and
    `HeaderMismatch` (-32020);
  - a revision it does not speak, 400 and `UnsupportedProtocolVersion` (-32022), naming
    those it does, `2026-07-28` first; no `clientCapabilities` in its `_meta`, 400 and
    -32602;
  - `server/discover` (its revisions, its capabilities, who it is), `tools/list` and
    `tools/call`; any other method, 404 and -32601; a notification, of which none is
    defined over HTTP, accepted and ignored;
  - each result `resultType: "complete"`, with who answers in its `_meta`
    (`io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`); `server/discover` and `tools/list` with
    caching hints, the same for every caller and stale at once (`ttlMs` 0,
    `cacheScope` public): asking again costs a caller tens of microseconds (PM M196),
    and a cache a client kept past this instance would not see a newer server's tools;
  - a `run`'s program ended by its connection closing, which is the revision's
    cancellation (D136); a session ID ignored.
- **The revisions before it** (2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26), a request without
  that `_meta`: as D60 and D136 serve them, `initialize` choosing among them and
  beginning a session; `MCP-Protocol-Version`, where given, one of them, or 400 and
  -32022 as above; with it `2026-07-28` but no `_meta`, 400 and -32602.
- **For both**, as 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 ask of every server over HTTP: an `Origin`
  header, which a browser sends, is refused, 403 (no web page is a caller: callers are
  agents on sockets of their own); a method but POST, 405 with `Allow: POST`.

Tested: in crates/server, on Linux, `the_current_revision_is_answered_request_by_request`,
`headers_that_differ_from_their_body_are_refused` (each header missing or other, a name in
Base64), `what_the_current_revision_refuses` and
`earlier_revisions_and_what_every_revision_refuses`; on real microVMs,
`the_in_vm_server_speaks_each_revision`: an agent asks as a client of 2026-07-28 does
(discover, list, call `whoami` and `run`), with its headers wrong, its revision unknown,
its capabilities missing, an unknown method and an origin, each refused as above; and
begins a session of 2025-11-25. Mutation-checked: each of the three headers unchecked, Base64
unread, any revision spoken, capabilities not required, an unknown method answered 200, a
result not complete, a list without its caching hints, an origin answered, an earlier
revision's header unchecked, 2025-11-25 not spoken: each fails a test.
### D137. A build never held by its builder's memory, nor outlived by its builder

CI run 38198639601 (dev fd9da553, x86_64 Linux): `a_builders_memory_is_plugged_as_its_
build_needs_it`'s first build ran past its 120 s, where it takes about 33 s (runs
38197041559 and 38189388050), and what it said was lost, its pipes held open by its builder,
which outlived the `shards build` the test killed. Three faults, each fixed here; the
cause of that build's stall left no evidence, so what the next one leaves is fixed too.

- **Memory that stopped coming held the build** (D133). A build past its `memory.high` is
  slowed, never ended, until memory comes; its grower asked for memory, waited 5 s
  (`STALLED`, a thousand times the 5-7 ms 1 GiB took, PM M193), said so on the builder's
  console, which a build does not show, and, once it had asked for all the builder may
  have, asked no more. Linux's virtio-mem driver tries a plug it could not make (ENOMEM in
  the guest, BUSY from the host) again at once on a configuration change, or else on a
  timer of 50 s doubling to 300 s, and never where too many of its blocks are offline
  (drivers/virtio/virtio_mem.c, `virtio_mem_run_wq`, Linux 6.18): with nothing else
  changing, the build waited those out, or for ever. Now:
  - the device tells its driver again when asked again, a configuration interrupt with
    the configuration and its generation unchanged, so the driver tries again at once;
  - where nothing comes for `STALLED`, the grower asks again, saying what it asked for,
    what came, and the kernel's last words of its driver (/dev/kmsg); where nothing comes
    for as long again, it lifts the build's `memory.high`: the build runs on what the
    builder has, as one booted with that much would, and is ended by the kernel where it
    needs more (exit code 137, as one past all its memory is), never held;
  - what the grower says is said in the output of the step that runs as it says it,
    through a pipe init relays as that step's stderr;
  - and where the kernel ends a process of the build for want of memory (any of its OOM
    killers, `memory.events` `oom_kill`), the grower says why in the kernel's words, of
    its last report (/dev/kmsg): what asked and of what order, each zone's free memory
    against its watermarks, and what it ended. A builder's kernel log goes nowhere a
    build shows, and a kernel build whose compilers were ended at 20 s (once in four,
    under a host's load of 23) said only "Killed signal terminated program cc1"; a run's
    is told where clients look for it (`State.OOMKilled`, the `oom` event). Tested by
    `a_kill_is_said_in_the_kernels_words` (crates/init, a builder's real report from
    6.18.48) and `a_builders_memory_is_plugged_as_its_build_needs_it` (the step past all
    its builder's memory says the kernel's "Out of memory: Killed process"); the relay off
    fails the latter.
  - **Said by the step's runner, before its end (2026-10-16).** The grower said it as it
    woke, after the kernel ended the step's process, and init relayed the grower's notes
    only while the step's stdout or stderr was open: a step ended for want of memory
    closes both as it dies, so its note came after the relay had stopped, and the step's
    error went without it. CI's x86_64 Linux jobs saw so in 6 of 175 failed jobs
    (`a_builders_memory_is_plugged_as_its_build_needs_it`, the error and its 137 there,
    the kernel's words not). The step's runner says it now (crates/init build.rs), once
    the step is reaped and before its end is reported: where the step's cgroup counted
    an OOM kill (`memory.events` `oom_kill`, which the kernel counts before it sends the
    SIGKILL: mm/oom_kill.c `__oom_kill_process`, "Raise event before sending signal"),
    the kernel's report, read until it says what it ended (`oom_said`); the
    grower says no kill. Mutation-checked: the runner saying none fails the test every
    time.
- **A killed build left its builder running.** A builder's VM ended as its build dropped
  it, or as its guest powered off on its connection closing: a killed `shards build` drops
  nothing, and a guest held at its memory hears nothing. The VM now ends as its `--attach`
  socket closes, which the build holds for as long as it holds the VM, killed or not; its
  network process goes with it, as it goes with every VM (D31).
- **And left its sockets' directory.** A builder's and a build proxy's directory of
  sockets in the temporary directory holds a lock (flock) its build holds while it lives,
  put in place only once held, so that one in place and free is a dead build's; each build
  removes those, its user's, before it makes its own.
- **What a command said before it hung is kept** (tests/common `run_shards_with`): a
  command past its deadline shows its output so far, not only that another process held
  its pipes.

Tested: in crates/init, on Linux, `memory_asked_for_comes`,
`memory_that_comes_slowly_is_waited_for`, `memory_that_stops_coming_is_asked_for_again`
and `memory_that_never_comes_is_given_up` (after `STALLED` twice, with what came); in
crates/vmm, `requests_are_whole_blocks_within_the_most` (a request repeated tells the driver
again, its generation unchanged); in shards, `a_sweep_removes_what_dead_builds_left` (a free
lock's directory removed; a live build's, one whose lock is not yet in place, and one not a
build's, kept); on real microVMs, `a_killed_build_takes_its_builder_with_it` (the build
killed as a step runs, its VM gone within 10 s, its directory left, and removed by the next
build), and `a_builders_memory_is_plugged_as_its_build_needs_it`, unchanged.
Mutation-checked: a request repeated telling the driver nothing, a stall not asked for
again, a free lock not swept, a held lock swept, the builder outliving its build, and no
sweep before a build: each fails a test.

### D136. Code mode: a program run in a sandbox, with its caller's grants and no more

AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §5's last part, decided by the user with D60 (§12 answer 18): the server
describes every tool open to its caller as a typed API, and takes a program that calls
them, run in a sandbox with the caller's grants and no more, many calls in one round trip.
It is shards' own MCP's, and its runtime shards' to choose (AGENTFILE_ARCH §11 row 997).

- **The tool.** `run` (`{code, timeout_ms?}`), beside `whoami`, `mcp`, `peers`, `send`,
  `receive` and `answer`: `code` is the body of an async function, in strict mode, with
  `shards` in reach, each tool an async function of it that returns the tool's value or
  throws its refusal as an `Error`. What the program returns comes back as JSON, the
  tool's text; what it throws, a syntax error, or its time running out, as an error
  (`isError`) in JavaScript's words (`TypeError: boom`) with its stack, whose lines and
  columns are the program's as sent (the function it is the body of opens on lines
  numbered -1 and 0, which QuickJS-NG records no position on). The tool's description
  declares `shards` in TypeScript: the typed API.
- **The engine.** QuickJS-NG 0.16.2, through rquickjs 0.14.0, against Boa 0.22.0 (PM
  M196): 0.80 MB added to the binary against 5.69; a call into the host in 44-47 ns
  against 95-121 (p50); the reference program made and run in 95-110 µs against 200-230
  (p50), 139-302 against 1312-1656 (p99), Boa's tail its collector's; and 0.6 MiB at its
  peak against 4.8. Its C is vendored (`vendor/rquickjs-sys`, checked against crates.io's
  index) and compiled for the guest by zig, as AWS-LC's is (D60). A program has
  ECMAScript's intrinsics and `shards`: no module, `require`, `fetch`, timer, `std` or
  `os`.
- **The sandbox.** The instance's filter forks no process (D59's `--processes=none`), so
  as it begins, before it confines itself, it starts a helper: its own binary again
  (`/proc/self/exe`, `shards-server sandbox`), exec'd fresh, so it holds none of the
  instance's keys, with one descriptor, its control socket. The helper confines itself at
  once to that socket's messages, polling, forking, and reaping and killing its workers
  by pidfd. For each program it forks a worker, which holds the program's socket alone
  and loads a filter of its own before it reads the program: reading and writing, its
  memory, futexes, the clock, the kernel's randomness and exiting; any other call, or one
  of another ABI (x32), kills it (`SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS`). A worker opens nothing: no
  file, socket, process or descriptor. Each tool it calls is a frame to the instance over
  its socket, which the instance answers as it answers its caller's MCP call of that tool,
  under the same grants, with the same refusals. Helper and workers are the instance's
  uid, gid and cgroup, its agent's (D60): a program's memory and CPU are its caller's,
  under the domains' memory policy, and need no limits of their own. `shards top` shows
  them as `shards-sandbox` and `shards-program`.
- **Bounds.** A worker's frames, a call or its value, are at most 1 MiB, as a request's
  body is: a program makes its instance hold no more for it than a request does. A call
  past it is thrown, for the program to catch, and never sent; a value past it fails the
  program. The instance's frames, the program and each call's answer, are read whole: a
  `receive` may hold more than 1 MiB, as an MCP call of it may.
- **Its end.** A program ends with its value or its failure; past `timeout_ms`, its worker
  killed; or when its caller lets it go. MCP's `notifications/cancelled` (2025-03-26 to
  2025-11-25) names a request by its ID in the caller's session, so the instance begins a
  session at `initialize` (`Mcp-Session-Id`, 128 bits from the kernel's CSPRNG) and a
  cancellation reaches only its own session's program: another client of the same agent,
  with a request of the same ID, keeps its own. A connection that closes ends the program
  it awaits, as closing a request's stream is its cancellation in MCP 2026-07-28's
  Streamable HTTP; an answer in JSON has no stream to resume, and none to reach once its
  connection is gone. A program that awaits what nothing will settle (no job left to run)
  ends at once, saying so. The helper reaps each worker and says how it ended: one its
  filter killed "made a system call its sandbox refuses".
- **What it saves.** The model's turns: one for each call made one by one, one for a
  program making them all. Not time between an agent and its instance (PM M196): a
  program costs its caller about 0.4 ms of its own (p50 408 µs, p99 558, for one that
  makes no call), what a process made for it costs, and a call within it as much as one
  over MCP, about 23 µs.
- **Recorded difference.** MCP asks a cancelled request's receiver not to answer it. Over
  HTTP, where the request waits on its connection, the instance answers it with JSON-RPC
  error -32800 (`request cancelled`, LSP's code, as MCP names none), which the client is
  to ignore, so that its request ends rather than holding its connection open.

Tested: in crates/server, on Linux, `a_program_calls_its_tools_over_its_socket`,
`a_refused_call_is_thrown` (an oversized call thrown, unsent),
`the_call_beneath_the_tools_is_out_of_reach`, `what_a_program_came_to` (null, a value JSON
cannot hold, a throw, an error's positions, a syntax error's, a promise nothing settles),
`frames_are_read_whole_and_within_their_bound`,
`a_worker_is_ended_for_a_call_its_filter_refuses` (`openat`, and x32 on x86_64, SIGSYS),
`initialize_begins_a_session`, `a_cancellation_names_a_request_in_its_own_session`,
`a_programs_call_is_its_callers`; on real microVMs,
`code_mode_runs_a_program_with_the_callers_grants`: a's program finds itself, its peers,
sends b a request (b receives it) and is refused one to c; c's see no `require`, `fetch`,
`std`, `os` or `XMLHttpRequest`, throw, fail to parse, overflow the stack and run past
300 ms; a cancellation from another session reaches nothing, the program's own session's
ends it; an abandoned program's worker goes; and once all is done the run holds three
instances, three sandboxes and no program. `the_in_vm_server_knows_each_agent`: each
instance and its sandbox run as the instance's ids. Mutation-checked: a cancellation that
ignores its session, a worker allowed to open files, the call beneath the tools left in
reach, a call past its bound sent, a pending program not said, positions counted from 1,
no session begun, an abandoned program left to run, no deadline, a cancelled request left
unanswered, the sandbox unnamed: each fails a test.

### D135. What git says as a build keeps a repository, and the advice asked for

`BUILDKIT_GIT_ADVICE` (D92) asks BuildKit's git for its advice; shards' Git (D48) runs no
git, and said none (AGENTFILE_ARCH §11 row 958). PM M195 measured what each builder says:
BuildKit v0.34.0's and Docker 29.3.1's git print the same lines, git 2.52's, of a fetch and
a checkout, most of them about BuildKit's own repository; and with the repository's `.git`
kept, git's advice on the detached HEAD it is left at, which v0.34.0 prints only when asked
and Docker always.

- **What is said**, as before: the commit a ref resolved to, and each submodule's two
  lines. And now, for a repository whose `.git` a build keeps (`ADD --keep-git-dir`, a
  context kept by `BUILDKIT_CONTEXT_KEEP_GIT_DIR`), what git says as it checks it out:
  `HEAD is now at <abbreviation> <subject>` (builtin/checkout.c `describe_detached_head`):
  the commit's abbreviation as git makes it among the repository's objects (object-name.c
  `repo_find_unique_abbrev_r`, `core.abbrev` unset: half the bits of their count, rounded
  up, 7 digits at least, and more while another object shares them), and its one-line
  subject (pretty.c `format_subject`: the first paragraph, each line without the
  whitespace it ends with, joined by spaces). Before it, where the build asks
  (`git.advice`), git's advice on the detached HEAD, git 2.52's sixteen lines as both
  builders print them, after a note naming the commit (`Note: switching to '<commit>'.`),
  where BuildKit's names `FETCH_HEAD`, the ref it fetches into its own repository.
- **What is not**: git's lines about BuildKit's own repository (`Initialized empty Git
  repository in /var/lib/buildkit/runc-overlayfs/snapshots/snapshots/34/fs/`, `From
  file:///var/lib/...`, the refs fetched into it, a probe's `fatal: Not a valid object
  name ...`): paths into a builder's store, which name nothing a build has.
- **Each line stamped**, a log line of its step, in the form `--progress=plain` gives every step's output (`#5 0.486
  <commit>`); they were said without the time.
- **Recorded difference.** Docker 29.3.1 prints the advice whatever `BUILDKIT_GIT_ADVICE`
  says: its solver, BuildKit v0.28.1, reads no `git.advice`, and git advises unless told
  not to. shards prints it only when asked, as BuildKit v0.34.0 does, which is what the
  frontend's plan means by it (D92).
- **Tested**: `add_fetches_git_repositories` (a kept repository's lines with the advice and
  without, each stamped, and none of them for a source whose `.git` goes);
  `a_commits_subject_is_gits` and `an_objects_abbreviation_is_gits`, against git itself:
  subjects of every shape; 7 digits in a small repository, 8 in one of over 16,384
  objects, 9 for two blobs that share 8. Mutation-checked: the advice not said, `git.advice`
  not read, the commit not abbreviated, the checkout's lines not said, the abbreviation
  not lengthened past a shared prefix or by the objects' count, a subject's lines not
  trimmed: each fails one.

### D134. Cache mounts at virtio-blk's speed: their layers EROFS images on the builder's join disk

D114 kept a cache's content as the layers its steps' changes made, and moved it in and out
of the builder over the build's connection: the host made a tree of a record's layers and
sent it, a frame of 1 MiB at a time, and the guest sent back what the step changed, which
the host applied to that tree and wrote as a layer. PM M194 measured where that went, for
a cache of 10,000 files of 4 KiB and two of 128 MiB: a build that mounted it and did
nothing spent 707 ms at the median sending its tree, 680 of them waiting on the builder
to take and write it; one that filled it spent 962 ms reading its changes back and
applying them (8.6 s at p90 under load) and 170 writing their layer. Now nothing of a
cache crosses the connection, and the host never makes a tree of one nor applies its
changes.

- **A record's layers are EROFS images**, files of its own (`cachemounts/v2/records/<id>/
  layers/<n>.erofs`): a step's changes as overlayfs left them in its upper directory
  (whiteouts as character devices 0:0, opaque directories by `trusted.overlay.opaque`,
  xattrs, owners, modes, times, a file of several names one inode), the first content of a
  cache from something (`from=`) written on the host from its source's snapshot, or
  layers merged. Version 1's records go at the next collection, as the store drops a
  layout it no longer reads.
- **The builder's join disk takes writes** (D119's, `shards run --kernel --attach FD`): the
  host attaches each layer's file to it, read-only, once for the builder's life, and for
  each cache a step writes, a file of its own for the changes, as large as the store has
  room for (`SHARDS_MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`, within what the disk has free past
  `SHARDS_KEEP_FREE`) and taking none of it until written. The VM process serves the
  attaches on a socket of the builder's (`DISK_ATTACH`, `DISK_DETACH`), and writes only to
  the ranges given writable. Ranges are never given twice, so what the guest has cached
  of one is never another's.
- **The guest** mounts each layer once, from a read-only loop device over its range
  (LOOP_SET_FD and LOOP_SET_STATUS64, as a joiner's root is made), which reads the range
  straight from the join disk (LOOP_SET_DIRECT_IO, Linux 4.4), not through the disk's page
  cache as well as the layer's: read twice so, a build held 256 MiB short of what it held
  kept the join disk's copy of its reread at the read's pace, in no cgroup its hold holds,
  its host throttling it for 15 minutes; read once, its step took 27.7 s (PM M350). Every
  range starts on a mebibyte (virtio `RANGE_ALIGN`), which the kernel's alignment for
  direct reads takes whatever the disk's block size. It stacks a cache's layers
  with overlayfs under the step's upper directory, and after the step, whatever its
  status, writes an EROFS image of that directory into the cache's writable range, syncs
  it, and says its length (`MOUNT_END`, a `Kept`): the host lets the range go, trims the
  file to the image, syncs it, and names it the record's next layer. Changes past the
  room fail the build, said so (the guest's image would pass its range), and nothing of
  them is kept.
- **Few layers, few bytes past what it shows.** A step mounts every layer of a record, and
  each costs it a loop device and a mount and each lookup that misses a layer; overlayfs
  stacks 500 at most (fs/overlayfs/params.h, `OVL_MAX_STACK`). A record's layers are
  kept as the logarithmic method keeps sorted runs (Bentley and Saxe, "Decomposable
  searching problems I. Static-to-dynamic transformation", J. Algorithms 1(4), 1980):
  each weighs more than twice the one above it, its weight its bytes and those of the
  files below it that it hides (which the guest counts as it writes the image, through a
  read-only mount of the layers); the topmost that weighs at least half the one below it
  is merged into it, and on down while what they come to does. A record of n bytes then has at most
  about log2(n / 4 KiB) layers, and each byte is merged at most as often. And what its
  layers hide stays under half of what they hold, as a copying collector holds at most
  twice what it keeps (Cheney, "A nonrecursive list compacting algorithm", CACM 13(11),
  1970): past it every layer is merged into the lowest, and what is hidden goes. That
  merge copies what is shown, no more than what is hidden: each byte hidden was written
  once, and is gone after. Merges are the host's, as the step that kept a layer lets the
  record go, while it still holds it: each run planned under the key's lock, merged
  without it, and put in its place under it again if no other merge took it meanwhile.
  A merged layer's files go once the record no longer names them; a step that took them
  still reads them, as each layer's file is opened as a step takes the record.
- **A file of several names stays one file**, as a directory keeps it. overlayfs alone
  copies up one name of a file of several, and its others show the old file below
  ("breaking the association with a lower hard link", copy_up.c). The cache's overlay
  has the inode index (`index=on`), which copies such a file up once, under every name it
  is reached by in the step, and records its origin, the layer's volume UUID and the
  inode; at the step's end, the names below that its changes did not reach are written
  into the image as links of the copy, where nothing above them hides them. The index
  tells layers apart by their UUIDs (super.c, `ovl_lower_uuid_ok`), so each image has one
  of its own: random in the guest, and on the host from the record and what it holds.
- **The builder's swap disk**, which none is given, is told from its join disk by serial:
  init swapped to `/dev/vda`, which the join disk is in a builder without disks.
- **Measured** (PM M194, against D114's, both arms in turn under one load, n = 20): a
  build that mounts that cache and does nothing ends 859 ms sooner at the median ([-1035,
  -790]), and costs what one mounting an empty cache does; one that fills a new one ends
  782 ms sooner ([-1005, -715]), its slowest of 20 at 1.2 s where D114's was 12.4 s. Filling one costs
  the image's writing: 247 ms for 295 MiB of files at the median, and 26 to trim, sync and
  name its file and record it.
- **Tested** on an M5 Max, macOS 26.4.1: `a_caches_changes_are_layered_as_a_directory_shows_them`
  (build.rs): two builds' listings as a directory would show them (files made, rewritten
  and removed, a directory removed and made again, a file made a directory and a
  directory a file, symlinks, a FIFO, owners, modes, a `user.` xattr, a file of two
  names), a file of two names rewritten through one and moved, twelve builds that each add
  1 MiB keeping each layer more than twice the one above, one that removes all but one
  file leaving one layer, a cache from a stage, and changes past the room; D114's tests
  unchanged; the store's records, plans and merges (`mounts.rs`, `merge.rs`), an image
  read back whole (`read_tree`), and its UUID. Mutation-checked: links not completed, no
  inode index, what changes hide not counted, whiteouts or opaque directories dropped, the
  room past the store's limits, a failure to write the changes not said, no merges, the
  rule of what is hidden gone, a merge at the bottom keeping its whiteouts, a directory
  that replaced something left not opaque, and a run put in place where it is not whole
  each fail one; a copied-up file's links counted against its names only spares a scan.
- **Recorded differences.** A step whose cache's changes are past the room the store has
  runs to its end and fails as they are kept, where BuildKit's step meets a full disk as
  it writes (no store of BuildKit's limits a cache). A cache from something counts its
  first content among its bytes (`system df`, `buildx du`): it is a copy of its own,
  where BuildKit's names its source's snapshot as its parent (D114).

### D133. A builder's memory, plugged as its build needs it (virtio-mem)

A builder may have half the host's memory, Docker Desktop's VM's share (a default open in
docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md, to derive from what the host can give), but the memory a
guest boots with costs it its page structures as it boots: about 21 MiB and 4 ms per GiB, a
builder of 64 GiB 1.4 GiB and 434 ms (PM M82). A builder now boots with 512 MiB, and is
given the rest as its build needs it, up to what it may have.

- **The device.** A virtio-mem device (VIRTIO 1.3 §5.15, device 24), the machine's last,
  so no other device's window moves for it: its region at the first GiB boundary after RAM
  (pmem regions after it), in whole Linux memory blocks (128 MiB, the unit Linux adds memory
  in), plugged in 2 MiB blocks, the usable region the whole region. Requests are answered as
  the specification has it: ERROR for blocks not of the usable region, unaligned, none, or
  plugged already (unplugged already, for an UNPLUG); NACK for a plug past the size asked
  for; BUSY where the host could not plug or unplug, which the driver retries. The driver
  must accept VIRTIO_MEM_F_UNPLUGGED_INACCESSIBLE. Linux's driver reads a 64-bit field in
  two halves, so the transport's ConfigGeneration counts the device's every change of
  size.
- **Unplugged memory is no one's.** Its pages go back to the host, and the range is left
  inaccessible: fresh anonymous memory, PROT_NONE, mapped over it (Windows: decommitted).
  macOS's MADV_FREE_REUSABLE and MADV_FREE gave nothing back while Hypervisor.framework
  mapped the memory, and replacing a mapped range in the host alone left the guest the old
  pages and its writes unseen by the host (PM M193). Hypervisor.framework's stage 2 holds
  the pages it maps, so a block is mapped into the guest as it is plugged and unmapped
  before its pages go back; KVM's follows the host's mapping, so the region is one memslot
  from the start (`hv::Stage2`, `Vm::add_hotplug`). The host's devices are refused blocks
  not plugged (`GuestMemory::host_ptr`); plugging and unplugging hold guest memory, so no
  device's access is between finding a block plugged and touching it. A guest that touches
  an unplugged block breaks its promise: on HVF its access is MMIO to nothing, on KVM its
  vCPU's run fails.
- **The guest asks, within what the host gives.** The guest knows when it needs memory, so
  it asks, through the control page (`HOTPLUG_SIZE`, what it may have; `HOTPLUG_REQUEST`,
  what it asks for, in whole blocks and at most that), and the device asks its driver for
  it (`requested_size`). The host keeps the bound: what it may have is what a builder booted
  with all of it had, and a step past it is ended as one was then.
- **The builder's init** holds the build, itself and every step (each in a cgroup of its
  own, so that each step's memory is counted and held apart), in one cgroup whose `memory.high` is what the
  build holds and what is free, less the kernel's reserve: 64 MiB and the page structures
  of the next memory plugged, a 64th of it. Past it the kernel slows the build's allocations
  and ends none, and says so in `memory.events`; a process of init's in the root cgroup,
  which nothing slows, wakes on it, asks for twice the memory the builder has, in whole
  memory blocks (so what is plugged ahead of the build is at most what it holds, and a build
  that comes to all of it asks a logarithm of times), raises `memory.high` as each block
  comes online, and lifts it once all of it is plugged, or once memory asked for stops
  coming (D137). Plugged memory comes online as the
  kernel's own (`memhp_default_state=online_kernel`): a builder gives no memory back, and
  memory online as movable alone can leave the kernel short with memory free
  (memory-hotplug.rst, "ZONE_MOVABLE Sizing Considerations").
- **What the kernel sized by the memory it booted with** is raised to what it sizes by all
  of it, so that a step sees what it saw in a builder booted with all its memory: the
  layers' tmpfs (`size=` and `nr_inodes=` of all of it, where `size=100%` would be of 512
  MiB); `kernel.threads-max`, the user namespaces' maxima, epoll's watches, `tcp_mem` and
  `udp_mem`, each in proportion to the memory; `fs.file-max` by the memory added, a file
  for each 10 KiB, as the kernel's own sizing has it (a proportion came out short on
  x86_64); TCP's buffers within their caps; TCP's orphans and TIME-WAIT buckets by its
  table's sizing; inotify's watches, which the kernel holds at 8192 below about 1 GiB, in
  their proportion to epoll's; and init's RLIMIT_SIGPENDING, half the threads, which
  every step inherits. Its processes are Docker's build steps', unlimited, as are its open
  files (1048576) and locked memory, whatever the memory (2026-10-12, PM M211: a step had
  kept the builder's kernel's own, 1024 of 4096 files).
- **No snapshot.** Memory plugged is not saved, so a snapshot of a VM with memory to plug
  is refused, and `--memory-max` with `--snapshot-dir` up front.
- **`shards run --kernel K --memory M --memory-max N`** boots a guest with M MiB that may
  have N in all.
- **Measured** (PM M193): against a builder booted with all it may have, half the host's
  (64 GiB), M82's three RUNs end 199 ms sooner at the median ([-223, -158]), the builder
  holding 96 MiB at its peak where it held 1424; a RUN that writes 4 GiB, the builder growing
  to hold it, ends 67 ms sooner ([-88, -40]), the builder holding 1.2 GiB less. A guest has
  1 GiB online 5 to 7 ms after it asks, and gives it back in 10 to 21.
- **Tested** on an M5 Max, macOS 26.4.1: `a_guest_grows_and_gives_back_its_memory`
  (boot.rs) plugs 1 GiB into a guest booted with 256 MiB, which writes 896 MiB of it and
  gives it all back, its VM process holding none of it as it ends (`hotplug_held_kib`, the
  OS asked page by page: a page Hypervisor.framework has unmapped is out of the footprint,
  held or not); `a_builders_memory_is_plugged_as_its_build_needs_it` (build.rs): a step that
  touches 1.5 GiB and a layer of 1 GiB in a builder booted with 512 MiB, its steps' limits at
  least a guest's booted with all of it and within a tenth more, and a step past all of it
  ended with 137, as before; unit tests of the device's every answer, guest memory's
  refusals, the control page's registers and `--memory-max`. Mutation-checked: the
  configuration interrupt, the request's lower bound, guest memory's check of plugged
  blocks, giving the pages back, Hypervisor.framework's mapping, init's request, its
  `memory.high`, its raised limits and its tmpfs's size each fail one.

### D132. A guest that is itself a hypervisor: EL2 on Hypervisor.framework

D13 plans KVM on arm64 Linux hosts. GitHub's arm64 runners give no nested
virtualization, so the record's test path is a guest booted at EL2 by shards' own HVF
backend, its kernel a KVM host (docs/research/measurements/nested-kvm). That path now
works: `shards run --kernel K --nested` boots a guest at EL2 on a Mac that gives one (an
M3 or later on macOS 15), and its KVM comes up as a hypervisor.

- **The VM.** `hv_vm_config_set_el2_enabled` (macOS 15), bound on first use as every
  framework call is (`hv_vm_config_get_el2_supported` says whether this Mac can). The
  framework gives no reset state (Apple's answer on its forum, thread 775546), so every
  entry, boot or PSCI CPU_ON, sets PSTATE to EL2h with DAIF masked and puts back the
  SCTLR_EL2 the framework had at creation, MMU and caches off, as booting.rst asks.
- **PSCI by SMC.** At EL2 the kernel's own HVCs are its own (its hyp stub), so the DT
  names `smc`; the backend already served PSCI by either.
- **The GIC's virtualization interface.** The DT gives the GIC its maintenance interrupt,
  PPI 9 (INTID 25, `HV_GIC_INT_MAINTENANCE`); the EL2 physical timer was already the
  timer's fourth interrupt (PPI 10).
- **EL2 registers the framework holds** trap to the VMM when the guest reaches them
  (CNTHCTL_EL2 first, as Linux sets its timer access): for an EL2 VM each of the 25 in
  hv_vcpu_types.h is read or written through the framework, where before every trapped
  write was dropped.
- **No SME at EL2.** The M5 has SME, but the framework leaves SMCR_EL2 undefined at the
  guest's EL2, where Linux's `__finalise_el2` sets the streaming vector length: the
  instruction faulted for ever (ESR_EL2 EC 0, ELR at `msr SMCR_EL2, x0`). An EL2 VM's
  ID_AA64PFR1_EL1 says no SME.
- **No snapshot.** The EL2 state is not saved, so a snapshot of such a VM is refused, and
  `--nested` with `--snapshot-dir` up front. x86_64 refuses `--nested` until it is
  built there.
- **The kernel.** KVM is not in the kernel every guest boots: the pinned kernel's `kvm`
  variant (resources/kernel/kvm.config), built and released by the same reproducible
  workflow, carries it. KVM costs no boot or restore time measurably (PM M192), but its
  800 KiB of text would be in every guest's image for a need few runs have.
- **Tested** on an M5 Max, macOS 26.4.1: `a_nested_guest_is_a_kvm_host` (boot.rs) boots
  the `kvm` variant with 2 vCPUs, and the guest says "CPU: All CPU(s) started at EL2"
  and "kvm [1]: Hyp nVHE mode initialized successfully", its vgic on IRQ 9, and powers
  off by PSCI over SMC; a Mac that gives no EL2 prints SKIP, and x86_64 is held to its
  refusal. Mutation-checked: the SME mask, the EL2 registers' forwarding, the EL2h
  entry, the maintenance interrupt and the SMC conduit each fail it.
  `devicetree_matches_the_boot_contract` holds the DT both ways.

### D131. A throttle waited out within the window the registry names

CI's pulls from ghcr.io failed on a throttle that outlasted shards' waits (PM M191). The
waits, up to 50, 100, 200, 400 and 800 ms, a random share of each, were chosen for ECR
Public's random throttling (PM M112). ghcr.io says more: its 429 names the window its
allowance is counted over, `retry-after: 301.718µs, allowed: 44000/minute`. A throttle
counted over a minute is a crowd's, and ends within that minute.

- **Waited out within the window.** Where the registry names a window of a minute or
  less, a 429 is waited out within it. The window comes from `allowed: N/second` (or
  `minute`) in its refusal, or from the `w` of its `RateLimit-Limit` field. The waits go
  on past the schedule, doubling to 6.4 s each, a random share of each, until the
  window is spent. Within such a window, `ratelimit-remaining: 0` is a crowd's, not a
  quota spent.
- **A quota counted over longer is still not waited for**, unless `Retry-After` says
  when: Docker Hub counts pulls over six hours (`w=21600`), and an hour's or a day's
  allowance is a quota alike.
- **A HEAD's refusal says nothing.** A throttled manifest HEAD is asked again as a GET,
  whose refusal names the window, which an answer to a HEAD has no body to say (RFC 9110 §9.3.2); containerd asks for a refused HEAD's body with a GET too
  (405, and 403's `withGETErrorBody`). A blob's HEAD keeps its method, since a GET would
  fetch the blob.
- **What the registry said stays said.** The client reads a 429's body ahead
  (`Response::peek`), so a refusal passed on still carries the registry's words.
- **Unlike Docker, recorded:** dockerd gives up on TOOMANYREQUESTS at once
  (`retryOnError` marks it `DoNotRetry`, moby v29 daemon/internal/distribution), and
  containerd asks again at once, five times.
- **Tested:** `a_throttle_named_for_a_short_window_is_waited_out_within_it` (registry
  pull): six throttles, one past the schedule, pulled under a minute's window, and not
  under an hour's or where none is named. The refusal still says the registry's words.
  Mutation-checked: the window, its one-minute bound, the GET and the read-ahead.

### D130. Frontend inputs, as docker/dockerfile:1.27.1 reads them

shards' frontend (D113) refused frontend inputs: definitions a client gives the frontend
whole, which BuildKit hands it through the gateway's `Inputs` call. It now reads them as
dockerfile's frontend does, so these builds work through it:

- **What buildx v0.37.1 gives as inputs:**
  - **bake's `target:` contexts.** `contexts = { base = "target:base" }` builds `base`
    first and gives its result as the input `base`, `context:base=input:base`, and its
    image config in `input-metadata:base`. A build of several platforms gives one each,
    `base::linux/arm64` and the like.
  - **A remote bake definition's target in a directory of it.** buildx copies the
    directory out of the repository (`set context to DIR`) and gives the copy as both
    the `context` and the `dockerfile` inputs.
  - **A Git context with a query**, where `BUILDX_SEND_GIT_QUERY_AS_INPUT` is set: buildx
    makes the Git source itself and gives it as both inputs.
- **Where dockerui reads them** (`initContext`, `NamedContext`, `forwardGateway`):
  - Where the context is the client's, not Git or HTTP: the Dockerfile from the
    `dockerfile` input unless `dockerfilekey` names the client's, and the context from
    the `context` input. The context is scoped by `contextsubdir`, and no `.dockerignore`
    applies to it.
  - An `input:NAME` context, where it is loaded; with a Git or HTTP context, that is the
    only read, and it fails as the inputs do.
  - A build handed on to another frontend gets each input marshalled anew.
- **`llb.NewDefinitionOp`, exactly:**
  - Each op is written again as it came, so its digest and those its readers name stay
    the same. Ops nothing reads are left out.
  - Each output of an op that is read is a vertex of its own (DefinitionOp's input
    cache), and each adds the op's source locations again.
  - Metadata is kept as `NewOpMetadata` and `mergeMetadata` keep it: every capability
    marked needed, export cache and progress group as given. An op that is the same as
    one of the build's own is one op, its metadata merged (`marshal`'s cache by digest).
    The root's capabilities follow from all of it.
  - Source maps are written where the marshal first meets them, one kept of those alike
    (`equalSourceMap`: the same file, language and data). A bake whose targets share a
    Dockerfile writes it once. Each map's own definition is marshalled anew, as
    `sourceMapCollector` does. Maps within maps are read without recursion.
- **Refused in BuildKit's words** (`a_definition_given_is_refused`, PM M190):
  - `NewDefinitionOp`'s refusals, prefixed `failed to get frontend inputs:` where
    initContext reads the inputs: a definition of no metadata, an op that is no `pb.Op`,
    a location in a map the definition lacks, a last op that reads nothing.
  - The marshal's refusals (`DefinitionOp.Validate`): an op of no metadata, and a root
    read at a negative output.
- **Deliberately unlike docker/dockerfile, recorded:**
  - **The marshal's refusals come when the input is read.** BuildKit's frontend refuses
    only once a marshal reaches the op, so it ignores a broken input the build never
    uses. It also crashes on an op that reads one the definition lacks (a nil
    dereference) or an output at a negative index (a slice index). shards refuses all of
    these up front.
  - **A context input's source map is compared with the Dockerfile's by file, language
    and data alone.** In a build of several platforms, or with
    `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=context`, BuildKit also compares the two maps' definitions once an
    earlier marshal has set one, so its answer depends on what it marshalled before. No
    BuildKit client sends a context input that has source maps.
  - **Malformed protobuf is refused in protobuf-go's words**, without its checks of an
    op's every field. BuildKit's server decodes every input before it sends one, so it
    sends none malformed, and its solver checks an op's fields when the op reaches it.
- **Found while measuring, fixed:**
  - dockerui reads Docker's other casing, `dockerfile`, from whatever it reads the
    Dockerfile from. shards' frontend tried it only in the client's directory. It now
    tries it in a Git or HTTP context and in an input too.
  - A capability the worker lacks, refused before the Dockerfile's source or an HTTP
    context is solved, is the client's own error. dockerui says it after `failed to
    resolve dockerfile:` (`failed to resolve httpcontext:`), and shards' frontend now
    does too (`Gateway::solve_as`). Docker's own BuildKit lacks `source.git.mtime`, which a
    Git context needs under SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, so such a build is refused there by both.
- **Tested:**
  - `scripts/frontend/compare` on Docker's own BuildKit (v0.28.1) through `buildx bake`
    and `buildx build`: `target:` contexts with one Dockerfile shared, with one each, and
    for two platforms; a remote bake target in a directory; Git queries given as inputs,
    one with a lowercase `dockerfile`; on BuildKit v0.33.0, a Git context with a lowercase
    `dockerfile`; on Docker's, a Git context refused. The repositories are served over
    git:// in `shards-dind` (`scripts/frontend/git-serve`). Every case is equal to
    docker/dockerfile step by step, image by image and refusal by refusal (PM M190).
  - `a_definition_given_is_marshalled_anew_as_it_came`,
    `a_definition_given_is_refused` and
    `a_refused_capability_is_said_as_readentrypoint_says_it` (frontend).
  - The merge, source map and refusal tests in `llb`.

### D129. SBOM attestations from shards' frontend, as docker/dockerfile:1.27.1 makes them

shards' frontend (D113) refused `attest:sbom` ("makes no SBOM attestations yet"), so
`docker buildx build --sbom=true` failed with it. It now makes them as dockerfile's
builder does.

- **What is asked** (dockerui `attestations.Parse`, `Validate`, `Client.init`):
  - `attest:TYPE` and `build-arg:BUILDKIT_ATTEST_TYPE`, the type lowercased. Where both
    name one, Go's map gives either; shards takes `attest:`.
  - Each value's CSV fields are the attributes; a field without `=` has an empty value.
  - Any type but `sbom` and `provenance` fails the build: `unknown attestation type "foo"`.
  - The generator, BuildKit's scanner unless named, is normalized with its tag
    ("failed to parse sbom scanner …" otherwise). The other attributes are the
    scanner's `BUILDKIT_SCAN_<KEY>` parameters.
- **The scan** (`CreateSBOMScanner`):
  - The generator's config is resolved for the first build platform, under no name of
    the frontend's, before any platform is built.
  - Each platform's result is scanned once every platform is built. The scan runs the
    scanner's command over the result mounted at `/run/src/core/sbom`, with each extra
    target (a stage `BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE` names, the context with
    `BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_CONTEXT`) beside it, `/tmp` a tmpfs and `/run/out` its output.
  - It asks no cache where the target asks none. `Plan.ignore_cache` now says so, and
    `shards build`'s own scan (D81) heeds it too.
  - The scanner's source is `llb.Image`'s: unnamed and pinned by no digest.
    `sbom::plan` takes both as arguments; shards build keeps its named, pinned source.
- **The attestation**: each platform's scan output, a `Bundle` with `reason=sbom`,
  `sbom-core=sbom` and the SPDX predicate type, keyed by the platform's ID. It is returned
  in the gateway's `Result.attestations` (field 12), which `shards_gateway` now writes.
- **Why not leave it to BuildKit.** BuildKit scans a result that comes back without an
  SBOM itself (`proc.SBOMProcessor`), but its scan has no extras. dockerfile's frontend
  makes its own, so this one does too.
- **Tested**:
  - `scripts/frontend/compare`, on Docker's own BuildKit (v0.28.1): one platform, the
    extras, two platforms, and an unknown type refused, each equal to docker/dockerfile
    step by step. The images match whole, except the SPDX documents' creation time and
    namespace, which the scanner makes anew each run. The harness's `sbom` cases set
    those aside, with the attestation manifests' and index's digests that follow from
    them and the scanner's log clock (PM M189).
  - `attestations_are_written_as_gateway_proto_has_them` (gateway) and
    `attestation_options_are_read` (frontend).

### D128. Build policies over OCI layouts, and a policy's own errors, as buildx ends a build

Found while D127 measured OCI layout contexts: `shards build` asked its policies (D101) of
an OCI layout as if it were a registry's image, and it said a policy's own errors as
BuildKit says a denial. Both now go as buildx v0.37.1 on BuildKit v0.28.1 has them (PM
M186).

- **An OCI layout is asked of as itself.**
  - buildx builds no policy input for an `oci-layout://` source ("oci-layout not
    supported yet", policy/validate.go). A build under any policy with an OCI layout named
    context fails: "failed to solve: failed to build policy input: unsupported source
    scheme: oci-layout".
  - `shards build` asked of the layout's image as `docker-image://docker.io/library/NAME@DIGEST`,
    the stand-in name dockerui gives a layout, NAME being the context's. A policy that
    allows `alpine` by name allowed a layout named `alpine`, whatever it held.
  - It now asks of the layout as itself and is refused as buildx is (build.rs
    `policies_hold_over_remote_contexts`).
  - An input of shards' own for layouts would be a schema buildx has not defined, which a
    policy written for buildx would misread. When buildx defines one, shards takes it.
- **A policy's own error is the build's, said alone.** Such an error is its input not
  built, or its Rego failing (`eval_conflict_error`).
  - buildx's callback answers BuildKit with a gRPC status.
  - BuildKit's grpcerrors says an error whose chain holds a status as that status, its
    wrappings dropped (ToGRPC, errorHasMoreContext).
  - buildx thus prints "failed to solve: Dockerfile.rego:7: eval_conflict_error: complete
    rules must not produce multiple outputs" at the FROM line's excerpt.
  - shards wrapped it in a denial's words (build.rs `a_policys_own_error_ends_the_build`; "IMAGE: failed to resolve source
    metadata for IMAGE: could not resolve image due to policy: ...").
  - `policy::Refused` now says who refused: a decision, the policy itself, or BuildKit's
    evaluator.
- **The policies' step fails only for a denial.** buildx closes it with the build's error
  only where DenyMessages or isPolicyEvaluationError finds a denial; for any other error it
  ends done. shards failed it for every refusal.
- **Tested**: `a_policys_own_error_ends_the_build` (a Rego conflict
  over an image and over the Dockerfile's own source, and an OCI layout context, each
  word for word as measured, the step done); `refusals_say_who_refused`; mutation-checked.

### D127. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from a build's sources, as docker/dockerfile:1.27.1 takes it

docker/dockerfile:1.27.1 lets SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH name where a build's time comes from,
not only give it in seconds (epoch.go): `context`, a named context, or a stage whose one
remote ADD is the source. `shards build` took a stage's Git or HTTP source's time and
gave `context` none, whatever the context was; shards' frontend (D113) refused every
name. Both now take each as that frontend takes it, held to it in `shards-dind` (PM M185).

- **What the value names**, in the frontend's order (`resolveSourceDateEpochState`):
  - a number: its seconds;
  - `context`: the build context's source;
  - a named context, as dockerui's `NamedContext(value, ContextOpt{})` finds one: the
    value parsed as a reference first, so `SRC` is refused whatever the stages ("invalid
    context name SRC: invalid reference format: repository name (library/SRC) must be
    lowercase"); then the context keyed with the frontend's platform
    (`src::linux/arm64`), or without;
  - else a stage of that name, case folded, its one remote ADD the source, made as
    `llb.HTTP` and `llb.Git` make it, the stage's ARGs expanded without SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH;
  - else "invalid SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH: VALUE".
- **The source's time** (`resolveSourceDateEpochFromState`, `sourceDateEpochFromMetadata`),
  from the one source op the state holds; none for scratch, an image, an OCI layout or a
  local directory, which say none:
  - a Git source's commit: its committer's time, in the committer's zone, which the
    image's history and `created` keep (`2026-08-05T17:35:52+02:00`; gitobject's
    `parseActor`, now shared with the build policies' commit input, D102). A committer
    line with no well-formed time gives none;
  - an HTTP source: its Last-Modified where no checksum pins its bytes; else its file
    downloaded and the newest regular file of the archive it is (none where it is no
    archive; one that decompresses past the image limits fails the build, as a layer
    does);
  - each resolved under the step BuildKit names ("[internal] resolve main build context
    metadata", "... SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH named context src", "... source stage src").
- **A named image or OCI layout context is loaded for no platform**, as dockerui loads it
  with `ContextOpt{}`. BuildKit keys a metadata step by the source's identifier and the
  platform asked, its own (`platforms.DefaultSpec()`, `linux/arm64/v8` here) where none
  is (bridge.go `resolveSourceMetadata`), so the load and the time's resolution are one
  step, printed under each name in turn: progressui prints a vertex that runs again by the
  name it runs under (measured). The planner's resolver now takes "no platform"; `shards
  build` keys its steps as BuildKit does and shows the one step so.
- **BuildKit's daemon decides first.** Docker 29.3.1's BuildKit (v0.28.1) refuses any
  SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH that is no number before a frontend runs ("failed to solve: invalid
  source-date-epoch: strconv.ParseInt: parsing "src": invalid syntax: ..."); v0.33.0
  leaves it to the frontend. shards' frontend, run by either, does as dockerfile's does
  there. `shards build` takes the value as v0.33.0 does: an input Docker 29.3.1 refuses
  and newer BuildKit builds.
- **Where shards does better.** The time is resolved once a build, in both. dockerfile's
  frontend resolves it again for each platform, all at once, so buildx shows the steps
  once or more as they happen to overlap, and a source that changes between the two
  answers (an HTTP file's Last-Modified) gives the platforms different times.
- **Found on the way**: shards' frontend read a remote context's Dockerfile where `-f`
  named a local one (`dockerfilekey`), a D113 defect `epoch-context-git` found; it reads
  the local one.
- **Tested**:
  - `scripts/frontend/compare`, 11 cases in `shards-dind`. Each is built by
    docker/dockerfile:1.27.1 and by shards' frontend on BuildKit v0.33.0, one on Docker's
    own v0.28.1. They are equal step by step and, where an epoch resolves, image for image
    byte for byte. The cases: the context (a Git URL, and a local directory, which says
    none); a stage's Git source, HTTP Last-Modified and an archive's newest file; a named
    Git context, image and OCI layout; a name refused; two platforms; v0.28.1's refusal.
  - `source_date_epoch_is_taken_from_a_named_or_remote_context` (`shards build`):
    - a named HTTP context before the stage of its name;
    - the refusal;
    - a named image's one step (mutation-checked);
    - a named Git context, and a Git context, keeping +02:00 (mutation-checked);
    - `source_date_epoch_is_taken_from_a_source_stage` as before.
  - Unit tests:
    - what the planner asks for each value, a named image resolved for no platform
      (`a_named_context_gives_the_time_before_a_stage`);
    - history at the answer's time and zone (`a_source_stage_gives_the_build_its_time`);
    - zoned times written as Go writes them (`times_in_a_zone_print_as_gos`).

### D126. Keyless signing, as cosign signs without a key

D116 signed OSI artifacts with cosign's keys and left keyless signing out: it needs
Fulcio and Rekor, and the public instance was not to be used without the user. The user's
answer (2026-10-10): "Let's test both", the public instance and a local one. `shards sign
agent|harness|mcp NAME` without `--key` now signs as cosign v3.1.3 signs without one
(`shards_sigstore::keyless`, over sigstore-go v1.2.2's `sign.Bundle`).

- **The services** are the signing config's: Sigstore's public instance's from its TUF
  repository (`signing_config.v0.2.json`, carried beside the trusted root and refreshed as
  it is, D104), or `--signing-config`'s; the trusted root likewise, or `--trusted-root`'s.
  Each kind is chosen as sigstore-go chooses (`signing_config`): the newest valid service of
  the highest API version, one per operator, then ANY, EXACT or ALL.
- **The identity token** is found as cosign finds it.
  - `--identity-token`: a token, or a file holding one. cosign takes only an RS256 JWS as a
    token and reads any other as a file's name; shards takes each algorithm Fulcio's
    issuers sign with.
  - Else cosign's ambient providers, in its order (Go initializes their packages by import
    path): Buildkite's agent, `SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN`, `/var/run/sigstore/cosign/oidc-token`,
    GitHub Actions, Google's workload identity (the metadata server, or Application Default
    Credentials: a service account's key, an impersonated account, federation from a file
    or URL), Google impersonation (IAM's generateIdToken), SPIFFE's Workload API (gRPC on
    its socket, over the frontend's HTTP/2 client, D113). `--oidc-provider` names one,
    `--oidc-disable-ambient-providers` none.
  - Else it signs in (`--fulcio-auth-flow`, cosign's flows): in a browser on a terminal
    (PKCE; the code brought back to a listener on this host, or typed in), by a device
    code without one, or by client credentials. Each token is checked as go-oidc checks it:
    its signature by the provider's keys, issuer, audience, expiry, and the nonce and
    access token hash oauthflow checks.
- **The signature.** An ephemeral ECDSA P-256 key, never written, signs the DSSE envelope of
  cosign's `sign/v1` statement.
  - Fulcio certifies the key for the token's subject, the key's proof of possession over
    it.
  - Each timestamp authority the config selects stamps the signature (RFC 3161; the
    request byte for byte OpenSSL's and digitorus/timestamp's).
  - Each log it selects logs it. Rekor v1: a `dsse` v0.0.1 entry as rekor's client
    proposes it, its answer made the bundle's entry as `tle.GenerateTransparencyLogEntry`
    makes it. Rekor v2: a `hashedrekord` v0.0.2 over the envelope's PAE digest, which needs
    a timestamp authority, as cosign refuses it without one.
  - The bundle (v0.3, the leaf certificate) is verified against the trusted root before it
    is kept, as `sign.Bundle` verifies what it made; then it is kept and pushed as D116's.
- **Before an identity goes into a log** shards says what will be published and where:
  cosign's statement for the public instance, and always the token's subject and the logs,
  which cosign does not name. On a terminal it asks cosign's question unless `--yes`;
  elsewhere it says it and goes on, as cosign signs with a token unasked.
- **Policies** already held an artifact to its keyless signatures (`input.image.signatures`,
  D116 over D105's verifier), against Sigstore's root.
- **Where shards does better**, each where cosign's behaviour is a defect, not a contract:
  - The device flow waits RFC 8628's 5 s where the provider names no interval (oauthflow
    asks again at once), and grows it by 5 s on `slow_down` (§3.5).
  - Fulcio's or a timestamp authority's last 5xx answer is reported. sigstore-go reads the
    answer it closed and says "http: read on closed response body" (seen in the oracle).
  - GitHub's token endpoint refusing is said; cosign decodes the refusal as a token.
  - `SPIFFE_ENDPOINT_SOCKET` is read as the SPIFFE spec writes it, `unix://PATH`, too.
  - Messages go to stderr, which shards keeps for people (oauthflow prints some to stdout).
  - `-h` is help on `shards sign` and every action of `shards agent|harness|mcp`.
- **Not taken**: Google federation from AWS or from an executable (its file and URL sources
  are taken), and SPIFFE's Workload API on Windows (a named pipe). A signer there gives the
  token itself with `--identity-token`; no demand for either has been seen.
- **Tested**:
  - Against a local Sigstore (PM M184): shards' signatures and cosign's, of each signing
    config (Rekor v2 with a timestamp authority, Rekor v1 with one and without), each
    verified by the other; identities signed in for at Dex in a browser and by a device
    code. `shards_and_cosign_keyless_signatures_verify_as_cosign_verifies_them`,
    `shards_bundles_hold_what_cosign_s_hold` and `a_changed_keyless_signature_is_refused`
    verify M184's bundles offline.
  - Against cosign's own libraries (`scripts/keyless/generate`: sigstore-go's Fulcio,
    timestamp authority, Rekor v1 and v2 clients against test servers): each request byte
    for byte, each answer's entry, the bundle, the services selected and tokens' subjects
    (`keyless_oracle.rs`, seven tests); six mutants killed.
  - Against Sigstore's public instance: `.github/workflows/keyless.yml` signs with the
    job's GitHub identity, cosign verifies; cosign signs, shards' policies verify both.
    Its first run (38158860635, 2026-10-11, D126's commit): shards' signature of
    `keyless.yml@refs/heads/dev`, logged at Rekor's index 3211368250 and stamped by
